News.title: Inside ruthless contest to be Britain’s best bingo caller – and how game’s ‘nearly-man’ finally won after 30 years
News.content:
Next

MOVE over Strictly and I’m A Celeb – the biggest showdown of the week unfolded on an industrial estate in Leeds.

The nation’s biggest bingo callers descended on the city’s Buzz Bingo to face off in a ruthless, high-stakes contest to be crowned the best.



If you thought a World Cup penalty shoot-out was tense, you have never witnessed the raw passion of a bingo hall when the title of National Bingo Game Caller of the Year is up for grabs.

More than 400 guests packed into the venue with dabbers at the ready, many having arrived at the crack of dawn on coaches from all corners of the country to support their local callers.



They were armed with motivational banners, custom T-shirts, and wearing face masks of their favourite contenders.

“I haven’t been this nervous since I was waiting on the number 88 for a full house back in 2021,” joked one punter from Wales, who was carrying a thermos she assured me was “just tea”.

She added: “Our girl is going to smash it today. She’s the Tom Jones of the bingo world, she is.”

As the Entertainment Editor of The Sun, I’m used to rubbing shoulders with showbiz royalty, but on Sunday ­afternoon, I found myself among bingo’s finest.

I took my seat on the ­judging panel alongside the formidable Nicole Garrett, CEO of The Bingo Association, and the legendary Donna Kunyo, who took the crown in 2019, in part thanks to her belting rendition of Dame Shirley Bassey’s This Is My Life.

And these contenders were not just there to call the bingo into a microphone. Oh no.



Like Donna, they also had to put on a show-stopping entertainment ­performance to start the session.

We were judging them on a strict, Simon Cowell-style set of criteria including knowledge of the game, stage presence, personality and sheer technical ability.

The pressure was on. Launched back in 1999, the nationwide contest had whittled down hundreds of ­callers to just six elite finalists.



Taking to the stage were hall heavyweights Eve Cunningham from Carlton Bingo, Livingston; Debra Phillips from Castle Bingo, Merthyr Tydfil; Josie Douthwaite of Mecca Bingo, Hull; Garry McWilliams from Castle Bingo, Barnes Hill, Birmingham; and Adam Vickery from Buzz Bingo, Plymouth.

Eve opened proceedings with a rousing performance of Amy Winehouse’s Back To Black, while Adam went leftfield with an amusing game of stand-up bingo.

Disaster nearly struck when Josie and Debra opted for the same choice of song in what was quickly dubbed The Battle Of The Tinas.

Both callers took to the stage in gold sequin dresses for their own unique versions of Tina Turner’s Proud Mary, with merry pensioners from Debra’s local club in Merthyr as her backing dancers.



But there was one man who had the crowd eating out of the palm of his hand. Enter Anton Fletcher, representing Castle Bingo Bootle.

For Anton, 53, this was his ­Leonardo DiCaprio moment.

Widely respected as the gentleman of the bingo industry, he had sadly become the “nearly-man” of the caller world.

Starting out as a caller in 1992 aged just 18, at Butlin’s Margate, he had stayed in the game for more than three decades. He reached the grand final in 2022 and 2024 but went home empty-handed both times. On Sunday it was his third time lucky.



He sealed his legendary status with a rendition of Neil Diamond’s Sweet Caroline, complete with bespoke bingo-themed lyrics, which, he told me, took him weeks to write.

Swapping the chorus to It’s Bingo Time, the entire 400-strong crowd was on their feet, waving their dabbers in the air and belting it out.

Cheering him on was his girlfriend Tracy. They first met as teenagers at Gala Bingo in Southport in 1991, and were each other’s first love. But as young lovers do, they drifted apart.

A chance encounter 11 years ago at a Mecca in Southport, where Tracy worked as a caller, saw them rekindle their romance. She looked on nervously as we judges took to the stage, but she needn’t have worried as our verdict was unanimous — Anton was the Bingo Caller of the Year.

Overwhelmed and clutching his trophy, an emotional Anton, who also won £1,000, told me: “I am so happy. It has been a long time coming — 30 years of bingo and here I am. It’s years of striving towards the pinnacle of the bingo industry.



“It’s hard to explain how much it means to me, because I’m so close to crying. I can’t wait to celebrate with my club and represent the bingo industry over the next ­couple of years.

“No matter what’s going on in my life, I’m up there calling the numbers.

“That’s my stage. That is my ­performance.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ever the professional, Anton had to hop on a coach back to Bootle in time for his shift that evening — and not even a three-hour traffic jam could stop him.

Now that’s what I call Top of the Shop.

News.title: Fury as traveller site with permission for 6 trailers ‘QUADRUPLES’ in size within days as 30 caravans park up
News.content:
CARAVAN CHAOS Fury as traveller site with permission for 6 trailers ‘QUADRUPLES’ in size within days as 30 caravans park up







Next

A TRAVELLER site has allegedly quadrupled in size in a matter of days – with nearly 30 caravans now parked on the land despite permission for just six.

Furious residents claim their quiet village has been turned into an “industrial housing estate”, with children racing around on motorbikes at all hours.



Maidstone council chiefs are now investigating the reported expansion at Thistlemere Stables, in Headcorn, Kent.

The site was originally granted permission for three mobile homes and three caravans.



But one resident claims the number has now rocketed to between 25 and 30, with a further five static caravans claimed to have arrived on Monday alone.

Families living nearby have bemoaned the impact the impact of the travellers on their leafy community.

One resident, who did not want to be named, said: “It’s a living hell.

“It’s an absolute disgrace they have been able to expand by four times with no permission.

“They can do whatever they want. It’s a joke.



“Residents have been abused verbally while walking by and being sworn at. They think they own the village now.”

He also claimed raw sewage was coming from the site and that the road had been turned into a “race track” by children riding motorbikes.

The man described two separate incidents in which he claimed to have seen a man covered in blood and bruises, including one who had allegedly been doused in petrol.

There is no suggestion the travellers were responsible for either incident.

He said police, including armed officers, had been called to the area but claimed nothing had been done.



An elderly resident added: “This should be such a lovely village. They spoil it.

“Whenever a local resident applies for planning permission for anything we have to jump through hoops.

“These people can do whatever they like. It’s so upsetting.”

Planning boffins initially gave the green light for one mobile home and one touring caravan at the site in 2023, alongside a day room and hardstanding.

A further two mobile homes and two caravans were approved in 2024, with additional hardstanding and another day room.



A retrospective application to change the layout was also approved in September this year.

Headcorn Parish Council has urged Maidstone council to take “robust enforcement” action if any breaches are identified.

A spokesman said: “Maidstone council must act without delay to establish whether planning rules have been breached and take effective enforcement action where necessary.

“Rural communities cannot be left to face the consequences of inappropriate development through prolonged inaction.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Maidstone council spokesman said: “The council is aware of the site at Love Lane, Headcorn and is currently investigating the matter.



“The council is assessing the development and will determine whether any breach of planning control has occurred and what appropriate enforcement action is necessary.”

News.title: Could Glasgow shooting footage reveal vital clues after gangster’s girlfriend ‘blasted FIVE times’?
News.content:
Next

COPS hunting a mob gunman who shot a law graduate five times are poring over doorbell camera footage for clues.

Police have gathered CCTV from neighbouring homes in the street where innocent Lauryn Wishart, 27, was blasted in a botched hit.



It is hoped the recordings may reveal the identity of the maniac — who had been hunting Lauryn’s gangster boyfriend Josh ‘Sheep’ Stevenson, 31.

One resident told The Scottish Sun: “One of the neighbours has doorbell footage which could have captured the gunman in the street beforehand.



“Plain-clothes officers were going from door to door speaking to residents and looking for anything that could help.

“The street would have been deserted at that time of night, so the camera might have picked up something important.

“It could be crucial in helping police identify whoever was behind this senseless attack.”

Lauryn was left fighting for life following the ambush at a property in Lambhill, Glasgow, on Monday night.

We told how cops had issued a so- called Osman warning to Stevenson after learning his life was in danger.

The hood previously tried to forge careers as a personal trainer and a pet food supplier.



Last year, he set up JKS Personal Trainer Ltd — which was dissolved the day after Lauryn was shot.

His pet venture The Finest Bulls Ltd was set up in 2021 and folded in 2023.

An underworld source said: “Stevenson was recently registered as a personal trainer but he never appears to spend any time in a gym.



“He spends most of his time trying to avoid being seen and keeps changing his routine — presumably because so many unsavoury people are looking for him.”

We previously revealed how the house where recruitment consultant Lauryn and Stevenson were attacked is owned by gangland figure Robert Daniel, 52.

It is claimed Stevenson is being stalked by a crime gang seeking revenge over a £100,000 drugs fall-out.

Lauryn remains critical but stable in hospital with police by her bedside.

News.title: Vincent Van Gogh painting completed two months before his death and later ‘stolen by Nazis’ sells for record £144m
News.content:
Next

A VINCENT van Gogh painting said to have been grabbed by the Nazis has sold for a record £144.74million.

Chataigniers En Fleurs beat the previous auction best for the Dutch artist, and became the second highest price for any work of art sold at Sotheby’s.



A day before the New York auction, Sotheby’s announced an agreement between the ­Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting since 1975, and the descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, who sold it in 1936.

A lawyer for the Fischer heirs had asked for the sale to be postponed until Sotheby’s showed the painting had not been sold under duress.



The auction house said that in recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the ­Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution.

It did not disclose details of the agreement.



The Fischer heirs said that they were grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family.

They said it made it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era.

Van Gogh painted Chataigniers En Fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom) in a burst of creativity after his release from a psychiatric asylum in 1890.

He took his own life two months later.



It was part of a collection of art which sold for £591.46million.

Austrian painter Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth ­Lederer (1914-16) sold last year at Sotheby’s for £180million.

News.title: Thomas Markle is mentally fit to stand trial for child sex abuse images, Florida court finds
News.content:
MARKLE ON TRIAL Thomas Markle is mentally fit to stand trial for child sex abuse images, Florida court finds







Next

THOMAS Markle Snr has been deemed mentally fit to stand trial over child sexual abuse material charges.

A psychiatrist found he had “sufficient ability to understand the nature and consequences of the charges against him“, a Florida court heard.



Meghan Markle‘s estranged dad appeared in a Tampa federal court on Thursday for the hearing.

Judge Lindsay Griffin had asked for the probe to determine if Markle Snr could understand the proceedings.





With a reasonable degree of medical certainty, a psychiatrist ruled he understood the charges, according to a report discussed in court.

Markle Snr’s lawyer Mary Wolf said she would not contest the findings at this stage.

But Wolf said she may contest the findings once he is moved to California.

She said: “I reviewed the report with Mr Markle. I suspect he would want to contest it but I do not.”



Prosecutors accepted the findings.

The Philippine National Police (PNP) filed three charges against the Duchess of Sussex’s 82-year-old estranged father over an alleged stash of child abuse images in the Philippines.

He has been charged with two counts of offering, distributing, selling, exporting or importing any form of Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Material (CSAEM) and one count of possessing CSAEM.



Markle Snr was charged with possessing child sexual abuse material in the US earlier this month after allegations against him were revealed by The Sun.

He has previously called the allegations “sick lies” and is yet to enter a plea.

He was arrested when FBI agents raided his US care home amid a deepening probe into child sex abuse images.

Agents seized approximately 78 items from storage units rented by Markle.

It included slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse material from two storage units rented by Markle.



Following his charge, Markle Snr was ordered by a judge in a Tampa court to be released on bail to the facility with an ankle bracelet.

Leaving court, Markle was told he couldn’t have access to any smart devices or the internet.

The 82-year-old was then pictured glaring into the lens in an orange prison jumpsuit after being arrested for allegedly removing an ankle tag.



Thomas Markle Jnr, 60, said he believed his “monster” father deliberately tore off the device so he could get free medical care behind bars.

Markle Snr was taken back into custody in the US after being accused of cutting off the electronic ankle gadget ­while under house arrest.

His jail photo was released by the Pinellas County sheriff’s office following his ­re-arrest, just five days after he was held in an FBI swoop and charged.

According to first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli, Markle Snr appeared in federal court in Tampa, Florida, after authorities learned he had cut off the tag at 1.45am (6.45am UK time).

Griffin ordered Markle to stay in custody until the end of his trial, having “violated the ­conditions of his pretrial release”.



She said he should be detained separately, as far as possible, from the general prison population.

The Sun revealed how Thomas Jnr reported his father to Philippines cops after finding alleged child sex abuse material.

News.title: Fury as Burnham wants YOU to pay for new Channel migrant crackdown and EU projects under shameful Brexit ‘reset’ deal
News.content:
Next

TAXPAYERS may have to foot the bills for a crackdown on Channel migrants and EU projects in Andy Burnham’s Brexit deal.

Brits could have to bankroll development in poorer European regions and pay more to tackle the small boats crisis, leaked documents show.



A 15-page draft joint statement about the PM’s Brexit Reset, seen by The Sun ahead of today’s summit in Brussels, raises fresh questions over the price of closer ties to the bloc.

Access to the EU’s electricity market would be in return for paying tens of millions a year into infrastructure projects in poorer countries in the bloc.



The draft also opens the door to more financial contributions towards tackling Channel migrant crossings — on top of the £662million already agreed — and proposes working together on “returns to third countries” — like the Rwanda scheme Labour axed in 2024.

The pact will also see regulation and red tape scrapped on food exports by aligning to EU rules the UK will have little say over.

The Treasury say it will eventually lead to £5billion of benefits every year.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch last night told The Sun: “Andy Burnham’s EU summit is more about the Labour Party’s interests than the national interest.



“The last thing the country needs is to start paying money to the EU to have laws set by foreign courts.”

It was also revealed yesterday that the PM has agreed to 100,000 visas for young Europeans up to the age of 31 to live and work here as part of a youth mobility deal.

Concerns were growing last night that millions could be lost with visa fees or due to the NHS surcharge being waived.

And the price of plans to slash tuition fees for youths from the continent studying here could be £485million, one analysis reveals.

The summit comes days after the PM said the hard Brexit deal had hit growth.



He said: “We have lost more than we have gained.”

News.title: Fiona the hippo dies after eating hat flung into enclosure as zoo shares ‘extreme sadness’
News.content:
Next

FIONA the hippo who became a global sensation after surviving a premature birth has tragically died after swallowing a child’s woolly hat in a freak accident.

The beloved nine-year-old, who captured hearts around the world with her miraculous fight for survival, died on Thursday despite a desperate battle to save her.



Vets at Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio had been fighting to keep the 2,400lb giant alive after the hat became lodged in her digestive system.

Keepers even resorted to bizarre vibration therapy in a last-ditch bid to shake the object through her body.



But despite round-the-clock treatment and a string of emergency procedures, Fiona could not be saved.

Heartbroken zoo bosses announced the devastating news on Thursday, saying staff had tried everything to rescue their much-loved star.



In an emotional statement, Cincinnati Zoo said: “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency.”

They added: “The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week.



“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.

“The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.

“We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are.”

Fiona’s fatal ordeal began on November 8 when a child’s knitted hat landed inside her enclosure following a freak chain of events.

The youngster had tossed the cap into the air near the hippo’s viewing area when it became caught in a ceiling fan.



It was then catapulted through a tiny gap above the viewing windows and landed inside Fiona’s habitat.

The curious hippo swallowed the hat, sparking a frantic fight to prevent a potentially deadly blockage.

As her appetite began to decline, worried vets sedated Fiona twice to carry out a series of urgent examinations.



An ultrasound revealed worrying bunching in her intestines, while further tests showed she was slightly dehydrated.

Medics attempted a colonoscopy using a nine-foot scope borrowed from Columbus Zoo, but were unable to reach the swallowed object.

Vets also pumped Fiona with fluids and administered medication while tempting her with her favourite foods.

Devoted keepers even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she had always loved, in a heartbreaking attempt to lift her spirits.

But the beloved animal’s condition failed to improve, and the zoo’s desperate rescue efforts ended in tragedy.



One heartbroken fan of the much loved hippo wrote: “Rest in peace, Fiona. The queen of the Queen City.”

The shocking death comes nearly a decade after Fiona first defied the odds in a remarkable fight for life.

Born six weeks prematurely at Cincinnati Zoo on January 24, 2017, the tiny calf weighed just 29lbs.



She was a staggering 25lbs lighter than the lowest previously recorded birth weight for a Nile hippo.

Her survival was initially uncertain, but dedicated keepers nursed her through the critical early weeks with round-the-clock care.

Fiona’s miraculous recovery transformed her into a worldwide celebrity, inspiring books, a beer range and even her own bobblehead.

Her every move became internet gold, with millions falling in love with the cheeky hippo’s antics, from her spectacularly loud farts to her lazy lounging and playful splashing in the water.

She even managed to steal the spotlight during a couple’s marriage proposal, cementing her status as one of the zoo world’s most unlikely superstars.



Dubbed an internet queen by her adoring fans, Fiona sparked a frenzy of online devotion that became known as “Fionamania”.

Her enormous personality earned her a Facebook reality series and a collection of children’s books, turning the once-fragile calf into a global phenomenon.

She became a big sister in 2022 when her mum Bibi gave birth to a healthy male calf named Fritz.

News of her latest health battle had sparked an outpouring of concern from devastated fans across the world.

Some furious supporters demanded punishment for the visitor responsible for the hat landing in her enclosure.



One wrote: “I hope you revoked that visitor’s pass.”

Another demanded: “Was the person arrested that threw the hat in?”

But zoo bosses insisted the incident was entirely accidental, describing the chances of the hat landing inside Fiona’s habitat as incredibly slim.

Zoo spokeswoman Michelle Curley said: “We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident.”

In a final tribute, Cincinnati Zoo urged devastated supporters to remember the staff who had fought tirelessly to save Fiona.

They said: “Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news.

“They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.”

News.title: Woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband speaks out as abusers found guilty
News.content:
A woman who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband has said she will "never feel completely safe" after four men were found guilty of sexually abusing her, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said: "The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire. He invited men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to the couple's home without her knowledge.

On Thursday, Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it."

On the steps outside the court, she said: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to."

News.title: Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
News.content:
The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.

The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.

That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.

The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimesâ¦ we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".

It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attachÃ© in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.

Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.

Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".

Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.

He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.

She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

News.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
News.content:
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than Â£30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

News.title: William and Catherine's India tour was 'particularly special', aide says
News.content:
The most senior advisor to the Prince of Wales has said this week's visit with the Princess of Wales to India was "particularly special" and described the royal couple "as very much a team".

Prince William and Catherine are now back in the UK after spending three days in Mumbai and Delhi - the first time they have travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.

The visit focused on the prince's Earthshot Prize which were hosted in Mumbai. His wife last attended the Earthshot awards when they were held in Boston in 2022.

"The prince has really enjoyed having the princess alongside him for Earthshot, and for her to see first-hand how much it has grown in scale since she last attended in Boston," Ian Patrick, the prince's private secretary told reporters.

"She's enormously proud of what he's achieved, and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together. They are very much a team."

The prince and princess also met the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at his residence in Delhi where they discussed UK-India partnerships.

In a social media post after the meeting, the prime minister said it had been "a pleasure to meet their Royal Highnesses" and praised the Earthshot Prize for "showcasing Indian ingenuity in addressing global environmental challenges".

The meeting was a late addition to the prince and princess's plans. Prime Minister Modi altered his schedule to return to India from a summit in the Philippines to ensure he could meet the royal couple.

"The prince and princess have had a thoroughly enjoyable time in India. They've been incredibly touched by the warmth of the welcome they've received," said Patrick.

News.title: Discrimination claims by McDonald's workers can go ahead, court says
News.content:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to "change the way they treat younger employees".

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

BBC correspondent Noor Nanji looks at the latest developments.

News.title: UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
News.content:
After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews., external

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.

GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.

Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating, external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".

One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.

The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.

News.title: Dutch watchdog tells people not to buy AI smart glasses
News.content:
The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.

While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.

The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under â¬100 (Â£84) to over â¬500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.

Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.

It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.

The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.

Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.

Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.

The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.

But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.

News.title: Timetable set out for dismantling leasehold system in England and Wales
News.content:
The government has set out a timetable for when the leasehold system in England and Wales will be dismantled.

Under the plans, most new flats - with only limited exemptions - will be sold as commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

The government says a modernised commonhold model is expected to be up and running around 2029, followed by a ban on the sale of most new leasehold flats, expected around 2031.

Meanwhile, a Â£250 cap on ground rents - the annual fee paid by leaseholders to their freeholder - is expected to come into force in 2028, six months after a new law passes.

Ground rents will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

There are around five million leasehold homes in England and Wales, where people own the right to occupy a property via a lease for a limited number of years from a freeholder.

Under commonhold, there is no ground rent or expiring lease.

On Thursday, the government introduced the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, external to Parliament.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months, and the measures in the bill will not come into force straight away.

News.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
News.content:
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas, 59.

News.title: Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims patients unnecessarily bled to death
News.content:
Dr Habib, who has worked in General Surgery & HPB (liver, pancreas and bile duct) since 2014, said he thought several hundred patients had come to harm from an excessively high rate of complications.

He said he had tried his best to use the whistleblowing procedures but the institutions he had contacted had failed to act as robustly as they should have.

He said he first became aware of avoidable surgery-related deaths in 2016.

In July 2021, he formally raised serious concerns about what he believes were dozens of avoidable deaths.

In February 2024, he spoke to Police Scotland.

Habib said he believed NHS Grampian was guilty of "wicked recklessness and an indifference to patient deaths" and called for a corporate homicide investigation.

The consultant said the 2022 external expert report, which was never made public, concluded that 19 deaths out of a case study of 45 were avoidable (42%).

He said he had contacted the first minister and health secretary on numerous occasions since June 2023 but the Scottish government had said it had "no jurisdiction" to investigate whistleblowing claims.

Habib also said that the Independent Whistleblowing Officer (INWO) refused to progress his complaints.

He also wrote to the chief executive of NHS Grampian, Laura Skaife Knight, in December 2025.

She replied six months later saying she needed Healthcare Improvement Scotland to complete its enquiries.

In response to the latest allegations from Habib, Skaife-Knight said: "A thorough investigation has already taken place into these matters, with some elements of that work ongoing.

"Any new evidence or information will be carefully considered, and NHS Grampian will continue to respond through the appropriate clinical, governance and legal processes."

A Scottish government spokesperson said they recognised the "courage shown by this whistleblower" and reiterated that a "very significant level of intervention and an unprecedented level of support" was being given to NHS Grampian.

News.title: Letby prosecutors knew expert witness was under investigation
News.content:
Police and prosecutors knew an expert witness against Lucy Letby was under investigation over his fitness to practise when he gave evidence at her trial.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh testified that he believed that two babies Letby was accused of attempting to murder had been poisoned with insulin.

Before the first of his two court appearances, however, Hindmarsh had been referred to the General Medical Council (GMC).

The BBC has learned the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) knew this before he went on to appear for a second time.

The Guardian has reported that the CPS told Letby's defence team it would oppose telling the jury about the GMC investigation because it had not concluded, external.

The CPS said it had "met all its disclosure obligations... and no objections were raised by the defence at any stage in relation to expert evidence".

Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others - one on two occasions - and sentenced to 15 whole-life prison sentences.

Prof Hindmarsh, who voluntarily removed himself from the GMC register before the investigation concluded, declined to comment to the BBC.

News.title: England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain
News.content:
England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association Â£12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

News.title: Tourist jailed for damaging Belfast's Big Fish
News.content:
A man has been jailed for five months after causing an estimated Â£10,000 worth of damage to Belfast's Big Fish sculpture.

Peter Smith, 44, of no fixed abode, admitted criminal damage and possessing items with intent to damage property.

He is believed to have used a hatchet, a hammer and a sledgehammer to smash ceramic tiles around the sculpture's left eye.

District Judge Francis Rafferty told Belfast Magistrates' Court: "I regard it as a targeted attack, but it remains unexplained."

Police were called to Donegall Quay shortly after midnight on 20 September. A witness saw Smith striking the sculpture with a long-handled object and detained him until officers arrived.

Smith was carrying a hammer and a small hatchet in his backpack and officers later found a sledgehammer in nearby bushes.

Defence barrister Garrett O'Kane said Smith was visiting Belfast from England and that he had a psychiatric disorder following a car crash four years earlier in which two of his sons were killed.

O'Kane said Smith told him that he had found the tools and used them to attack the sculpture.

The court heard that plans for repairing the sculpture remain unclear.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after councillor stabbed
News.content:
A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.

Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.

West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.

The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".

Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.

A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.

News.title: Flag injunction case 'spiralling out of control'
News.content:
The co-founder of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has said an interim injunction banning him and others from putting flags on lamp-posts in Birmingham is "spiralling out of control", as he learned the case could go to trial.

The High Court granted Birmingham City Council the order on Wednesday against Ryan Bridge and others, after thousands of union jacks and St George's flags were put up across the city.

The council argued that they posed a hazard on lamp-posts, signs and other highway structures, and fuelled community tensions.

On Thursday, Bridge attended another hearing where he was told the injunction had come into force and would be in place until a trial or further court order.

The 45-year-old heard that if the council sought a permanent injunction, the case could involve at least three to four days of evidence.

He said: "It's spiralling out of control, isn't it?" and added that he did not "want to exploit any more of the public purse and the council's money".

Bridge, from Blackwell, near Bromsgrove in Worcestershire, said he stopped putting up flags in Birmingham when he first heard about the injunction.

He said the other defendants in the case, which include six other named individuals and "persons unknown" who may put up flags, thought the case was "done".

News.title: Trump posthumously pardons late controversial baseball star Pete Rose
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned the late baseball star Pete Rose, who was embroiled in controversy over tax crimes and a gambling scandal.

“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND, whose record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday.

Trump then listed off some more of the former Cincinnati Reds first baseman’s stats and then said he, “just like the Great Roger Clemens, who won 354 games, was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess!”

Rose was banned from the MLB in 1989 after the league found that he violated its rules by repeatedly betting on the Reds as a player and manager from 1985 to 1987.

He was then sentenced in 1990 to five months in federal prison for filing false income tax returns. “I will serve my sentence, pay my debt to society and get on with my life,” Rose, who had pleaded guilty to the tax charges, said, according to a New York Times article published at the time of sentencing. Rose later died at age 83 in September 2024.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned the late baseball star Pete Rose, who was embroiled in controversy over tax crimes and a gambling scandal ( Getty Images )

During an impromptu White House press briefing with his longtime friend Trump earlier this month, UFC chief Dana White was asked about the president potentially pardoning Rose.

“The president has said he might consider a pardon for Pete Rose. What is your advice to the president about that pardon?” a reporter asked White, who was at the podium after Trump semi-jokingly offered him the job of White House press secretary. The role remains vacant, though White never ruled it out.

“I don't advise the president on anything ever, but I think it's fair. I think it's fair to pardon Pete Rose,” White said.

Trump then chimed in: “I'd give Pete Rose a pardon. I think Pete Rose was very mistreated...he was caught gambling. Now it's legal, right? But he was gambling on his own team. He wasn't gambling against.”

“He shouldn't have done it. But he went through 40 years of hell. And they should have given him a pardon. They should have given him into the Baseball Hall of Fame a long time ago,” the president continued.

Since Rose was banned from baseball, he was not allowed into the Hall of Fame, but after he died, his ban was lifted, making him eligible for a posthumous award.

open image in gallery Trump also said last month that he would give fellow former MLB star Roger Clemens, who had his own fair share of scandals, the Presidential Medal of Freedom ( Getty Images )

Trump also mentioned Clemens, a two-time World Series Champion with the New York Yankees who had his own fair share of scandals.

Clemens’ former trainer, Brian McNamee, claimed that he injected the baseball star multiple times with steroids and human growth hormones from 1998 through 2001.

It was also reported by the New York Daily News in 2008 that Clemens had a decade-long affair with the now-late country music star Mindy McCready.

Nonetheless, Trump announced during a midterm rally in Texas last month that he will honor Clemens with the Presidential Medal of Freedom — the highest civilian honor.

“This supersedes anything that obviously I've done in my playing career, and to get it from this man, this president, there wouldn't be another president I'd want to get it from,” Clemens said after Trump welcomed him on stage.

This is a developing story...

News.title: Jodie Foster admits ‘superstitious’ movie premiere ritual
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Jodie Foster has attended dozens of movie premieres across her five-decade acting career, but she still gets superstitious.

The Oscar-winning Silence of the Lambs actor revealed on the red carpet for her new animated movie Hexed that she partakes in several “lucky” rituals before a premiere, but the main one is wearing a specific perfume.

Foster, 64, told People at the Los Angeles event that she is sure to “always wear a certain perfume,” adding that she never wears perfume “pretty much ever, except when I go to a movie premiere.”

“It’s vetiver,” Foster said of the scent.

“Beyond that though, I think it’s more just make sure you have the right underclothes,” she added of her preparation for big events.

open image in gallery Jodie Foster voices Queen Celeste, the ruler of the witches, in the new movie ‘Hexed’ ( Getty )

Foster added that she’s often trying to manifest good outcomes, saying that she’s become “a little more superstitious as I get older.”

“I feel like I have many superstitions,”the Taxi Driver star said. “I don’t know if it’s superstitions, but I do things to ensure a good outcome. If it doesn’t work, I don’t care, but I just want to make sure that I put my finger on the scale a little bit.”

“So, I have lucky things, I do, I suppose, and it seems to get more and more as I get older. I get a little more superstitious as I get older,” she continues. “You would think it would be the opposite, but it’s getting worse.”

Hexed, a Disney animation, follows teenager Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who discovers that she and her mother, Alive (Rashida Jones), are witches with the ability to travel to a magical realm. Foster voices Queen Celeste, the witches' evil ruler.

Foster has opened up about her superstitions before, previously telling Jimmy Kimmel Live that when she is traveling, she makes a specific decision about the underwear she wears on flights.

“I do wear underwear on the plane that has, like, a very bright color,” she said. “Just for the plane. Just, like, these are other superstitions that I have.”

open image in gallery Jodie Foster has said she has become ‘a little more superstitious’ in recent years ( AP )

Foster made her acting debut in a television commercial for sunscreen in 1965 aged three. At the age of six, she made her feature film debut in Napoleon and Samantha, and continued to play smaller roles on television and in films, including Becky Thatcher in Tom Sawyer (1973).

She earned her first Oscar nomination for best supporting actress for Martin Scorsese’s Taxi Driver, which she appeared in aged 12.

She won her first Academy Award for Best Actress for her role as waitress Sarah Tobias in 1988’s The Accused and her second for playing FBI agent Clarice Starling in the 1991 film The Silence of the Lambs.

Her most recent Oscar nomination was for her work as a swimming coach in 2023’s Nyad.

News.title: Thirteen train heist suspects charged with stealing $22 million in cargo from major retailers
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

More than a dozen people have been charged over a massive train heist operation targeting $22 million in cargo from major retailers.

A federal indictment unsealed Thursday describes how an organized group targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country.

Trains that transport products to stores and customers around the country have become a big target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have affected the world's largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon.

The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise.

The men shared numerous photos and videos in group chats of themselves busting into the hulking train cars and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise.

They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars as police helicopters descended overhead.

Thirteen men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo in connection with the heists and two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers.

If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison.

News.title: John Travolta shares update on his love life six years after death of his wife
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

John Travolta is open to finding love again.

“Well, love everything is part of my personality,” Travolta told Craig Melvin while appearing on Monday’s episode of Today. “So you know, am I open to it? Yes.”

The 72-year-old Grease star has been focused on his two children: Ella Bleu, 26, and Benjamin, 15, since the death of his wife Kelly Preston, who died in 2020 from breast cancer. The couple also shared a son, Jett, who died in 2009.

“It’s been an interesting six years to take care of my son, who was only nine when this happened,” he said.

Travolta said he wanted to get his kids “squared away and all sort of settled out about their future and what happened.”

open image in gallery John Travolta and Kelly Preston photographed in 2007 ( AFP/Getty )

“You’re both a mother and father when one of the parents leave, so I felt that in a very big way,” he said. “They’re both becoming happier each year and recovering more from it. So we’re good.”

Last week, his daughter Ella Bleu – who starred in his directorial debut Propeller One-Way Night Coach – had presented him with the Cultural Icon Award at the Dwight D. Opperman Excellence in Leadership Awards in Washington.

“It meant everything to me and she did such an elegant, eloquent job of acknowledging her father,” he said.

“It was just a big moment … my gorgeous daughter delivering this speech that was very touching, made me cry,” he continued. “We've always had a great relationship, Ella and I.”

During the speech, Ella called Travolta her “pilot, both in life and in the skies,” referring to him having his pilot's license.

“For the past 26 years, I’ve had a front-row seat to someone who has never lost their excitement for life. Someone who continues to learn… someone who lives without ever expecting anything in return, someone who is kind,” she said.

open image in gallery John Travolta has said he’s open to love again after the death of his wife six years ago ( Getty )

“While the world celebrates a cultural icon, my brother Ben and I get to celebrate our hero,” she continued. “Congratulations, Dad.”

On October 13, on what would have been his wife’s birthday, Travolta shared an Instagram post of his daughter with the caption: “Look at your baby girl now Kelly!! Happy birthday, you should be so proud!!”

Travolta met Preston while filming the 1989 comedy The Experts. They wed in 1991. Their first child, Jett, was born in 2009. He died aged 16 after suffering a seizure while the family was on vacation in the Bahamas.

Preston, best known for her roles in Twins and Jerry Maguire, died in 2020 aged 57.

Travolta made his directorial debut earlier this year with Propeller One-Way Night Coach, and received the honorary Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival. He unveiled his new look at the festival, wearing different colored berets and round wire-frame glasses. He told the press that it was to channel his auteur persona.

The Pulp Fiction actor wrote, directed and co-produced Propeller One-Way Night Coach, which is based on his own 1997 children’s novel of the same name.

The movie follows a young aspiring pilot named Jeff and his mother as they embark on a cross-country journey to Hollywood. Ella plays a flight attendant in the film, which will begin streaming globally on Apple TV in May.

News.title: Royal secretary shares insight into William and Kate’s relationship after ‘special’ trip
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

William’s private secretary says the Prince and Princess of Wales are “very much a team” after their three-day trip to India to stage the Earthshot Prize.

William and Kate travelled to Mumbai to celebrate Anglo-Indian links, young people and William’s environmental awards, which fulfilled their belief that royal tours should have “purpose, meaning and impact”.

The visit was also significant for Kate, marking her first long-haul overseas trip since she announced her cancer diagnosis in March 2024.

William’s private secretary Ian Patrick said the prince had been particularly pleased to have Kate alongside him.

“The prince has really enjoyed having the princess alongside him for Earthshot, and for her to see first-hand how much it has grown in scale since she last attended in Boston,” he said.

“She’s enormously proud of what he’s achieved and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together.

“They are very much a team.”

open image in gallery The Prince and Princess of Wales at the 2026 Earthshot Prize Awards (Aaron Chown/PA) ( PA Wire )

Earthshot CEO Jason Knauf described Kate as a key figure in the background, and when debating whether to go ahead with the initiative, the princess was the “loudest voice saying yes”.

During the visit, the future King announced the launch of a five-year personal accident insurance scheme for temporary rangers on the “front line” protecting “precious wildlife”.

The scheme, developed and launched by William’s United for Wildlife initiative, aims to address the problem of India’s temporary rangers not being covered by policies that protect permanent staff, potentially leaving their families with no income and compensation if they were killed or injured on duty.

It will provide protection for 10,000 temporary rangers across seven states from December.

The states covered are Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Assam, Uttarakhand, Maharashtra, Kerala and Rajasthan.

open image in gallery William highlighted the risks faced by conservation workers, who often patrol remote areas and face difficult conditions while protecting wildlife. ( PA )

William announced the scheme as his India visit ended and highlighted the efforts of the workers: “Day and night, India’s wildlife rangers stand on the front line of protecting this precious wildlife. They patrol remote forests, endure difficult conditions and face significant dangers, all in service of safeguarding nature for future generations.”

The prince had announced similar initiatives following Earthshot Prize events in Rio de Janeiro in 2025 and Cape Town in 2026, extending support for wildlife rangers in several regions.

The royal couple also held bilateral talks with India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on Wednesday evening, the last day of the tour, to strengthen diplomatic ties between the two countries.

open image in gallery Prince William and Kate with India's prime minister Narendra Modi ( India's Press Information Bureau )

William’s aide said the couple want their international engagements to deliver meaningful outcomes, rather than simply serve as ceremonial visits.

“The prince and princess want their overseas travel to have purpose, meaning and impact,” Mr Patrick added.

“It’s about building stronger relationships, creating opportunities for collaboration and supporting projects that deliver real results.”

The couple attended the inaugural Children’s Earthshot during their visit and described the youngsters who had created solutions to tackle environmental challenges in their local communities as “incredible”.

Mr Patrick said: “One of the strongest themes of this visit has been young people. They believe passionately that the next generation must have a voice in shaping their own future.

“They don’t want young people to feel unheard or that the challenges facing the planet and society are beyond their control. They want them to feel optimistic, empowered and part of the solutions.”

News.title: Drone footage posted on YouTube of Mauricio Pochettino’s first Man United training session
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Drone footage showing Mauricio Pochettino leading his first training session as Manchester United manager has been posted online.

The 12-minute clip, which was filmed above United’s Carrington training complex, was uploaded to YouTube.

In the video, Pochettino can be seen working alongside the squad, which had been split into three separate groups.

Addressing the upload, the drone operator wrote: "For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn’t fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the manager’s first training session, there are many media there so certainly won’t be the only footage of training released."

Man United are currently in the relegation zone ( Getty )

Manchester United have declined to comment on the footage.

The session marked Pochettino’s opening training session following his appointment as United’s new head coach last week. He succeeds Michael Carrick, who was dismissed during the international break with the team currently in the relegation zone after winning just one of their 10 Premier League matches.

After overseeing his final match with the United States - a 2-0 victory over Haiti that concluded early on Wednesday morning UK time - Pochettino arrived in Manchester later that day.

His first match in charge will see United take on old rivals Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday afternoon.

Andoni Iraola’s side are currently 10 points above United in the table, and will be hoping to spoil Pochettino’s Premier League return.

Pochettino is taking charge of his fourth Premier League club, having previously managed Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea.

However, he has made it clear that he has been an admirer of United for a long time, and was cheering them on when they completed the Treble by winning the 1999 Champions League final against Bayern Munich in Barcelona.

“I was in Barcelona in that final, that was an iconic final,” he said in his first interview as manager. “We were shouting for Manchester United.

“From there, it was so exciting to see Manchester United, and more with the admiration of Sir Alex Ferguson – for me, the best coach in the history of the sport. I always admired him.”

News.title: Matthew Rhys reflects on ‘terrible joke’ during James Bond audition that may have cost him role
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Matthew Rhys has shared how a disastrous joke during his James Bond audition brought his hopes of playing 007 to an abrupt end, after he suggested that the famous secret agent should walk with a limp and wear an eye patch.

The Welsh actor, 52, who recently enjoyed a remarkable night at the Emmy Awards with two leading actor wins, recalled his unsuccessful attempt to secure one of cinema’s most coveted roles during an appearance on Conan O’Brien’s podcast.

Rhys was considered for the part in the early 2000s, prior to Daniel Craig, 58, being chosen to succeed Pierce Brosnan, 73, making his debut in 2006’s Casino Royale.

The audition took place inside the Bond producers’ offices overlooking Green Park in London.

Asked by Conan O’Brien, 63, how the meeting had gone, Rhys replied: "Well I’m not playing Bond, nor have I been."

The actor explained he had visited the offices of the Broccoli family, who have overseen the James Bond franchise for decades, for a meeting about potentially taking over the role.

During the interview, Rhys was asked if he had read Casino Royale, the Ian Fleming novel that introduced the British secret agent.

However, the conversation took an unexpected turn when the audition panel asked him to explain how he would approach the character differently.

The panel asked: “So what would you do different with Bond?”

open image in gallery Rhys made history at the 2026 Emmy Awards, becoming the first performer to win two leading actor prizes for different programmes in the same year ( Reuters )

Rhys said: “As a terrible joke, I said, ‘Limp’.”

Rather than changing course, the actor continued with the joke, suggesting his version of Bond should also wear an eye patch.

He recalled: “It went very quiet and then I just fell apart.”

The meeting failed to secure Rhys the role, which eventually went to Daniel, whose interpretation of the British spy began with Casino Royale and continued through four further films.

Daniel went on to star in Quantum of Solace, Skyfall, Spectre and No Time to Die, ending his 15-year tenure as 007 in 2021.

Despite missing out on Bond, Rhys subsequently established himself as a leading television actor, becoming particularly well known for playing Soviet intelligence officer Philip Jennings in the acclaimed spy drama The Americans.

The series, which ran for six seasons, starred Rhys opposite Keri Russell, 50, who played his on-screen wife Elizabeth Jennings. The pair also became partners away from the cameras.

Rhys won an Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for his performance in The Americans in 2018.

His other notable credits include playing lawyer Perry Mason in HBO’s period crime drama of the same name, as well as appearances in Brothers and Sisters, A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood and The Post.

open image in gallery The Bond role eventually went to Daniel Craig ( Eon Productions )

Rhys’s career has recently reached another milestone after he made history at the 2026 Emmy Awards, becoming the first performer to win two leading actor prizes for different programmes in the same year.

He won Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series for Widow’s Bay, the Apple TV horror-comedy created by Katie Dippold, 46.

The series follows Mayor Tom Loftis, played by Rhys, as he attempts to transform a mysterious New England island into a tourist destination comparable to Martha’s Vineyard, despite the community’s reputation for supernatural occurrences.

He also received Outstanding Lead Actor in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for Netflix’s psychological thriller The Beast in Me, in which he stars opposite Claire Danes, 47.

Rhys plays wealthy property developer Nile Jarvis, a man whose involvement in the disappearance of his first wife becomes central to the mystery.

Claire plays author Aggie Wiggs, who becomes increasingly fascinated by her neighbour while investigating his past.

The two victories also made Rhys the first male performer to win leading actor Emmys across drama, comedy and limited series categories, following his earlier success with The Americans.

His Bond audition has resurfaced amid renewed interest in the franchise following the announcement of Robert Pattinson, 40, as Daniel’s successor.

Robert, best known for playing Edward Cullen in The Twilight Saga and Bruce Wayne in The Batman, is set to take over the role for the next film, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, 59.

The franchise is entering a new chapter following Amazon MGM Studios’ assumption of creative control from longtime producers Barbara Broccoli, 66, and Michael G Wilson, 84.

News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”

Inflation increased in October as a result of surging fuel prices for motorists.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October to 174.7p, the highest level since August 2022.

The ONS said diesel rose by 7p to 199.5p per litre last month – the highest since records began in 1996.
