News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” added the ASA, who launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

Voy said the ads were retracted while the investigation was underway, adding that they will not run them again.

Dr Earim Chaudry, Chief Medical Officer at Voy, said: “Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance”.

News.title: Saucepan racks, fitted sheets and dehumidifiers: Your tricks for drying laundry in winter
News.content:
As temperatures drop and laundry piles up, drying clothes indoors can become a headache. But when Laura de Barra gave her verdict on the best heated clothes airers, Telegraph readers had a lot to say. So, we asked you what works in your homes.

While some of you have relied on heated airers for years, others have found a standard clothes horse or an overhead airer paired with a dehumidifier preferable. Several of you argue that you can’t beat the efficiency of a tumble dryer.

Here are your tried and tested tips...

Heated airers

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.



After seeing a review for the Lakeland heated airer printed in The Telegraph in 2008, Clive Ruffle, 67, from Surrey, felt enticed to buy one. “It had a price offer and a coupon to send to the newspaper,” he recalls.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

The options to fold the airer away flat and use only half of it, where one side is folded down, are the two major features that attracted Clive to the product.

“The drying speed is good, and we’ve never felt frustrated by it,” he says. “The heated bars are very effective and if we choose to heat, clothes are usually done in the day. They take a bit longer without the heater.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

For a more affordable option, Caroline Morrell, 65, from Greater Manchester, recommends buying a tiered Minky heated clothes airer, which she uses with a Beldray cover.

Sports.title: How Mauricio Pochettino fell in love with Man Utd attending 1999 Champions League final with future goalkeeping coach
Sports.content:
Next

MAURICIO POCHETTINO fell in love with Manchester United watching Alex Ferguson pull off the greatest smash-and-grab in Champions League history.

Now 27 years later, the Argentine has got his hands on the keys to a different kind of Old Trafford drama.



The new Old Trafford boss was at the Nou Camp in 1999, cheering on the Red Devils as they ripped Bayern Munich’s hearts out with two dramatic stoppage-time goals to win 2-1.

Sat next to Catalonia-based ­Espanyol team-mate Toni ­Jimenez — now goalkeeping coach at Carrington — Pochettino was swept up in the madness of the comeback.



It secured United an unprecedented Treble after their Premier League and FA Cup triumphs, transformed Ferguson into Sir Alex, made his players legends and turned a 27-year-old Poch into an admirer.

Little did he know that nearly three decades later, he would be the man expected to glue the club back together.

Pochettino said: “In 1999, I was in Barcelona in that final. That was an iconic final, Toni and I were shouting for Manchester United.

“From there, I was so excited to see Manchester United and had more admiration for Sir Alex Ferguson — the best coach in the history of the sport.

“I always admired him and then had the opportunity to meet when I went to Southampton and then we played in Old Trafford in 2013.

“That was a dream come true and then the possibility of meeting him in a restaurant in London.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“That is all the memories I have about that club. Now being a head coach is an honour and a privilege.”

United were seconds from defeat to Bayern when Teddy Sheringham (below) levelled before Ole Gunnar ­Solskjaer landed the ­knockout blow from a second David Beckham corner.

Pochettino said: “That type of game where you stay sitting in your place and you’re so excited.

“It was an amazing game. What happened in the end — it’s impossible not to empathise with that team.



“That made me pay more attention to United, Ferguson and the players who are all legends.”

Ex-Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino, now 54, has spent the best part of ten years flirting with the Old Trafford job, watching the club tumble from one false dawn to another.

With Louis van Gaal’s position in ­jeopardy in May 2016, Ferguson requested to meet then-Spurs boss Pochettino at a London restaurant.

Jose Mourinho was being lined up as Van Gaal’s replacement but that did not stop Fergie asking the League Managers Association secretary for Pochettino’s number.



A lavish two-hour seafood lunch at Scott’s in ­Mayfair might have remained private had ­paparazzi not snapped the pair with Pochettino’s No 2 Jesus Perez outside.

United have since appointed five permanent managers but Poch never disappeared from the conversation.

When Solskjaer was given the caretaker job in December 2018, a league victory over Pochettino’s Tottenham at Wembley the following month was viewed as a positive sign by United.

Two months later, Solskjaer signed a three-year contract.



Quizzed before that meeting almost eight years ago, Pochettino had revealed: “I remember when Ole scored after 90 minutes at the Camp Nou. I was there and shouted for United’s goal.”

Spurs sacked Pochettino in November 2019 — just five months after taking Spurs to the Champions League final.

His availability became an awkward sub-plot to Solskjaer’s reign.

One reason the Norwegian lost the dressing room by November 2021 was his frequent ­references to glory days his players felt so far removed from.



Michael Carrick fell into the same trap, citing Fergie, Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney, Sir Bobby Charlton and Sir Matt Busby during a box office five-minute monologue to open one of his final press conferences.

Nostalgia is no longer accepted as a substitute for success at Old Trafford.

And the club Poch inherits is worlds away from the one that stole his heart in Spain, with United in the relegation places.

He said: “We must start from zero. Culture is the most ­important. We need to create the environment and platform for the players to perform.



We need to understand the history of the club, try to create a new culture and philosophy that can respect that identity but at the same time, perform.

“If we don’t perform, the responsibility is mine.”

There is no gentle introduction as Poch’s first assignment is a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on Sunday.

He has urged his new players to be “fearless” after just ONE Prem victory in ten games, a 5-2 win over newly- promoted Ipswich 82 days ago.



Pochettino’s form as USA boss is in stark contrast to United’s, winning all SIX games since ­losing in the World Cup round of 16 to Belgium, scoring 20 goals and conceding just three.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Red Devils have lost seven of their 15 games this term with their only clean sheet coming against Azerbaijani minnows Sabah FK in September.

United are 18th in the Prem but could be bottom by kick-off on Merseyside if Crystal Palace and Sunderland both win on Saturday.

Sports.title: How Man Utd’s ‘midfield flex’ could SHOCK Liverpool and see Pochettino unleash ‘butcher’ Lisandro Martinez
Sports.content:
Next

MAURICIO POCHETTINO faces a baptism of fire in his first game as Manchester United boss when he takes his side to Anfield on Sunday.

The Argentine has inherited a side leaking too many shots and missing injured midfielder Carlos Baleba ahead of the massive clash with Liverpool.



But here SunSport’s tactical expert Dean Scoggins reveals how ruthless defensive calls, a surprise attacking set-up and an unlikely “midfield flex” could see Pochettino bamboozle the Reds….

BALEBA is not going to be in the XI, and United need to make a decision about how they are going to combat that in midfield.



I don’t think Youri Tielemans has been anywhere near the player that Manchester United have wanted him to be so far.

So here’s something a bit more radical – how about they go with Lisandro Martinez as the holding midfield player in this game?

Leave out Tielemans, bring in Harry Maguire and move Kobbie Mainoo over to the other midfield shape.

That gives you a bit of Argentinian muscle, which Pochettino may well like in that midfield position where Martinez can flex his muscles a little bit and be the holding player in there.

Martinez has got that ability on the ball as well, and having someone like him in there means Mainoo will get more licence to go forward.

Shifting Martinez into the engine room leaves a void at the back against a £400million Liverpool frontline boasting Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

With United conceding 5.1 shots on target per game so far this season, Pochettino cannot afford to throw young centre-backs Leny Yoro and Aiden Heaven into the deep end together.

Ruthless changes in defence are needed – if you’re going to play against Liverpool, then you need someone who’s going to head it.

You have to have Maguire in that team. There’s lots of talk of Heaven and Yoro at centre-back, but this is Anfield and this is the first week.

Look, Harry Maguire has a lot of faults. There are lots of mistakes he’s made in previous weeks.



But if Liverpool are going to cross and load the box as they do, you’ve got to pick Maguire and be ruthless with the youngsters in this first game.

Pochettino also has a big call to make up top, where fans are clamouring to see target man Joshua Zirkzee lead the line as a focal point.

However, Pochettino could snub the Dutchman in favour of overloading the flanks with Bryan Mbeumo, Amad Diallo and Matheus Cunha.

We know from previous jobs that Mauricio Pochettino loves to have the pivot point in the attack, the post, and Zirkzee is one of the names on all the fans’ lips.



Think back to his Tottenham days, where he’s got Harry Kane, or brought Fernando Llorente into the squad.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

However, Liverpool are quite susceptible in the spaces between the full-back and the centre-back, where Milos Kerkez loves to go out and chase the ball and leaves space in behind him.

In order to get the numbers around the side in that area, you don’t want the post in the middle of the field – start with Mbeumo, and if you go to Zirkzee later in the game, that’s an option.

Sports.title: Newcastle ‘closer than ever’ to announcing 65,000-seater ‘Allianz Arena-style’ new stadium in £1.3billion project
Sports.content:
Next

NEWCASTLE could be ready to end 134 years of history at St James’ Park.

Toon have occupied the famous old stadium since 1892, but their Saudi owners seem to have settled on building a new £1.3billion home over redevelopment.



The Daily Mail claims that club chiefs met representatives from Goldman Sachs this month to discuss funding plans for a 65,000-seater home in Leazes Park.

Newcastle have reportedly conducted surveys around animal and plant life after concerns were raised about the presence of bats in the potential site.



Expanding St James’ is another option, but a new ground is the easiest path to competing with the best clubs in Europe in the age of FFP.

Early designs by KSS architects were compared to Bayern Munich’s Allianz Arena and Atletico Madrid’s Wanda Metropolitano by those who saw them, per the Mail’s report.

Debts would fall on the club, as opposed to its Saudi backers and a decision could be announced early next year.

Newcastle host Arsenal on Saturday looking to climb the table after a sluggish start.

Under-fire boss Matthias Jaissle revealed that he begged Bruno Guimaraes not to join the Gunners and admitted he hasn’t been able to replace him.

Jaissle said: “I met Bruno really shortly in the pre-season, but the decision was already made from him to join Arsenal.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“I tried my best at least in the end to convince him, but the decision was made.

“I tried to tell him we counted him on as a leader and to explain the role he would have with us. But again the decision was made.

“He informed me. But it’s my job to do my best anyway, and at least I can look in the mirror and say I tried.

“When those conversations started with Newcastle, of course, that was a key player for us, and I hoped until I arrived that he will stay as I was planning with him.

“But the decision was then finally made when I joined the camp, and we need to deal with that.



“That’s the past. Again, we have now a squad who are capable to do better and we work on that.”

Toon are winless in three matches and Jaissle is running out of time to find answers — even if the questions stem from before his time in charge.

Sports.title: Former Premier League star, 40, appointed as manager of Scottish third tier club six months after retirement
Sports.content:
Next

CONOR SAMMON will kick off his managerial career with a return to Scottish League One side Alloa Athletic.

Sammon, 40, takes the reins at Recreation Park with the side sitting bottom of the third tier.



He told the club website: “I’m really excited at the opportunity to come and manage the team.

“It’s a club that I have such fond memories of as a player – having just retired in May, I didn’t think I’d be back quite as quickly, though I always thought one day it would be something I’d be interested in.



“I’m absolutely delighted and looking forward to getting to work with the group. I know the quality that’s in the dressing room, and I’m excited by the challenge to turn things around.”

Alloa chairman Martin Ross added: “We are delighted to welcome Conor back to Alloa Athletic.

“He brings a wealth of experience, strong understanding and the qualities we believe are needed to take the team forward.

“We look forward to supporting him in the role.”

Former Wigan and Derby striker Sammon is tasked with turning around a dismal run of form that has seen the Wasps lose their sting in a run of five consecutive defeats across all competitions.



They have only managed three league wins so far this campaign, which led to predecessor Andy Graham being given his marching orders.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

A statement released after Graham’s dismissal read: “We fondly remember Andy’s place in Alloa history as a winning club captain and manager and deeply appreciate those achievements.

“However, following discussions between Andy and the board, both parties felt it was right that a fresh approach is needed to give the club the best possible chance of achieving its goals this season.”

Their most recent result came in the form of a 4-1 defeat away at East Kilbride, but a quick impact from Sammon could make a huge difference.

A tightly-congested table sees the Wasps just a point adrift of eighth-placed Peterhead and three behind Cove Rangers in seventh.



His first game in charge is away at Montrose on Saturday.

Sports.title: Bromley sign forgotten Premier League wonderkid, 27, who ‘pocketed Mesut Ozil’ in first transfer since Andy Woodman axe
Sports.content:
Next

BROMLEY have announced the shock signing of Reece Oxford on a free transfer.

The former Premier League starlet made his name at West Ham after an unforgettable debut.



Oxford, 27, made his debut in England’s top flight for the Hammers in 2015 and helped them to a 2-0 win over Arsenal at the Emirates.

Playing as a defensive midfielder, Oxford pocketed German star Mesut Ozil during his 79 minutes on the pitch.



The prospect went on to play just 17 times for West Ham despite his fantastic debut.

He had loan spells at Reading and Borussia Monchengladbach before joining Augsburg in 2018.

He played 77 times in the Bundesliga and scored twice, however he was released by the club in May 2025.

After a year without a club, Oxford began training with the Ravens this season and has now been handed a contract.

He is the first signing at the club following the arrival of new manager Karl Robinson, who replaced Andy Woodman earlier this month.

Oxford said: “The new gaffer came in, hopefully I can help him out now, help the team and we can get some wins.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“I’ve been here for a few weeks now, getting my fitness levels up.

“Everyone has been great. All I can do is give something back to them now.”

Bromley are currently bottom of League One and three points away from safety.

Oxford could make his debut for the club on Saturday against Reading at the Madejski Stadium.

He has been handed the No39 shirt at Bromley.

Sports.title: Swansea appoint FOUR interim managers including Match of the Day pundit, 42, after ‘acknowledging’ Vitor Matos exit
Sports.content:
Next

SWANSEA have finally confirmed that Vitor Matos has left the club.

Strasbourg announced the Portuguese manager had taken over on Wednesday.



Almost 24 hours later, the Swans followed suit with a curt statement.

It devoted just one line to the former boss, which read: “Per RC Strasbourg’s announcement, Swansea City acknowledges that Vitor Matos and his coaching staff have left the club.”



Former captain Ashley Williams will lead a temporary coaching team filled with ex-Swans stars against West Brom on Saturday.

The statement added: “Swansea City can confirm club greats Ashley Williams, Leon Britton, Joe Allen and Kris O’Leary – a quartet boasting over 1,400 appearances in black and white – will be at the helm for Saturday’s game against West Bromwich Albion.



“Additionally, head of academy goalkeeping Paul Whitfield has stepped up to the senior set-up, with the group taking today’s (Thursday) training session at Fairwood.

“The club wants to place on record its thanks to Ashley, Leon, Joe, Kris and Paul for making themselves immediately available without hesitation, and we are grateful to have people with such a great passion for Swansea City guiding us through this period.”

Williams, 42, has been working as a pundit on Match of the Day, while O’Leary and Britton are the only members of Matos’ backroom team to stay put.

Diogo Medeiros, Toze Mendes, Goncalo Ricca and head of goalkeeping Pedro Pereira are set to leave.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Matos had agreed a new deal running through to 2030 and Strasbourg are expected to pay compensation in the region of £5million, per the BBC.

Former Wales and Swansea star David Giles thinks Matos’ departure will upset summer signings.

Speaking on Radio Wales Breakfast, he said: “Swansea have started off this year really brightly and that’s down to the players that he has brought in, that’s the sad thing.

“A lot of the players will feel let down because they probably signed for Swansea City because of Vitor Matos.

“He sold them the dream with the way that he wants to play – it’s really bright, attacking football and they are quick and travel with the ball going forward.”

Beckham, 51, co-founded Studio 99 which created the four-part Netflix documentary about his own life.

Becks, 51, wore the No 7 shirt at Manchester United for six years from 1997, as did Belfast-born Best decades ­earlier during his many years with the Red Devils.

Afterwards Becks paid tribute to him as a “football legend” and “one of the greatest players to have ever graced the game — and a great person”.

Northern Irish-born George became a Manchester United legend after making his debut aged just 17 years old.

Nicknamed the “fifth Beatle” for his rock-star style fame, his off-the-pitch antics later took the light off his record on the pitch.

Los Angeles Rams receiver Puka Nacua has been suspended for three games for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy.

The suspension begins immediately and Nacua will be eligible for reinstatement on December 14, following the Rams' Week 14 game against the San Francisco 49ers.

The All-Pro receiver won't be paid during his suspension but, thanks to the timing of his suspension, won't miss any games because he is currently out due to knee and toe injuries.

Nacua went on injured reserve last week and he is eligible to return from both IR and his suspension when the Rams (6-4) host the Dallas Cowboys on December 20.

The Rams and Nacua have been awaiting his probable suspension for nearly a year. The suspension of Nacua stems from an incident on New Year's Eve in 2025, where he allegedly made an antisemitic remark and bit a woman.

The accuser filed a civil lawsuit on March 25 against Nacua for assault and battery, while Nacua's attorney denied his client made any such statements and described the biting as "horseplay."

Nacua entered a holistic care facility earlier that month, before he was sued, the concluded his time in the rehab facility in time to be part of Los Angeles' off-season program in mid-April.

Sports.title: Drone footage of Pochettino's first Man Utd training session leaked online
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino’s first Manchester United training session today has been leaked online in a major security breach.

The 12-minute drone footage over their Carrington training ground was uploaded onto YouTube.

It shows Pochettino doing various tactical drills with his new team as they prepare for their clash with Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

Liverpool

Manchester United Sunday 22nd November 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

United have signs around the Carrington area warning that use of drones are "strictly prohibited" and anyone caught "will be reported for prosecution and subject to civil action".

Image: A "No Drones" sign is pictured outside Manchester United's Carrington Training complex

The uploaders of the drone footage, CC Overview, claimed to have not breached any laws.

On the video they posted: "For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it, the drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required.

"As for leaking team news/ tactics, it was half an hour into the manager's first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The training today was a closed session and not open to the media.

Manchester United declined to comment when contacted by Sky Sports News.

Analysis: Leaked drone footage 'a significant tactical advantage to Liverpool'

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett:

"This 12-minute video starts off innocuously. We see large numbers of Man Utd players on a separate pitch doing what is known as rondos, those small groups of six or seven players with one or two in the middle trying to intercept the ball. It's the classic pre-training warm-up. That's pretty innocuous. That won't give Liverpool or anyone else much of an insight into what Pochettino's tactical thinking might be for his first game in charge.

"But then on the next pitch, as the drone moves across, it zooms in, and the zoom is quite incredible. You can make out faces and we see Pochettino hands-on, walking them through certain match scenarios. At one stage Pochettino calls all those players in for a huddle and a briefing.

Image: Mauricio Pochettino speaking to players on his first day at training as Man Utd boss

"I'm not going to give you any information about who those players are. But these 11 players Pochettino calls in - 10 outfield players and one goalkeeper. We shouldn't assume this is his starting XI, necessarily.

"Saturday would be the day we'd expect United to do their specific tactics and shape to prepare for the game at Anfield the next day. If this was drone footage of that session it would be even more damaging, even more explosive.

"But the fact it's 11 players separated from the group... it's a very difficult situation for Pochettino and Manchester United.

"I don't think [Pochettino and the players] were aware of it at the time.

"It's questionable whether the person handling the drone has done anything illegal. All around Carrington training ground, they have a large numbers of signs up saying drones are prohibited. But it's clear from these images the drone was not flying directly above United's property. It was to the side of United's property and zoomed in.

"There's absolutely no suggestion Liverpool are involved in this, they are clearly not. But you have to say, it could be advantageous to Liverpool and Andoni Iraola if he's planning his tactics for Sunday's game to look at this and get an idea of how Manchester United might be lining up and what Pochettino might be thinking.

"While it seems as though there are probably no laws that have been broken here, nevertheless it's an awful lot of very specific footage which Manchester United and Pochettino would not want out in the public.

"If you look at the impact of what we're talking about, Man Utd earlier today released some images of the training session and it showed Harry Maguire and Patrick Dorgu among the main training group. Both of those have had injury concerns of late. So those official images told me, Man Utd supporters and Liverpool's tactical preparation experts that Maguire and Dorgu may be in line for possible selection.

"It's gone a stage further now with this leaked drone footage because that has shed even more light on that. It gives a pretty clear picture of who's fit, who's out on the training field, who's involved and who isn't.

"That has to be a significant tactical advantage to Andoni Iraola and Liverpool as they go into this huge game on Sunday."

Sports.title: FIA to introduce full-time F1 stewards
Sports.content:
The FIA has announced it will introduce full-time Formula 1 stewards from 2027 with the aim of having "greater consistency in decision-making".

The use of full-time stewards has been a consistent talking point in F1 as different stewards, who adjudicate all racing and technical matters on a race weekend, are used at each event over the season.

There has been an argument that this can lead to inconsistencies in decision-making when it comes to imposing penalties, or the severity of a penalty.

But the FIA announced on Thursday, ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, they will begin to recruit full-time stewards with a phased introduction from next year with the aim of establishing 12-15 full-time stewards over the coming years.

Currently, there are four stewards drawn from a large FIA pool of officials and one of those is a former racing driver. The new structure will continue to use the knowledge of driver stewards at each event and the FIA say full-time stewards will "allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making".

The news comes a month after the opening of the FIA Remote Operations Centre at Biggin Hill in the UK, following a reorganisation of Race Control in 2022 after the controversial 2021 season which saw Max Verstappen overtake Lewis Hamilton on the last lap of the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Image: The "significant financial turnaround" under FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's has helped create the full-time stewards programme

"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport," said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.

"Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships."

Sports.title: Mardle: The Worlds is now the 'incentive' for Littler
Sports.content:
Sky Sports Darts' Wayne Mardle believes Luke Littler has to use winning the World Darts Championship as his motivation following his Grand Slam of Darts loss; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

The World Darts Championship is now the 'incentive' for Luke Littler after Grand Slam of Darts loss, says Wayne Mardle

Wayne Mardle says he doesn't know how Luke Littler will feel ahead of the World Championship, after crashing out of the Grand Slam of Darts

Luke Littler suffered a shock 10-8 defeat to Jermaine Wattimena at the last 16 stage of the Grand Slam of Darts and Sky Sports Darts' Wayne Mardle believes the world No 1 now has to throw all his energy into being ready for the World Darts Championship.

Littler was attempting to become the third player ever to win the Wolverhampton event three times in a row alongside Phil Taylor and Michael van Gerwen.

However, he came up against an incredible performance from Wattimena, in which he was hitting T20s for fun and averaged over 101.

With Littler also missing the Players Championship, which is the last major before Alexandra Palace in December, the next time we will see Littler on the TV stage is when he plays his opening Worlds match on Friday December 11 as the reigning champion, live on Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the second-round match between Luke Littler and Jermaine Wattimena at the Grand Slam of Darts

Littler went into 2026 targeting a clean sweep of majors and while he won the Premier League, Masters, UK Open, and World Matchplay, his loss in the second round at the World Series Finals to Dirk van Duijvenbode has started a run without a major win.

He has since not defended his World Grand Prix title, Grand Slam title, or clinched the European Championship, which has eluded him.

For Mardle, Littler has to put everything else to one side, use his time away to get fresh, practice, and win the major that just has something a bit different to the rest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Luke Littler is out of the Grand Slam of Darts after being beaten by Jermaine Wattimena in round two

"There is no doubt that every player gets more motivated. The Worlds is different," Mardle said.

"The run-up is different and the build-up to it is gigantic.

"He went basically nine months into the year holding this belief and everyone else thinking he's going to do the clean sweep.

"So it was nine months of all this and then it ends, but the Worlds is out on its own. The incentive is that it is the Worlds. That is all the incentive you need. It is the biggest and it is the best event.

"If he loses in that then he will have gone four months without a major.

"The Worlds is the one, and Michael van Gerwen said this for years: what is the point in winning anything else? You only need to win this one.

"I think that is just the same with Luke's mentality."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Luke Littler sent Sky Sports commentators Wayne Mardle and Dan Dawson wild with his audacious three-bullseye checkout

'You are better winning the Players Championship'

The talk has already turned to whether Littler's time away from the TV spotlight will be a positive or a negative as he attempts to become the second player ever, alongside Taylor, to have won the World Darts Championship three or more times in a row.

Mardle insists that, while it would be better for Littler to be heading into the Worlds as a potential Players Championship winner after his loss at the Grand Slam, if he brings his A-game, it is his to lose.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Incredible scenes in Wolverhampton as Luke Littler appeared to ask his team if he should go for three bullseyes, then duly delivered on the incredible 150 checkout!

"I don't know how he really feels about losing here at the Grand Slam but what I do think going forward, because he's not playing in the Players Championship, so his next outing will be at the Worlds.

"This is the way that I would frame it - would he be better not playing, or would he be better winning the Players Championship? You are better winning the Players Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player John Part and Mark Webster try to recreate Luke Littler's triple bull finish from the Grand Slam of Darts

"But that is the kind of situation that you don't know. You don't know if he goes to the Players Championship, wins it or loses.

"If he loses, it is like maybe he shouldn't have gone to that, in hindsight and everything else.

"I really believe for Luke, if he can turn up fresh, if he can turn up ready, if he can turn up with anywhere near his A-game, he probably wins the Worlds again. That will be three times on the bounce by the age of 20, which is ridiculous."

'It reminds me of trying to beat Taylor'

Wattimena picked up the biggest win of his career against Littler at the Grand Slam but it is not the first time he has come out on top against 'The Nuke' as he beat him in August on the way to winning a Players Championship title.

Wattimena said that win gave him confidence and reinforced that Littler is "not a robot" and Mardle believes that win can be credited for the performance we saw from the Dutchman in the Grand Slam.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player An emotional Jermaine Wattimena gives his reaction to his win over Luke Littler at the Grand Slam of Darts

"I know this is a thing. I was about when Phil Taylor was hardly ever beaten and until you actually beat him, you don't believe you can," he said.

"You see others beat him, there were loads throughout the years. There was Andy Callaby. Adrian Gray beat him. There were others that beat him that were not as good as me.

"I remember thinking why can't I ever beat Phil? It is not until you do that you know that someone's not a robot.

"So that win was massive for Jermaine and it was one of the reasons why he won yesterday.

"Now going forward after yesterday, he can beat anyone on that stage. Luke Humphries has to watch out if he plays Jermaine. Gerwyn Price, they should all watch out now.

"It is really important to have belief. Now he has got it and he has got the ability."

Friday at the Grand Slam of Darts

2x Quarter-Finals

Jermaine Wattimena v Kevin Doets

Gerwyn Price v Niko Springer

The last 15 fixtures played in this slot immediately after an international break have averaged a whopping 3.5 goals per game. All 15 have cleared the over 1.5 goals line, while 11 have produced three or more goals.

There's another layer to this argument, too. The Premier League is currently running below expectation in the goals department. We're seeing 2.73 goals per game despite the underlying expected goals data suggesting that figure should be closer to 2.92.

That's a sizeable gap. And one I'd expect to narrow as the season progresses such is the attacking talent on show.

Bournemouth vs Nottingham Forest, Saturday 3pm

Bournemouth don't get nearly enough credit for just how good they are without the ball. There's a perception that they're all about high-octane pressing, attacking intent and causing chaos. But dig beneath the surface and you'll find one of the most disciplined defensive units in the Premier League.

No team has conceded fewer shots inside their own penalty area this season than Bournemouth's 59, while their expected goals against figure of just 1.13 per 90 is the third-best in the division.

And who's sitting second in that particular metric? Nottingham Forest at 1.10.

So we're dealing with two teams whose defensive foundations are among the strongest in the league. That's usually my cue to start sniffing around the unders market.

Chelsea are 17/20 favourites with Sky Bet, with Leeds available at 29/10 for the away win.

That's a significant gap between two sides who could produce a much tighter contest than those prices suggest.

Leeds have become an awkward opponent to shake off under Daniel Farke. They possess a granite chin, defend their penalty area with determination and are happy to make life uncomfortable for the opposition without much worry about the aesthetics of their performances. The managerial merry-go-round is spinning again. Crystal Palace have jumped aboard, handing Thomas Frank the keys to Selhurst Park. New hope. But a new manager doesn't necessarily mean new results.

In fact, recent evidence suggests quite the opposite for teams in trouble.

The famous 'new manager bounce' is one of football's most romanticised theories. A fresh face walks through the door, standards supposedly rise overnight and points start rolling in.

Shame the numbers don't back it up.

Of the last six Premier League teams sitting in the bottom eight to change manager between November and March, five actually saw their points-per-game average drop across the following five matches.

Vitor Pereira at Nottingham Forest. Igor Tudor at Tottenham. Rob Edwards at Wolves. Graham Potter at West Ham. Ivan Juric at Southampton.

It's a fascinating trend that should serve as a warning to Palace supporters expecting Frank to arrive waving a magic wand, especially with Frank having plenty to prove in that he can operate to the level expected without the comfort blanket of the Brentford structure. The markets still haven't quite cottoned on to what Roberto De Zerbi is cooking up either. The reputation remains one of chaos, risk-taking and goals galore. But the reality? Something very different.

Hall is also the most fouled defender in the Premier League, drawing an average of 2.2 fouls per 90 across his last 12 matches in all competitions. His willingness to carry the ball into dangerous areas and take opponents on makes him a magnet for contact.

One speculative effort and one mistimed challenge from an Arsenal player will do the business.

3h ago 14.00 EST Head-to-head record: As mentioned, this will be the 13th meeting between Arsenal and OL Lyonnes, making it the joint-most-played fixture in WCL history, level with Lyon’s encounters against Wolfsburg. The French giants have historically enjoyed the upper hand, winning eight of the previous 12 meetings, with Arsenal recording three victories and one draw. However, the rivalry has become increasingly competitive in recent seasons, with all three of the Gunners’ wins coming since 2022. The clubs met three times last season, beginning with a league phase encounter at Meadow Park. Despite Alessia Russo opening the scoring after just seven minutes, a Melchie Dumornay double secured a 2-1 victory for Lyon. They were subsequently drawn together in the semi-finals, with Arsenal taking a 2-1 advantage from the first leg thanks to Olivia Smith’s winner. However, Lyon responded in France, claiming a 3-1 victory to progress 4-3 on aggregate. Jule Brand scored in both legs, while Wendie Renard also found the net in the return fixture. Interestingly, Arsenal have won just three of their 17 matches against French opposition, with all three victories coming against Lyon. Meanwhile, the French side’s first-ever defeat on a trip to England came against Arsenal in April, ending an impressive 10-game unbeaten away record. Share

Sports.title: Fifa sparks tension with demand for tax-free status in UK for Women’s World Cup
Sports.content:
Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four football associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the 2035 Women’s World Cup.

The UK bid to host the tournament is due to be ratified at an extraordinary Fifa congress in Zurich on Monday and the Guardian has learned there is tension behind the scenes over many of Fifa’s requirements, which multiple sources involved in the discussions have indicated will not be met.

Fifa is understood to have requested blanket exemptions on tax for all football-related activities for it and its broadcast and commercial partners, as well as its suppliers and staff. It also wants ticket sales – projected to reach 4.5m for the 48-team competition – to be VAT-free and for currency exchange fees to be waived.

Government sources have told the Guardian such blanket exemptions will not be granted for financial reasons and the optics of giving tax breaks to Fifa, which has cash reserves of more than $4bn (£3bn).

Fifa’s governance crisis has also complicated matters, with the prime minister, Andy Burnham, having called on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to resign on multiple occasions, and the FA preparing to endorse France’s Philippe Diallo at March’s presidential election.

Negotiations involving Fifa, the Treasury and the domestic FAs will continue after the UK bid has been ratified. Some carve-outs may be granted but the government is adamant the World Cup will not receive the wholesale tax-free status Fifa is seeking.

An FA spokesperson said: “We provided every guarantee that we can provide under the laws of the country and flagged any deviations transparently. Our approach is also consistent with every major event the UK has hosted or is due to host, including London 2012 and Euro 2028.”

Fifa identified in its evaluation report of the bid the UK’s tax and legal framework as a “medium risk” for the tournament, which would need to be addressed.

Fifa’s tax requirements have proved challenging for many tournament hosts in recent years, including last summer’s men’s World Cup. After months of negotiations with the US Treasury, Fifa succeeded in securing a late exemption from federal taxes for the 48 competing teams, although many were forced to pay state and city tax on their World Cup earnings depending on the location of their matches.

The tax adviser Oriana Morrison, who has worked for many national associations, said: “Fifa will ask for the world but ultimately accept the minimum that enables the tournament to be commercially viable. There are likely to be some difficult conversations ahead as the tournament will not generate anywhere near as much money as the men’s World Cup, so the margins are far tighter.”
