It may also choose to disrupt ship-to-ship transfers of oil, or target Gulf infrastructure or alternative export routes that allow Gulf countries to bypass some Tehran’s restrictions in Hormuz, he said.

Tehran also appears to be lowering the threshold for retaliation. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Tuesday said it targeted American radars in Bahrain following unspecified “US drone violations of Iran’s airspace.” It has also warned Bahrain’s Sunni rulers against mistreatment of the majority Shiite population.

Iran has warned countries against allowing the US to use their territory to attack it. National security chief Rezaei said last week that “all military bases… from Western Asia to Europe, will be legitimate targets.”

“There will be no safe distance or safe haven for aggressors,” he warned, adding that “no base will remain immune.”

This shows that Iran may not only be looking to expand its scope of operations, but is now “signaling that even violations of its airspace could trigger attacks against American assets,” Azizi said.

Others believe there is not much else the Islamic Republic can do that can bring Washington to agree to a deal that works for Iran.

Parsi of the Quincy Institute said that further action by Iran will not make a difference. What could make a change, he said, is the one thing that Iranians are disinclined to do: give Trump a “symbolic” victory that is “ego-soothing and face-saving.”

The Iranians, he said, are more opposed to a symbolic loss than a substantive one, which only adds to the stalemate.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei speaks at a press conference in Tehran on November 15. Xinhua/Shutterstock

Meanwhile, a third US aircraft carrier strike group recently entered US Central Command’s area of responsibility, where it is expected to – at least temporarily – join ongoing operations that include enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and escorting commercial ships willing to transit the strait.

Washington may be misjudging Iran’s breaking point, experts said.

Tehran’s latest operations fit into a “broader shift in Iranian military thinking toward more proactive deterrence,” Azizi said.

“If the leadership concludes that its leverage over Hormuz is weakening while the American blockade continues to impose economic costs, it may decide to go further, potentially even challenging US naval forces more directly,” he said.

This would be considerably riskier, he said “but Iran may see it as necessary to break the blockade rather than allow its position to deteriorate gradually.”

World.title: The Trump team’s messaging problems on tech outages, broken down
World.content:
Two weeks after the GOP’s shellacking in the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is embroiled in a crisis that it has often made worse with its messaging.

A series of tech outages impacting air travel, banks, online communications and even a highly classified network used by the National Security Agency has Americans spooked — and often wondering what’s going on.

And the messaging from the administration has been so confusing — or, in some cases, largely absent — that it’s fed into the growing unease.

It’s gotten to the point where former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt on Tuesday took to pointing out when members of the administration actually get it right, in her estimation.

Former Trump Homeland Security spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin added on X: “Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”

Here’s a look at how some of the main players — including some who could succeed Trump as the GOP presidential standard-bearer — have handled things.

Trump: The man who isn’t there

President Donald Trump is now telling Americans concerned about the tech outages to “relax.”

“Tell them to relax. Everything’s good. These are individual events,” the president told Fox News in an interview in China that aired Wednesday night.

Largely, his problem has been his absence — his lack of any public presence on the issue and his lack of reassurance in a scary time.

He said virtually nothing for two days about Friday’s rare and chaotic full ground stop at the nation’s airports, even as he posted repeatedly on social media about renovation projects like Washington’s public golf course. By Sunday, he posted blaming the Biden administration and asking Congress for more money to modernize the Federal Aviation Administration.

By Monday, he said he didn’t “take any responsibility” for the ground stop. He said he had been working in the Oval Office when it happened but had delegated the messaging to others.

“I didn’t think there was any reason for me to do (it),” Trump told reporters while departing the White House for Asia.

And his comments are making him look increasingly out of touch. Before telling Americans to relax about the tech outages, he effectively shrugged them off.

“It’s life,” Trump said after landing in the Philippines when asked whether he was concerned about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

One of the main lessons of the 2026 election was that voters saw Trump as unconcerned about their priorities. His response to these outages has been a case in point.

Trump has never been good at empathizing. But he doesn’t even seem to be trying.

Perhaps nobody has come in for criticism like Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Even MAGA-aligned conservative commentators have called him “a buffoon” and “unfit for office,” with Megyn Kelly saying she has “zero faith in this man.”

The reason has been a characteristically unsteady stream of messages, compounded with a highly questionable decision to fly to a college football game on Saturday, even as many Americans were still stranded. (Mullin has stressed that he’s required to fly in a government plane because of his job.)

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton speak with each other before the start of a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on November 18. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

Mullin kicked things off Friday amid the ground stop by saying that he didn’t “want to say this is a crisis, but it is.” He then began Friday night’s press conference with a pretty tone-deaf joke about how it was Friday the 13th. (There are few people with less of a sense of humor than the stranded traveler.)

By Monday, he was offering speculation about what was happening with the tech outages based on “one guy that’s very smart with tech” but was “not Elon (Musk).” It was a performance more befitting of a TV pundit than the guy in charge of responding to the crisis.

But Mullin’s biggest optics problem was deciding to go to the Texas-LSU football game on Saturday, which was first reported Tuesday morning by the New York Post. When challenged about that decision Tuesday on CNBC, Mullin noted that the airspace at the time was “completely open” — although many people were still stranded — and said that even as he’s working hard, “we’ve still got to live our life at the same time.”

Talk about tone-deaf.

Mullin kept trying to explain at a congressional hearing Wednesday, telling the House Homeland Security Committee that canceling his travel plans would have looked like “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly.” But that sounds quite different from his initial explanation. And it seems a little too cute by half.

The thing is, to those familiar with Mullin’s TV appearances even before he became DHS secretary, he’s always had this in him. The former Oklahoma senator gets things wrong. He’s often off-message. It’s just that this is the first time it’s been front and center for the American public. And he compounded that with a Ted Cruz-level travel gaffe.

Duffy: A message even Republicans don’t want to hear

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s problem has been his choice of message — basically blaming the ground stop on a lack of FAA modernization funding from Congress.

The first problem is that he previously scoffed at this kind of blame-shifting. As CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski reports, after a 2023 ground stop under the Biden administration, Duffy suggested the problem was leadership rather than funding.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy walks through the US Capitol on his way to attend a Senate GOP luncheon on November 17. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

“They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over Covid,” Duffy said on Fox News at the time. “And now they’re gonna come back and say, ‘We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren’t able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning aircraft couldn’t, couldn’t fly.’”

The second is that while Duffy has been consistently asking for more money, he’s rubbed even Republicans the wrong way with his latest request.

After previously asking for $30 billion more for FAA modernization, he quickly jacked that up to $50 billion — but without saying why. Congressional Republicans have balked both at the implication that they were to blame for what happened Friday and at the idea that they should just shovel money on top of the $12.5 billion that Congress approved in the GOP’s spending and policy bill last year, when that hasn’t all been marked as spent yet.

Clayton: Some rare competence

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has increasingly been dispatched — including at Wednesday’s hearing — in an apparent effort to steady the ship.

During a Fox Business appearance Tuesday and at Wednesday’s hearing, he’s sought to underscore the administration’s conclusion that the tech outages aren’t due to some malign foreign actor.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said at the hearing. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

It was pretty standard stuff from the administration, but it was delivered with the kind of confidence and authority that has been lacking elsewhere.

Leavitt on Tuesday praised the decision to dispatch Clayton — the implication being that he was an improvement on the others.

Rubio: Some rare empathy

Leavitt has also conspicuously praised Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has stepped forward to offer the empathy and concern that Trump hasn’t.

Rubio acknowledged while in the Philippines this week that the outages highlight important questions about “vulnerabilities” in our technology. He also nodded to people being “nervous” and “anxious.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio prepares to speak to the media at the Solaire hotel in Paranaque, Metro Manila, Philippines, on Wednesday. Carlos Barria/Reuters

He added at another point: “We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling, to see these reports, day after day, of some technical failures. … We get it.”

“We take these things very seriously,” Rubio added. “Obviously, we’re always vigilant.”

Again, standard leader stuff. But it underscored the lack of similar comments from Trump.

Vance: Canceling his plans (unlike Trump)

Vice President JD Vance hasn’t said as much as other players, but he did make some pretty big news Wednesday by abruptly canceling his appearance at the New York Times’ DealBook Summit. The stated reason: He was asked to attend meetings in Washington amid the tech outages.

It’s unclear what (or who) specifically prompted the last-minute cancellation. Vance has clearly been trying to craft a brand somewhat independent of Trump. And Wednesday’s was an interesting move, given the president’s lack of public attention to the issue and that fact that some have questioned whether he should have canceled his own plans to travel to Asia.

Vance has also wandered into some trouble, though. After he echoed the party line of blaming the administration’s predecessors for the state of the nation’s air travel system, even Fox News’ Laura Ingraham balked.

“Well, you guys have been in charge the last two years,” Ingraham interjected, adding: “Why hasn’t it gotten fixed?”

The White House press secretary: Still conspicuously nonexistent

The entire episode has also underscored the strange lack of a replacement for Leavitt.

It’s been nearly three months since she left her job in late August. It’s also been almost a month since her initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, was fired after just five days.

These are moments when the administration could really use disciplined messengers fully devoted to briefing the media every day. But apparently they can’t find the right person — and those filling the void have struggled.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: UN top court finds Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against Rohingya minority
World.content:
Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s long-persecuted Rohingya minority, the United Nations’ top court found Thursday, an unprecedented ruling that survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear.

The historic judgement marks the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history — and the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar.

The court’s decision – by nine votes to six – also comes at a time when the broader idea of international justice has come under fire from the Trump administration.

For the Rohingya, the ICJ’s judgment is a “turning point.”

“It is the difference between being told our history was a tragedy, and being told our history was a crime that must be answered for,” said Murshid Alam, who was just 12 years old when he was driven from his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.

Myanmar army members burn Rohingya houses in Mandru, Myanmar, on September 6, 2017. Yousuf Tushar/LightRocket/Getty Images

A Bangladeshi man helps Rohingya Muslim refugees to disembark from a boat on the Bangladeshi shoreline of the Naf river after crossing the border from Myanmar in Teknaf on September 30, 2017. Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images Rohingya women and children wait to get distributed meals at Moynarghona refugee settlement near Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, November 24, 2017. Susana Vera/Reuters

The ICJ’s rulings are final and binding, but the court – which hears disputes between states – doesn’t have the power to enforce its decisions. Its orders, however, are sent to the UN Security Council, which could decide to implement the court’s ruling through a resolution.

Between 2016 and 2017, the military in Buddhist-majority Myanmar targeted villages and towns home to Rohingya communities, looting, burning and slaughtering their inhabitants, and expelling hundreds of thousands from the country.

CNN reporting at the time documented harrowing stories from Rohingya who saw their family members raped or killed by soldiers, and in some case their Buddhist neighbors joining in the massacres. Photos showed streams of terrified people fleeing burning villages on foot or piling into overcrowded boats as they sought to reach neighboring Bangladesh and safety.

This case against Myanmar was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, a country thousands of miles from where the killings took place, in a world-first. The United States and Canada previously declared the atrocities as genocide.

After seven years of weighing evidence and hearing witness testimony, the ICJ found that the scale and nature of Myanmar’s atrocities “went well beyond what would be required to punish the population and are instead characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group,” presiding judge Iwasawa Yuji said during a nearly three-hour reading.

“The court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy” the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.

An aerial view shows the Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on November 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP/Getty Images

In its judgement, the court established the military “engaged in indiscriminate killings” and gave particular weight to the “widespread acts of sexual violence, and extreme acts of violence against children” as well as security forces’ attacks on “Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.”

Myanmar had denied its “clearance operations” were intended to destroy the Rohingya population, and said the military was conducting legitimate counter-terrorism operations against a Rohingya insurgent group. The court rejected that defense, saying the Myanmar military did not distinguish between militants and civilians.

CNN has reached out to Myanmar’s military-backed government for comment on the ruling.

‘The world sees our suffering’

Murshid Alam was a child when he was forced out of his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state by a hail of gunfire. In the chaos of the escape, he was shot in his ear — a “terrifying experience,” he told CNN. The wound has healed, but the “secondary trauma of losing my home and seeing my community destroyed” has not.

Alam was one of more than 740,000 Rohingya people who fled to Bangladesh to escape the massacres. The sprawling refugee camps that he came of age in have since become the world’s largest, hosting more than 1.2 million people.

“Our generation has grown up in displacement. We have known nothing but statelessness,” said Alam, 22, who now works to educate and advocate for young people in the Cox’s Bazar camps as founder of the Rohingya Youth Union.

The genocide ruling, he said, “tells us that the world sees our suffering and refuses to let it be erased.

Dawda Jallow, Minister of Justice of the Republic of Gambia. Phil Nijhuis/AFP/Getty Images

Following The Gambia’s successful application to bring the case, the ICJ allowed South Africa to bring a case against Israel over its war with Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Israel denies the genocide charge.

That has led to concerns among some the court could come into collision with the Trump administration – already on a campaign to “dismantle” another institution, the International Criminal Court. Last month, its UN ambassador Mike Waltz accused the ICJ of trying to lower the threshold for a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case that he claimed could potentially be “weaponized” against American soldiers.

What next for the Rohingya?

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya, including to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence and reunification of families,” and return all property lost or damaged. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure their future protection from discrimination and persecution.

It is unlikely Myanmar will adhere. The head of the Myanmar military during the massacres, Min Aung Hlaing is now the country’s leader after he overthrew the elected government – and has dismissed the Rohingya identity as “imaginary.” His military-backed government has shown little interest in allowing Rohingya to return.

Mohammed Shoaib, 7, who was shot on his chest before crossing the border from Myanmar in August, shows his injury outside a medical centre after seeing a doctor, at Kutupalong refugee camp near Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh November 5, 2017. Adnan Abidi/Reuters Armed Myanmar soldiers patrol a village in Maungdaw located in Rakhine State as security operation continue following attacks by armed militant Muslims in October 2016. AFP/Getty Images

What they would return to is another question. In the Rohingya homeland of Rakhine state, the military-backed government is not in control. An ethnic armed group called the Arakan Army controls the vast majority of the state, including areas that border Bangladesh, and has been accused of widespread abuses against civilians in its areas.

Meanwhile, the military has ramped up airstrikes across the state as part of its grinding civil war, dropping bombs on civilian markets and hospitals, in response to territorial losses.

Rohingya now living in the camps cannot work and face dire conditions, including trafficking, exploitation, meagre food rations, and a lack of basic education.

Alam, in the Bangladesh refugee camp, hoped the ruling could pave the way for a return to the home he fled as a young boy.

“The Rohingya do not want to live in refugee camps forever. We want to return to our homeland in Rakhine state with our rights, our citizenship, and our dignity fully restored,” he said.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: Mortada Mansour referred to trial over defamation of actress Elham Shahin
World.content:
The Public Prosecution on Wednesday ordered the referral of lawyer and former club president Mortada Mansour to the Economic Court to stand trial on charges of insulting and defaming veteran actress Elham Shahin.

The court has scheduled the opening hearing for December 3.

The prosecution’s decision follows a formal criminal complaint filed by Shahin against Mansour in his capacity as the owner and administrator of his verified official Facebook page.

The move runs parallel to a separate regulatory complaint lodged with the Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), chaired by Khaled Abdel Aziz.

Shahin petition’s requested that the media council’s findings be formally forwarded to the Public Prosecutor’s Office and merged with her original criminal complaint, as both address the same alleged offenses.

She implored the authorities to take immediate steps to suspend and block the Facebook account in question.

Upon receiving Shahin’s complaint, the Supreme Council for Media Regulation referred the matter to its Complaints Committee—headed by media executive and council deputy chair Essam al-Amir—to initiate appropriate legal proceedings in accordance with Egyptian media law.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Honoring Anwar Sadat: The weight of a historic medal and a lesson in loyalty
World.content:
The US Congressional Gold Medal derives its prestige from the institution that bestows it, the legislative journey required to earn it, and the enduring place it secures in public memory.

In honoring President Anwar Sadat with this distinction, Washington acknowledges that a decision made by an Egyptian leader continues to shape regional security and diplomacy decades after his passing. Behind this milestone lies a sustained effort by advocates who believed Sadat deserved this recognition and worked tirelessly to realize it.

As Congress’s highest expression of national appreciation for distinguished achievements and contributions, the medal traces its lineage back to George Washington in 1776 and has since honored figures such as Winston Churchill and Nelson Mandela. Every award requires its own dedicated act of legislation—a process that imbues the honor with an institutional weight extending far beyond the ceremony itself.

In Sadat’s case, the bill authorizing the medal was signed into law on December 13, 2018, following a bipartisan effort supported by both Republicans and Democrats.

The legislation mandated a posthumous award in recognition of his historic achievements and courageous contributions to Middle East peace.

The significance of that framing warrants close reading.

The law explicitly links the Camp David Accords and the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty to regional stability, partnership, dialogue, and American strategic interests—reflecting Washington’s stated reading of Sadat’s legacy.

From an Egyptian perspective, however, this moment also recalls the nation’s ability to translate military triumph into a diplomatic path that reclaimed sovereign land, and the courage to make a pivotal choice that profoundly reshaped the country’s future.

This honor affords us a valuable opportunity to tell our own story on our own terms: how did Sadat arrive at his decision? What did he set out to achieve? How did he balance military strength with diplomacy? And what did Egypt ultimately gain? These are the essential questions that must remain front and center whenever we present his legacy to the world.

In this regard, Mohamed Shafik Gabr merits clear recognition and appreciation.

Anyone who knows him is well aware of the high esteem in which he holds Sadat—a reverence he channeled into a concrete mission, shouldering much of the effort to champion the medal initiative and build momentum behind it.

Serving as International Chairman of the Medal Committee, Gabr helped organize a November 2018 reception on Capitol Hill in the US Senate to rally support for the legislation, bringing together prominent American and Egyptian figures.

Undertaking such an endeavor demands deep institutional fluency, sustained engagement, and the ability to unite supporters across diverse political lines.

Throughout this campaign, Gabr stood as one of its driving forces, working in concert with American partners and bipartisan lawmakers.

His persistence and loyalty deserve to be recorded as an integral chapter in the story of this tribute.

His role carries a broader lesson worthy of reflection in our public life: what becomes possible when an Egyptian leverages his network and experience in service of his nation’s memory and standing, pursuing a public goal over the course of years until it becomes reality.

Egypt’s global influence expands not only through statecraft, but also through the initiatives of its citizens and their capacity to forge alliances around causes they believe in.

With Sadat himself, honoring his memory leaves ample room for candid debate over his presidency.

One can disagree with certain choices he made while simultaneously acknowledging his courage and the magnitude of his impact.

Ultimately, this tribute celebrates an Egyptian president who altered the course of history, while the campaign that brought it to fruition offers a lesson in loyalty and perseverance. And much of the credit belongs to Shafik Gabr, whose devotion found lasting expression in a milestone that will endure.

World.title: Photos: US Congress bestows highest honor on Anwar Sadat’s timeless legacy
World.content:
The US Congress posthumously bestowed the Congressional Gold Medal upon late Egyptian President Mohamed Anwar Sadat during an official ceremony at the US Capitol in Washington on Wednesday, in recognition of his historic role towards forging peace in the Middle East.

Attended by senior American and Egyptian officials, diplomats, and political and media figures, the tribute drew reflections from Sadat’s son Gamal Sadat, current Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, and Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty.

Gamal Sadat: Peace remains my father’s enduring legacy

Accepting the medal on his late father’s behalf, Sadat emphasized that peace stands as Anwar Sadat’s defining legacy.

He added that President Sisi continues to play a pivotal mediating role in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, guided by the conviction that living together in peace far outweighs the human toll of endless war.

Hailing the ceremony as a deeply meaningful milestone for the Sadat family, Gamal remarked, “If my father were here with us today, he would truly feel the profound value of this honor.”

He portrayed his father as a modest man who wielded presidential authority to improve the lives of his citizens and advance regional stability, backed by the resolve needed to see those goals through.

Gamal also paid tribute to his late mother, Jehan Sadat, noting her steadfast support throughout his father’s peace initiative despite knowing the personal peril his bold decisions carried.

“Together, they shared a deep love and mutual respect for one another and for their country,” he said, adding that his parents instilled that same patriotism and devotion in him and his sister.

Recalling the pivotal events of 1977, Gamal cited his father’s pledge before the world to alter the course of history—telling the Egyptian people he would travel to the ends of the earth, even to the Israeli Knesset, in pursuit of peace, where ten days later he famously declared, “No more war.”

Forty-seven years on and that peace endures, Gamal said, expressing his pride that President Sisi continues to champion those very principles amid ongoing conflicts across Africa and the Middle East.

President Sisi: A timeless model of political courage

In a statement shared on his official Facebook page on Wednesday evening, President Sisi expressed his profound appreciation to the US Congress for honoring the late president.

He described the award as a tribute to Sadat’s historical legacy and his ability to achieve peace through political will and decisive courage.

President Sisi stated that this distinction reflects international recognition of the vital role peace plays in averting conflict and fostering stability.

He referred to Sadat’s historic journey as a model of visionary leadership capable of making watershed decisions for the region.

Underscoring the urgency of reviving the spirit of peace amid delicate regional circumstances whose repercussions reverberate globally, Sisi stressed called for prioritizing dialogue, preventing further escalation, and securing a more stable future.

Peace, he affirmed, remains essential to safeguarding nations, protecting their resources, and unlocking new horizons for development—a goal demanding concerted international effort and steadfast political resolve.

Foreign Minister Abdelatty: Peacemaking as the highest form of leadership

Representing President Sisi at the Capitol ceremony, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty delivered an address affirming that honoring Anwar Sadat reflects global recognition that the courage to make peace is the highest form of political leadership.

Abdelatty traced the defining milestones of Sadat’s diplomatic trajectory—from his November 1975 address before the US Congress and his historic 1977 visit to Jerusalem, to the 1978 Camp David Accords and the 1979 Egyptian-Israeli Peace Treaty, which restored Egypt’s full sovereignty over the Sinai Peninsula.

He noted how Sadat bequeathed a lasting legacy carried forward by successive generations in the ongoing pursuit of regional stability.

The foreign minister underscored that the nearly half-century strategic partnership between Egypt and the US has been anchored in diplomacy, mutual respect, and a shared commitment to peace.

Calling Gaza a defining test for the world, Minister Abdelatty stressed that cementing the ceasefire, delivering aid, and rebuilding the enclave must lead to a two-state solution along the 1967 borders with no Palestinian displacement.

He concluded by thanking the US Congress and reaffirming that under President Sisi— who hosted the 2025 Sharm El-Sheikh Peace Summit—Egypt remains a trusted mediator committed to peace as a strategic choice.

World.title: Cairo’s Qasr El Nil Bridge to close for 15 hours on Friday for maintenance
World.content:
The Cairo General Traffic Department will implement traffic diversions across the Qasr El Nil Bridge on Friday to complete maintenance work on the structure’s metallic expansion joints.

The operation will require a full closure of the bridge’s westbound carriageway—affecting traffic approaching from Tahrir Square—for the duration of the repairs.

Work will be scheduled to run for 15 hours — from 12:05 am until three pm — with the westbound lanes set to reopen fully to vehicular traffic immediately upon completion.

Alternative routes and traffic diversions

Under the traffic management plan, authorities will close the Tahrir Street approach leading onto the Qasr El Nil Bridge from Tahrir Square.

Motorists will be diverted around Tahrir Square onto Meret Basha Street, continuing to Abdel Moneim Riad Square to access the 6th of October Bridge ramp toward Giza, before exiting onto El Gezira Street.

Additionally, the on-ramp leading to the Qasr El Nil Bridge from the Kamal El-Din Salah Tunnel will be closed.

Traffic will instead be rerouted along the Nile Corniche toward Abdel Moneim Riad Square, connecting to the 6th of October Bridge toward Giza and exiting through the El Gezira Street off-ramp.

The Cairo General Traffic Department will deploy additional officers throughout the area in coordination with the executing contractors, while installing clear signage and safety barriers to alert motorists to the ongoing roadwork.

This aims to prevent congestion and maintain smooth traffic flow.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Ministry of Justice In Contempt Trouble, As Court Summons AG Betty Lamin-Blamo Over Defiance Of Release Order
World.content:
IB Atlantic, Seven Crew Member Still Held In Custody

Judge Banwon orders Justice Minister to appear Friday to explain why she should not be held in contempt after vessel and crew remain detained beyond court-imposed deadline; continued detention raises fresh questions about government’s respect for judicial authority.

By Willie N. Tokpah



Monrovia-The Ministry of Justice’s failure to obey a court order directing the release of the mysterious vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has escalated into a direct confrontation with the judiciary, with Criminal Court ‘A’ summoning Justice Minister and Attorney-General Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo to answer allegations of contempt.

In an escalation of the unfolding maritime controversy, Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon has issued a writ of summons commanding Lamin-Blamo to appear before Criminal Court ‘A’ at the Temple of Justice on Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.

The court wants the Attorney-General to show cause why she should not be held in contempt for allegedly disobeying its order directing the release of the IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members.

As of Thursday, November 19, when the writ of summons was issued, both the vessel and its seven crew members remained in state custody. Their detention continued despite the expiration of the court-imposed deadline of 4:00 p.m. Wednesday, November 18.



The development has placed the country’s chief legal officer directly before a judicial proceeding over the government’s alleged failure to comply with a court order, raising serious questions about the Ministry’s obligation to respect judicial authority.

The summons, dated November 19 and issued under the authority of the First Judicial Circuit, Montserrado County, marks an escalation in a case that has dragged on for nearly three months without a comprehensive public explanation of the vessel’s activities or the legal grounds for its prolonged detention.

AG Summoned To Answer

The writ is explicit about the reason for the summons.

It commands the Minister of Justice and Attorney-General to appear before the court and explain why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the order directing the release of the vessel and its seven crew members.

The summons were issued by the Assistant Clerk of Court Gideon A. Eshun and directed to the Montserrado County Sheriff, H. C. Sulonich, or his deputy, for service.

The court further instructed the sheriff to make an official return to the Clerk’s Office, stating the manner and form in which the summons were served.

Although the issuance of the writ does not constitute a final finding of contempt, it represents a serious judicial step requiring the government’s chief legal officer to account for the Ministry’s alleged failure to comply with the court’s directive.

The summons also raised an important institutional question on whether government authorities can continue holding individuals and property in state custody after a court has ordered their release without obtaining further judicial authorization.

Ministry Still Holds Vessel and Crew

The latest development follows the Ministry’s failure to meet Wednesday’s 4:00 p.m. deadline.

Judge Banwon had ordered the release of the IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members following a habeas corpus petition challenging their continued detention.

But by approximately 5:00 p.m. Wednesday and up to the time of the summon, FrontPageAfrica observed that the court’s directive had not been implemented.

The seven crew members remained detained, while lawyers representing them confirmed that their clients had not been released.

Judge Banwon was also observed leaving the court premises at approximately 4:00 p.m., around the time the deadline expired, with the vessel and its crew still under state custody.

More troubling, the situation had not changed by Thursday, November 19, when the court issued the contempt summons.

The vessel and all seven crew members were still being held, notwithstanding the court’s directive.

The continued detention suggests that the Ministry had not acted on the release order even after the deadline had passed, leaving the court to take the additional step of summoning the Attorney-General.

When contacted late Wednesday evening to establish whether the release had been effected and to explain the apparent delay, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah declined to provide a substantive explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPageAfrica.

His response left unanswered the central question confronting the Ministry, on what legal basis were the vessel and its crew still being detained after the court-imposed deadline had expired.

Government Struggle To Explain Detention

Sources within the Ministry of Justice, who spoke to FrontPageAfrica on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly, previously disclosed that the Ministry was struggling to formulate an explanation for the continued detention.

According to the sources, the difficulty was linked to the government’s earlier public statements that investigations were being conducted into the vessel’s movements and the circumstances surrounding its interception.

The sources indicated that authorities were under pressure to explain why the vessel and its crew remained in custody despite the court’s directive and the absence of publicly disclosed investigative findings establishing grounds for their continued detention.

They further disclosed that the Ministry was contemplating releasing the vessel and its crew early Thursday morning, November 19, in an effort to comply with the court’s order.

However, as of Thursday, November 19, when the contempt summons was issued, that anticipated release had not taken place.

The continued detention now placed the Ministry in a difficult legal position, with its head expected to explain before the court why the order was not obeyed within the time prescribed.

The Ministry’s position, including any legal justification for the continued detention, remains important and should be presented before the court.

The IB Atlantic IV first attracted attention in August after its unusual presence off York Island in Grand Cape Mount County raised concerns among residents and security authorities.

The Comoros-flagged vessel reportedly remained within Liberian coastal waters before moving farther offshore, prompting a pursuit by Liberian security forces, including the Armed Forces of Liberia Coast Guard.

On August 4, then Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Major General Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were pursuing the vessel.

The ship reportedly evaded the initial pursuit before being intercepted by Ivorian authorities on August 9.

Its interception in Côte d’Ivoire transformed the incident into a cross-border maritime security matter, raising questions about how the vessel had moved from Liberian waters into the custody of a neighboring country.

On August 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah confirmed that the vessel had been arrested by Ivorian authorities and disclosed that the Liberian Government was engaging its Ivorian counterpart to facilitate its return.

The government also disclosed that a Liberian fishing vessel had reportedly gone out to sea to meet the IB Atlantic IV, prompting the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority to investigate the circumstances surrounding the encounter.

Questions subsequently emerged about the vessel’s cargo, movements, possible activities, and the circumstances surrounding its initial presence along Liberia’s coastline.

Although allegations and speculation about possible contraband circulated during the incident, no publicly established findings have confirmed those allegations.

Following diplomatic and security engagements between Monrovia and Abidjan, the vessel was returned to Liberia in late August, reportedly arriving on August 27 under the command of the Liberian Coast Guard.

Its return was expected to provide Liberian authorities an opportunity to conduct a comprehensive investigation and publicly account for the circumstances surrounding its interception.

Instead, the vessel and its seven crew members remained under state custody, with no comprehensive public account of the investigation’s findings.

The prolonged detention eventually prompted the vessel’s management and the seven crew members to seek judicial intervention through a habeas corpus petition.

The petition challenged the legality of their continued confinement and resulted in Judge Banwon’s order directing their release by Wednesday afternoon.

The Ministry’s failure to meet that deadline, followed by the continued detention of the vessel and crew on Thursday, has now triggered the issuance of a contempt summons against the Attorney-General.

For the seven crew members, the case represents months of uncertainty and detention aboard a vessel whose presence in Liberian waters has remained shrouded in unanswered questions.

The Attorney-General will have an opportunity to explain the Ministry’s position and show cause why contempt proceedings should not proceed.

The country’s chief legal officer has now been summoned to answer before that same court.

The IB Atlantic IV controversy has therefore entered a new phase, one in which the government is not only being asked to explain a mysterious vessel, but also to account for its continued detention of the ship and its crew after a judicial order for their release.

All eyes are now on the Temple of Justice on Friday, November 20, when Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo is expected to appear before Criminal Court ‘A’ and answer the court’s summons.

World.title: Liberia: 23 Years After the Guns Fell Silent, Opposition Arrests and Prosecutions Test Liberia’s Post-War Bargain
World.content:
Monrovia – In 2003, a group of Liberian women nearly gave up on the peace talks in Accra because they had no money. Leymah Gbowee told a gathering in Monrovia this week that a US$10,000 grant from the African Women’s Development Fund kept them going. To women who had buried husbands, sons and neighbors, she said, it felt like a million dollars.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The war they were trying to end had reached every corner of the country. There was “not a single home in this country that had not been touched by the war,” Gbowee recalled. An estimated 250,000 Liberians died between 1989 and 2003.



Also speaking at Monday’s gathering was former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, who led the country out of those ashes. Sirleaf, who turned 88 last month, delivered a warning. Twenty-three years of unbroken peace, she said, could be undone if Liberia’s leaders fail to build unity, inclusion and equal opportunity.

She did not name President Joseph Boakai or any case. But her words land at a tense moment. A former House speaker faces a retrial over the burning of the Capitol. A former vice president sits in Monrovia Central Prison awaiting a drug trial. And the main opposition party says the justice system has been turned into a weapon against it. Critics fear the government’s approach, whatever its legal merits, could chip away at the fragile consensus that has held Liberia together since 2003.

“Peace is not enough”

Sirleaf spoke at the West African Women Peacebuilding Convening, hosted by the Gbowee Peace Foundation Africa. Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti was also on the program.



She traced Liberia’s unraveling to the April 1980 coup that toppled President William R. Tolbert, Jr. From there, she said, the country lost not only its peace but almost everything it had built. She urged Liberians to celebrate 23 years without war, then warned that peace alone was not enough. It had to be matched by unity, inclusion and equal opportunity, and those in power, she said, should beware.

She also told the women in the room that their work was unfinished. “Women brought the peace, now women must help keep the peace,” she said.

Coded as it was, the message was not hard to read in Monrovia. Exclusion, a sense that the state belonged to one group, was a thread that ran through the grievances of 1980 and the wars that followed.

A warning from someone who knows the cost

Few Liberians are better placed to issue such a warning, and few carry more of the history it touches. Sirleaf took office in January 2006, little more than two years after the Accra peace agreement ended 14 years of civil war. She inherited a country with no electricity grid, gutted ministries, disarmed but restless ex-fighters and roughly 15,000 UN peacekeepers on the ground.

Over 12 years, she oversaw two elections, debt relief, the UN mission’s drawdown and, in 2018, the first peaceful transfer of power from one elected Liberian president to another in decades. The 2011 Nobel Peace Prize she shared with Gbowee recognized that work.

Her record is not without question marks.

In 2009, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission recommended that she be barred from public office for her early support of Charles Taylor, a recommendation the Supreme Court later held unconstitutional. Critics also accused her government of nepotism and of letting corruption take root.

But on the narrow point she raised this week, her experience is hard to dismiss. Her government kept rivals inside the tent, including some who had fought on opposite sides of the war. The peace she managed was built on the idea that no group should feel it had been pushed outside the system.

The cases

The former speaker. J. Fonati Koffa was Speaker of the House when a fire tore through the Capitol Building’s joint chambers on December 18, 2024, at the height of a bitter fight over his removal. In 2025, a special grand jury handed down a 63-count indictment against him and 13 others, including sitting lawmakers, on charges ranging from arson to attempted murder.

FrontPageAfrica’s own reading of that indictment found no direct evidence tying Koffa to the planning or execution of the fire, only hearsay and links through his staff. Koffa resigned the speakership in May 2025. On January 2, 2026, the trial judge dissolved the jury, citing alleged juror misconduct. In August, the Supreme Court rejected Koffa’s petition and cleared the way for a retrial. Nearly two years after the fire, he still has no verdict.

The former vice president. On August 19, Jewel Howard-Taylor was on her way to catch a flight to Accra, where she was due to give a keynote speech, when authorities stopped her at Roberts International Airport. Prosecutors charged her with drug trafficking and money laundering tied to the cocaine network behind Liberia’s largest drug busts. They allege she accepted payments and met members of the network in Dubai. She denies the charges.

On September 24, Criminal Court “C” denied her bail. The 63-year-old former senator, who lost her son Philip in January, has been held at Monrovia Central Prison since. Reports say the leaders of Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire and Rwanda privately questioned the circumstances of her arrest. Former President George Weah has called her detention political persecution.

The others. Former Finance Minister Samuel Tweah was acquitted by a jury in May in a US$6.2 million corruption case. Last week, former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and others were sentenced to 10 years over Saudi-donated rice. In August 2025, police helped carry out a court-ordered eviction that ended with the demolition of the CDC’s Congo Town headquarters. And Weah himself now faces unconfirmed talk of being called in for questioning, which the government has dismissed.

The government’s case

The Boakai administration rejects the charge of persecution. Officials argue that a government elected on a promise to fight corruption and impunity cannot exempt people because they belong to the opposition. The Unity Party has pointed to the drug crackdown as proof that the law is being applied evenly.

Boakai made the point bluntly after the CDC headquarters was torn down. “The law is the law,” he told reporters, insisting the police were enforcing a court ruling, not a political decision.

The record is not one-sided. Juries have acquitted as well as convicted. Tweah walked free, and two defendants in the rice case were sent for retrial after jurors could not agree.

Kemayah’s conviction came after a full trial, and he keeps his right to appeal. The cocaine seizures were real, and the pressure on Liberia to confront trafficking is coming from its own citizens and its foreign partners alike.

The opposition, for its part, has not always backed its claims of selective prosecution with evidence. But perception matters in a country where the line between political defeat and personal danger was once very thin.

Why critics fear for the peace

The worry is less about any single case than about the pattern, and about what it tells the losers of Liberia’s elections. Since 2003, the country’s peace has rested on an unwritten bargain: you can lose power without losing your freedom, your property or your life.

The CDC says it kept its side of that bargain. Its leaders like to point out that the party conceded the 2023 election when Weah lost by a razor-thin margin. “We conceded the election peacefully with a margin of just 17,000 votes,” Janga Kowo, then the party’s secretary-general, told supporters in June 2025, warning that the government had crossed a red line. When the party’s headquarters came down, Weah urged supporters not to take the law into their own hands. That restraint has held. The fear is that it will not hold forever.

There is also a double standard that many Liberians notice. The government moves quickly against today’s opponents, but justice for the war’s victims keeps slipping. The TRC recommended a war crimes court in 2009. Boakai has backed one, but lawmakers will not take up the bill until January 2027, and the proposed US$1.2 billion national budget sets aside no money for it. Many of the men accused of atrocities in the TRC report have died without facing a judge.

For families who lost a father at a checkpoint or a daughter in a massacre, that contrast is hard to accept. Accountability that reaches the current opposition but not the warlords can look less like justice and more like politics.

What is at stake

Liberia heads toward the 2029 elections with its peace intact but its politics raw. How the courts handle Koffa’s retrial and Howard-Taylor’s case will shape whether Liberians see a government cleaning house or settling scores.

The test implied by Sirleaf’s warning is simple to state and hard to meet. Prosecutions must be swift, transparent and visibly evenhanded. They must reach allies as readily as rivals, and they must sit alongside a real reckoning with the war, not in place of one.

Gbowee’s generation of women prayed outside the negotiating rooms in Accra until the men inside signed. The peace they won has now outlasted the war that came before it. Whether it outlasts this moment depends on whether every Liberian, in power or out of it, still believes there is a place for them inside the system.

World.title: Liberia: Justice Ministry Defies Court Order to Release IB Atlantic IV, Seven Crew Members
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Ministry of Justice has failed to comply with a court order directing the release of the mysterious vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members by 4:00 p.m. Wednesday, November 18, raising fresh questions about the government’s continued detention of the vessel and its crew despite judicial intervention.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon of Criminal Court ‘A’ for Montserrado County had ordered the Ministry of Justice to release the vessel and its crew by the stipulated deadline following a habeas corpus petition challenging their continued detention.



However, as of approximately 5:00 p.m. Wednesday, FrontPage Africa observed that the court’s order had not been carried out.

The seven crew members remained detained aboard the vessel, while lawyers representing them confirmed that their clients had not been released.

Judge Banwon was also observed leaving the court premises at approximately 4:00 p.m., around the time the deadline expired, with the vessel and its crew still under state custody.

The apparent failure to comply with the order has raised questions about the Ministry’s handling of the case and the legal basis for the continued detention of the vessel and its crew.



When contacted late Wednesday evening to confirm whether the vessel and its crew had been released and, if not, to explain the delay, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah declined to provide an explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPage Africa.

Ministry Struggles To Explain Continued Detention

Sources within the Ministry of Justice, who spoke to FrontPage Africa on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly, disclosed that the Ministry was still struggling to formulate an explanation for the continued detention of the vessel and its crew.

According to the sources, the difficulty stems from the fact that the public had previously been informed that an investigation was underway into the vessel’s movements and the circumstances surrounding its interception.

The sources said authorities were facing pressure to explain why the vessel and its crew remained detained despite the court’s directive and the absence of publicly disclosed investigative findings establishing grounds for their continued custody.

They further indicated that the Ministry was contemplating releasing the crew members and vessel early Thursday morning, November 19, in an apparent effort to comply with the court’s order, although the Wednesday deadline had already passed.

Such a move, if carried out, would come after the government had missed the deadline established by the court.

As of Wednesday evening, however, no official confirmation had been issued that the release had taken place.

Nearly Three Months In Custody

The detention of the IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has become one of Liberia’s most unusual maritime security cases, beginning with the vessel’s unexplained presence off York Island in Grand Cape Mount County in August.

The Comoros-flagged vessel initially attracted attention after lingering in Liberian coastal waters, prompting concerns among residents and security authorities about its presence, movements and possible activities.

The situation escalated when Liberian security forces, including the Armed Forces of Liberia Coast Guard, reportedly attempted to intercept the vessel as it moved farther offshore toward Rivercess County.

On August 4, then Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Major General Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were pursuing the vessel.

The ship reportedly evaded the initial Liberian pursuit before being intercepted by Ivorian authorities on August 9, transforming the incident into a cross-border maritime security matter.

Its interception in Côte d’Ivoire raised additional questions about how the vessel had moved from Liberia’s coastal waters into the custody of a neighboring country and what authorities had discovered during the operation.

Liberia’s Investigation And The Vessel’s Return

On August 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah publicly confirmed that the vessel had been arrested by Ivorian authorities and disclosed that the Liberian Government was engaging its Ivorian counterpart to facilitate its return.

The government also disclosed that a Liberian fishing vessel had reportedly gone out to sea to meet the IB Atlantic IV, prompting the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority to investigate the circumstances surrounding the encounter.

The development widened the scope of the investigation, placing additional focus on the relationship between the foreign vessel and the Liberian fishing boat.

Questions also emerged over the vessel’s cargo, movements, initial presence off York Island and whether any prohibited materials or other suspicious items had been discovered.

Although allegations and speculation about possible contraband circulated during the incident, no publicly established findings have confirmed those allegations.

Following diplomatic and security engagements between Monrovia and Abidjan, the vessel was eventually returned to Liberia in late August, reportedly arriving on August 27 under the command of the Liberian Coast Guard.

Its return was expected to provide Liberian authorities an opportunity to conduct further investigations into its activities and the circumstances surrounding its interception.

Instead, the vessel and its seven crew members remained under security control, with no comprehensive public account of the investigation’s findings.

Court Intervention

The continued detention eventually prompted the vessel’s management and the seven crew members to seek judicial intervention through a habeas corpus petition challenging the legality of their confinement.

Judge Banwon’s order directing their release by 4:00 p.m. Wednesday represented a significant judicial intervention, placing the Ministry of Justice under a clear deadline to act.

The failure to release them by the stipulated time has brought renewed attention to compliance with judicial orders and the constitutional protections afforded to persons held by state authorities.

For the crew members, the ordeal has meant weeks of detention aboard a vessel whose movements have attracted national and regional attention.

For the government, the case presents an increasingly difficult challenge: explaining the circumstances that led to the vessel’s pursuit, its interception in Côte d’Ivoire, its return to Liberia, the prolonged detention of its crew and the apparent failure to comply with a court order directing their release.

As Wednesday night approached, the IB Atlantic IV remained in custody, its seven crew members were still detained, and the public continued to await answers to a maritime mystery that began off Liberia’s coastline and has now become a test of compliance with judicial authority.

World.title: Liberia’s First Foreign Policy:A Feminist Bet in a Retreating World
World.content:
Monrovia – For 179 years, Liberia conducted its foreign relations without a written foreign policy. On Tuesday, November 17, that changed. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched what it calls the first foreign policy document in the nation’s history, and with it a Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy that the government bills as Africa’s first.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The launch drew foreign ministers, Nobel Laureate Leymah Gbowee and leading figures of Africa’s women’s movement to Monrovia. It gives Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti a signature achievement weeks before Liberia takes the presidency of the United Nations Security Council.



But a close reading of the government’s own announcement raises questions the ceremony did not answer. Who pays for it? How will success be measured? Can it survive a change of government? And how does a policy built around protecting rights square with some of the deals Monrovia has already struck abroad?

From presidential statements to a written policy

Since independence in 1847, Liberia’s foreign policy has lived in the speeches of its presidents rather than in a document. According to the Foreign Ministry, the last update came in 1971, when William R. Tolbert, Jr. restated the country’s foreign policy after succeeding William V. S. Tubman.

Much has changed since Tolbert. The Organization of African Unity became the African Union. ECOWAS and the Mano River Union took on larger roles.



Liberia went through civil war, peacebuilding and democratic consolidation, and is now an elected member of the UN Security Council for 2026–2027.

A written policy is a genuine step. It gives diplomats, investors and partners something to hold the government to. The ministry says the drafting was led by seasoned diplomats, including former ministry officials, with input from ambassadors and missions abroad.

One detail stands out. Cabinet endorsed the policy on May 28, 2026, almost six months before Tuesday’s launch. The ministry has not explained the delay, and the press release does not say where the public can read the full document.

Is it really Africa’s first?

The government’s headline claim needs a qualifier. In 2021, Libya’s then Foreign Minister Najla Mangoush announced at the Generation Equality Forum in Paris that Libya was committing to a feminist foreign policy. At the time, gender-policy trackers recorded Libya as the first African nation to do so.

Libya’s commitment, however, never became a working policy. Analysts noted that its transitional Government of National Unity could not implement it alone, and Mangoush was dismissed in 2023.

Liberian officials have themselves used more careful language in the past. When it validated its feminist foreign policy roadmap, the ministry described Liberia as the first country in Africa to formally commit to a feminist foreign policy, following a government decision in February 2024. The defensible claim is narrower than the headline: Liberia is the first African country to formally adopt and launch a written gender-responsive foreign policy.

Joining a club that is shrinking

Liberia is adopting a feminist foreign policy just as several of its pioneers walk away from it. Sweden coined the concept in 2014 and dropped it in 2022 after a change of government. The Netherlands, Argentina and Germany have since followed, making Germany the fourth country to introduce such a policy and then abandon it.

The pattern is consistent: the policies were tied to a party or a minister, and they did not outlive them. A November 2025 report on the field asked openly whether feminist foreign policy was facing its obituary. Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Spain remain among the active adopters.

The lesson for Liberia is direct. The policy carries the stamp of President Joseph Boakai and Minister Nyanti. Unless it is written into law, funded in the national budget and built into the Foreign Service, it could be shelved by whoever wins the 2029 election.

What the policy promises

The broader foreign policy rests on six priorities: economic diplomacy, national sovereignty, regional integration, peace and security, citizen protection and international cooperation.

The gender-responsive component, which dominates the government’s announcement, has five pillars:

* Women’s rights

* Women’s economic empowerment and inclusive trade

* Women, peace and security

* Climate justice and natural resource governance

* Women’s political representation and leadership

The ministry says the policy grew out of a review that found gaps between Liberia’s gender-equality commitments and the actual presence of women in foreign policy and diplomatic leadership. The Ministry of Gender validated it, and UN Women supported the process, which has run through stakeholder dialogues since at least 2025.

Earlier ministry events produced concrete promises that can now be tested. These include quarterly gender audits at the Foreign Ministry, a Women in Diplomacy Fund, and plans to revise the Foreign Service Manual to require gender parity in training and promotions.

What the announcement leaves out

No price tag. The press release names no budget, no timeline and no targets. A policy without a budget line is a statement of intent, and the government’s reliance on UN Women raises the question of how much of it Liberia owns.

No role for the Legislature. The policy was endorsed by Cabinet, not passed into law. That makes it easy to launch and just as easy to reverse.

Little on hard diplomacy. Six broad priorities get a single sentence. There is nothing on how Liberia will manage relations with the United States and China, its place in a divided ECOWAS, or how economic diplomacy will bring in investment.

The citizen-protection test. “Citizen protection” is listed as a core priority. Yet the government has agreed to accept third-country deportees from the United States, a deal now under scrutiny in the US Senate through Resolution 886. The ministry has not said how that arrangement fits the new framework.

Women at home. A foreign policy that puts women’s political representation at its center will be judged by Liberia’s own numbers. Women remain a small minority in the Legislature, and the ministry has not published how many of Liberia’s ambassadors and senior diplomats are women.

The first test: December at the Security Council

The policy’s first real test comes quickly. Liberia holds the Security Council presidency in December, giving it control of the Council’s agenda for a month. Ministry officials have already pledged to prioritize women’s issues during Liberia’s Council term, and in September President Boakai launched the country’s third National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security in New York.

If the December agenda carries the policy’s pillars into the Council chamber, the launch will look like the start of something. If not, critics will call it a ceremony.

The questions for the government are plain:

1. How much will the policy cost, and where is it in the budget?

2. Where can the public read the full document?

3. What will change in Liberia’s embassies by the end of 2027?

4. Will the government ask the Legislature to write the policy into law so it outlasts this administration?

5. Why did the launch come almost six months after Cabinet’s endorsement?

World.title: Liberia: ArcelorMittal Certifies 40 Liberian Railway Workers, Deepens Local Skills Development
World.content:
A cross-section of the newly certified Train Assistants and Dispatchers alongside Training and Rail Management of ArcelorMittal Liberia.

ArcelorMittal Liberia has certified 40 Liberian railway professionals as 38 Train Assistants and 2 Dispatchers, marking another significant milestone in the company’s commitment to developing local talent and building a highly skilled workforce to support its expanding mining, railway and port operations.

The newly certified personnel completed more than a year of intensive theoretical and practical training, demonstrating the technical competence, operational discipline, and safety awareness required to work in one of Liberia’s most critical industrial sectors. The certification ceremony, held on November 18, 2026, at AML Railway Headquarters in Buchanan, celebrated not only individual achievement but also the growing success of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s long-term workforce localization and human capital development strategy.

As the company advances its multi-billion-dollar expansion program and increases production capacity, developing Liberian talent to take on technical and leadership roles remains a key priority.



The latest graduates join a growing number of switch tenders, train assistants, dispatchers, shunt drivers, train drivers, maintenance personnel, and other railway professionals who have been trained and employed through ArcelorMittal Liberia’s structured Operations technical development programs.

Building skills for Liberia’s industrial future

Railway operations are among the most safety-critical and technically demanding aspects of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s business. Every train movement, operational decision, and communication has a direct impact on the safety of employees, equipment, and infrastructure. For that reason, the company has invested heavily in establishing a structured competency-based training career pathway aligned with international railway operating standards.

The newly certified employees underwent extensive classroom training and practical field exposure covering subjects such as train handling, hazardous commodities, safe train movement, shunting operations, rail safety procedures, wagon operations, dispatching systems, speed and acceleration management, gradients, and yard operations.



The program also included rigorous theoretical and practical assessments to ensure participants met competency requirements before certification.

Speaking during the ceremony, the AML Manager for Operations Training and Compliance, Ruth Negash, praised the graduates for their hard work, safe learning, dedication to excel and perseverance.

She noted that certification was earned through commitment and demonstrated competence, stressing that ArcelorMittal Liberia’s training standards are intentionally rigorous because “we want excellence.”

Negash emphasized that safety remains at the center of every railway role, reminding graduates that their responsibility is to protect themselves, their colleagues, and the equipment that enables operations.

“The railway is Liberian. It’s not going anywhere. It belongs to you and you must take your job very seriously to excel in your careers with high standards for safety, competency and productivity.” she said.

She further highlighted the company’s continued investment in developing future train drivers and railway leaders, noting that certification represents only the beginning of a lifelong learning and career development journey.

Competence before Certification

Manager, AML Operations Training and Compliance, Ruth Negash

The certification exercise formed part of a broader Rail Operations Technical Training and Compliance initiative aimed at strengthening technical competency, operational efficiency, and drive towards best and sustainable safety performance across the railway system.

According to Rail Operations Technical Trainer Madalitso Chabwera, the certification process was designed to verify that participants had successfully met all prescribed competency requirements.

“Our goal is to develop personnel who are technically competent, operationally disciplined, and committed to continuous improvement,” he said.

He noted that the certification was not simply recognition for attending training, but confirmation that each participant had demonstrated the knowledge, practical skills, and professional judgment required to perform safely and effectively in railway operations.

Chabwera described the certification exercise as an important foundation for structured career progression and continued workforce development within ArcelorMittal Liberia’s railway operations.

“Competence is built when theory is understood and practice is respected,” he told participants.

Supporting workforce localization

Rail Operations Technical Training Specialist, Madalitso Chabwera

The certification reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s broader vision of empowering Liberians to take increasing ownership of the country’s industrial infrastructure.

Over the past few months, the company has strengthened its rail training systems through technical gap assessments, competency evaluations, development of structured career pathways, added switch-tender training programs, and upgraded the design of new operating procedures aimed at improving safety, performance and productivity.

General Manager for Railway Operations, Felix Lage, said the achievement demonstrates the immense potential of Liberian talent when given access to training and development opportunities.

“Liberians have talent. We just need to find them, develop them, train them, and put them to work,” he said.

He encouraged the graduates to view the certification not merely as securing employment, but as the beginning of a professional career with long-term growth opportunities.

“You do not have a job. You have a career,” he told the graduates.

Career Pathways and future opportunities

For many of the graduates, becoming a certified Train Assistant or Dispatcher is only the first step on a structured career pathway that can lead to higher technical and supervisory positions.

Deputy General Manager for Railway Operations, Mulbah Gbozee, challenged the graduates to continue building their skills and preparing for greater responsibilities within the operation.

He noted that graduates could progress through several levels of railway operations, including Shunt Driver, Train Driver, Dispatcher, Superintendent, Rail Operations Manager, and other leadership positions.

“This is just the start,” Gbozee told participants. “The opportunity is in your hands.”

The company recently completed gap assessments, theory refreshers, technical assessments, and competency verification exercises, ensuring that employees meet the international railway standards required for advancement within the newly developed AML Railway Operations training pathway framework.

Deputy General Manager for Railway Operations, Mulbah Gbozee

Training Liberians to drive expansion

The certification comes at a critical time as ArcelorMittal Liberia continues implementing its expansion plans, which will significantly increase mining and railway activity.

The focus on workforce development aligns with ArcelorMittal Liberia’s longstanding commitment to skills transfer, localization, and sustainable economic development. Through structured training programs, apprenticeships, learnerships, scholarships, and technical development initiatives, the company continues to create opportunities for Liberians to acquire world-class industrial skills while building long-term careers.

A proud achievement

On behalf of the graduates, newly certified Train Assistant Victor James thanked the company, trainers, supervisors, and mentors who supported their development throughout the program.

He described the certification as an important milestone that has opened new opportunities for career growth and professional advancement.

For the graduates, the certificates represent the successful completion of hundreds of hours of training and practical experience. For ArcelorMittal Liberia, they represent something much larger: another step in building a highly skilled Liberian workforce capable of supporting one of Africa’s most significant mining, railway, and logistics operations.

As the company continues its expansion, the investment in people remains as important as the investment in infrastructure. By equipping Liberians with internationally aligned technical skills and creating clear pathways for advancement, ArcelorMittal Liberia is helping to build the next generation of Railway professionals while contributing to Liberia’s broader human capital development and economic transformation.

World.title: Liberia’s Embassy Hails Washington’s Report, but Leaves Out ‘Corruption’
World.content:
MONROVIA — The U.S. State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement on Liberia makes two arguments. First, the economy is improving. Second, the state is still failing the investors it wants to attract.

On Tuesday, the Embassy of the Republic of Liberia in Washington answered with a press release. It praised the first argument in detail and wrapped the second in diplomatic language.

What the Embassy praised



The Embassy said it was “particularly heartened” by six findings:

• Growth of 5.1 percent in 2025

• A 31.5 percent rise in export volumes

• Inflation down to 8.5 percent by December 2025



• Investment opportunities in mining, agriculture, energy and other sectors

• Laws allowing up to 100 percent foreign ownership in many sectors

• Membership in international arbitration systems, a $40 million World Bank trade project, and modernization of the Freeport of Monrovia

It also listed President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s governance initiatives: asset declarations, reviews of public contracts and work toward a specialized anti-corruption court.

None of that is false. The report does acknowledge it. As FrontPageAfrica reported earlier this month, the statement acknowledges what the government likes to say: growth reached 5.1 percent in 2025, exports surged, and inflation cooled.

What the Embassy left out

The word “corruption” appears nowhere in the Embassy’s release. Neither do “bribery,” “cronyism,” “extortion,” or “procurement.” The report’s criticism is reduced to one sentence about “areas requiring continued attention.” It lists those areas as “institutional effectiveness, regulatory administration, infrastructure, access to finance.”

The report itself is much blunter. It says:

• Stakeholders widely regard corruption as the main brake on Liberia’s democratic consolidation and economic growth.

• Some officials put short-term personal gain ahead of the investment climate.

• Political cronyism often influences decisions that should be based on merit.

• Businesses can easily operate illegally if they pay the right political interests. Companies that follow the rules get little help and may be targeted for bribes.

• Corruption is worst in government procurement, contract and concession awards, customs and taxation, regulatory approvals and government payment systems.

• Multinational firms often report being charged fees that are not in their investment agreements. Accounts of extortion “at multiple levels of government are common.”

• Civil society groups investigating corruption report being targeted with bribe requests, visa threats and unfounded legal allegations.

Calling all of this “regulatory administration” is not a summary of the report. It is a rewrite.

Same reforms, different weight

The two documents also disagree on how far reforms have gone. The Embassy presents Boakai’s anti-corruption measures as accomplishments. The report calls them “nascent reform efforts.”

The details matter. According to the report, the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission is still advocating for a specialized criminal court, and the Legislature is still considering removing the statute of limitations on corruption prosecutions. The Embassy does not mention the statute-of-limitations amendment, arguably the most concrete reform in the pipeline.

The report also says Liberia’s membership in the ECOWAS, African Union and UN anti-corruption conventions “has not produced measurable reductions in corruption.” It says the laws are on the books but enforced inconsistently, and that even-handed enforcement is “the exception rather than the rule.”

The quiet pushback

The most telling paragraph in the release is its most diplomatic. The Embassy notes that “such assessments draw upon multiple institutional, public, and private-sector sources.” It offers to “enrich the analysis with updated official statistics” toward a “more balanced understanding.”

In diplomatic language, this politely questions Washington’s sources. The report’s corruption findings rest on business surveys and U.S. Embassy reporting, meaning what investors say happens to them. Official statistics can update a GDP figure. They cannot rebut a company’s account of being charged an unofficial fee at the port.
