World.title: Trump urges nuclear arms control in historic meeting with Putin and Xi
World.content:
SHENZHEN, China — It’s unclear what decisions may come from this historic meeting.

But the spectacle of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping may be what delivers the defining image.

On Thursday, Trump, Putin and Xi met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. Sitting around a huge, doughnut-shaped table at the Kylin Villa resort were leaders of three of the world’s most powerful nations: the U.S. with its largest economy, Russia with its biggest nuclear arsenal, and China its largest standing army and manufacturing sector.

“We are really making history,” Trump said.

The sight of Trump expressing such warmth toward two authoritarian strongmen will have left many American allies outside the room dismayed. After Trump called Putin his “friend,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X, “God, protect us from such friends.” Russia has invaded Ukraine and waged a yearslong campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and misinformation against the West.

Others were concerned about the prospect of a “Yalta 2.0,” a reprise of the 1945 Yalta Conference in which the U.S., Britain and the then-Soviet Union met to carve up the postwar world.

After Thursday’s meeting finished, Russia and China issued a brief statement that was light on detail or major announcements. The U.S. did not immediately release a version.

The “China-Russia-U.S. Declaration on Peace” agreed to “reform” the United Nations “so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges.” (Russia and China have long sought to shift the body away from Western human rights concerns, while Trump has been a strident critic of the world body.) The declaration agreed to boost the production and supply of petroleum products, which have been disrupted by the Ukraine and Iran wars, and it rebuked the International Criminal Court not to abuse its power. (The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin.)

The final point was that the leaders vowed to take steps to avoid nuclear war, although no specifics were mentioned.

The last remaining treaty between Washington and Moscow, New START, lapsed in February, but China, which has a far smaller nuclear arsenal than the other two, has resisted calls to be included in a new agreement.

“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers, by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in the public section of the meeting.

“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them, it’s very hard to give them up,” he added. “That’s the way life works.”

World.title: Classified NSA network is still down, leaving some staff working from home
World.content:
An internal classified computer network used by the National Security Agency remained down on Thursday, resulting in some employees being ordered to work from home for a third day in a row, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

The network first went down on Tuesday due to a technical problem that occurred when maintenance on the network was underway. Both sources told NBC News the issue has created an inconvenience but has not affected the NSA’s work collecting electronic intelligence around the world and overseeing cybersecurity.

There is no sign that the outage was caused by a cyberattack, the sources said.

Even though the NSA’s network issue came amid an unusual series of mass outages that have wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails over the past few days, U.S. officials have said say there is no indication that the technical problems were caused by a coordinated cyberattack.

Nonessential staff at the NSA are being told to check in with their supervisors and find out if they need to come into the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland. Otherwise, they are advised to work from home, according to a telephone information line for the workforce and the two sources familiar with the matter.

While the NSA does not release the precise number of agency employees, former officials have said it employs tens of thousands of people. In 2024, a Maryland state government document put the number of NSA employees at 39,000. The agency has since made some workforce reductions as part of broader cutbacks across the federal government.

The outage also affected a worksite in Georgia that handles the NSA’s electronic intelligence work in the Middle East, the sources said.

In a statement Tuesday, the NSA acknowledged experiencing a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”

“While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the statement said. “NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

The NSA, which oversees the nation’s vast electronic surveillance efforts, is considered one of the world’s most sophisticated cybersecurity and electronic spy agencies.

With powerful eavesdropping and code-breaking tools as well as a well-educated workforce, the NSA prides itself as a center of digital expertise.

While it is not uncommon for government networks to suffer brief disruptions or outages, such a high-profile technical problem threatens to tarnish the reputation the agency has built, according to former officials and experts.

World.title: My boss canceled our 1:1 so I could keep playing ‘GTA’
World.content:
Within the first 20 minutes of playing “GTA 6,” I’ve been Tased, driven a boat, ransacked a remote drug dealer’s compound, stolen their cash and made my getaway in a plane.

“Drive” by The Cars plays through the speakers as I get behind the wheel for the first time. That first ride in a new “GTA” still hits different. This time, it’s down a rainy road, lit by the glow of warm lights. It’s nostalgic and new at the same time.

Yes, my boss knows this is happening. And no, I do not have my driver’s license in real life.

But given that “Grand Theft Auto” is such a cultural phenomenon, I was given the green light to chronicle my adventures behind the virtual wheel.

For the uninitiated, “GTA” is one of the biggest entertainment franchises in history. Fans of the property have been waiting 13 years for Rockstar Games, the game’s publisher, to release its new installment. The adventure series almost always involves vehicle driving (and sometimes robbery), heist missions and exploring fictional cities that are modeled after real-world places.

To prepare for the game, I clocked over 700 hours in “Red Dead Redemption 2,” Rockstar’s previous major release. The new installment of “GTA VI” clearly carries shades of everything that made “RDR2” mesmerizing and addicting. From the reactive nonplayable characters (NPCs) — characters players don’t even control and only sometimes interact with — to the lifelike graphics.

“GTA VI,” however, feels even more alive and almost overstimulating. There’s so much happening at once, both to you as a player and the world around. You can also, for the first time, play as both the male and female leads. Jason Duval (a male) and Lucia Caminos (a female), the protagonists, are a couple that find themselves “in the middle of a criminal conspiracy” across the fictional state of Leonida (inspired by Florida).

Here’s a play-by-play of the chaos that ensued in my first few hours of gaming.

Hour 1

It’s chore time! This game is low-key turning into a drywall installation simulator.

I just fed my snake, and I am hanging drywall in my bedroom. The snake’s name is Dolores BTW.

My snake. Rockstar Games

And now I am painting. I got to choose between three colors: a blue, green and peach. I went with peach.

Paint time. Rockstar Games

I am thinking about stealing a boat. Do I steal a boat?

Pondering Jason's next move. Rockstar Games

Wait. The boat has scuba gear on it. Are we going scuba diving?

We are going scuba diving.

In my gear. Rockstar Games

OK, stole the boat. We’re going offshore to get to deeper water to dive!

Boat life. Rockstar Games

UHHH, SOMETHING JUST EXPLODED IN THE WATER.

OH, THERE IS A BOAT ON FIRE AND A BODY FLOATING IN THE WATER.

I’ve encountered a shark.

World.title: Palestinians flee as Israeli tanks cross Gaza ceasefire’s ‘yellow line’
World.content:
Israel’s ground operation across the yellow ceasefire line in Gaza, which forced Palestinians to flee their makeshift shelters, marks a fresh escalation in the conflict and risks undermining an already floundering truce with Hamas, analysts said Thursday.

As tanks rolled into central Gaza on Wednesday, residents could be seen carrying blankets and other belongings away from their tents in pictures and video taken shortly after the Israeli military began what it said was an operation targeting a “terror tunnel.”

Others could be seen rolling away mattresses on carts and pushing loved ones in wheelchairs away from the scene near the Nuseirat camp in central Gaza. At least one person was reported to have been killed in an Israeli airstrike near the raid, Palestinian medics said, according to Reuters.

“Bullets were fired at us,” Amna al-Gasar, 49, told NBC News after she fled the scene with her young children, her baby in a pink fluffy sweater strapped to her chest. She said her family had received “evacuation orders” from the Israeli military and that tanks had advanced on the area.

“This is the 14th time that we’re getting displaced,” al-Gasar said, who added that she is from Gaza City in the north of the enclave which is now on the side of the “yellow line” occupied by Israeli forces. “Where should we go? We are exhausted. This is not a life,” she said.

Muna Abu Shehadeh, 37, said in a separate interview that along with some of her relatives, she left “with nothing but our children — no bedding, no food, and no water.” She added that she had a daughter who was ill, as well as a baby, and that they had to leave behind what few supplies they had.

The Israeli military told NBC News the ground operation was the first to be executed beyond the yellow line — the boundary marking the roughly 60% of Gaza that remains occupied by Israeli forces — since the U.S.-brokered ceasefire with Hamas came into effect in October 2025.

Separately, in a joint statement with the Israel Security Agency, or Shin Bet, the Israel Defense Forces said the operation was a “targeted” assault aimed at dismantling a tunnel that “posed an immediate and direct threat” to troops.

World.title: Fiona the hippo dies after eating hat, Cincinnati Zoo says
World.content:
Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo, Fiona, has died following complications from eating a hat that was tossed by a visitor and ended up in her enclosure, the zoo announced Thursday.

“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a statement.

She had ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat “by accident” last week, zoo officials said.

“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said in a statement. “The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.”

“We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are,” the statement said.

The zoo asked the public to keep her caretakers in their thoughts.

The knit hat got into Fiona’s habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and got caught by a ceiling fan that catapulted it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, The Associated Press reported, citing zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.

Fiona became a global celebrity soon after her premature birth nearly a decade ago.

She was born six weeks early in January 2017 and the world followed her progress online, rooting for the baby hippo to survive. Fiona quickly became a star: books were written about her, she inspired a line of beer and a couple got engaged in front of her exhibit.

World.title: Consumers stock doomsday pantries as tech outages cause jitters
World.content:
Public anxiety over a string of technology failures is driving some Americans to plan for the worst.

Jittery shoppers are stocking up on generators, shelf-stable canned goods, bottled water and other disaster-planning supplies at retailers such as Costco and Walmart, according to businesses and Wall Street analysts.

What's usually perceived as fringe behavior is starting to spread into the mainstream, according to RBC Capital Markets retail analyst Steven Shemesh.

"We've seen some evidence of it happening across the consumer retail space," he told CBS News, citing recent concurrent tech outages affecting online banking platforms, the Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system and even the National Security Agency. "Right now, on the margins, people are preparing more than they have in the past."

"People want to be comfortable knowing that if we did have an outage for a couple of days, they'd have food in the house," Shemesh added.

Data from market research and analytics firm Circana show that purchases of common emergency-prep staples rose for the four weeks ending Nov. 1. Sales of water germicidal tablets, which remove contaminants from drinking water, surged 154% compared with the same period a year ago. Sales of disinfecting wipes rose 72%, while moist towelette sales increased 20%, according to data from RBC Capital Markets.

Shemesh said that Walmart, which reported its third-quarter earnings on Thursday, told RBC that it is seeing a spike in sales of doomsday staples such as soup, water and ready-to-eat foods.

"It's not enough to move the needle for a company that does $8 billion in sales per year, but they are seeing those kinds of behaviors play out," Shemesh said. "Things could need to escalate quite a bit for this to go from level one to level three, which would maybe start to move the needle for some companies."

Nik Modi, global consumer and retail research co-head at RBC Capital Markets, is also seeing signs of panic shopping by consumers.

"A convergence of government action and social media anxiety has pushed 'doomsday prepping' into mainstream consumer behavior over the past several months," Modi said in a research note this week.

He traces the shift in purchasing behavior to a Pentagon military readiness initiative in late September that was misinterpreted and amplified on social media as an impending "blackout."

"Tailwind" for some prep categories

Big grocery chains, including Albertsons and Kroger, could benefit from a sales boost if the demand for such goods continues, Shemesh added.

"At current magnitudes, the stockpiling trend is a modest tailwind for a narrow set of categories: shelf-stable proteins, water purification, disinfecting hygiene formats and a handful of dry pantry staples," Modi said in his note to investors.

Earlier this week, investment firm Mizuho Securities said that consumers flocked to Costco after tech vulnerabilities heightened concerns about the risk of a major cybersecurity incident.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report.

He added that shoppers are "pantry-loading" and also depleting the retailer's inventory of "high-ticket generators," which were sold out online as of Sunday night.

Tractor Supply, which sells a range of tools, clothing, and heating and cooling equipment, told CBS News that it has seen increased demand across "several preparedness-related categories." It's selling more generators, liquid storage tanks, propane and accessory tanks than it did during the same period last year.

World.title: Fiona the hippo has died, Cincinnati Zoo says
World.content:
Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely almost a decade ago, and whose story captured hearts around the world, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.

"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a news release. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, had ingested a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure by accident last week, the zoo said, and despite the team's efforts to get it out of her system, "it was ultimately too much to overcome."

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning 3 on Jan. 23, 2020. John Minchillo/AP

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said. "She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many."

Before Fiona's death, veterinarians closely monitored her health, turning to an unconventional method to try to help her pass the blockage by borrowing a vibration plate from a horse farm. They had Fiona stand on the device several times a day, hoping the vibrations would help move the material through her digestive system.

Fiona would have been 10 years old this January. Her birth in 2017 drew the attention of millions on social media after she was born prematurely, weighing just 29 pounds, far below the typical 55–120 pounds for a newborn Nile hippo. Fiona was the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in 75 years.

Fiona with a zookeeper in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden on Jan. 10, 2018. John Minchillo / AP

To support baby Fiona, zoo staffers worked around the clock to care for her, including bottle-feeding her and helping her learn to swim.

In August 2022, Fiona's little brother, Fritz, was born at the Cincinnati Zoo.

"Fiona was a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati," Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said in a social media post. "She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world. Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."

World.title: Stocks plunge as investors take cover amid growing uncertainty
World.content:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged more than 1,100 points on Thursday, while other stock markets also slid, amid fears that the boom in artificial intelligence stocks may be deflating.

The Dow tumbled 1,101 points, or 2.2%, to close at 49,097, while the S&P 500 slipped 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.3%.

The swoon in markets was broad, with more than 90% of S&P 500 stocks nosing down.

Wall Street analysts said no single catalyst accounted for the plunge, but rather pointed to ongoing concerns about the durability of financial markets that lean heavily on AI's financial prospects. Despite those concerns, Anthropic had a successful stock market debut, with its shares rising as much as 34% in Thursday trading after staging the biggest initial public offering in history.

"The slump has set off a scramble of headline searching as people scour the wires to find the most negative sounding news flash," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a research note. "People just don't have much enthusiasm for this market, and rallies tend to bring out sellers instead of chasers (there is still a lot of hesitation when it comes to being long AI-linked names, especially picks-and-shovels, and the defensive stuff is quite extended after the recent rally)."

For weeks, investors have fretted about the financial strength of the AI sector amid concerns that the torrent of capital pouring into data centers may not deliver the productivity and profit growth companies are counting on.

More recently, investors were shaken by the resignation earlier this month of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after the revelation that he had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Some lawmakers have increased scrutiny of Nvidia's sales to China and to companies in southeast China, while the Commerce Department this week signaled it plans to tighten export controls on AI chips.

On Thursday, shares of AI-related stocks went from morning gains to afternoon losses. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared amid the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8% before swinging to a 1.8% loss. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents access to them to customers via the cloud, went from a 10.5% morning gain to a 5.5% drop.

Nvidia erased an early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 2.7%. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with the worries that have been dogging the entire industry.

It wasn't only tech stocks that tumbled on Thursday. Williams-Sonoma dropped 15.3% after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street's forecast.

Walmart sank 1.2% even though the retailing giant reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts' expectations.

World.title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
World.content:
Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.

"Seminal" moment

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.

"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.

"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.

The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to investment bank Renaissance Capital, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).

Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, and Daniela Amodei, co-founder and president, center left, during the company's IPO at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.

Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.

Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.

"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.

At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.

"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.

Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.

"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.

While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

World.title: Photos, videos show devastating South Florida flooding
World.content:
South Florida communities are reeling in the aftermath of widespread flooding that forced evacuations and school closures this week, as residents braced for additional rainfall on Thursday.

Parts of central Florida were under a flood warning until Thursday night as rain lashed coastal areas east of Orlando, dumping as much as eight inches there by early afternoon. In the city of Palm Bay, near Cape Canaveral, officials announced a mix of mandatory and voluntary evacuations for different neighborhoods and offered to transport residents away from their homes by boat.

A stop sign stands in a flooded street in Cocoa, Florida, on Nov. 19, 2026. Cyndy Paulin via AP

Parts of Florida's Broward County, which includes Fort Lauderdale and the nearby coastal city of Hollywood, have received more than 15 inches of rain since Tuesday, and up to a foot of rain has fallen in other areas. Photos and video footage show neighborhoods inundated, with residential properties and vehicles partially submerged in water.

Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue shared multiple videos to social media that captured its crew members either driving or wading on foot through knee-high waters. In several of them, rescuers were seen collecting debris and approaching vehicles that had become stranded on flooded roads.

FLFR High Water Teams are out assisting folks who need help in the flooding. pic.twitter.com/VXkqSrlgce — Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue (@FLFR411) November 18, 2026

One video, shared by X user Sruly Meyer, showed floodwaters rushing over a Hollywood street where his Uber was driving. The water appeared to create small waves that lapped against tree trunks and inched up the surrounding driveways.

"Insane flooding. Uber to airport," Meyer captioned the video.

Insane flooding. Uber to airport. Stirling off 67th in Hollywood. pic.twitter.com/Fayxd6jNDW — Sruly Meyer (@SrulySaysStuff) November 18, 2026

Law enforcement officers have been conducting rescues since Wednesday in particularly hard-hit locations. Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said they rescued more than 70 residents, in addition to 20 or 30 pets, from a flooded Hollywood apartment complex on Wednesday, CBS Miami reported.

The officers used high-profile vehicles to navigate deep floodwaters and help residents evacuate, including one resident who posted on Instagram about being trapped inside the complex as water levels began to rise.

Law enforcement officers from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission help evacuate a cat from a flooded neighborhood in Hollywood, Florida, on Nov. 18, 2026. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

No injuries or deaths have been reported in connection with the torrential rain or flooding, but officials and local residents told CBS Miami a number of families "lost everything."

Knee-deep floodwaters were reported inside some people's homes and ground-level apartments.

Floodwaters inundate the area around a home in Hollywood, Florida, on Nov. 18, 2026. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

People walk their bikes along a flooded street on Nov. 18, 2026, in Hollywood, Florida. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Multiple school buildings and at least one medical facility also flooded on Wednesday, with Broward County Public Schools reporting waters had breached classrooms inside schools in Hollywood as well as the nearby town of Davie.

One hospital also reported a breach, leading it to temporarily suspend visitations. The rain also caused the roof of a synagogue to collapse.

Capt. Jeff Carroll, a law enforcement officer from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, is pictured asking a resident of Hollywood, Florida, if they need help evacuating on Nov. 18, 2026. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Broward County officials activated a countywide state of emergency early Wednesday as conditions worsened.

Some motorists were forced to abandon their cars overnight as flooding made roads impassable and caused the vehicles to stall, Broward County officials said at a Wednesday news conference to announce school closures. The town of Davie also closed all public facilities for the day, including town parks and trails, according to CBS Miami.

Pounding rain also flooded on- and off-ramps leading to and from one Florida interstate highway, and a section of the state's turnpike filled with water.

World.title: Iowa residents asked to evacuate Friday ahead of Army detonation
World.content:
A plume of dust containing toxic lead particles is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Friday, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, following a planned U.S. Army detonation of unstable explosives.

The detonation is scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people four hours west of Chicago near the Mississippi River.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the AP.

The Army says moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," she told the AP. The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.

A plume of dust containing toxic lead particles is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Friday, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces. National Weather Service

Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.

Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.

The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.

Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.

This photo provided by the U.S. Army shows the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on May 14, 2024. (Shawn Eldridge/U.S. Army via AP) Shawn Eldridge

EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.

The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.

CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.

Community concerns grow ahead of Friday

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.

U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region are canceling classes Friday, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.

"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.

The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.

World.title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
World.content:
Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.

Sponsor Message

Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.

The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.

That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.

Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

Sponsor Message

In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.

Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.

'Time is of the essence' at East Potomac

Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.

Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.

Sponsor Message

But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.

Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.

The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.

Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.

The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).

Sponsor Message

Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.

Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.

Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.

Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.

Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.

Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.

"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.

Sponsor Message

Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."

"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"

Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.

Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

World.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
World.content:
The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

toggle caption i Richard Drury/Getty Images

Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.

She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."

Sponsor Message

It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)

As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?

David and Nina's Four L's

When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:

Love. "You gotta love each other."

Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."

Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.

Sponsor Message

Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.

toggle caption i Kerry Thompson/NPR

The Magic Six

I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn . She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection , where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.

Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?

The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six .

Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.

Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.

Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.

Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.

Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.

Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.

Sponsor Message

State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.

Listen. Don't Fix.

Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.

"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.

Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."

It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.

Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.

Find Your Rhythm

Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?

Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.

Sponsor Message

As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."

So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."

World.title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
World.content:
The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years

With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.

Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.

It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.

Loading...

Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.

Nearly 50 House seats flipped

So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.

That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.

It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

The biggest House majority in a generation

This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.

If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.

Loading...

Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.

This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.

Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.

World.title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
World.content:
The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

toggle caption i Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images

The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.

Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.

Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.

But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.

"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."

Sponsor Message

Genocidal campaign

For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.

The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.

toggle caption i Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images

Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.

"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."

She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."

Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."

"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."

Rejected defense

Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.

Sponsor Message

"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.

toggle caption i Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.

She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.

"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.

The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.

A group long denied recognition

In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.

Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.

The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.

But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.

Sponsor Message

In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.

Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."

The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.

However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.

The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.

Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.

Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.

Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.

"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.

She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.

Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

World.title: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
World.content:
World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets

toggle caption i John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPR

Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)

The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.

Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.

Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.

toggle caption i NOAH SEELAM/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

Let's eschew the euphemisms

World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott , the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.

Sponsor Message

This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.

There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp , the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.

toggle caption i DefeatDD

toggle caption i Haag/ullstein bild/via Getty Images

toggle caption i Kristina Ketelsen

Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?

The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.

Sponsor Message

What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab , who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.

toggle caption i NurPhoto/via Getty Images



So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.

A toast to toilets

Let's end by reflecting on the present day.

"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."

If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.

I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.

World.title: Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
World.content:
Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

🎧 Jeffries, who has served as the top Democrat in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December.

in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December. ➡️ Rep. Robert Garcia, poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, sent document-preservation letters to more than a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members in preparation for investigations starting in January. These letters focus on four main areas: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the White House Epstein cover-up."

Sponsor Message

Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Xi and Putin met separately the night before the trilateral meeting. Trump also had one-on-one meetings with Putin and Xi. It's the first time the three leaders have held a summit together.



🎧 The three leaders had different agendas as they went into their meeting, NPR's Jennifer Pak says. Trump aimed to prioritize nuclear arms control. He said that they had a unique opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons, a stance Beijing has typically resisted due to its smaller stockpile compared to the U.S. and Russia. Putin sought discussions to end the war in Ukraine, but on Moscow's terms. The complexity of these issues makes substantial outcomes unlikely, Pak says. Xi aimed to position China as a stabilizing global force by bringing together Russia, its old ally, and the U.S., its direct competitor.

Anthropic is set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange today. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. The company sold 956 million shares at $83 each, surpassing its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares as part of the IPO, and the company's prospectus outlines plans to introduce an extra $26 billion in shares through private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.



Sponsor Message

🎧 In its IPO filing, Anthropic was optimistic that AI would have a bigger impact on the economy than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The company's paperwork suggested that the addressable market for Anthropic's products could be as big as $40 trillion annually, exceeding the GDP of the United States.
