But CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the danger of losing control over AI. The prospectus flagged some political risks, including the company's current dispute with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. Ruwitch says that now that Anthropic and SpaceX are on the market, OpenAI could potentially join next year.

Watch this

toggle caption i Nickolai Hammar/NPR

Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.

Ben Shapiro says he remains committed to his values during Trump's turbulent presidency. The conservative podcast host voted against Trump in 2016, but actively campaigned for him in 2024. Shapiro expressed disappointment in the president's tariffs, alleged corruption and the handling of the war in Iran. He says that Trump's strict immigration policies and the "whiff of corruption" surrounding the White House contributed to the GOP's midterm losses. The co-founder of the media company The Daily Wire warns that Republicans face an "uphill road in 2028," and he doesn't see Vice President JD Vance as the right GOP presidential candidate. Shapiro argues that Vance could alienate key voter groups like Hispanics, the working class, women and the college-educated. In conversation with Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep, Shapiro discussed who he thinks could be a potential 2028 GOP candidate, his new movie, Confession, and the recent decline in his show's YouTube subscriptions.

Sponsor Message

Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.

Today's listen

toggle caption i Odd Andersen/AFP via Getty Images

The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra is an ensemble founded by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim nearly 30 years ago in Germany to unite Middle Eastern musicians. Despite the deep personal grief and heightened tensions following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the Gaza war, members of the orchestra strive to confront, rather than sidestep, political realities. Longtime musicians say Barenboim has helped them bridge painful cultural divides and foster enduring cross-border friendships. The space has also given some participants a safe space to discuss Gaza, allowing music to resolve the dissonance.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Fadel Dawod/National Book Foundation

Abdelrahman ElGendy has won the National Book Awards' non-fiction prize for his memoir, Huna, which recounts his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. "Choosin' Texas" singer Ella Langley won six of the seven categories she was nominated for, including song of the year, at the Country Music Awards. In this week's edition of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Esme Nicholson sends greetings from a Berlin square, where children play around a Käthe Kollwitz bronze cast. In the wake of World War I, the German artist's work often portrayed undernourished children in their mothers' arms.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
World.content:
Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.

Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.

"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.

Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.

Sponsor Message

The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.

"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."

She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.

But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.

Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.

The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.

Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.

"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.

Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.

The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer. The web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: With Putin in the room, Carney condemns Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned Russia's war with Ukraine while Russian President Vladimir Putin, the man prosecuting that war, was in the room for leaders' speeches at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China.

Carney's speech principally focused on the government's efforts to boost the economy and make the country a more favourable place to invest for Asian partners.

However, toward the end of those remarks to the plenary session on Thursday, he veered into the yearslong conflict that has threatened Ukraine's territorial integrity, killed tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians and shaken the global economy.

"Sustained prosperity also depends on a stable international environment. Geopolitical crises, including Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine, continue to have material economic consequences across the Asia-Pacific and beyond," Carney said, according to a copy of his prepared remarks shared by the Prime Minister's Office.

WATCH | Carney on Russian sanctions: Sanctions on Russia are 'biting' and will increase, Carney says | Duration 1:32 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from China on Nov. 18, said sanctions on Russia remain 'absolutely' necessary. 'Not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground,' Carney said, adding, 'sanctions are very real and they're going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on.'

Wars like Putin's "underscore the importance of reliable partners who respect international law and territorial integrity while building resilience among like-minded countries," he said.

This is believed to be the first time these two leaders have ever been together in the same space since Carney became prime minister.

Before making those comments, Carney was more pointed in a news conference when asked about Putin's claim that sanctions on his country are ineffective and "a thing of the past."

"Mr. Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he'll find out that they're very real, they're biting and they're absolutely necessary because of his illegal and unjustified war. Canada is speaking with action," Carney said.

Carney and United States President Donald Trump leave the family photo at the summit, which also included Russian President Vladimir Putin. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

When asked if he was willing to be blunt with Putin face-to-face, Carney praised former prime minister Stephen Harper's 2014 decision to personally chastise Putin for invading Crimea.

At the time, Harper said to Putin: "I guess I'll shake your hand, but I only have one thing to say to you: you need to get out of Ukraine."

According to an account of that moment in Harper's recently published memoir, Putin told him in response, "I'm not in Ukraine."

"Well, that's why it's a waste of my time to talk to you," Harper said he told the Russian leader.

Carney said he was willing to say something similar.

"If I have the occasion to be next to him, I will make that clear. But it is already clear, and not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they're going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on," he said.

After his speech taking issue with Putin's war, Carney did pose for the usual leaders' family photo as the summit wrapped.

Putin was one row down and two leaders over from Carney, but it wasn't apparent if the two ever spoke.

The Russian Embassy in Ottawa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World leaders including Carney, Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are seen in the family photo on Thursday. (Greg Baker/Getty Images)

Since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin has largely avoided international summits where Kyiv's Western allies are present. He hasn't been to APEC, for example, in years.

But he was in Shenzhen, China, this year for a rare trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping where the war with Ukraine was a major focus.

Putin also had a one-on-one meeting with Trump, who greeted the Russian leader at the start of their bilateral discussion by saying: "He's my friend," a comment that has been roundly condemned as inappropriate given Putin's alleged war crimes.

Trump shakes hands with Putin as Xi looks on before the APEC summit welcome banquet. (Iori Sagisawa/AFP/Getty Images)

Trump hailed the visit as "Highly Consequential" on social media as he returned to Washington. But it wasn't clear what, if anything, had been accomplished beyond a vague commitment to avoid nuclear war.

Xi said the meeting focused on "promoting world peace."

Putin, for his part, said the countries "hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."

Leaders from the Coalition of the Willing, comprising some 34 Western nations supporting Ukraine in this war, met later Thursday to discuss the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.

Carney was in the air on his way back to Canada but his defence minister, David McGuinty, attended in his place.

According to a readout from McGuinty's office, the minister "reaffirmed Canada's unwavering support for international efforts and emphasized that any peace agreement must preserve Ukraine's sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, while strengthening rather than weakening Euro-Atlantic security."

Canada's position is that Ukraine "must be fully involved in decisions regarding its own future," the readout said.

World.title: Canada seeking interim trade arrangement with U.S. by end of year: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is seeking to reach an interim tariff arrangement with the Trump administration by the end of the year, according to members of the federal government's Canada-U.S. advisory committee.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc met with the committee on Thursday. Sources told CBC News that the government's goal of an interim arrangement would cover Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum, auto and lumber — as well as Section 338 tariffs imposed on Canada in August after previous talks broke down.

After the talks fell apart, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to slap higher levies on Canadian autos, car parts and steel on Jan. 1.

Not a hard deadline: committee member

Committee member Valérie Beaudoin cautioned that the end-of-year ambition isn't a hard deadline.

"Maybe it's going to go fast, but it can take a longer time. And we know when they deal with Donald Trump — and this is my opinion — it's not always straightforward, it's not always easy," Beaudoin told CBC News Network host Andrew Nichols.

Jean Simard, another member of the committee and head of the Aluminium Association of Canada, told CBC News that it's "the opportune time" for Canada to negotiate.

"Next year there's a new Congress being sworn in, a new Senate being sworn in with Democratic majorities in both — even though they cannot repeal a [presidential] veto. But still, they will take over part of the agenda," he said.

The president's Republican Party suffered massive losses in the recent U.S. midterms and some Democrats have pledged to try to end tariffs on Canadian goods once they officially take control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

But Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association and a member of the advisory council, told CBC News that "it appears that the dynamics in Congress have not yet hit the negotiating table."

"The question would be: Is this the best time to do a deal with an administration that would like to take an issue off the table itself, without looking like it was forced to do by the new Congress? Or, is this an opportunity for the administration to fight with Congress and show that they're really in charge?" Volpe said.

"It's my read of it that different parts of this administration have a different opinion on it."

Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading back to Ottawa after a nine-day trade mission to Europe and Asia.

Speaking virtually to the Dealbook summit from China on Wednesday, Carney said Canada continues "to have a series of issues" when it comes to trade with the U.S.

The prime minister indicated that there had been progress toward an agreement in recent weeks but said they're not at the point of putting anything to paper.

Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump in China on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit — a conversation he described as "reasonably direct" but one that didn't produce a trade breakthrough.

WATCH | 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy,' Carney says: 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy': Carney | Duration closed caption 2:22 At the APEC summit in China, Prime Minister Mark Carney met face-to-face with U.S. President Donald Trump for the first time since trade talks fell apart. Carney, who secured a number of global deals at the summit, said if the U.S. still isn't ready for a deal, 'we're busy.'

During his latest trip, Carney brokered free trade deals with the Philippines and the 11-nation ASEAN bloc — and secured meaningful market access for Canadian commodities in return for allowing a relatively small number of Chinese EVs to be imported at lower tariff rates and adjustments to import rules for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.

"We'd like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy," Carney told the summit's audience in New York.

Peter Navarro, one of Trump's top trade advisers and a frequent critic of Canada, blasted Carney on Wednesday for seeking a more open trade relationship with China.

"Are you really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme," Navarro wrote in a social media post.

The White House official again criticized Canada's negotiating tactics on Thursday.

"The arrogance and dishonesty of Ottawa on trade and misreading of their position is really something else," he said.

"They are like a high school team taking on the New York Knicks. That doesn’t end well for Canada."

World.title: Fiona the hippo dies after ingesting visitor's hat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after ingesting a visitor's hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure.

"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said in a statement.

The zoo said Monday that the nine-year-old hippo was undergoing care around the clock after swallowing the hat more than a week ago.

Before she died, veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said.

They even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move things along through her digestive tract.

"Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome," the zoo said. "The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover."

'Symbol of perseverance and joy'

Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval posted on social media that the city was heartbroken.

"Fiona was a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati. She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he said.

Grace Brooks, of Cincinnati, and her two children, ages three and five, had Fiona on their minds when they arrived at the zoo Thursday, before her death was announced. Her kids have been talking about Fiona at preschool, she said.

"They know all about Fiona, and we have lots of books about her," Brooks said.

The zoo was mostly empty, though a small crowd was gathered inside the "Hippo Cove," where two other hippos were swimming.

Even without Fiona in the cove, her presence was felt.

There's a holiday-themed Fiona statue just outside the entrance, and the gift shop has an entire wall filled with hippo-themed shirts, coffee mugs, glasses and books, including A Very Fiona Christmas and You've Got This, Fiona.

Fiona got her own speacial birthday cake on her third birthday in 2020. (John Minchillo/The Associated Press)

Fiona was under close care

Fiona captivated people worldwide after her premature birth in 2017. She swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and catapulted the hat through a small opening above the area's viewing windows.

Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said it was an accident.

Before she died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.

An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 2.7-metre scope, but he said they were unable to detect anything.

Fiona, seen here in June 2018, was only 13.2 kilograms when she was born. (John Minchillo/The Associated Press)

Surgery not an option

According to the zoo, specialists told them that surgery wasn't an option for full-grown hippos.

Hippos have a digestive system that would make Fiona's situation tricky, said Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, before the hippo's death was announced.

"They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don't regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does," Kottwitz told The Associated Press in an email.

Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge for many reasons, he said.

In order to find the hat, multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, he said. But hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have skin more than five centimetres thick in places.

Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona's situation was difficult because it was hard to tell exactly where the hat was.

"You just don't know because you can't do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses," Hawkins said.

Other zoo animals have also died from eating foreign objects and zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.

Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.

Fiona was born premature

Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 13.2 kilograms, which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.

Fiona was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.

Her survival brought an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was shot and killed in 2016 when a child got into his enclosure.

World.title: Petition asks Netflix to cancel The Body for 'blasphemous' and 'anti-Christian' content
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The new Netflix show The Body is taking heat for being "blasphemous" and "anti-Christian," with more than 110,000 people signing a petition calling on the streaming giant to cancel the show.

The Body, which released on Netflix on Nov. 11, is a coming-of-age drama by writer, actor and director Quinn Shephard. It tells the story of a dance team at a Catholic school.

In the show, the girls perform a mock satanic ritual at a Halloween party, pretending to offer one of their classmates as a virgin sacrifice. Afterward, the girls begin having prophetic visions, sparking hysteria in their town.

The petition on CitizenGO calls it: "A blasphemous anti-Christian series featuring satanic ritual."

"Parents cannot screen every show teens press play on. Netflix is counting on that," it says.

As of publication, the eight-episode series is third in Netflix Canada's top 10. According to Variety, it drew 5.1 million views in its first five days in the U.S.

WATCH | The Body official trailer:

The petition was launched before the show's premiere and initially called on Netflix not to release it. As of Nov. 19, just over a week after the show was released, it had received more than 118,000 signatures.

The petition also criticized Netflix's marketing campaign for posting photos portraying the show's characters as saints.

Not the first program protested

The petition also criticizes previous Netflix releases, including The First Temptation of Christ — a Brazilian comedy released in 2019 — for mocking Jesus. It also mentions the 2020 French drama Cuties, saying it "sexualized eleven-year-old girls."

Despite protests, streaming platforms rarely respond by removing content from their libraries.

In 2019, more than 20,000 people signed a petition to cancel the series Good Omens, claiming it mocked God and normalized Satanism. However, protesters mistakenly addressed their petition to Netflix rather than Amazon, which produced the series. Good Omens went on to have a second and third season.

In 2021, about 100 Netflix employees staged a protest outside the company's headquarters in Los Angeles over Dave Chappelle's comedy special, The Closer. Protesters said the special was transphobic. Netflix kept the special available on its platform.

The animated sitcom South Park has also faced numerous controversies involving various groups, including Christians, Muslims, Mormons and the Trump administration. The series is now in its 29th season.

CBC reached out to Netflix for comment on the petition but did not receive a response before publication. Netflix has yet to confirm whether the series will be renewed for a second season.

World.title: Almost half of women in B.C. report intimate partner violence: StatsCan
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Almost half of women in B.C. have reported experiencing intimate partner violence at least once since the age of 15, according to a new Statistics Canada report released on Wednesday.

In the study, intimate partner violence is defined as psychological, physical and sexual abuse. It can range from name-calling and manipulation to physical and sexual assault.

The study showed 47 per cent of B.C. women reported experiencing intimate partner violence. That figure, calculated from 2025 data, has held steady since the last report, which examined numbers gathered in 2018.

Nationwide, 45.1 per cent of women reported intimate partner violence, up from 44 per cent.

The study is based on the 2025 Survey of Safety in Public and Private Spaces, which was administered both online and via the telephone, and included over 46,500 respondents in the 10 provinces.

The study found that across the country, more younger women — aged 15 to 24 years old — are reporting intimate partner violence. (khuncho007/Shutterstock)

Younger women reporting more

At the same time, the study found that across the country, more younger women — aged 15 to 24 years old — are reporting intimate partner violence.

That number has bumped up to 58.5 per cent, up from 55.75 per cent.

Angela Marie MacDougall, executive director of Battered Women's Support Services, said the uptick may be the result of an increased willingness to report — a change from previous generations.

"The time of where survivors, victims, didn't report, they just had to deal with it like my mother and my grandmother," said MacDougall of what those previous generations went through.

Angela Marie MacDougall, executive director of Battered Women's Support Services, says the increases may be the result of an increased willingness to report — a change from previous generations. (CBC)

She said a greater willingness to report also comes at a time when there have been regressions in women's rights.

"There's more of a push back within the culture against the forces that would want to entrench violence against women," said MacDougall.

She said accountability work from community organizations and media is making victims feel like reporting intimate partner violence will create a meaningful result.

"It's more like if I report, I have a better chance of having a result that is going to help me be safer," said MacDougall.

She said her organization has seen an 80 per cent increase in requests for services since the same time last year.

Racialized women less likely to report: worker

The new Statistics Canada numbers also show that racialized women — defined in the report as those who are not white and not Indigenous — are reporting intimate partner violence at a lower rate than their white counterparts.

About 29.4 per cent of racialized women reported having experienced intimate partner violence at least once since the age of 15.

This number was 48.7 per cent for non-racialized women.

Syma Nehal of Nisa Homes says she's seen first-hand why immigrant women are often the most reluctant to report intimate partner violence. (Bismah Mughal/CBC)

But Syma Nehal said this doesn't show the full picture.

She works directly with immigrant women at Nisa Homes, which provides transitional housing for women fleeing intimate partner violence.

Nehal said she's seen first-hand why immigrant women are often the most reluctant to report.

"They're unfamiliar with systems … or they're isolated from their communities," said Nehal. "And so some of these abusers will exploit those fears by threatening deportation."

She said there is a lack of effort to recognize the unique cultural barriers these women face, which is why progress on making it safe for women to report intimate partner violence is still slow, even as immigration continues to grow.

World.title: More cadets, more money, less training: Military defends controversial suspension
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The second-in-command of Canada's military stood behind the decision to suspend most cadet training in various parts of the country, suggesting the program is swamped by an increase in participation and struggling not to blow its annual budget.

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee, the vice chief of the defence staff who is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the military, testified Thursday before the House of Commons public accounts committee.

A set of leaked emails obtained by a number of media outlets, including CBC News, show weekend training and participation in competitions by cadets has been halted until the end of the fiscal year in March. Mandatory weekly parade nights, however, will continue at least for the time being.

Topshee told the tri-party committee that membership in the cadets program has jumped by roughly 20,000 in the last few years and funding for the program has increased to $265 million annually.

WATCH | Topshee on cadet training cuts: Military's 2nd-in-command says increase in cadets led to temporary cuts | Duration closed caption 2:01 Asked by Conservative MP William Stevenson why some cadet training activities have been cancelled, deputy minister of defence Christiane Fox noted that the program received a $27-million budget boost in the spring of 2026 and Vice-Chief of the Defence Staff Angus Topshee said most of the funding had been 'front loaded' into summer training.

"Unfortunately, a lot of the cadet funding is front-loaded. It happens during the summer months," Topshee said.

"And so they spent a large part of that expanded budget on summer training. And we didn't factor in the sizable increase in the number of cadets participating in the program."

The answer to questions from Conservative MP William Stevenson represent the clearest explanation to date from the military about the reason for the decision, which has angered many Canadians.

A written statement from the Department of National Defence (DND) late Wednesday referenced the increased participation and the higher budget, but focused on the fact that both the cadet and junior ranger programs were being reviewed.

Topshee added more clarity to the military position.

"Despite the fact the budget has grown, they have run up against a hard cap on the amount of money that they've been given," Topshee said.

"They are now on track to exceed that and they are living within their means, as all of us within the Department of Defence are," he added. "We are required to live within the budget we've been given and they spent theirs a little bit faster than they were intended to."

The written statement from the department implied that it was too early to say what "the full extent of any changes" would be because of the ongoing review.

WATCH | CAF pauses most cadet training over budget constraints: Canadian Armed Forces pauses most cadet training over budget constraints | Duration closed caption 1:47 The Canadian military is pausing most cadet training across the country due to budget constraints, CBC News has learned.

Deputy minister of defence Christiane Fox told the same committee that she supports the restoration of the training that has been put on pause.

"It is an essential program, not just for the military and the forces, it is an essential program for young Canadians to develop confidence, leadership, skill sets that we need," Fox said.

The decision to rein in the cadet program budget is just one part of a series of internal belt-tightening measures at DND.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has drastically ramped up defence spending and has largely exempted the department from its expenditure review program. But it has not entirely escaped the fiscal axe.

DND has been told to focus its billions of dollars in new investment on priority areas, including the purchase of new equipment.

At the same time, it is still subject to reductions planned in a previous federal budget, passed by the Trudeau government.

Those reductions in operations and maintenance funding continue to roll out this year with DND expected to find $459 million in savings this year.

World.title: Alberta government to revise policy as school boards say new flag regulations could cost millions of dollars
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta’s education minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school boards collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new outdoor flagpoles.

On Thursday, Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides told reporters at the legislature that school boards buying new flagpoles should “pause until we’re able to provide some additional direction."

Nicolaides has also said he believes the money would be better spent by directing it to classrooms.

A flag display regulation , made public in late October to accompany new legislation from last spring, says schools must fly the Canada and Alberta flags outside their buildings and on separate poles to satisfy national flag protocol.

The provincial regulation says any work needed to ensure the flags fly on separate poles is supposed to be done by Jan. 4, 2027.

CBC News reached out to eight school divisions to ask about how many of their schools have just one flagpole and how much money they anticipated they would need to spend to satisfy the provincial regulation.

The Calgary Board of Education, the province’s most populous school division, counted 223 schools and leased sites with a single flagpole. Spokesperson Joanne Anderson said in a Wednesday email that the division estimated it would cost $4 million to install a second pole on every site. The regulation says that work is supposed to be done by Jan. 4, 2027.

“We will not be able to meet the Jan. 4 outdoor flag installation requirement as we will need to procure and install the flags and flagpoles,” Anderson said in an email.

Calgary’s Catholic school division said 122 schools would need a second flagpole, and each pole could cost $20,000 to $30,000 to purchase and install.

In Northland School Division, which has locations across northern Alberta, 12 schools would need additional flagpoles, and each would cost at least $20,000, spokesperson Curtis Walty said in an email.

“Meeting the Jan. 4, 2027, deadline would be impossible,” his email said. “Installing additional flagpoles would place significant pressure on education funding.”

Edmonton Public Schools said more than 170 sites would need a second flagpole, and 77 Edmonton Catholic Schools would need a second flagpole. Neither provided cost estimates.

The Fort McMurray Public School Division plans to install wall-mounted flagpoles on some schools that cost $2,000 each as a temporary measure, before installing permanent flagpoles in the ground next summer, a statement said.

Opposition raises lack of consultation

The issue came to a head at a meeting of the Alberta School Boards Association (ASBA) in Edmonton earlier this week, where members passed a resolution calling on the government to suspend the flags regulation, restore school board authority over flag displays and eliminate the mandatory costs for installing flags and poles.

Smith attended a breakfast event with trustees in Edmonton Tuesday and held a fireside chat with ASBA president Shali Baziuk.

NDP MLA Janis Irwin said she was at the meeting and heard the exchanges.

On Tuesday, she told reporters she believes the premier seemed to be unaware of the costs and challenges of installing flagpoles because her government fails to consult with affected people before introducing new rules.

“It should have been a wake-up call for her to recognize that she's making decisions without understanding the consequences on the ground," Irwin said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to the media in Calgary on Oct. 21, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Baziuk declined an interview request Wednesday.

Smith was asked about the ASBA meeting in question period at the legislature on Wednesday.

"Admittedly, we didn't know that it is common to only have one flagpole at a school," she said.

Changes coming, minister says

CBC News requested interviews with eight school board chairs on Wednesday. Although all declined, Fort McMurray Public School Division chair Tim O’Hara said in a statement that he appreciated the premier’s willingness to listen and "her recognition that 'You don’t know what you don’t know,' as she stated in response to finding out how many schools exist with less than the newly required two flagpoles.”

O’Hara said the event highlights why meaningful exchanges with school boards are important to identify practical obstacles before the government introduces legislation and proclaims it into law.

Nicolaides also met with ASBA members in Edmonton, but on Monday.

On Wednesday, Nicolaides told reporters at the legislature he would be changing the regulations.

Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides says he will review new school flags regulations after school trustees said hundreds of buildings need a second flagpole to fulfil the incoming rules. (CBC)

He said he would consider removing the requirement for the Canada and Alberta flags to be displayed outside schools, but didn’t have more details on what the changes would entail.

“We don't want school boards to be absorbing these kinds of significant costs,” Nicolaides said.

Flag protocols could dictate costs

Gary Komusi, a Calgary business owner who runs Signs Talk, installs and repairs flagpoles as part of his work. In an interview with CBC News, he said following national protocol around the Canadian flag prompts some limitations around how a school could fly a second flag.

For example, he said if the Canadian flag is flying alongside an Alberta flag, the Canadian flag must be on the left-hand side and on a taller pole.

The height of the pole each school requires would depend on what their existing pole is like, Komusi said. Once ordered, a pole could take six to eight weeks to arrive, he added, potentially making the Jan. 4 deadline impossible to meet.

Komusi said the cost would depend on the length of the flagpole and the time of year it is installed, but he estimates it would be at least $5,000 per flag.

Installers would have to pour a cement footing with metal components for each flagpole base, then erect the pole onto it.

Flags themselves aren’t expensive, Komusi said, but schools have to ensure the Canadian flag is the correct dimensions — twice as wide as it is long.

Komusi said he is sympathetic to schools that have to spend money to meet the requirements.

“I'm not looking at this as a windfall for Signs Talk, or the flag industry, which I guess it is, but it's a hardship on the schools,” he said. “If this all went away, that would probably be for the best.”

World.title: Armed forces in Haiti push to oust gang members from corridor on edge of capital
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country's capital to its western and southern regions.

It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.

Haiti's National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.

Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti's police posted a video of armoured vehicles rumbling through the community.

Gangs entrenched for years

Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country's economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.

LISTEN | The Trump administration and Haiti: Front Burner 36:28 Why is Trump so focused on Haiti?

Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.

The fight to control Martissant began in June 2021, when gangs from Grand-Ravine and Village-de-Dieu attacked the Ti-Bois gang. Armed men set fire to homes, killed families, destroyed businesses and seized control of Martissant's police station.

The clashes forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes and affected some 800,000 people overall, according to a July 2022 United Nations report.

Several years ago, gangs operating between Tabarre and Carrefour would demand some $380 US from those transiting through Martissant, according to a 2023 UN report.

Last year, Haiti's Center for Analysis and Research in Human Rights noted that ever since Martissant fell, hundreds of public and private institutions were relocated and more than one million people were forced to flee their homes.

UN-backed force putting pressure on gangs

As the fight in Martissant continues, a UN-backed Gang Suppression Force also has made recent inroads against gangs in a push to not only displace them but prevent their return.

Vehicles belonging to the Gang Suppression Force are seen patrolling in the Tabarre neighbourhood of the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince last month. (Odelyn Joseph/The Associated Press)

"Operations are entering a new phase: increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling more strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas," the force wrote Thursday on X.

The Gang Suppression Force said it's working in places including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and in Haiti's central Artibonite region, which has come under repeated violent attacks by armed men.

The force said it has come under fire as it advances along Route 5, "removing obstacles established by gangs to isolate communities and control key routes."

The force said it also cleared and secured a church and school that gangs had been controlling north of Gros-Morne.

"It is about restoring freedom of movement, reopening access to public institutions, and re-establishing State presence for communities that have endured years of gang control," the force wrote Sunday on X.

El Salvador embraces fight against gangs

Also fighting gangs are some 2,500 troops deployed by El Salvador last month when four of their own went missing after an Oct. 18 attack in Haiti's capital.

Following orders by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the troops have attacked the main homes of two of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, this month. Neither one was killed.

Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and the deployment of Salvadoran soldiers to fight armed gangs in Port-au-Prince. (Patrice Noel/The Associated Press)

Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Bukele, but experts have criticized the unilateral operations of Salvadoran troops and noted that the use of explosive drones has claimed a growing number of innocent victims.

A small group of Salvadorans are separately working with the Gang Suppression Force.

In late September, El Salvador's legislature passed a law authorizing the participation of that group in Haiti for another 12 months until October 2027. The law was championed by Bukele and overwhelmingly approved by the country's congress, controlled by Bukele's party.

The ongoing clashes with gangs continue as Haiti prepares for its first elections in more than a decade. The country hasn't had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed in July 2021.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Unabashed Racist Far Right Emerges in Cuba
World.content:
The Cuba proposed by Voluntad Nacional is one featuring militarily uniformed assault squads that would take to the streets to combat “communism.”

By Angry GenXer

HAVANA TIMES – You can publish just about anything on the internet… as long as it isn’t censored.

But on September 20, a new initiative emerged on Cuban social media: the page Voluntad Nacional Noticias (National Will News). It not only promotes an imagined Nazi future for Cuba but also actively recruits followers, interacting in large online groups whose members its promoters consider potentially sympathetic. The platform targets Catholic groups, especially those made up of young people, which anyone can access.

It is hard to believe, but it is true. And dangerous. We are no longer talking about KKK costumes on Halloween or SS uniforms at a rock event (incidents from years ago that scandalized many people). This is outright racism disguised as religion.

In their Manifesto, published on October 30, the people behind Voluntad Nacional openly preach racial, intercultural, and intergenerational hatred.

Interspersed among news posts criticizing the situation in Cuba, typical of any digital media outlet independent of the government, the page features content promoting openly racist ideology.

Beyond its anti-communism, Voluntad Nacional’s visual imagery revives the grotesque, buffoonish “classic” racist caricatures (so “acceptably” widespread in Cuba, the United States, and other countries until nearly the 1970s). It also invokes the stylish “sex appeal” of the powerful mass-militarist aesthetics of 20th-century totalitarian regimes, famously associated with the German SS uniforms manufactured in Hugo Boss textile factories.

The AI-generated posters from Voluntad Nacional look like they were taken from Nazi propaganda of a century ago. This one sates: I couldn’t care less about the socialists.

In a recent post, we see a caricature: on the wall of a house are the words “Long Live Fidel” and the emblem of the CDR (Committees for the Defense of the Revolution). On the other side of the window, a Black man—depicted as a buffoon, as though copied from a Klan pamphlet—is swigging from a bottle of rum. To the right marches a muscular white man wearing a cap, military boots, and a uniform resembling that of the SA (the German Nazis’ stormtroopers).

The caricature accompanies the “Manifesto of a Generation,” written by those promoting the “project,” who distance themselves both from their “grandparents”—who entangled Cuba in a socialist revolution—and from millennials, who, in their view, have lost all ethical direction and no longer respect social “hierarchies.”

A hundred years ago, when fascism was emerging around the world, representing a new generation was precisely one of its slogans (including in Cuba, where the ABC party existed).

Cuba has not yet experienced the worldwide social protests associated with “Generation Z,” except perhaps for last year’s student strike. But this “Manifesto” is something very different. Instead of the symbols used by Gen Z activists in various countries, here we see ridiculous representations dating back a century.

They defend traditionalism and “Hispanism,” attack Zionism, Afro-ancestral religions, “reparterismo” (the Cuban urban culture associated with reparto music), Freemasonry (which they associate with Jose Martí), and socialism. They proclaim a political stance typical of the “Third Position”: outside both “communism” and capitalist “liberalism/libertarianism.”

The ultraconservative and racist Hispanism defended by Voluntad Nacional differs from the marginal and favorable Hispanic tendency found in Iberian countries. For Voluntad Nacional, racial mixing is the ultimate evil.

Among Cubans, there are other voices (or are they the same people?) advocating the “reincorporation” of our archipelago into the Spanish state.

What strikes me most is the response in Catholic social media groups, where Voluntad Nacional’s posts are neither deleted nor banned, and the comments focus on debating Afro-Cuban religions rather than opposing anti-Black racism and hostility toward people of mixed racial ancestry.

However, among the many commenters, Catholic priest Rubén Trinidad has stood out, intervening several times with well-reasoned responses opposing the hate group.

Perhaps they hope to attract minority segments, such as rockers who enjoy NS metal (National Socialist metal) or ultratraditionalist Catholics. But the proposal is serious, with a well-written manifesto that displays a certain degree of coherence. This is not a “make-believe political party” like those that sprang up following the recemt presentation of the Orthodox Liberal Party.

The manifesto may appeal to a certain segment of well-off Cuban youth who reject reggaeton culture (“reparterismo”), crime, and unruly street behavior (which are not the same thing). Such young people are already quite visible on Cuban streets.

But Voluntad Nacional’s racism, pro-Nazi aesthetics, and potential for totalitarian authoritarianism may prove a significant obstacle to gaining their acceptance.

Still, we should not forget that the principal social base of fascism and Nazism came from segments of the “middle class”: the obedient “respectable people.” It was only the more “mystical,” resentful, and organized groups that served as the “romantic” initiators of those movements, which later co-opted the petty bourgeoisie and other “disciplined” social sectors.

Catholic priest Rubén Trinidad has actively opposed the racist propaganda of Voluntad Nacional.

A clerical, racist, pro-Nazi far right may be too “troglodytic” for many enthusiasts of law-and-order totalitarianism. But the fact is that the fascist “garage sale” offers ideologies that do not profess racism, clericalism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, or “toxic” nostalgia.

That deserves another article. It is something worth considering in a country searching for a future, where so many people are desperate to march under the banners of a Bukele, the El Salvador president.

So far, the Voluntad Nacional Noticias page has not been censored by Facebook, a platform that is extremely strict about other types of content.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Thursday, November 19, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Thursday, November 19, 2026.

Trump Blasts ICC, Praises Presidents Xi and Putin at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit

Nov 19, 2026

The leaders of Russia, China and the United States — Presidents Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump — have wrapped up an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, with what Chinese media is calling a landmark “peace declaration.” The four-point plan calls for the three nations to reduce nuclear risks, increase oil refining, promote reforms to the United Nations and limit the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. This is President Trump.

President Donald Trump: “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I’ll be suggesting ways to protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction.”

President Putin faces an ICC warrant seeking his arrest for war crimes committed in Ukraine, including the unlawful transfer of children from Russian-occupied areas. Neither the U.S., nor China, nor Russia is a party to the Rome Statute that established the International Criminal Court.

During the summit, President Trump lavished praise on President Xi and referred to President Putin as “my friend.” That prompted Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to write on social media, “God, protect us from such friends.”

Democrats Nominate Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker as Progressives Dissent on Healthcare, Gaza and ICE

Nov 19, 2026

Image Credit: Reuters/Jonathan Ernst

On Capitol Hill, House Democrats voted 251-11 on Wednesday to nominate New York Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Jeffries is poised to make history as the first African American to fill the role. The vote came during a closed-door caucus meeting. Afterward, seven incoming Democratic congressmembers issued a joint statement explaining their opposition to Jeffries. They wrote, “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues.”

Israeli Tanks and Bulldozers Push Past Gaza’s “Yellow Line,” Further Displacing Palestinians

Nov 19, 2026

In Gaza, thousands of Palestinians have been forced to flee again after Israeli tanks and bulldozers pushed past the ceasefire’s “Yellow Line” on Wednesday and into Palestinian-held territory. Israeli troops operating east of the “Yellow Line” have gradually pushed the boundary westward and now occupy about two-thirds of Gaza’s territory, with 2 million Palestinians trapped in an increasingly narrow strip of land, most of them forced to live in tents. This is Salam Aql, a Palestinian woman who says she was displaced for the 15th time on Wednesday.

Salam Aql: “They ordered an evacuation, but we wanted to stay because we are exhausted from being displaced so many times. We are tired. I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started coming in. The boy was sitting in front of the tent and was hit in the leg. Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer. We are scared.”

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said the military is ready to take more land and turn the newly seized areas into permanent parts of Israel’s security zones. The Palestinian Health Ministry says Israeli forces have killed over 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza since last October’s so-called ceasefire.

Israel Extends “Administrative Detention” of Gaza Hospital Director Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya

Nov 19, 2026

An Israeli court has once again extended the detention of Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, by six months. Dr. Abu Safiya was seized by the Israeli military along with several of the hospital’s staff and patients during a raid on Kamal Adwan in December 2024. He’s been held without charge ever since. Dr. Abu Safiya’s legal team condemned the latest extension of his imprisonment as “neither a fair nor a transparent process.” The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has said that it has received information that Dr. Safiya “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care.”

World Court Finds Burma Committed Genocide Against Rohingya in 2017

Nov 19, 2026

Judges at the International Court of Justice have found that Burmese security forces committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during military operations nearly a decade ago. It’s the first time the court has held a nation accountable for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The ruling follows the 2017 military crackdown by government forces and ethnic Rakhine mobs that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. Ahead of today’s verdict, survivors hoped the ICJ would deliver justice and pave the way for them to return to their homeland. Hasina Khatun is a Rohingya refugee who was forced to flee her home when a mob burned her village to the ground.

Hasina Khatun: “To save our lives, we fled into the jungle, where we spent five days. Our children suffered from the cold, as we had no warm clothes, blankets or tarps. We endured immense hardship. Later, as the Myanmar military continued its attacks, we left the jungle and returned to the village before moving to the riverbank for shelter. But even there, we were not safe. We witnessed Myanmar soldiers taking away my husband and other men from the area right before our eyes.”

Venezuela Restores Military Ties with U.S., Months After Abduction of President Maduro

Nov 19, 2026

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise visit to Caracas on Wednesday, where he announced the U.S. and Venezuela have signed an agreement to restore military ties. Under the deal, the two countries will work together on areas such as joint training, intelligence sharing and border security. It’s Hegseth’s first visit to Venezuela since U.S. forces violently abducted former President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, National Assembly deputy Cilia Flores, back in January. The deal comes after months in which Washington has effectively controlled Venezuela’s oil sales. This is Defense Secretary Hegseth.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth: “In the last year, the country that previously sent its oil wealth to Cuba or to China from rigs built by Americans and Venezuelans has now signed a historic oil deal with the United States through the Department of War that is bringing energy dominance for the benefit of Americans and for Venezuelans for decades to come. In fact, this makes the Strait of Hormuz a nonfactor for the Western Hemisphere.”

Hegseth also traveled to Colombia Wednesday, where Colombia’s Trump-backed right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, turned down a U.S. plan for joint operations against drug cartels.

Anthropic Valued at $1.5 Trillion Ahead of Initial Public Offering

Nov 19, 2026

Anthropic has become the first major AI lab to become a publicly traded corporation, after completing what’s become the largest initial public offering in history. On Wednesday, Anthropic said it had raised a record $107.3 billion, giving it a valuation of more than $1.5 trillion. This comes after Anthropic warned in its IPO filings that, without proper safeguards, its technology poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Study Shows Advanced AI Models Flagged Civilian Infrastructure as Military Targets

Nov 19, 2026

Image Credit: Instagram/@morybndhaa

New research has shown that advanced AI models repeatedly flagged civilians and civilian infrastructure as military targets in simulated scenarios. Anthropic’s models performed worst overall, according to the study by the independent evaluation company Vals AI. In tests using real satellite imagery of southern Iran, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 misidentified the school in Minab — which was hit by a U.S.-Israeli attack in February, killing more than 120 children — as a military target in most hypothetical runs. The Pentagon has touted its heavy reliance on AI models in its war with Iran.

CISA Urges Users of Java to Immediately Patch a Security Flaw

Nov 19, 2026

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is urging users of the computer language Java to immediately patch a serious security flaw, which could allow hackers to take over a server without needing a password or login. The bug was discovered by the cybersecurity startup Calif on Tuesday, using advanced AI tools. Java has been described as the “backbone of the internet”; it runs on billions of devices across government agencies and is used by the majority of Fortune 500 companies.

DHS Secretary Mullin Grilled over FAA’s Nationwide Ground-Stop Order

Nov 19, 2026

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin faced a grilling by House Democrats on Wednesday over last Friday’s nationwide ground-stop order that paralyzed air travel, leading to over 18,000 canceled flights and 28,000 delays. This is Congressmember Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee.
