World.title: ODPEM employee was not PNP actor, says Opposition
World.content:
Dayton Campbell

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The People’s National Party (PNP) has strongly rejected claims that a senior Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) employee, who resigned amid an investigation into the handling of hurricane relief supplies, was affiliated with the Opposition party.

In a statement on Thursday, the PNP said a thorough review of its membership records found no evidence that the former employee had ever been a member of the party or acted on its behalf.

PNP General Secretary Dr Dayton Campbell described attempts to portray the former employee as a political saboteur as predictable but deeply concerning.

“That the Government and its surrogates would once again try to create a distraction and pass the blame for their failed relief effort is not surprising. What is shocking is the claim that one employee in logistics could have caused all of this on his own,” Campbell said.

Campbell argued that attributing the reported failures to a single employee raised serious questions about the Government’s oversight and management of the relief operation.

“If one employee could direct donor funds, keep containers sealed for a year, stop homes from reaching homeless families and allow food to spoil while mould ran rampant, then that speaks to the gross incompetence of a Government that failed not only to manage the relief effort but to manage its own staff,” he said.

He further questioned who authorised the transactions, who was responsible for supervising the employee, and when the minister with responsibility for ODPEM would be held accountable.

“Jamaicans who gave generously, and families still without a roof, deserve the truth. Who authorised these payments? Who supervised this employee? And when will the minister responsible accept accountability?” Campbell asked.

The Opposition has also called on Prime Minister Andrew Holness to provide a full account of ODPEM’s management of relief supplies following Hurricane Melissa, in light of the findings outlined in a report by the Auditor General’s Department. The October 2026 compliance audit identified several deficiencies, including 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables, 15 unopened containers not recorded in ODPEM’s inventory and approximately $780 million in shipments omitted from the agency’s donation schedules. READ: ODPEM audit finds expired food, insect-infested supplies and millions in unaccounted donations ODPEM has since responded to the findings, disputing claims of missing funds and housing units. READ: No missing houses, no missing money

The PNP maintained that the prime minister must answer for the agency’s operations, particularly given his decision to bring ODPEM under the Office of the Prime Minister immediately following Hurricane Melissa.

According to the Opposition, the findings point to serious failures in the management and distribution of disaster relief supplies.

“This can only be described as an abject failure of leadership and accountability by the prime minister,” Campbell said.

World.title: BOJ increases policy rate to 6.5% as inflation pressures persist
World.content:
The Bank of Jamaica in Kingston.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) has increased its policy rate for the second consecutive month, raising it by 50 basis points to 6.5 per cent, effective Thursday, as the central bank moves to contain persistent inflationary pressures.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the BOJ said its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) unanimously agreed to the increase amid concerns that inflation could remain above the bank’s target range until late 2027, signalling a more prolonged period of elevated prices than previously anticipated.

The policy rate represents the interest paid by the central bank to deposit-taking institutions on balances held in their current accounts at the BOJ.

The decision comes despite a slight easing in headline inflation, which declined to 8.2 per cent in October 2026 from 8.6 per cent in September, according to the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (STATIN). However, it said inflation remains significantly higher than the 2.9 per cent recorded in October 2025.

The BOJ attributed the continued inflationary pressures primarily to rising food prices, transportation costs and electricity rates compared with the previous year.

Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes agricultural food products and fuel, increased to 5.4 per cent in October, up from 5.3 per cent in September and 3.7 per cent in October 2025.

According to the central bank, the increase in core inflation suggests that higher agricultural and fuel prices are beginning to affect the cost of processed foods and certain services. However, relative stability in the foreign exchange rate has helped to moderate some of these pressures.

The MPC also highlighted continued uncertainty surrounding the inflation outlook, particularly due to ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

It warned that prolonged conflicts, coupled with worsening agricultural production conditions resulting from an intensifying El Niño phenomenon, could further drive inflation expectations and place additional pressure on consumer prices.

Despite these risks, the BOJ indicated that the policy rate increases implemented so far should be sufficient to support a timely return of inflation to its target range.

READ: BOJ increases policy rate to 6% to contain inflation

World.title: No missing houses, no missing money
World.content:
Director general, Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), Commander Alvin Gayle addressing a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew on November 18. (Photo: JIS)

THE Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) has challenged findings in the Auditor General’s report suggesting discrepancies in accounting for 200 prefabricated houses donated by the Republic of China, insisting that all units were received, handled, and stored appropriately.

Speaking at a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday, ODPEM Director General Commander Alvin Gayle sought to clarify the report’s findings, maintaining that all prefab houses received in the aftermath of last year October’s Hurricane Melissa were accounted for.

“I need to address something that has come to me in the media space, regarding the fact that only some 31 prefabricated houses that were donated to the GOJ [Government of Jamaica] by the Republic of China [have] been accounted for. This is not the case. What is the case is this — 200 houses were donated to the GOJ, they were received by the ODPEM, 169 of those units have been distributed and 31 remain in our custody,” said Gayle, using the moment to also declare that all monies channelled through the agency were accounted for.

His comments came in response to an Auditor General’s Report tabled in Parliament on Tuesday, investigating the agency’s management of resources received under the Hurricane Melissa relief initiative. It charged that ODPEM had several instances of inefficient receipt, storage and distribution of donated fixed assets.

The report said 200 prefabricated houses were received by the agency, valued at more than $139 million. That donation is represented among a revised ODPEM schedule in July 2026, reporting that 1,332 fixed assets valued at $443 million were donated to the Government of Jamaica by various countries and entities in support of Hurricane Melissa relief efforts.

However, the report claimed that ODPEM had provided warehouse receipt forms to support only 1,084 assets donated, while the remaining 248 were unseen.

“We have so far verified the existence of the 11 motor vehicles, 31 prefabricated houses, and the 353 chainsaws. We found no evidence that the internationally donated fixed assets were recorded in ODPEM’s inventory records or fixed asset register. Further, receipt forms were not provided for the remaining 248 assets noted on ODPEMs schedule,” the report said.

It also highlighted that ODPEM’s records bore no evidence of receipt forms for the prefab homes.

The audit report outlined that omitting donated assets from the fixed asset register risked creating inaccurate financial and asset records, and infringed on ODPEM’s ability to track, monitor, and maintain the assets entrusted to its care.

Acknowledging that risk, Gayle told the media briefing on Wednesday that ODPEM had initiated corrective action before the latest attorney general report was made public, including changes to leadership, logistics operations, and measures to improve warehouse management.

The director general said the agency has committed to strengthening its inventory management and operational capacity, pointing to a new standard of operating procedures introduced to fortify the receipt, recording, storage and distribution of relief supplies across its warehouses.

“To support these measures, ODPEM is upgrading its integrated management accounting system to improve the tracking of donated goods, strengthen audit trails and reduce reliance on manual processes. Existing warehouse and inventory policies are also being reviewed to ensure compliance with government financial and asset management requirements, while donated fixed assets are being reconciled with ODPEM’s asset register,” added Gayle.

Among its corrective measures, Gayle also pointed to ODPEM’s enlistment of the Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency to investigate internal discrepancies involving relief supplies and assets, including weaknesses in inventory management and warehouse controls. Gayle noted that ODPEM was fully cooperative with the ongoing investigation, and clarified that anyone found culpable of wrongdoing will be held accountable in accordance with the law and disciplinary procedures.

He further acknowledged the auditor general’s findings concerning the use of approximately $45 million from donated funds to facilitate the customs clearance of relief supplies consigned to third parties.

Gayle told the media briefing that such payments were used as an exceptional measure to facilitate the urgent clearance of humanitarian shipments and prevent delays in the delivery of relief supplies to affected communities, but admitted that they were unapproved for use in such circumstances.

“While the expenditure was undertaken in the context of the emergency response, ODPEM acknowledges that the payments fell outside the approved purpose of the donated funds and that the necessary financial controls and supporting documentation should have been maintained.

“Steps have since been taken to restore the funds to their designated account. Approval has been granted for an additional allocation, and the donation account will be reimbursed in full upon receipt of those funds,” he said.

The director general maintained, however, that all prefab homes were accounted for, with only 31 left for distribution.

“Two hundred were donated, 169 were distributed and 31 remain in our custody. And those 31 were seen by the attorney general as reported in the report,” he continued.

World.title: Tufton outlines measures to tackle shortcomings in the public health sector following worrying review
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton addressing the House of Representatives on Tuesday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

MINISTER of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton has pointed to a raft of measures that is being implemented to address the “systemic problems” besetting the country’s ailing health-care sector.

Tufton outlined the measures in Parliament on Tuesday after he tabled a report which detailed shocking shortcomings faced by patients including delayed admission and treatment, late diagnosis, lack of treatment, long waiting lists and discourteous staff. These were among more than 1,000 client (patient) complaints recorded at hospitals across Jamaica’s four Regional Health Authorities (RHAs) during the first quarter of the year.

The Jamaica Observer reported on the review findings on Wednesday, highlighting that just over 10 per cent of the complaints have been cleared up. The findings are contained in a 50-page Ministry of Health and Wellness Report titled, ‘Institutional Performance Review’ that was ordered by Tufton.

Tufton had vowed to be open and transparent when he ordered the review, and on Tuesday he said it was “self-imposed”.

“This is a new effort that we’re embarking on. I know it lends fodder for those who like to criticise because there’s a lot to criticise here,” Tufton said at the conclusion of his presentation, a seeming acknowledgement of the numerous deficiencies in the public health-care system.

Tufton pointed to the health ministry’s implementation of the accountability framework scorecard, which rates 13 public health entities against 18 governance and accountability indicators, and the client care connect, which managed 1,045 client feedback cases across the four RHAs. He suggested the review also offered a blueprint for the way forward.

By way of action, he said all regional health authorities have been mandated to implement plans to clear their backlog of open cases, and expand the QR Code feedback system launched by the South East Regional Health Authority so every patient can be heard and every concern tracked to solution.

The minister said that by January 2027, the portfolio score should reach at least 60 per cent and one in four client cases should be resolved within the quarter.

“By April 2027, no entity should remain in the critical category and at least half of all cases should be resolved,” he stated.

Beginning in the 2027/28 fiscal year, the service level agreements with each regional health authority will incorporate the framework indicators and targets for resolving patient concerns.

“We will follow the resources to ensure that primary healthcare and prevention gets adequate support at the level of the regional authorities,” Tufton assured.

He also committed to meet personally with board chairs and each will be asked to submit a 90-day recovery plan by November 30 and report monthly to the health ministry. “Where there is no measureable improvement by January, the performance of the board will be reviewed,” Tufton said.

For hospitals with the highest number of patient complaints, beginning with Cornwall Regional, St Ann’s Bay and Kingston Public, the ministry will meet with the board chairs, regional directors and chief executive officers and require reviews of the level of the individual departments. “This is to identify which units are struggling and why, and learn from those that are doing well,” said Tufton.

He highlighted that Cornwall Regional Hospital was doing well in a few areas. “Their physiotherapy department is excellent, their dialysis department is world class. They don’t keep patients in A&E, they triage them to wards. These are examples that we could teach many other institutions,” said the minister.

Regarding Cornwall Regional, he was careful to point out that the review was not a condemnation of an entire institution, but rather “it is recognising the weaknesses and correcting them”.

He told the Parliament that the review represents the first integrated assessment of two principal mechanisms through which the ministry measures organisational performance and accountability. Pointing out that government mechanisms were already in place to do that, Tufton explained that “we have come up with a format because we believe it agitates more aggressively for the value for money preposition”.

The accountability framework scorecard evaluated 13 public health entities against 18 governance, leadership and accountability indicators, while the client care connect tracked and monitored over 1,000 patient feedback cases across the four regional health authorities.

“Taken together, these instruments provide a comprehensive review of how well our institutions are governed, how effectively they respond to the public they serve, and where improvements are required, to strengthen performance and public trust,” said Tufton.

Significantly, the review found that no regional health authority was performing at the highest level on both governance and client (patient) experience.

“While some institutions demonstrate strong compliance on governance requirements, that strength is not always reflected in the patient experience,” Tufton acknowledged. He pointed to the North East Regional Health Authority as an example, noting that it achieved the highest governance score in the portfolio, yet it resolved less than one per cent of the client cases reported during the review period.

“That finding should give us pause because accountability is not measured by the number of reports that we produce, the meetings we hold, or the policies we approve. Accountability is measured by outcomes, it is measured by whether concerns are addressed, whether service is improved and whether citizens feel heard”.

Meanwhile, Tufton acknowledged that nearly 90 per cent of patient complaints remain unresolved and identified several recurring challenges across the public health portfolio. These relate primarily to management and client services. Monthly performance reporting was flagged as a weakness, so too the absence of timely audited financial statements; digital transformation initiatives were progressing too slowly, and inconsistent measurement of governance breaches was also present. Of particular concern is that complaint resolution mechanisms lacked the responsiveness that citizens expect and deserve.

Tufton argued that these are not merely administrative concerns. He argued that “unresolved complaints represent a missed opportunity to learn, delayed reports constrained decision-making, while weaknesses in governance increase risks, and inefficiency consumes resources that could be directed to patient care”.

World.title: Jahshii counts blessings on début EP N.U.M.B
World.content:
Dancehall artiste JahshiiContributed

For an artiste whose musical identity has long been rooted in resilience, learning to acknowledge his blessings is proving just as important for Jahshii as overcoming the obstacles.

The entertainer is therefore making room for gratitude, reflection, and personal growth with his forthcoming début EP, N.U.M.B (Never Underestimate Mi Blessings).

A seven-track collection, Jahshii says he hopes the project will encourage listeners to appreciate their own journeys while remaining determined to overcome life’s challenges.

Set for release on November 27, N.U.M.B represents a personal milestone for the Born Fighter deejay, who says the music draws heavily from his thoughts, lived experiences, and the lessons gathered along the way.

“The project means a lot to me. It’s seven songs with wah deh pan mi mind, me life experiences and dem thing deh. Das why me call it N.U.M.B (Never Underestimate Mi Blessings) because it’s all about acknowledging my blessings and not taking dem for granted,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Produced by Sweet Music Production and distributed worldwide through ONErpm, the EP finds Jahshii exploring themes of gratitude, faith, resilience, and self-awareness, while maintaining the motivational messaging that has become a recurring feature of his music.

For the artiste, the intention is not simply to entertain but to leave listeners with something they can carry beyond the music.

“Mi fans can expect motivation from it, self-awareness and ultimately determination. My music always have dat, messages fi get people fi stay determined. Memba a we say born fighter ennu, so this is a project weh means a lot and I hope the people take a lot of lessons from it when dem listen,” he added.

That fighting spirit runs through the project’s track list, which includes Glory, Manifest, Survivor, Learn Enough, Prove Dem Wrong, Pretend Teeth, and Powers.

The upcoming release comes amid a period of continued musical activity for Jahshii. In October, he released 4th Charge alongside UPSTATE, followed by Fighter, a collaboration with Carlostha1st and ikeed. His recent appearance at Appleton Estate Livewire in Clarendon has also kept him connected to Jamaica’s live entertainment circuit.

Beyond the music, Jahshii has increasingly spoken about the importance of using his platform to encourage young people and promote positive messages, sentiments that align with the project’s emphasis on personal development and determination. His reflections on fatherhood have also formed part of this broader outlook.

With N.U.M.B, however, the artiste is offering listeners something particularly personal: A collection of music inspired by what occupies his mind, the experiences that have shaped him and, perhaps most importantly, the blessings he refuses to take for granted.

As he prepares to deliver his first official EP, Jahshii is reminding listeners that being a fighter does not mean focusing solely on the struggles. Sometimes, it also means recognising how far you’ve come, appreciating what you have, and finding the determination to keep going.

World.title: Witness testifies to being paid ‘extra’ during Ruel Reid political campaign
World.content:
Former Education Minister Ruel Reid (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

A government employee in service to former Education Minister Ruel Reid testified Wednesday that he was paid extra money, between $30,000 and $330,000, for time spent working while Reid campaigned for a position as Member of Parliament (MP).

That series of payments, as well as who exactly bore responsibility for paying stipends to students engaged in a government programme at Caribbean Maritime University (CMU), were the subjects of testimony in the ongoing fraud trial of Reid and his co-accused when trial resumed at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court.

Two witnesses took the stand — one, an employee of the Universal Service Fund who was cross-examined, and the former government employee.

The court heard testimony from the man who had worked closely with Reid, of him spending significant amounts of time daily with the then minister between 2016 and 2019.

After identifying Reid in the courtroom, the witness detailed work trips around Kingston as well as other parishes that the then-minister had undertaken, including, in particular, St Ann.

When questioned by the prosecution on why Reid would have gone to St Ann, the witness told the court that at the time Reid was aspiring to become the Member of Parliament for St Ann North Western and would visit the area for graduations, funerals, etc.

At that time, the witness detailed that his base salary was just over $100,000 per month for work that often saw him putting in extended hours.

The witness testified about a conversation with Reid where the then-senator expressed concern about the long hours the witness and another employee were spending alongside him as he worked towards his aspiration to become MP, indicating that he wanted to assist them with giving him their undivided attention.

“So he said he would speak to the PS [permanent secretary] about assisting us with a stipend,” the witness explained.

He further testified that the stipend, paid directly to his account around eight or nine times, started out at $30,000 before being raised to $60,000, then $100,000, then after looking back at his statement, added that it went up to $120,000.

He also indicated that another one-off payment of $330,000 for use of his vehicle was made.

The witness also testified that he had deposited money on behalf of Reid to different banks.

The USF employee, on the other hand, was grilled by Hugh Wildman, who represents former head of CMU Fritz Pinnock, on an agreement between CMU and the USF regarding the Technology Advancement Programme (TAP) financed by the USF and partly carried out by CMU.

The witness gave testimony that the programme targeted unattached youth, meaning unemployed young people who were out of school, and indicated that CMU was engaged to carry out a three-month teaching component of the course.

She maintained, after several questions from Wildman, that under the agreement there was no provision for stipend or financial support to be provided to students by CMU.

She added that there was, however, a $10,600 weekly stipend to be provided to students in the programme, paid bi-weekly, entirely by the USF.

Wildman suggested that the witness’s response that USF had paid the students was incorrect, to which she disagreed.

The witness testified that in order to be paid, the students would have had to provide their banking information, and acknowledged that not all students in the cohort had bank accounts at the start of the programme.

Wildman asked multiple questions of the witness concerning CMU’s role, if any, in the payment of stipends, questioning whether the school had filled the gap for students who did not have bank accounts at the start of the programme, to which the witness responded, “I do not know if CMU had to fill the gap.”

Wildman went on to query whether the employee knew if CMU had submitted vouchers to the USF for reimbursement for paying stipends to the students, to which she responded, “To my knowledge, CMU did not pay stipends to the students.”

The attorney suggested to the witness that CMU paid a $10,600 stipend to students who were without banking information, an arrangement that only ended after the students were able to provide banking information, to which the witness responded that she had no knowledge of that.

He went on to ask the witness about national coordinators engaged by CMU to assist with the TAP programme, suggesting to her that coordinators paid stipends to the students on behalf of CMU.

Senior Parish Judge Sanchia Burrell intervened initially but eventually allowed Wildman to proceed, putting his suggestion to the witness, to which she said, “I disagree with your suggestion.”

When Wildman suggested to her that the coordinators would submit bills to CMU for repayment of money given to students, the judge intervened, indicating to the witness she did not have to answer.

During re-examination, the prosecution asked the witness whether the students who did not have bank accounts were eventually paid by USF, she responded that once their banking information was shared, USF paid all stipends due to those participants from the beginning of the programme up to when they provided their banking details.

Testimony is expected to continue tomorrow in the matter in which the defendants Reid; Pinnock; Reid’s wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle Reid; and Jamaica Labour Party Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence are accused of participating in a scheme that siphoned off $25 million from the Ministry of Education and the CMU.

World.title: FULL ‘SPEID’
World.content:
Jamaica winger Renaldo Cephas (left) evades Mexico goalkeeper Raul Rangel and gets through on goal but didn’t convert the opportunity during their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final second-leg football match at the BBVA stadium in Monterrey, Mexico, on Tuesday night. (Photo: AFP)

Despite the Reggae Boyz missing out on the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals, interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid says there’s no shame in losing to Mexico and believes they deserved more from the contest.

Jamaica’s hopes of advancing were dashed as Mexico advanced 3-3 on aggregate on the away goal rule after their 1-0 second-leg quarter-final defeat at the BBVA Stadium in Monterrey on Tuesday.

Jamaica only needed a draw to book their spot in the last four but were unable to hold onto their first-leg advantage as Jesus Corona found the all-important goal in the 35th minute.

It was a tough pill to swallow for the Boyz who, at one point, held a 3-0 aggregate lead at the National Stadium in Kingston on Saturday.

Speid was pleased with his team’s effort but says they fell short offensively in the second leg.

“I always thought we had to score a goal coming to Mexico, I thought we were one goal short coming from Jamaica,” he said. “But it’s Mexico, the number 13 ranked team in the world. They went through on [away goals] so that’s a positive.

“I thought we should have kept that lead and made it much harder for Mexico but I still believe even if they were two goals behind us, they would still have put pressure on us. I just thought we needed to score a goal no matter the result.”

Winger Renaldo Cephas had Jamaica’s best opportunity of the game when he went past goalkeeper Raul Rangel, who was well off his line. However, he was unable to convert as he was caught by Erik Lira.

Cephas, who scored in the first leg, admits he should have been more efficient on Tuesday.

“I think we should have put away the game from the first half.” he said. “I got two chances and if you don’t score, they will score — this is football.”

However, Cephas says the team deserves credit for pushing Mexico to the limit.

“Mexico are a very good team, so we just came out and tried our best.” he said. “We stuck to the plan and fought to the end. I can say congrats to the boys on everything, we stood and fought but it is what it is.”

Jamaica have yet to beat Mexico away from home but Speid doesn’t believe the conditions or atmosphere played a role this time.

This is the third time we’ve played in Mexico since this year so we’re used to that, it didn’t affect us in any way,” he said. “Mexico were very good but I thought we fought very well and got the better chances and probably should have scored even one.”

Mexico Head Coach Rafa Marquez got his first win on his sixth attempt since being appointed in July after the FIFA World Cup. He was relieved that the team improved on their first-leg display.

“Their attitude and concentration were better,” he said. “The team made a physical effort, they were more intense, and in the final minutes, some important players got tired, but those who came on put in a good effort. We’re still lacking in finishing, though, because we create a lot of chances but we don’t convert them.

“I’m happy because we achieved what we were looking for, we sought our first victory. It was a great first half, we had many chances but we couldn’t finish them, we had to improve, the team gave its best effort.”

The result means Jamaica will not only miss out on a semi-final clash with the USA but will now have to play in a Concacaf Gold Cup Qualifier, as they had to advance to the competition last year. They will face Aruba over two legs in March for a spot in the Gold Cup, set for June 17 to July 11.

The Reggae Boyz, however, will meet the USA in a different setting next month when the two teams clash in an international friendly at Inter Miami Stadium in Florida.

World.title: Creativity Shines @ Alexander’s Restaurant
World.content:
Courtleigh Hotel & Suites Executive Chef Ainsley Lambie presents a selection of dishes from Alexander’s lunch and dinner menu. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

In the bustling heart of New Kingston, Alexander’s Restaurant at the Courtleigh Hotel & Suites remains a standout gem for discerning palates. Consistently reimagining traditional fare, the eatery pairs rich Jamaican heritage with inventive modern twists. Thursday Food returned on Monday, November 2, having been wowed the week before by the new six-month old lunch and dinner offerings.

The menu options entice right from the start with offerings such as the Shrimp Alexander — sautéed shrimp tossed in a coconut red curry sauce and topped with an Asian cucumber slaw — alongside salads like the island-spiced tandoori chicken and apple, or the baked goat cheese tart salad. Pescatarians are well-catered to with standouts such as the Jamaican Blue Mountain coffee-rubbed salmon and the plantain-crusted snapper. However, the true stars are the new bowls, featuring boneless oxtail with plantain, as well as a miso coconut grilled chicken. Add the Beach Lander — a surf-and-turf of grilled lobster and beef tenderloin with a rum cream velouté and jerk butter, served with vegetables and sweet potato au gratin — and deciding what to order becomes a delightful challenge.

Fresh ingredients and culinary creativity remain the core philosophy of the menu, according to Courtleigh Hotel & Suites Executive Chef Ainsley Lambie.

“One of the things we truly push here is authentic ingredients — like yam, sweet potato, and fresh ginger — sourced

from the parishes of St Elizabeth, Westmoreland and St Ann. We have a lot of returning guests, so we didn’t want to change too much, but we wanted to incorporate ingredients that haven’t been utilised as much while cutting down on imported items,” Lambie shared with Thursday Food.

Anchoring that creative shift is the boneless oxtail and plantain bowl, which has quickly emerged as one of the menu’s standout hits.

“The dish was designed to evoke a traditional Sunday dinner, packing every quintessential element — oxtail, coleslaw, fried plantain, and avocado — into one hearty bowl. And because the oxtail is boneless, it is an easier eat,” Lambie noted.

The Shrimp Alexander, a familiar fixture on the menu, has received a revamp. It is now served with a refreshing cucumber and seaweed-infused salad, finished with Scotch bonnet peppers and tomatoes.

Initial feedback on the new menu has been favourable, especially among Alexander’s most devoted patrons.

“The feedback has been excellent! We’re fortunate to have such a loyal following, and watching our guests enjoy themselves has been the real highlight,” Lambie said.

Driven by the continuous desire to experiment with island-grown ingredients, the new menu showcases Lambie’s fearless approach to pleasing every palate.

“There’s a distinct uniqueness to every dish we create. While our offering is diverse, we thrive on flexibility — if a guest craves something custom, we will happily prepare it,” Lambie said.

Positive feedback on the new menu is just the beginning for Lambie, who is already setting his sights on new creations for 2027.

“We already have several exciting dishes in the pipeline, including a goat cheese, apple, and avocado tart that we’re thinking of adding to the board. We’re also looking forward to introducing a sweet chilli fried lobster, as well as a honey-glazed salmon,” Lambie said. “We strive to stand out in everything we do. We innovate, and we take pride in owning that creative identity across the board.”

Alexander’s Restaurant

Courtleigh Hotel & Suites

85 Knutsford Boulevard, Kingston 5

Opening Hours: Lunch 12:00 pm to 3:00 pm daily

Dinner 6:00 pm to 10:30 pm

Tel: 876-929-9000

World.title: How to watch the UK-EU summit like a pro
World.content:
On tech, British firms are concerned that they could be shut out of parts of the EU public administration market because of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) and its new sovereignty requirements. They’ve lobbied hard for reassuring language in talks, both with the negotiators working on the law and with those drafting the joint statement.

On health, the U.K. and EU are looking to strike a deal to tackle medicine shortages by sharing intelligence on supply disruptions and stockpiles. As Brussels steps up efforts to manage medicine shortages across the bloc, Britain risks being left out of the increasingly joined up system. Closer cooperation could help both sides “avoid procurement battles” for limited stocks and “tit-for-tat export bans, as happened during the pandemic,” said Mark Dayan, Brexit lead at the Nuffield Trust.

One area the statement will definitely cover is the question of tuition fees. EU countries want European students studying at British universities to qualify for lower domestic fees, as they did before Brexit.

The U.K. is open to the idea but wants, in turn, assurances its businesses won’t be hit by new EU Made in Europe rules. Brussels says it can’t give those assurances yet, so the statement is likely to include a compromise to delay talks by up to six months. Only then will we find out how much lower tuition fees might get.

Another key question is whether the implementation of the agri-food, emissions trading and youth mobility deals will be contingent on a successful outcome for tuition fee talks — which some member countries have been pushing for. This will be determined by the wording of the final statement, but the latest version does not make this link explicit.

What does Burnham want to talk about?

Since Labour Party conference in September, Burnham has talked up building a closer relationship with the EU — ditching some of the caution that characterized his predecessor’s approach to European relations.

World.title: The web is held together by volunteers. AI could tear it apart.
World.content:
The PHP Foundation, which was only established in 2021 despite the coding language itself existing since the early 1990s, has two members of staff and 13 contractors. “Having very few individuals responsible for some key piece of infrastructure is just problematic,” said Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member.

Out of office

Many tools like PHP have their origins in the 1990s, when foundational software and programming languages were developed in the messy, community-minded early days of the web. Those that worked well or were useful were gifted as a common good, picked up by other software developers and became building blocks for a vast number of digital technologies on which governments, critical infrastructure and citizens now rely.

Many open-source software libraries form the basis for widely used software like Android. Facebook was originally built using PHP, and household names like Spotify, Etsy and Wikipedia are just some top destinations that still use it as the basis for their services and websites.

The homepage of the PHP website is seen in Singapore on Oct. 22, 2026. | Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images

When cybersecurity agencies and companies issued an urgent warning in October that there were major flaws in PHP identified with the help of AI, and that they should either update their systems or shut them down, it was a public revelation that the architecture upon which our digital world relies is almost comically fragile.

Adermann explained that it is common for people who have worked on a PHP project for years in their spare time — developing a level of specific expertise that’s very hard to replicate — to duck out when they start families or can no longer find spare time.

That became especially apparent during the process of fixing the recent PHP flaws: One person involved in pushing out technical updates had a scheduled medical procedure and “was simply not available,” he said. “It was like, ‘okay, how do we figure it out, who can even do this now?’”

World.title: After Putin talks, Trump tells Europe it could save lives and cash if Ukraine war ends
World.content:
Momentum for a peace deal has grown in recent weeks after a flurry of diplomatic activity and intensive talks in Europe, Russia and the Middle East. Trump’s meeting in China with Xi and Putin alarmed some of Ukraine’s allies and raised fears that the U.S. president could be won over to the Russian argument that Ukraine and its European supporters have prolonged the war, which began with Russia’s 2022 invasion.

Some of the officials familiar with the call described Trump’s tone as strongly critical of Europe’s ongoing support for Kyiv, while others said he was just communicating in his usual forthright style. One person briefed on the call said the president had merely emphasized how much all countries could save if the war ended and Europe no longer had to pay for aid to Ukraine.

A U.S. official briefed on the call said any suggestion that Trump had told leaders to stop funding Ukraine was “not accurate.” The president was making his long-held view clear that he “wants to bring this conflict to a close,” the official said.

A White House official rejected characterizations of the call as critical of Europeans, saying: “President Trump called into the Coalition of the Willing meeting today and was super upbeat about the prospects for peace and praised the leaders in the room. The President emphasized that the war is extremely costly in terms of human life and financing, and everyone should all be striving for peace because it will save lives and money that can be invested in our countries’ own defenses and prosperity.”

Trump’s argument was that if the war ends, European governments could be spending their money on rebuilding Ukraine or on their own people, the U.S. official said. The president sounded “optimistic” about the prospects for peace and praised the European leaders on the call for their efforts, the official added.

When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting in Berlin whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war.

World.title: Britain shouldn’t rush to a second Brexit referendum, say pro-EU Lib Dems
World.content:
There would be “an expectation” from the public a referendum would be held if Britain was to seek to rejoin because it is the way Britain left, he said: “The public would rightly ask the very difficult questions of a political party that did seek to make that move without going back to them.”

The debate around rejoining the bloc has fired up campaigners who backed Brexit a decade ago. They argue another referendum would again dominate time and attention in Westminster.

Pinkerton conceded it is an “entirely fair criticism” and “one of the reasons that I wouldn’t necessarily want to trigger that process right now, because I think there are so many domestic reforms that we need to be getting on with too.”

He is optimistic Britain could remain outside the euro and Schengen area, though warned there’s “no guarantee” the previous rebate negotiated under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s could be achieved again.

Tackling the populists

Pinkerton said he is not concerned Burnham’s willingness to discuss Britain’s ties to the bloc will leave the Liberal Democrats outflanked by Labour on the issue.

“I look at the whites of the eyes of so many of his own MPs and I can see that there’s not an appetite for him to go any further than the light flirtation that he’s been engaged in over the last few weeks,” he said.

Pinkerton said he is “deeply uneasy” about the prospect of the far right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen winning next year’s French presidential election as well as the recent state election performance of the Alternative for Germany, but said that shouldn’t “change our ambition” to be far closer to Europe as a vehicle for improving economic growth, something he argues could help neutralize populism.

“We’re not making our propositions through a blind adherence to the idea that Europe is entirely virtuous and has no flaws,” Pinkerton said.

World.title: Startups call on Commission to salvage or scrap EU Inc proposal
World.content:
They also sent a joint letter to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen earlier this week.

The European Commission published its proposal for a so-called 28th regime, also known as EU Inc., earlier this year, to harmonize how founders can incorporate a company and reward their personnel, so that startups can scale more easily across the bloc.

The scheme was seen as a challenge to the U.S. state of Delaware, which is known for its flexible incorporation laws.

Lobby groups now say that EU capitals have rolled back key provisions, such as the freedom to set up shop in any EU country and simplified insolvency rules. With their demand to withdraw and submit a new proposal, the groups hope that EU capitals will rethink their position.

“This is an opportunity for Member States to reconsider their positions and make sure EU Inc. delivers on its original promise,” said Simon Schaefer, president of Startups for Europe.

Jeannette zu Fürstenberg, managing director of General Catalyst, a fund that backed leading European companies such as Helsing and Legora, also criticized the EU Inc. proposal as it stands.

World.title: Video: EU-Gesundheitskommissar wird aus Protest gegen Pestizidregeln mit „Asche“ beworfen
World.content:
Die Kommission stellte das Omnibus-Gesetz als Möglichkeit vor, den Rückstau bei der Zulassung von Pestiziden abzubauen und den Landwirten das Leben zu erleichtern. Viele zivilgesellschaftliche Gruppen lehnen es jedoch entschieden ab.

Mehr als 2.000 Wissenschaftler haben einen Brief unterzeichnet, in dem sie fordern, den Vorschlag so lange auszusetzen, bis eine unabhängige Folgenabschätzung durchgeführt wurde. Die Verbraucherorganisation Foodwatch hat die Angelegenheit vor den Europäischen Bürgerbeauftragten gebracht und der Kommission Verwaltungsmissstände vorgeworfen. Außerdem haben Nichtregierungsorganisationen zahlreiche Proteste organisiert.

Mehr als 300 Nichtregierungsorganisationen – darunter Umweltverbände, Imkerverbände und Gruppen von Pestizidopfern sowie Ärzte und Wissenschaftler – aus 25 europäischen Ländern wollen sich am 24. November um 14 Uhr vor dem Europäischen Parlament in Straßburg versammeln, um ihre Unzufriedenheit mit dem Sammelgesetz zum Ausdruck zu bringen.

Video, aufgenommen am 19. November 2026 im „The Hotel“ in Brüssel. | Emma Pirnay/POLITICO

Várhelyi wischte sich sichtlich verärgert den Staub ab und fuhr wie geplant mit seiner Rede fort.

„Was für Leute seid ihr denn?“, bemerkte er. „Wie ich schon sagte: Guten Morgen. Ich bin ein bisschen überrascht, dass sie es wagen, im Namen der Krebsopfer die Asche der Verstorbenen zu verstreuen.“

„Das übertrifft alles, was wir uns hätten vorstellen können. Es tut uns leid“, sagte Elisabetta Zanon, Leiterin der European Cancer Organisation, vor dem Publikum.

World.title: Nigel Farage is back in Brussels
World.content:
Farage will attack that deal but go further to attack Burnham’s ambition of getting closer to the EU as negative and backwards looking, according to his spokesperson.

Instead, the veteran Brexiteer will try to paint a vision of an optimistic future of Britain outside the bloc — in stark contrast to how the U.K. public feels about the country's current status.

But before the speeches, Farage will be visiting the European Parliament on Thursday and Friday. It’ll be his first time back in the building since 2020, his spokesperson said.

Back then, just two days before Brexit was implemented after protracted negotiations, Farage received a final reprimand, for waving Union Jacks against the flag-bearing rules.

Farage used that final speech to say the looming formal departure from the EU, at 11 p.m. on Jan 31, 2020, was “the point of no return — once we’ve left we are never coming back.”

Whether that is true or not appears more up in the air today than it has done in the decade since the Brexit referendum.

World.title: Présidentielle : pourquoi les youtubeurs ne veulent pas être régulés comme les télés
World.content:
“On se demande comment une règle de pluralisme qui a été créée pour répondre à la rareté des fréquences télé et radio sur la TNT peut s’appliquer à des chaînes que vous pouvez créer en quinze secondes aujourd’hui, avec une adresse mail, sur YouTube ou TikTok”, pose d’entrée de jeu Gaspard G, qui a rejoint l’équipe de l’Umicc en 2024.

Et l’influenceur de poursuivre : “On ne peut pas programmer, à une certaine heure [comme le font les chaînes de télévision], un bout de leurs interventions pour respecter les règles de temps de parole et de pluralisme. Moi, par exemple, je sors une ou deux vidéos par mois.”

Les inquiétudes sont donc fortes du côté des créateurs à l’idée de devoir recevoir tout l’échiquier politique. “Tous les politiques ne voient pas l’intérêt de passer sur nos chaînes…”, souligne Gaspard G. Et pour cause : les candidats n’ont aucune certitude de faire des grosses audiences quand bien même l’influenceur qui reçoit est une star. “La vidéo sur Jean-Luc Mélenchon a fait 1 million, celle sur Gabriel Attal 250 000 vues. Mais je n’ai pas d’impact là-dessus, c’est l’algorithme qui décide et qui répond lui-même à une logique commerciale.”

Pour limiter la casse, la déléguée générale de l’Umicc a pris les devants et fait quelques suggestions au régulateur. “Au lieu de cibler idiotement la masse des 200 000 créateurs de contenu en France, on pourrait peut-être s'intéresser à ceux qui ont une influence sociétale”, estime-t-elle. Comprendre : seraient concernés les influenceurs dont 30% des contenus, sur les douze derniers mois, traitent de sujets d’intérêt public et qui ont touché au moins 5% de la population. Deux critères cumulatifs qui pourraient bien trouver leur place dans la recommandation — non contraignante — du régulateur, qui s’appliquera en principe aux créateurs à partir du mois de mars.

“Ils sont dans une logique de discussion. Ils se veulent hyper rassurants, concède Bénédicte de Kersauson. Mais on sait très bien que c'est glissant… Donc on reste vigilant”, conclut-elle.

“La creator economy mérite mieux”

World.title: 10,000 identical inflatable rings raise questions over Ceuta migrant crossing
World.content:
A police report points to possible logistical preparations ahead of the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta at the end of July, after detecting the use of thousands of inflatable rings of the same model, black with a printed design, during the crossing at Tarajal beach.

 

The officers believe that "it does not seem possible" for the migrants themselves to have bought the rings directly from shops or online, as there would not have been enough stock to meet a sudden purchase of thousands of units on the same day without prior planning or orders.

The analysis, based on aerial images and photographs from different points along the Tarajal border, suggests that a single large batch had been purchased in advance, then distributed at specific locations and widely used during the crossing.

Images on social media and in the press do not make it possible to clearly identify points of sale. However, some migrants interviewed said they had bought the rings in the Moroccan town of Fnideq, while others said they had acquired them on Tarajal beach itself, before entering the breakwater.

The judge requests information on the rescues

Judge María Tardón, who is handling the case at the National Court, has asked the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Tarifa for information about the rescues carried out on 30 and 31 July, when the mass crossing took place, including the times, locations, identities of the people rescued and the units involved.

The magistrate has also asked the organisation Hazte Oír, which has joined the proceedings as a popular prosecution, for photographs and videos of a Ford Focus with a Spanish number plate in order to identify its two occupants.

According to the complaint, the vehicle was parked on the Tarajal breakwater in the early hours of 30 July and its occupants provided assistance to only some of the people who were crossing.

World.title: Nobel economist Joseph Stiglitz deems youth protests across Europe 'legitimate'
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets in France, Denmark, Italy and Spain in recent weeks to speak out against rising living costs, housing crisis and poor pay.

 

Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz said he understands the youth's worries and that their concerns were "legitimate".

"Part of the problem [...] is inequality across generations," said Stiglitz.

"They can't afford housing. They're not given the education that would make them productive. AI is giving rise to new sets of anxieties," he said.

The former World Bank chief economist said that the world the next generation is inheriting is filled with uncertainties linked to rising inequality, climate change and other issues.

Protests have filled European countries' streets in recent months, fuelled by widening wealth gaps. "I think those are legitimate complaints," said Stiglitz. These pressures drive fear within younger generations that they may never match the living standards their parents enjoyed.

'I pay €460 for 5 square metres'

Last week, hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in Spain for the first nationwide 24-hour strike since 2012.

Marching through pouring rain, protesters in Madrid carried signs chanting "we have no home", speaking out against rising living costs.

"People work a lot, and it isn't enough to pay the rent, to pay for a house," said Paula Diaz, a 25-year-old theatre technician who lives with her parents.

Protestors block Madrid's Gran Via main avenue during a nationwide general strike in Spain, Wednesday, 11 November 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Arturo Leon, 24, is a student in Barcelona and pays €460 a month for a 5-square-metre bedroom in a shared apartment with four others. "We do not have a contract, and there are lots of things in the flat which are broken, but the landlord refuses to fix," he told Al Jazeera.

Sanchez called this month's election, initially scheduled for 2027, after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the demonstrations.

'We don't want mice in our schools'

In Italy, thousands of students called for more school funding as they marched, set up tent camps and occupied schools to make their demands heard.

"We don't want windows falling on our heads, and we don't want mice in our schools. We want clean buildings, and I want to live in a better world than this one," said Sofia Cataldi, a 16-year-old Roman student.

This call for a better life sounds like an echo of student protests that have been rumbling in France since the beginning of September.

Students chant during a demonstration demanding increased education funding in Paris, Tuesday, 10 November 2026. AP Photo/Teresa Suarez

"The state of schools, the state of hospitals, staffing levels in schools and hospitals, the way things are getting worse and worse across all public services — these are issues that really resonate with us," said Aurelane Thos, a 38-year-old nurse.

"We're stressed about our studies, but when you have a bunch of cops in front of the high school every morning, you only want to keep protesting," said Mathilde, a 17-year-old pupil in Paris.

Stiglitz backs taxing the rich

The 83-year-old American economist has been a long-time advocate of taxing the ultra-wealthy. He argues that governments would have room to respond to social demands if they were willing to raise more revenue.

"There is so much money at the top that even a small tax rate on the top generates a huge amount of money," he said.

Stiglitz backs proposals such as the suggestion by French economist Gabriel Zucman for a minimum levy of around two per cent of fortunes above €100 million.

There is so much money at the top that even a small tax rate on the top generates a huge amount of money Joseph Stiglitz Nobel Prize-winning economist

Such tax revenues would allow more money to be spent on public services and should be levied at the European Union level. He argues the bloc's free movement of people and capital made tax avoidance easier.

But the Columbia University professor warned that tax alone won't solve Europe's challenges. European countries should rethink parts of their public spending and implement more flexible pension systems that reflect longer life expectancy, while taking into account physically demanding jobs.

"Students may not fully understand," Stiglitz said, that beyond the usual budget pressures, "this is a particularly difficult time."

World.title: Turkish court blocks jailed Istanbul mayor from 2028 presidential race
World.content:
A Turkish court ruled on Thursday that jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu's university diploma was invalid, preventing him from running in the 2028 presidential election, according to media reports.

 

Imamoglu, considered one of the strongest opposition challengers to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, was arrested in March 2025 on corruption charges that his party says are politically motivated.

Turkish law requires presidential candidates to hold a valid university degree.

The State Council's decision to reject his appeal over his diploma is the latest legal setback for Imamoglu, a member of the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). He was elected Istanbul mayor in 2019, defeating Erdogan's preferred candidate.

The CHP later nominated Imamoglu as its presidential candidate.

Arrest sparks widespread protests

His arrest on 19 March 2025 on multiple corruption charges triggered widespread protests. Critics saw the move as an attempt to remove one of Erdogan's main political rivals.

A day before his arrest, Istanbul University cancelled Imamoglu's degree, claiming it had been obtained fraudulently.

Police raided his home hours later and detained him. He was subsequently jailed on the same day the CHP officially named him its presidential candidate.

A supporter of Turkey's main opposition Republican People's Party or (CHP) holds a poster of jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu during a rally, in Istanbul, March 18, 2026. AP Photo

Imamoglu defends his university degree

The diploma case went to trial in September 2025. Imamoglu told the court he had been admitted to a university in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is recognised only by Turkey, when he was 18.

He said he later transferred to Istanbul University to complete his degree, following the rules set by Turkey's Council of Higher Education (YOK).

Imamoglu defended the transfer, saying he had followed the university's application process.

"I saw the announcement for a horizontal transfer to Istanbul University, met the requirements, applied and was accepted, studied and graduated," he said.

World.title: Europe Tonight : NATO Secretary General’s Head of Policy Planning debriefs the latest APEC talks
World.content:
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping issued what they describe as a ‘joint declaration on peace’ after historical trilateral talks in China, saying nuclear wars must never be fought. The Russian President also says he has invited European envoys to Moscow to clarify their position ahead of peace negotiations.

 

To discuss the matter Euronews' evening show Europe Tonight welcomed Fabrice Pothier, head of policy planning in the private office of the Secretary General of NATO, he also oversees the review of current and future strategic policy issues facing NATO.

Discover the full conversation in the video above.

World.title: US defence secretary Pete Hegseth lands in Ecuador on Latin America anti-narcotics tour
World.content:
United States Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth landed in Ecuador on Thursday as part of his South American tour, after brief visits to Colombia and Venezuela, where he pledged to eliminate and defeat narcoterrorists.

 

Ecuador's president, Daniel Noboa, is ideologically aligned with the Trump administration and has driven a growing militarisation of the country's cities, in line with other conservative populist leaders in the region.

Hegseth's trip to Latin America comes after an attempt by United States lawmakers, including a Republican representative, to remove him from office, prompted by the war against Iran and by air strikes without legal backing on several vessels suspected of drug trafficking over the past year, causing the deaths of more than 200 people.

The Defence Secretary will later make a brief visit to Honduras, according to the country's press office, where he will meet at a nearby air base with Nasry Asfura, another leader allied with Trump. This is the Pentagon chief's first official visit to South America, which has included a meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez.

As part of his trip to Venezuela, Hegseth announced that he would increase military cooperation with the post-Maduro regime and promised to hunt down drug traffickers.

World.title: At least one dead and dozens missing after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal en route to Spain
World.content:
At least one person has died, and dozens more are missing after a boat carrying around 100 migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal while attempting to reach Spain, local officials have said.

 

The latest incident, which is thought to have happened in the early hours of Wednesday morning, comes amid a surge in departures towards the Canary Islands, with more than 11,000 people reaching the archipelago in the first half of November alone.

The boat, described by some sources as “rickety”, sank off the coast of Yenne, a town south of the Senegalese capital, Dakar.

“The accident happened around 3 a.m.," said Ousmane Sène, secretary general of the Yenne mayor's office.

“When we went to the scene, we saw the boat on the shore.”

Sène added that firefighters recovered one body while police arrested one survivor.

According to other survivors, there were around 100 people on board at the time it sank.

Sène confirmed that two other bodies were also recovered in nearby villages, but it’s not clear if they were people who drowned in this particular incident.

Recently, Senegalese coastal areas have become major departure points for migrants attempting the treacherous sea journey to Europe. Many of them are hoping to reach Spain’s Canary Islands, an archipelago off West Africa which lies more than 1,000 kilometres south of the European mainland.

According to Spanish government figures, more than 11,000 migrants reached the Canaries in the first half of November – that number was more than half the total for all of 2025.

This week’s sinking comes shortly after a disaster which saw at least 39 people die after a migrant boat sank near the town of Kébémer in northern Senegal.

Senegalese authorities are making efforts to crack down on people attempting the dangerous migration route and have made dozens of arrests.

On Wednesday, the country’s navy said it had “rescued” over 1,400 migrants at sea in just 48 hours.

Also on Wednesday, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye spoke out against the resurgence of migrant departures toward Europe and called for strengthened controls along Senegal's coasts, too.

“The acceleration and complexity of irregular migration demonstrate the urgency for the government to intensify... the diligent and efficient implementation of public policies concerning youth, education, vocational training, youth employment and entrepreneurship, as well as the economic empowerment of women,” said Faye.

World.title: Macron backs reopening 'the question' of Ukraine's NATO accession
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron backed "reopening the question" of Ukraine's NATO membership on Thursday, while urging Kyiv's allies to do the "maximum" to provide it with the necessary air defence systems.

 

"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," said Macron, following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, co-chaired by France and the UK.

Macron stated that Ukraine’s NATO accession had been set aside in early 2022, albeit in a "completely different" context.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Western allies ruled out Kyiv's NATO's membership for the short-term, fearing that admitting a country at war with Russia could trigger a direct NATO–Russia confrontation under Article 5.

Following two day US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared that US negotiators had floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.

He said that Kyiv was not prepared to concede territory, but said that "specific security guarantees" were being discussed with NATO and the EU.

"The question arises, including for us Europeans, of what happens the day after, because Ukraine will be a country with a very well-equipped and sizeable army. For our long-term security, Ukraine’s membership of NATO makes sense", stated Macron.

Macron's remarks came hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral in China.

Zelenskyy added that if Western countries laid out assurances, he would consult Ukrainian society on the proposition, saying he had “no right to make this decision alone”.

World.title: New regional security architecture will also benefit Europe, Pakistani FM tells Euronews
World.content:
Regional peace across the Middle East should now be established through a special mechanism, Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar told Euronews, as “we all have to see the new security architecture (...) and the consequences on the global economy” beyond the Gulf region.

 

In a wide-ranging exclusive interview in Islamabad for Euronews’ World Conversation programme, Dar outlined the complex diplomatic engagements led by the major regional powers, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and multiple countries in the region with Europe “towards bringing peace and stability to the region which will be effective and beneficial to the entire globe.”

Dar called the mutual defence Mecca Pact, signed by Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia in August for their collective and individual security and defence, a possible “beginning of the regional security architecture” because, in his view, it will help not only the region but countries beyond it too.

Pakistan’s foreign minister said the UK, France and Germany are engaging with the new security structure, and that Italy is also interested “to be part of the dialogue”.

In the exclusive Euronews interview, Dar revealed how his government took the initiative in the peace mediations between the US and Iran in the early phases of the war and how he urged his Iranian counterpart not to respond to the US-Israeli attacks.

“In the early morning of the first day of the war, 28 February, I called (Iranian foreign minister Abbas) Araghchi to please exercise strength and don't react, because I was wondering if they might react against the Gulf countries, which unfortunately they did,” Pakistan’s foreign minister said.

“The entire (diplomatic) process began on that day," Dar recalled.

He described how the Pakistani leadership “worked hard to bring them around table,” which resulted in the parties shaking hands and sitting down for negotiations.

“It was 21 hours of a marathon session with no real breaks, but only consultative breaks, and, after the fifth round, I was very sure that by the sixth round we have covered so much of the mileage that we reached a point (of agreement).”

“We didn’t give up,” Dar said, and this effort later became the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding to end the Iran war, signed on 18 June.

He told Euronews that one of the agreement's core points, “which almost every country on the globe supported, was that there should be no tolls, permits, fees or permissions” in the Strait of Hormuz, adding that the EU and the UK also supported this diplomatic process.

“I think that the sea lanes must be seen as a free movement and Pakistan has not given up” on this principle, Dar said, adding that all parties are still “working hard” on achieving this goal.

He also said that Pakistan “continue to persuade both parties to please respect and honour what you signed on 18 June”.

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.
