World.title: Colombia aplicará por primera vez la eutanasia química a 10 hipopótamos en un periodo de cuatro meses
World.content:
EL PAÍS ofrece en abierto la sección América Futura por su aporte informativo diario y global sobre desarrollo sostenible. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete aquí.

A la serie sobre los hipopótamos en Colombia se le suma un nuevo capítulo. Este miércoles, el Ministerio de Ambiente y varias corporaciones ambientales del país anunciaron que aplicarán un protocolo de manejo que incluye la eutanasia química de 10 hipopótamos en el departamento de Antioquia, en un plazo de cuatro meses. Estos ejemplares están ubicados en zonas cercanas a centros poblados y representan riesgos para las comunidades. El anuncio es el primer revés del ministro de ambiente, Fabio Arjona, quien prometió al ser nombrado un santuario para esta especie invasora “similar a Jurassic Park”. “Sale más barato mantenerlos que matarlos”, dijo entonces en una entrevista con EL PAÍS.

David Echeverri, jefe de la Oficina de gestión de la biodiversidad de Cornare (Corporación Autónoma Regional de las Cuencas de los Ríos Negro y Nare), celebra la decisión, a pesar de lo controvertido que es este tema en Colombia. “Ética y ambientalmente es la mejor medida. Y se tenía que tomar tarde o temprano. Es mejor ahora que hacerlo a las patadas después de que hubiera algún fallecido por un ataque”, cuenta por teléfono. Hasta el momento, se conocen al menos tres personas accidentadas en la zona del Magdalena medio. Uno de ellos, está en silla de ruedas. Otros, son pescadores que fueron atacados en plena faena.

El Plan para la Prevención, Control y Manejo del Hipopótamo Común en Colombia (Hippopotamus amphibius) contempla cuatro frentes de trabajo: conocimiento y monitoreo de la población; intervenciones de control y manejo; trabajo social y articulación institucional, y educación ambiental. Entre las medidas de intervención están la esterilización, la traslocación, el confinamiento y la eutanasia química. Si bien en 2009, se llevó a cabo la caza controlada del individuo conocido como Pepe, de concretarse este proyecto sería la primera vez en 40 años que se aplica la eutanasia química. Desde que Pablo Escobar trajo cuatro ejemplares a Colombia por primera vez -tres machos y una hembra- a la Hacienda Nápoles, la invasión ha pasado como una papa caliente de un Gobierno a otro.

Estas operaciones se llevarán a cabo en una primera fase piloto, con una inversión de unos 500 millones de pesos (137.000 euros) y en los próximos cuatro meses requeriría una inversión superior a los 8.000 millones (2,2 millones de euros). Este segundo presupuesto aún no está confirmado. Para Katherin Corrales Bravo, bióloga especializada en manejo de especies invasoras de Corpoboyacá, el anuncio es una excelente noticia, pero no se atreve a cantar victoria. “Una cosa es lo que se prometa y otra es lo que se haga”, narra por teléfono. “Llevamos muchos años escuchando a Gobiernos decir que se harán cargo. Toca ver... Lo que sí sé es que el equipo de Cornare está perfectamente preparado para llevarlo a cabo”.

Señalamiento de presencia de hipopótamos en el río Samaná (Colombia), el 22 de septiembre. Luis bernardo Cano

Esta corporación ambiental lleva 15 años en el manejo de esta especie. Desde 2009, ha desarrollado acciones de monitoreo y seguimiento poblacional, ensayos de confinamiento, 35 intervenciones quirúrgicas y procesos permanentes de educación ambiental con las comunidades. A estas labores se suma la castración de 58 hipopótamos y el traslado de varios individuos a zoológicos nacionales. Además de la corporación, el Ministerio contó que están trabajando también en la articulación con expertos del Gobierno de Sudáfrica para fortalecer las capacidades mediante capacitación y transferencia de conocimientos, “especialmente en procedimientos de captura y manejo de hipopótamos dentro del agua”.

Entre los que se someterán a la eutanasia se encuentra el hipopótamo por el que las madres de Puerto Nare, Antioquia, pusieron una tutela en septiembre. Este ejemplar apareció a finales de julio en el río por el que transitan diariamente 23 estudiantes en la ruta escolar hasta la escuela rural, poniendo en riesgo a los menores de edad, asi como a los pescadores y a los moradores del municipio. El río es para ellos la principal vía de acceso a los hospitales, funerarias, mercados y lugares de recreación. La tutela quedó recientemente archivada, según explicó el martes Juber Martínez, abogado de las demandantes. Lo que alegó el juez, lamenta, es que “no estamos cualificados para defender la tutela”. La noticia de la eutanasia a los 10 hipopótamos fue bien recibida con alivio y congoja a partes iguales en Puerto Nare. “Sé que muchos vecinos reniegan de esta medida, pero hay un colegio, unos niños... Tenemos que actuar. ¡Es tenaz!”, dijo el científico.

Otros de los seleccionados son los que aparecieron recientemente en un video viral en redes. Hace una semana, se podían ver cuatro hipopótamos a punto de ser arrollados por una tractomula en plena noche en el municipio de Puerto Triunfo. Las autoridades ambientales salieron a buscar la manada y pidieron a los conductores bajar la velocidad. Pero los vecinos afectados están cansados de que las únicas medidas que se tomen sean recomendaciones para aprender a vivir con este animal, que en África mata a unas 500 personas al año. Echeverri añade que hay otros dos núcleos más de individuos próximos en la minuciosa lista que confeccionaron junto al ministerio.

“Cuanto antes y sin dolor”

El procedimiento es complejo y tortuoso. Primero un equipo multidisciplinar se trasladará a los núcleos donde se encuentran los hipopótamos para ubicarlos, sedarlos y posteriormente aplicarles el medicamento mortífero. “Lo que queremos es que sea cuanto antes y sin dolor”, matiza Echeverri, de la corporación ambiental. El cuerpo del hipopótamo -que presumiblemente quedaría flotando en el río- sería extraído con ayuda de una grúa y enterrado bajo tierra para evitar que los animales carroñeros se contaminen con los potentes fármacos.

El biólogo insiste, sin embargo, en que esta es la primera parte de un plan a largo tiempo. “Podremos decir que el problema está acabado cuando los hipopótamos esterilizados se mueran de viejos y los problemáticos ya no estén”, resume. “Para eso, faltan años”. Ni Echeverri ni el ministerio descarta reubicar otros ejemplares a Vantara, un centro de rescate de fauna silvestre ubicado en el Gujurat, India, como se había considerado en el Gobierno anterior.

La eutanasia ha sido una petición recurrente para los ambientalistas del país, quienes llevan décadas estudiando el impacto negativo de estos cuerpos de hasta tres toneladas sobre los territorios de la zona del río Magdalena, la principal arteria fluvial del país. Desplazamiento de especies nativas, aplanamiento del suelo que pisan o contaminación fecal de las aguas en las que habitan… “La decisión de aprobar la eutanasia es muy necesaria para conservar nuestros ecosistemas”, aseguraba hace unos meses Nataly Castelblanco, bióloga y miembro del equipo de Biodiversos Colombia.

Actualmente, se reproducen un 4% más que en los países de donde son endémicos y suman unos 250 ejemplares distribuidos en un área de 2.000 kilómetros cuadrados. Una superficie mayor al tamaño de Bogotá. Recientemente, se encontró un hipopótamo en Barrancabermeja, a más de 300 kilómetros de la hacienda Nápoles. El Instituto Humboldt habla de la posibilidad de llegar a 1.000 en 2035 sin un control adecuado.

World.title: La defensora del pueblo en funciones elimina el área de Igualdad y diluye la de Migraciones un día después de asumir el cargo
World.content:
Los vientos de cambio ya han irrumpido en el organismo del Defensor del Pueblo. Un día después de ser nombrada titular en funciones tras agotar su mandato Ángel Gabilondo, Teresa Jiménez-Becerril ha eliminado el área de Igualdad de Trato y ha diluido la de Migraciones al meterla junto a la de Justicia y Seguridad. La nueva defensora, propuesta por el PP, era hasta ahora la adjunta primera, cargo que seguirá desempeñando hasta el nombramiento por el Congreso del nuevo titular de la entidad. Pero era la adjunta segunda, Patricia Bárcena García, la que tenía asignadas las carteras de Migraciones e Igualdad de Trato. Ahora, los temas de Migraciones pasarán a Jiménez-Becerril en un área más amplia, según consta en el organigrama publicado en la web de la institución, y la cartera de Igualdad de Trato no aparece.

La decisión de Jiménez-Becerril no es baladí. Estas dos materias han sido dos de los pilares del trabajo del equipo de Gabilondo durante el último lustro. “Se ha producido una quiebra del consenso sin precedentes”, señalan fuentes cercanas a la institución. “Sin previa información, diálogo o conversación alguna, se ha reorganizado la institución y se han impuesto cambios esenciales dirigidos a una acumulación de poder hasta el momento desconocida”.

Otra de las consecuencias de la reorganización es el equilibrio de competencias entre las dos adjuntías, ya que con los nuevos cambios la que ocupa Jiménez-Becerril absorberá una mayor cantidad de expedientes. “Tres de cada cuatro quejas ciudadanas quedan bajo la responsabilidad directa y exclusiva de la adjunta primera, ahora defensora en funciones”, subraya esta misma fuente, que afirma: “Refleja un giro desde un enfoque centrado en la atención especializada a las personas, la inclusión y el respeto a la diversidad, en otro basado en la securitización y en la desaparición práctica de la idea de igualdad de trato”.

La cuestión migratoria ha sido un reto para el equipo de Gabilondo. Dos de sus actuaciones de oficio más relevantes fueron sobre el salto de la valla de Melilla durante el verano de 2022 (en la que hubo 23 fallecidos) y otra después de la entrada masiva en Ceuta en julio de este año de más de 80.000 migrantes (y en la que murieron al menos 141 personas). Sobre la primera, concluyó que las devoluciones en caliente durante la tragedia fueron ilegales y pidió que se reforzasen “los medios materiales y humanos” de la Embajada y de los consulados en Marruecos, con el fin de “garantizar que los necesitados de protección internacional puedan acceder y tramitar sus visados para solicitar asilo en España, sin tener que arriesgar sus vidas ni utilizar vías irregulares de entrada”.

La segunda actuación de oficio sigue abierta después de que este agosto pidiera información al Gobierno, la Fiscalía y Ceuta tras la entrada masiva. Los resultados del posible informe y las recomendaciones recaerán en Jiménez-Becerril, ya que, no solo como defensora en funciones, sino como adjunta primera, será la encargada de liderar el asunto.

En cuanto al área de Igualdad de Trato, aunque ya no aparece en el organigrama, sigue constando en la web del organismo cuáles han sido sus líneas de trabajo: “El Defensor del Pueblo realiza actuaciones en relación con los distintos tipos de discriminación por motivo de género, orientación sexual, origen étnico, pertenencia a confesión religiosa, discapacidad o cualquier otra condición o circunstancia personal o social”. Sobre estos problemas destaca el informe Violencia vicaria de género. Las otras víctimas, publicado en noviembre de 2024. En él, entre otras cuestiones, urgía a una reforma de la Ley de Medidas de Protección Integral contra la Violencia de Género y pedía que los casos penales de esta tipología “sean competencia de los órganos judiciales que conocen de la violencia de género, independientemente de que haya denuncia previa de violencia sobre la madre”.

La institución, a través de su departamento de comunicación, ha respondido a este periódico que estos cambios “persiguen optimizar los procesos internos de funcionamiento de la casa para seguir trabajando en defensa de los derechos fundamentales de la ciudadanía”. En cuanto al área de migraciones, señalan que “mantiene toda su estructura y personal” y que el objetivo de su fusión con la nueva macroárea se ha llevado a cabo para que sea “más operativa en el marco de la protección humanitaria y social del fenómeno migratorio”.

Sobre la eliminación del organigrama de la cartera de Igualdad de Trato, la nueva defensora asegura que “el objetivo es precisamente reforzar su presencia en el trabajo de la institución, incorporando esta perspectiva a la supervisión que realizan todas las áreas en sus respectivos ámbitos para darle mayor visibilidad”. No explica si cada área contará con un departamento especializado para tratar estas quejas en cada ámbito social, laboral, económico, migratorio, judicial, etc. Ni tampoco si se contratará a más personal y cómo la nueva defensora ha podido diseñar esta transversalidad en un día de mandato.

Jiménez-Becerril (Sevilla, 1961) es licenciada en Ciencias de la Información por la Universidad Complutense de Madrid y cursó un máster de Diseño de Moda en el Instituto Marangoni de Milán, según aparece en la web del organismo público. Fue eurodiputada del PP entre 2009 y 2019 y, desde ese año hasta su nombramiento como adjunta primera de Gabilondo en 2021, trabajó como diputada por Sevilla en el Congreso.

Jiménez-Becerril destaca también por su labor como presidenta de la Fundación Contra el Terrorismo y la Violencia Alberto Jiménez-Becerril, asociación que lleva el nombre de su hermano, concejal de Sevilla del PP asesinado junto a su mujer en 1998 por orden del antiguo jefe de ETA Francisco Javier Arizkuren Ruiz, Kantauri. El atentado fue ejecutado por los miembros del comando Andalucía, José Luis Barrios y Mikel Azurmendi. Los tres fueron condenados por estos delitos hace más de una década.

World.title: Dutch embassy hit in Kyiv as Putin vows Crimea bridge revenge
World.content:
The Dutch embassy in Kyiv was hit during drone strikes on Thursday afternoon, damaging the building and surrounding area, though no one was reported harmed. Shortly thereafter, Russian president Putin pledged to respond to recent attacks on the Crimean bridge, which the Netherlands was involved in.

“Fortunately our colleagues are unharmed, though there is minor damage to the building,” Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen said. He said the ministry was looking into exactly what had happened and that its priority now was the wellbeing of its staff.

The Kyiv Independent reported that the projectile was a Russian drone which crashed close to the embassy, damaging cars and a security post and shattering windows in the building, during an hours-long attack on the capital. The site said it was not clear whether the drone had been aimed at the area around the embassy or had been shot down.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian attacks on Kyiv had once again damaged a diplomatic mission, broadcaster NOS reported. Ukrainian media also reported Russian drone attacks throughout the day, with air raid sirens sounding several times in the capital.

Crimean bridge attack

The strike comes two days after a Ukrainian attack on the Kerch bridge to Crimea, which Dutch arms maker Destinus publicly said it had been involved in. Destinus said seven of its Ruta missiles had hit the bridge and that it was “proud to support the Ukrainian army”.

On Wednesday, Russia’s embassy in The Hague said Moscow had been informed of Dutch involvement and asked whether The Hague was “openly taking part in the conflict”.

Berendsen told MPs that Russian embassies were being used to spread the Kremlin’s narrative. “They want to drive a wedge between us, so we have to see it through that lens,” he said.

In April, Russia’s defence ministry put a Destinus factory on a list of potential targets, which former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev said should be taken “literally”, NOS and other outlets reported.

Staff in Ukraine

On Thursday morning, NRC reported that Destinus employees had personally shot down Russian drones in Ukraine and helped the Ukrainian army launch attacks towards Russia.

The defence ministry told the paper that using a weapon system against a party in an armed conflict counts as direct participation in hostilities.

Destinus denies carrying out military operations and says it only provided technical support. Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz has declined to comment on NRC’s findings.

Experts told NOS that by going public, Destinus could increase the risk of Russian sabotage or cyberattacks against it. “We know that Russia has gone after companies like this in Europe,” missile expert Fabian Hoffmann said. Defence analyst Patrick Bolder said the company was already on a Russian list of targets “and would not easily come off it”.

World.title: Prostate cancer surgeries improving: fewer men left incontinent
World.content:
The share of men who end up incontinent after having a prostate tumour removed has roughly halved over the past few years, broadcaster NOS reports.

Until 2020, about 30% of patients in the Netherlands who got the operation were left incontinent afterwards. Between 2022 and 2024 that fell to 14%, according to insurers’ data analysed by the quality registry Dutch Prostate Audit.

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the Netherlands. Just over 16,000 men were diagnosed with it last year, and it killed 3,334 in 2024, according to CBS figures.

There has been a huge gap in outcomes between the hospitals that do the surgeries, which has also narrowed a lot in recent years.

A PhD study looking at operations between 2016 to 2020 found that one hospital had a 19% rate of causing incontinence by the operation and another 85%. Now the differences go from about 10% to 25% at most.

“That was hard to face, and it forced urologists in the Netherlands to work together more on improving things,” Rik Somford, a urologist at the Canisius-Wilhelmina hospital in Nijmegen who chairs the working group behind the push, told NOS.

Patients still can’t see how individual hospitals perform, and people want more transparency. Next year hospitals will start publishing some results, including complications within 90 days, whether the cancer was fully removed and whether patients are still incontinent a year later.

World.title: UN court in The Hague rules Myanmar committed genocide
World.content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority. It is the first time the UN’s highest court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Reading the judgment at the Peace Palace, court president Yuji Iwasawa said the court was “fully convinced” that Myanmar’s security forces had acted with the intent to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya population during a military crackdown in 2017.

The court found that soldiers killed thousands of Rohingya civilians (around 10,000, according to the evidence), committed widespread sexual violence and violence against children, and attacked people as they fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. More than 730,000 Rohingya crossed the border.

The case was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, with the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Netherlands and Canada said in 2020 that they would intervene in support.

Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says the operation targeted Rohingya militants who had attacked police posts.

The ICJ settles disputes between states and is separate from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is also in The Hague and prosecutes individuals. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed, but the court has no way of enforcing them.

The ruling could also affect South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, which is still before the court, the Volkskrant reported. The judges said other motives, such as fighting an insurgency, do not rule out genocidal intent. But they kept the bar high: genocide has to be the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence as a whole.

World.title: 1,100 new poplars to save historic tree-lined Maas riverbanks
World.content:
Some 1,100 new poplars are being planted along the river Maas to preserve the rows of trees that have lined both banks for almost a century, broadcaster NOS reported.

The trees, which stand 110 metres apart between Boxmeer and Geertruidenberg, were once used by skippers to navigate river. They are known as beacon trees (bakenbomen) and have become a defining part of the river landscape.

Many of the original trees are reaching the end of their lives, and for years dead trees were not replaced. Only 700 are left. The replanting will bring the total to 1,800 over the coming years.

The national government, the provinces of Noord Brabant, Gelderland, and Limburg, and 14 local authorities along the river are putting €4.6 million into the project.

They signed the agreement on national tree day (Boomfeestdag) and have committed to paying for maintenance for the next 100 years. North Brabant will coordinate the work. A network of volunteers and civic groups is also involved.

The new trees are black poplars, which the provinces describe as native to the Maas valley and good for biodiversity and nature restoration.

World.title: Corporations build 24,000 social homes, say state help needed
World.content:
Dutch housing corporations built almost 24,000 new social rent homes last year, but say they cannot keep up the pace without more help from the government.

Some 10,000 homes were lost to demolition and sales, giving a net increase of 13,000, broadcaster NOS reported, based on the annual report from housing corporation association Aedes. Corporations built 2,100 more social rent homes than a year earlier.

There are now 2.1 million social rent homes in the Netherlands. For new contracts, the rent on a social housing property can be no more than €932.93 a month.

Homes renting for up to €1,228.07 count as mid-market rentals, which corporations also build. Many corporation homes now have an energy label of A or better.

However, corporations are still spending more on each home than they take in in rent. Aedes puts the average shortfall at €44 per home, down from €48 a year earlier. Most of that improvement comes from higher rents and from selling homes. Corporations borrow to fund 52% of their investments.

“We know that this way of working cannot go on,” Aedes chair Liesbeth Spies said. Without new measures, corporations will face “painful choices between new construction, maintenance and liveability”, she said.

The cabinet plans to cut a tax paid by housing corporations from 2028. Aedes says higher interest rates and rising costs will swallow up the extra money.

World.title: FVD expels two members after neo-Nazi cage fight exposé
World.content:
The far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) has expelled two members and pushed a Den Bosch councillor to step down. The move follows a TV investigation that linked people in and around the party to a neo-Nazi network that organises illegal cage fights.

The investigation was done by current affairs programme Zembla and Flemish broadcaster VRT’s Pano, using an undercover infiltrator and hidden cameras.

This summer Zembla filmed Ramon van Asch, who led FVD’s group on Den Bosch council, leaving a cage fight in Oeffelt, North Brabant, with a baby in his arms.

Fighters and spectators repeatedly gave the Nazi salute. Van Asch said an acquaintance had invited him and that he went home once the fighting began.

Hitler commemoration

Two members of FVD’s youth wing fought at another event in Finsterwolde, Groningen, according to Zembla. One of them, Luc Kluytmans, is one of the two members the party has now expelled.

He was also secretly filmed in April at a Hitler commemoration in Luxembourg, run by the neo-Nazi group Wolvenrad, where he took part in burning books by Jewish writers.

In a statement on social media, FVD said “unacceptable behaviour and views” had been shown at the fight. It said it had asked Van Asch to step down and that he had done so.

“Not problematic”

Ralf Dekker, who leads FVD’s MPs, was less concerned when NOS showed him the footage. “Everyone should go where they want,” he said. “I don’t find that problematic at all.” He later said he had not known about the report when he was asked, although Zembla had already approached the party for comment.

The counter-terrorism coordinator NCTV says fights of this kind are meant to strengthen the “white race” physically. It says they pose no violent threat in the Netherlands for now, but could make violence more likely.

Ahead of March’s local elections, several FVD candidates were found to have links to extremist organisations. FVD leader Lidewij de Vos called their past activities “youthful indiscretions”.

The documentary is on NPO 2 tonight.

World.title: Regional bus and train strikes return on Monday and Tuesday
World.content:
Regional bus and train drivers across the Netherlands will strike on Monday and Tuesday, after union members rejected employers’ final offer for a new pay and conditions deal.

The FNV and CNV unions say more strikes will follow on December 3, 4, 14, 15 and 18 if the two-day walkout does not move employers, Het Parool reported.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, Transdev, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

The unions held a first nationwide 24-hour strike on October 14. They had planned to strike one day a week until Christmas, but suspended the strike after the employers’ organisation VWOV made a number of commitments and talks resumed.

The talks ended with the VWOV putting a final offer on the table. The employers said it allowed for pay rises while taking into account “the financial limits of our sector”. A large majority of FNV and CNV members voted against it.

The unions say pay is not the problem. They object to employers’ plans to raise the starting age of a scheme for workers over 50 to 53, and to cut the allowance for working irregular hours.

World.title: Dutch arms maker’s staff hunted Russian drones in Ukraine: NRC
World.content:
Employees of Dutch arms manufacturer Destinus have been actively participating in the Ukraine war, engaging in drone battles with Russian forces, according to an investigation by NRC.

The defence ministry says such actions amount to direct participation in hostilities, and experts warn the company’s activities could drag the Netherlands into the war.

On Tuesday, the company publicly announced its missiles had been used in a specific attack, the strike on the Crimea bridge. It has now confirmed to NRC that its staff “launched and operated” interceptor drones against incoming Russian attack drones, without live explosives and under the direction of Ukrainian soldiers.

NRC asked the defence ministry whether Destinus employees are allowed to use weapons against Russian drones or targets. The ministry said that launching or operating a weapons system counts as taking part in the fighting, and that anyone who does so loses the protection given to civilians under the laws of war. Explaining to soldiers how a system works does not, it said.

Legal risk

Jessica Dorsey, an international law lecturer at Utrecht University, said company employees who take a direct part in fighting can be treated as targets, and the Ukrainian army’s consent makes no difference. Liesbeth Zegveld, a professor of the law of war, said they could also face prosecution.

Zegveld also told NRC that the company could drag the Netherlands into the war. “The formal position is that the Netherlands is not at war,” she said. “But by supporting companies that take part in this way, you muddle your way into the war.”

Wimar Bolhuis, a left-wing PRO MP who sits on parliament’s defence committee, called the findings “worrying” and has asked the Defence ministry to explain how the drones were tested and how the export licences were granted. “We need to know what is really happening there,” he said. Volt leader Laurens Dassen also called for an investigation into whether Destinus lets staff take part in the war.

Battle testing

NRC spoke to more than 40 people, including current and former employees, investors and advisers, and drew on internal documents, messages and video. It found that from autumn 2024, a Destinus team in Ukraine tested the company’s Hornet interceptor drone against Russian-made Shahed drones, using drones shipped from the Netherlands.

Internal messages seen by NRC show that the drones crashed repeatedly, and one was nearly lost over a village. When the Ukrainian army asked whether the drone was ready for use, the team on the ground said it was not ready for combat missions. A team leader in Spain pushed for it to fly anyway.

Kokorich told NRC he did not recognise its descriptions of chaotic factories, of the drones’ poor condition or of a start-up mentality at the company, and said safety is “of the utmost importance” at Destinus.

Strike on Voronezh

NRC also reported that in June 2023, before Destinus moved its military arm to the Netherlands, employees went to the front near Kharkiv to test the company’s first attack drones. The aircraft carried explosives and were set to hit a military airfield near the Russian city of Voronezh, 180 kilometres across the border. According to the paper, Destinus staff were closely involved.

On the morning of June 9, a drone hit an apartment block in Voronezh and three people were injured. NRC said employees who saw footage of the strike suspected the drone was theirs, though it cannot be said with certainty where the Destinus drone came down.

Destinus said the Ukrainian army selects targets and decides on military operations, and the company provides “technical support in line with its contracts”. “Destinus does not carry out military operations,” it said.

Government backing

Destinus was founded in Switzerland in 2021 by Russian-born Kokorich and registered its military arm in Hengelo in 2024. In 2024 he settled US fraud charges over his previous space company, without admitting or denying them, and paid a $2 million penalty and accepted a five-year ban from running listed companies.

The Netherlands has since become a key customer. In June it agreed to pay for 700 Ruta cruise missiles for Ukraine, worth €250 million, a package the cabinet first described as drones.

In August, the defence ministry signed a contract with Destinus to develop a navy version of the Hornet, part of a project budgeted at €250 million to €1 billion.

The foreign ministry, which grants arms export licences for Ukraine, told NRC that manufacturers are responsible for safety defects and Ukraine is responsible for assessing the quality of the weapons.

On Wednesday, the Russian embassy asked whether the Netherlands was becoming involved in the war after the Crimea bridge strike. In a parliamentary committee debate on Wednesday, foreign minister Tom Berendsen said his ministry had no further details of Destinus’ role in the bridge attack. He said Russian statements of this kind are intended to sow division and stoke fear.

World.title: Poland hands e-commerce giant Allegro “greenwashing” fine for misleading tree-planting campaign

Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK, has fined Allegro, one of Europe’s largest e-commerce platforms, 55 million zloty (€12.3 million) for misleading consumers over a campaign that promised to plant trees in exchange for collecting parcels through its delivery service. The case is one of a series of investigations into so-called “greenwashing” launched by the authority against companies operating in Poland. UOKiK found that two of the Polish e-commerce group’s practices relating to the tree-planting initiative had infringed consumers’ interests. The first involved promotional claims suggesting that collecting 10 parcels through Allegro’s delivery service would result in a tree being planted. In practice, however, Allegro calculated the number of trees to be planted using forecasts prepared the previous year, rather than linking plantings to individual consumers’ parcel collections. This meant that decisions on the number of trees had already been made before customers collected their parcels. 🌳 Greenwashing ma swoją cenę! Blisko 55 mln zł kary dla Allegro – ekologiczne obietnice miały zachęcać do odbioru paczek, ale rzeczywistość nie była tak zielona. Milionów deklarowanych drzew nigdy nie posadzono. ❌ Ekościema nie może się opłacać 🔎https://t.co/yPQznKz0H1 pic.twitter.com/UDcWXWq3LI — UOKiK (@UOKiKgovPL) November 18, 2026 The second breach concerned the conditions attached to the campaign, which Allegro failed to communicate clearly to consumers. According to UOKiK, Allegro’s promotional messages could have led customers to believe that collecting 10 parcels through their delivery was sufficient to trigger tree planting. In fact, customers had to do it within a single calendar year and, from January 2024, submit a dedication for the tree within a specified period. Without a dedication, collecting the required number of parcels did not result in a tree being planted or assigned to the customer. UOKiK also found that the option to submit a dedication was unavailable for extended periods. Between March and November 2024, the feature was disabled for a total of 264 days, the watchdog said. The prolonged interruptions could have led customers to forget about the requirement or abandon their attempts to submit a dedication, meaning they would not receive the promised tree. UOKiK imposed a fine of 29.9 million zloty for the first practice and 24.9 million zloty for the second. Its decision can still be appealed in court by Allegro, which has not yet commented on the decision. “Green claims must be truthful, specific and verifiable; otherwise, they may mislead consumers and constitute an example of greenwashing,” said UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny. “If a consumer hears, ‘collect 10 parcels, and we will plant a tree,’ they have the right to interpret that literally,” Chróstny said, adding that “several million [trees] – more than half of the total number claimed by Allegro – were never planted at all”. When announcing its decision, UOKiK noted that, according to a 2025 consumer survey conducted by the European Union, 43% of Poles said that the environmental impact of a product or service influenced their choices. The Allegro case forms part of a broader crackdown on suspected greenwashing by companies operating in Poland. Alongside Allegro, UOKiK has brought charges against delivery companies DHL, DPD and InPost, mobility firm Bolt, retailers Tchibo and Zara, and cosmetics firm L’Oréal Polska. World.title: Poland deepens regional gas cooperation with Hungary, Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has signed memorandums with four of its neighbouring countries – Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania – pledging to strengthen regional cooperation on natural gas supplies and the security of infrastructure. The initiative comes amid Poland’s efforts to use its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity and transmission links to establish itself as a regional energy hub, helping its neighbours, especially landlocked countries to the south, diversify supplies and reduce their reliance on Russia. The two memorandums of understanding were signed in Warsaw during a ministerial meeting at the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC), co-organised by the US Department of Energy, Poland’s energy ministry and the Global Energy Centre run by the Atlantic Council. Rozpoczęliśmy 7. edycję Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC) – jednego z kluczowych forów współpracy energetycznej Stanów Zjednoczonych oraz krajów Europy Środkowo-Wschodniej. ⚡️ W Warszawie spotkali się przedstawiciele rządu Stanów Zjednoczonych, państw… pic.twitter.com/7t8kLluubF — GAZ-SYSTEM (@GAZ_SYSTEM) November 18, 2026 One of them, signed by Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – who collectively form the Visegrad Group – establishes a framework for closer collaboration between their gas transmission system operators and more effective use of existing infrastructure. In late 2022, for example, a new gas interconnector opened between Poland and Slovakia. However, since then, the pipeline has seen very little use, as Bratislava has continued to rely on Russian gas supplies. Hungary has also remained reliant on Russian gas. By contrast, Poland quickly phased out its imports of Russian energy after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It now receives most of its gas via a pipeline that runs from Norway through Denmark and through LNG that arrives by sea, sourced mainly from the US and Qatar. From autumn 2027, the EU will ban its member states from importing Russian gas. In September, Hungary’s energy minister said that his country will be ready to meet that deadline. Slovakia, however, is challenging the import ban at the European Court of Justice. As part of the new memorandum signed this week, the four Visegrad countries will assess the impact of phasing out Russian supplies on regional energy security. The second memorandum, signed between Poland’s Gaz-System and Lithuania’s Amber Grid and KN Energies – which operate gas and LNG infrastructure in the two countries – focuses on strengthening the resilience and security of energy infrastructure around the Baltic Sea. It provides for closer coordination between the companies, including information-sharing on threats and incidents, joint risk assessments, exchanges of expertise on infrastructure protection and crisis response, and joint training sessions and exercises. “The LNG terminals in Poland and Lithuania serve as critical supply hubs for…Central and Eastern Europe, significantly enhancing energy security and bolstering regional resilience,” said Sławomir Hinc, CEO of Gaz-System. But that “security depends on the resilience of every link in the chain”, added his counterpart at Amber Grid, Nemunas Biknius. “This regional agreement will enable us to strengthen that chain in a structured and coordinated way.” Poland has declared its ambition to become a hub for supplying gas to the CEE region, including Ukraine, in particular by expanding imports of LNG from the United States. In addition to its existing LNG terminal in Świnoujście, which opened a decade ago, it is planning to build two further floating storage and regasification units that will be located in the Bay of Gdańsk. The first of those, under construction in South Korea, is due to open in 2028. Last year, a record amount of natural gas was traded in Poland, surpassing the levels seen before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the energy crisis that followed. We cannot do what we do without your support. Police and prosecutors have detained 123 people across Poland as part of a major operation targeting online child pornography. Among those arrested were some who had used AI to produce content depicting the abuse of minors. Around 170 searches took place, with prosecutors seizing a total of 1,096 electronic devices. Initial analysis indicates that almost 2.8 million files containing child sex abuse material were contained on them, said the National Prosecutor’s Office, which oversaw the operation. Those detained are all men, ranging in age from 18 to 73, and include a teacher and a doctor. All were Polish citizens apart from one Ukrainian and one Belarusian. Policjanci Centralnego Biura Zwalczania Cyberprzestępczości zatrzymali 123 osoby i zabezpieczyli ponad 2,8 mln plików z materiałami przedstawiającymi seksualne wykorzystanie małoletnich ‼️ Działania pod krypt. „INFERNO”, to już kolejna – 9 operacja CBZC przeciwko przestępczości o… pic.twitter.com/XBdNAmLjKz — Centralne Biuro Zwalczania Cyberprzestępczości (@PolicjaCBZC) November 19, 2026 The police’s Central Cybercrime Bureau (CBZC) reports that the detained teacher claimed “he was studying to obtain expert qualifications and was collecting and analysing the [abuse] material to check whether his psyche could withstand the associated strain”. The doctor, an anaesthesiologist, was found to be in possession of around 75,000 files containing child sexual abuse material. Prosecutors have already charged 94 of the suspects with producing, possessing and/or disseminating materials related to the sexual exploitation of minors. Those crimes carry a jail term of up to 15 years. Thirty-one of the suspects have been placed in pretrial detention. “Among those detained were people who used AI technology to produce materials depicting the sexual abuse of minors,” wrote the National Prosecutor’s Office. One suspect is also accused of taking photographs and videos of himself and children naked at a public swimming pool. In May this year, prosecutors announced the results of a similar operation against child pornography, which, by coincidence, also resulted in 123 people being detained. Among those detained at that time was a teacher accused of recording and photographing children, as well as another suspect accusing of grooming minors through a messaging app before encouraging them to perform sexual acts. World.title: Polish Supreme Court rejects government’s position on Constitutional Tribunal
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s rule-of-law crisis has taken another twist, after the Supreme Court (SN) issued a resolution effectively opposing the government’s position towards another top court, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), and endorsing that of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. The SN found that TK rulings are only valid if issued by judges the president has sworn in and that they take effect even if the government refuses to publish them. Nawrocki has refused to swear in five TK judges, while the government has refused to publish 85 previous TK rulings. However, the government’s justice minister argues that the new SN resolution is itself invalid because it was issued by judges who were appointed unlawfully. Połączone izby Sądu Najwyższego o wyrokach Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jako podstawie wznowienia postępowaniahttps://t.co/DzgL6aDTGK pic.twitter.com/GpiGbWMvNn — Sąd Najwyższy (@SN_RP_) November 18, 2026 On Wednesday, the SN issued a resolution in response to questions over the validity of rulings issued by the TK. It found, among other things, that a valid TK ruling can only be issued by a panel of judges who, after being elected to the tribunal by parliament, have “taken an oath before the president, that is, in his presence”. Those latter words relate to a key dispute that has arisen around the TK. The government’s majority in parliament has this year chosen eight new TK judges, who would now form the majority on the 15-seat tribunal. However, Nawrocki has refused to receive the oath of five of those judges, citing concerns over the method of their appointment or their qualifications. Those five judges have instead arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies before a notary and then forwarded their oaths to the presidential chancellery. They and the government argue that this meets the requirement for them to take up their seats. However, Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former government, reject that position and say that the judges cannot take up their seats on the court until the president receives their oath in person. The Supreme Court has now effectively endorsed their stance. Meanwhile, the SN also addressed another contentious issue. Since March 2024, the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – has refused to publish any of the 85 TK rulings issued in that time. That is because, under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, three judges were unlawfully appointed to the TK. The current government argues that TK rulings only take force when published in the official Journal of Laws. Indeed, so did the former PiS government when, in 2016, it refused to publish TK rulings that contradicted its judicial policies. However, the SN has now deemed that valid TK rulings enter force even if not published. “In a situation where the body responsible for publishing TK rulings fails to fulfil this obligation…these abuses by the executive power cannot affect the universally binding force of TK rulings,” said SN judge Aleksander Stępkowski, quoted by the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily. However, the validity of the SN’s resolution is itself contested as it was issued by judges whose own status is questioned. That is because they were appointed to the court through the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS) after it was overhauled by PiS in a manner that brought it under political control and rendered it invalid, according to Polish and European court rulings. The current government has generally rejected decisions issued by such “neo-judges”, as it calls them. And that position was reiterated on Thursday by justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who wrote that “the neo-judges in the Supreme Court have adopted a so-called resolution”. “Any decision issued with the participation of even one person appointed through the politicised National Council of the Judiciary after 2017 is a non-existent judgement,” he added. Neosędziowie w Sądzie Najwyższym podjęli nibyuchwałę połączonych trzech izb (III CZP 41/26), uznając, że nieopublikowane rozstrzygnięcia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego mają moc powszechnie obowiązującą, a za wyrok TK można uznać tylko taki wydany przez osoby, które złożyły ślubowanie… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 The SN’s resolution comes as the TK itself is embroiled in a crisis. At the end of October, the eight new TK judges chosen by parliament this year took control of the tribunal and announced that its chief justice, Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, supported by Nawrocki and the SN’s chief justice, Zbigniew Kapiński (also a “neo-judge”), has rejected that move as an illegal “coup d’état” and claims he is still in charge of the tribunal. However, police have prevented him from entering the building. On Wednesday, just as the SN was issuing its resolution, the eight government-backed TK judges announced that they had lifted Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution at the request of Żurek. World.title: Disputed Polish constitutional court announces chief justice stripped of immunity to face charges
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. The government-backed judges who recently took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have announced that the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has been stripped of legal immunity in order to face criminal charges. Święczkowski, who was appointed to the TK under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, has condemned their takeover as an illegal “coup d’état” and says that any decisions issued by them have no validity. In a further development, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) announced yesterday that it has rejected a request by Święczkowski for an emergency order to suspend all proceedings against him at the TK. Trybunał Konstytucyjny zdecydował. Prokuratura może teraz stawiać zarzuty. Nikt nie stoi ponad prawem.https://t.co/trIEqa8Mh1 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 A statement published on Wednesday evening on the tribunal’s website announced that motions from the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, to strip Swięczkowski and the deputy head of the court, Bartłomiej Sochański, of immunity had been approved. The decision was made by the group of eight judges who dramatically took control of the TK on 30 October as riot police held back protesters outside. All of them were chosen by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, but opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them. After taking over the tribunal, they declared that Święczkowski and Sochański had been suspended for their failure to properly fulfil their duties. They also launched internal disciplinary proceedings against the pair, with hearings in those cases due to take place later this week. Separately, Żurek, who serves as justice minister in addition to being prosecutor general, filed multiple requests to the TK for Święczkowski and Sochański to be stripped of their immunity in order to face criminal charges. Most of those were approved today. Among the alleged crimes prosecutors wish to charge Święczkowski with are abuse of power and failure to fulfil duties for his refusal to allow five judges chosen by parliament this year to take up their seats on the court. Sochański is accused of the same offences. Święczkowski has argued that he cannot admit those judges because, under Polish law, they are obliged to first swear an “oath before the president” and have not done so. Prosecutors also allege that Święczkowski used violence against those five judges to physically prevent them from entering the judges’ chambers at the TK. The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026 Further allegations against Święczkowski relate to his time serving as national prosecutor under the former PiS government. Prosecutors say that he abused his powers by making unauthorised use of material gathered from surveillance. They also accuse him of abusing his power by “maliciously” reassigning prosecutors to different locations as a form of punishment, despite there being no legal basis for doing so. However, although the TK today approved the lifting of Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunities, it did not consent to them being arrested and held in pretrial detention. It also rejected two additional requests from Żurek to lift Święczkowski’s immunity for other alleged crimes. The TK found the motions contained “formal deficiencies”. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 Święczkowski immediately rejected today’s decisions, saying that they had no legal validity. He describes the eight judges who have taken control as “usurpers”. However, on Tuesday, Święczkowski suffered another setback in his struggle to retain control over the TK after the European Court of Human Rights announced that it had rejected a request from him and Sochański for an interim measure ordering that all proceedings against them be suspended. The ECHR found that “the applicants had failed to demonstrate an imminent risk of irreparable harm to the core of their rights”. The decision stands in contrast to one made in May this year by the ECHR, when it ordered that the five judges Nawrocki has refused to swear in be admitted to the TK. Święczkowski ignored that order, arguing that the ECHR did not have the authority to issue it. European Court rejects request for interim measure in case concerning Constitutional Court of Poland. 🔗 https://t.co/I15bGXeeKF — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 17, 2026 Święczkowski has received backing from some other Polish institutions. President Nawrocki continues to recognise Święczkowski as the chief justice of the TK and has condemned the government-backed judges’ takeover of the court. The chief justice of the Supreme Court (a separate body from the TK), Zbigniew Kapiński, has also sided with Święczkowski and Nawrocki. Speaking to broadcaster RMF on Wednesday morning, Kapiński said that any decisions made by the eight judges who have taken over the TK “have no legal force”. Kapiński’s own status has also been subject to dispute. He was appointed to the Supreme Court under the PiS government through a judicial body overhauled in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to various European and Polish court rulings. On Monday, the central bank, whose governor is a longstanding associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, announced that it was suspending all outgoing payments from the TK’s bank accounts due to uncertainty over who holds legitimate control over the court. Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a takeover by a group of judges backed by the government https://t.co/ZYkzoneojO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 17, 2026 The recent dramatic events at the TK follow a decade-long crisis around the Polish judiciary, triggered by the contested judicial reforms and appointments made by the former PiS government and PiS-aligned former President Andrzej Duda. The current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that came to power in 2023 – has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK due to the presence of unlawfully appointed judges. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. The eight judges it has appointed now have a majority on the 15-person court, although five of them have not been sworn in by Nawrocki. The remaining seven judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were appointed when PiS was in power. World.title: New Kraków mayor withdraws from metro plans and seeks to shrink clean transport zone
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The administration of Kraków’s new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has signalled that the city will withdraw from plans to build a metro system and will seek to shrink the size of the recently introduced Clean Transport Zone, which imposes additional costs on older, more polluting cars. “We won’t, like the previous administrations, make any promises regarding the metro,” deputy mayor Karol Wałachowski told local news service LoveKrakow. “We’re withdrawing from this project until central [government] or European funding becomes available.” The draft municipal budget for next year presented by Gibała allocates no funds towards preparation work for the metro, notes LoveKrakow. Instead, the new administration wants to establish seven new tram routes. For decades, Kraków has discussed the possibility of building a metro system, which would be just the second in Poland after Warsaw’s. In 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the idea. However, only in 2024 did the then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, who came to office that year, announce plans to build a metro. The city unveiled the planned route in 2025 and then, in July this year, it launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. Kraków has announced a €43 million tender for pre-design work on a planned new metro system, which would be only the second in Poland. The plans include a feasibility study, environmental report and assessment of the impact on existing buildings https://t.co/mB24RcVY96 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 But the idea now looks set to be abandoned after Miszalski was dismissed in a recall referendum earlier this year and Gibała was elected last month to replace him. While Gibała has often said that he would, in theory, like Kraków to have a metro system akin to Warsaw’s, he has argued that it would be impossible to build without significant funds from the European Union or Polish government. During this year’s election campaign, Gibała told news service Wirtualna Polska that he wanted to “honestly tell Kraków residents that, regardless of whether [Monika] Piątkowska [his opponent] or I win, there won’t be a metro anytime soon. We won’t build it without government funding”. Gibała said that, if elected, he would ask the government for a written guarantee of funding. “In my opinion, they won’t [give one], and the metro issue will die. I won’t spend millions more zloty on more expert teams and analyses [to prepare for the metro].” The issue has become tied up in national politics. Gibała is an independent while Piątkowska, his defeated rival, was from Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. LoveKrakow reports, based on sources, that, if Tusk loses power at next year’s parliamentary elections, a new national government may be more willing to provide funds for the metro project. In one of his first announcements since being elected, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of the annual LGBT+ equality march. He argues that the event has become too "partisan" https://t.co/SS2EbRy6Ob — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 This week’s announcement of withdrawal from the metro plans was criticised by one of Miszalski’s former deputy mayors, Stanisław Mazur, who told Radio Kraków that the project should have been seen as “an investment that would significantly support the development of Kraków’s economy”. Two former rectors of Kraków’s AGH University, Antoni Tajduś and Tadeusz Słomka, also told LoveKrakow that it was vital to continue with the preparatory work for the metro system because otherwise, if funding does become available, the city would not be ready to implement the project. Separately, Gibała’s new administration has also presented draft plans to reduce the size of Kraków’s Clean Transport Zone, which was introduced at the start of this year and levies additional costs on drivers of old, more polluting cars. The project has long caused controversy. It was initially meant to go into force in 2024, but was blocked by a court ruling. There have also been legal challenges to the measures finally introduced this year. Many local politicians and officials have argued that the zone unfairly burdens drivers from outside Kraków who need to enter the city, in particular people with lower incomes, who are more likely to drive older cars and are hit harder by the new costs. A court has rejected an attempt to overturn the Clean Transport Zone that was introduced at the start of this year in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, and which places restrictions on driving older, more polluting cars https://t.co/NoAKsDgUus — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026 During his election campaign, Gibała said that he wanted to reduce the size of the Clean Transport Zone, so that it covered only the city centre rather than the whole city. He also pledged to put any final decision about the zone to a public referendum. This week, another of his deputy mayors, Jan Hoffman, confirmed that city hall had presented draft plans to reduce the size of the zone. However, he noted that any change would have to be approved by the city council and also suggested that any final decision should be made in a referendum. Those plans were criticised by Kraków Smog Alarm, an NGO that fights for cleaner air. They said that reducing the scope of the Clean Transport Zone would harm residents’ health and result in tens of millions of zloty in fees being lost to the city budget. World.title: Polish government seeks to introduce maximum gas prices for consumers
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced plans to introduce a maximum price for natural gas to protect households from the continued impact of the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran earlier this year. The measure would be funded by a new special levy on certain energy companies. To enter into force, the bill must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record amount of legislation. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk noted that gas prices have been at elevated levels due to the ongoing crisis around the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East, which is normally a major conduit for both oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). Tusk pointed out that the European gas benchmark price recently surpassed €100 per megawatt-hour (MWh), which was its highest level in four years. The figure has since fallen to around €85/MWh, though that is still more than double the level in January and February, before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Such costs are “unacceptable for any Polish family”, said the prime minister. “We can’t allow people to suffer because of decisions made abroad… about war in the Middle East. We don’t want Polish families to pay for it.” The government therefore wants to introduce a maximum price of 197.29 zloty (€44.15) per MWh (which is the level of the current state-regulated gas tariff) for the whole of 2027. The energy ministry estimates that this will save households that use gas for heating up to 1,863 zloty over the year. As well as individual households and housing cooperatives, the maximum price will also apply to entities providing important public services, such as schools, nurseries, hospitals and shelters. Companies selling gas to such consumers will then receive compensation from the state to cover the difference if the maximum price is below what the level of gas tariffs would normally be at that time. The costs of this compensation “will be largely covered by a new monthly gas levy” charged to “energy companies holding licences to trade natural gas with foreign countries and selling high-methane natural gas on the domestic market”, says the government. The levy would amount to 10% of net revenues from domestic sales of high-methane natural gas in 2027. Companies holding capacity rights amounting to less than 10% of the total capacity at entry points to Poland’s gas-transmission system would be exempt. While the legislation is unlikely to face obstacles in parliament, it remains unknown what Nawrocki’s position will be. The president has previously pushed for the government to lower energy prices. However, he also blocked a windfall tax on energy companies to subsidise fuel-price cuts, before eventually relenting. President @NawrockiKn has backed down and signed into law the government's proposed windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits, which he had previously blocked. In response, the government has reintroduced measures to lower prices at petrol stations https://t.co/icGEST8NAo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Earlier this year, analysis by Allianz, the world’s largest insurance company, found that Poland was among a group of 11 countries “most at risk” from a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Poland has become a growing consumer of gas in recent years. As the country has moved away from its traditional reliance on coal, gas has increasingly been used for both electricity generation and home heating. Last year, gas accounted for a record 13.2% of electricity production, up from just 2.7% in 2015. The latest figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that in 2024 almost 21% of households use gas for heating, up from 10% in 2015. Gas consumption reached its highest ever level in Poland this week – breaking a record set in 2021 – amid freezing winter temperatures and as the fuel continues to play a bigger role in the country's energy mix https://t.co/2wEWLPCV9l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 10, 2026 The majority of gas consumed in Poland is imported – around 82% last year, according to the energy ministry. Around 43% of imports arrive in the form of LNG, delivered to a terminal at Świnoujście on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast. Last year, most of that LNG came from the United States (accounting for 30.7% of Poland’s total gas imports) and Qatar (11.2%). However, LNG exports from Qatar have been severely impacted by the difficulties around the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, Polish state energy giant Orlen exercised its right to terminate one of its two long-term LNG contracts with QatarEnergy, citing “the ongoing force majeure”. However, Orlen insisted that the decision “does not affect the security of gas supplies”. Most of Poland’s remaining gas imports come via the Baltic Pipe, which opened in 2022 and brings gas from Norway via Denmark. World.title: Poland’s central bank freezes constitutional court’s accounts amid leadership dispute
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a disputed takeover by a group of judges backed by the government. The National Bank of Poland (NBP), which holds the tribunal’s accounts and is headed by a governor appointed under the former government, said it was not the bank’s role to determine which side was legally entitled to represent the institution. Narodowy Bank Polski wstrzymał realizację zleceń płatniczych Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Powodem jest spór o to, kto jest uprawniony do reprezentowania TK i dysponowania środkami zgromadzonymi na jego rachunkach bankowych – poinformował NBP.https://t.co/KXwEBL6j9k pic.twitter.com/0h90bPdTLO — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 16, 2026 Last month, eight judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, has refused to swear in – took control of the court. They declared that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, both of whom were appointed to the TK under the former government, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties and launched disciplinary proceedings against them. Święczkowski denounced the move as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the court’s other six judges, also appointed under the former government. A few days later, Święczkowski submitted a statement to the NBP identifying himself as the sole person authorised to manage the TK’s accounts. Later that week, after the newly elected judges held their first meeting and made several key decisions, the NBP said it had also received documents “indicating, in principle, other persons authorised to dispose of the funds held in the Constitutional Tribunal’s bank accounts”. Meanwhile, Święczkowski also issued a legal challenge against the TK takeover at the Supreme Court, which on 10 November issued a ruling revoking the order to suspend Święczkowski and Sochański. However, the validity of that ruling is disputed. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has claimed leadership of the TK, said that only the tribunal itself can decide on the issue. Disciplinary hearings for Święczkowski and Sochański are due to begin later this week. Święczkowski, nevertheless, sent the Supreme Court ruling to the national bank as evidence that he remained the person legally entitled to manage the tribunal. The dispute around Poland's constitutional court risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/mtgutqSTQh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 The NBP’s governor by Adam Glapiński, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and is a longtime associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. On Monday, the NBP announced that it would suspend all payment orders relating to funds held in the TK’s accounts, citing “a set of documents, which mutually cancel each other out”. “This means that payment orders are not executed, regardless of who initiates them,” the NBP said in a statement. “The National Bank of Poland has no authority to decide who is legally entitled to control the Constitutional Tribunal.” Finance minister Andrzej Domański criticised the decision, accusing the central bank of becoming embroiled in the political dispute. “The National Bank of Poland should safeguard its independence, including its political independence,” Domański said. He added that the government would “explore all available options” to secure funding for the TK and ensure that it can continue functioning. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also condemned the NBP’s move, saying its “invocation of a non-existent document [the disputed Supreme Court ruling] to block funding for a constitutional body is…an attempt to protect an entrenched system”. Święczkowski expressed satisfaction that the NBP had denied access to the “usurpers” trying to take over the court but argued that he, as the legitimate chief justice, should be given control over the accounts, reports news website Onet. Prezes Narodowego Banku Polskiego próbuje paraliżować Trybunał Konstytucyjny, powołując się na rzekome orzeczenie Sądu Najwyższego z 10.11.2026 r.. Problem w tym, że ten papier wygląda jak wydany z pieczątką z ziemniaka, a w obiegu są już jego trzy różne wersje. Najpierw Bogdan… pic.twitter.com/7rWELZFIF0 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 16, 2026 Recent events follow a decade-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative PiS government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. However, Nawrocki has refused to accept the oath of most of those judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.
