World.title: FDI in Bulgaria in January-September 2026 was 3.96B euro
World.content:
Foreign direct investment in Bulgaria in the first nine months of the year stood at 3.96 billion euro, the equivalent of 3.1 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), statistics from the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) showed on November 19.

In January-September 2025, FDI was 2.38 billion euro, but the BNB originally reported 1.91 billion euro, which was revised upward later.

Investment in equity, including in the real estate sector, was 96.5 million euro (compared to an outflow of 10.5 million euro in January-September 2025) and the BNB figures showed 3.73 billion euro in re-invested earnings (compared to 3.33 billion euro for the first nine months of last year.)

Net receipts from real estate investments by foreign companies recorded an outflow of 11.1 million euro, compared to an outflow of 21.2 million euro in January-September 2025.

The central bank data showed 130.9 million euro in investment inflows as debt instruments, recorded as the change in the net liabilities of Bulgarian companies towards their foreign investor owners, compared to outflows of 935.3 million euro in the first nine months of 2025. Such financial flows include financial loans, suppliers’ credits and debt securities, BNB said.

By country, the largest direct investment in Bulgaria in the first three quarters of 2026 came from Greece (515.3 million euro), Luxembourg (487.1 million euro) and Switzerland (464.9 million euro). Notable net outflows were recorded towards the United States (-104.1 million euro) and Kazakhstan (-12.3 million euro).

According to preliminary figures, Bulgarian investment abroad increased by 406.8 million euro in January-September, compared to 379.2 million euro in the same period of last year, BNB said.

(Photo: Miroslav Sárička/freeimages.com)

World.title: Eric Rubin, former US ambassador to Bulgaria and former American Foreign Service Association president, dies at 65
World.content:
Eric Rubin, who was US ambassador to Bulgaria from 2016 to 2019 and subsequently served as president of the American Foreign Service Association (AFSA) died on November 17 at the age of 65.

“We extend our deepest condolences to Eric’s wife Nicole, daughters Liana and Rachel, his extended family, loved ones, friends, and the many colleagues whose lives were enriched by his kindness, wisdom, and unwavering sense of purpose,” AFSA said.

“We hope they find comfort in knowing that Eric’s legacy of service, integrity, and advocacy will endure. He will be deeply missed,” the association said.

At a ceremony on June 10 2019, Bulgaria’s highest state honour, the Stara Planina first degree, was conferred on Rubin for his contribution to the development of Bulgarian-US relations.

Before becoming US ambassador in Sofia , Rubin served as deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs, a position he held from 2011 to August 2015.

He was deputy chief of mission at the US embassy in Moscow, Russia from 2008 to 2011, executive assistant to the under secretary of state for political affairs from 2006 to 2008, and director of the office of policy and coordination from 2004 to 2006.

Before that, he was consul general and principal officer at the US consulate-general in Chiang Mai, Thailand from 2001 to 2004, resident associate and risk fellow at the Institute for the Study of Diplomacy at Georgetown University from 1999 to 2000, and special assistant to the under secretary of state for political affairs from 1998 to 1999.

He also served as assistant White House press secretary for foreign affairs and National Security Council director for public affairs from 1997 to 1998, special assistant to the Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs from 1996 to 1997, and deputy political counsellor at the US embassy in Kyiv, Ukraine from 1994 to 1996. Rubin had a BA from Yale University.

World.title: US Senate foreign relations committee approves Holder’s appointment as ambassador to Bulgaria
World.content:
In a 13 – 8 vote on November 18, the US Senate foreign relations committee approved Trump nominee Douglas Holder becoming ambassador to Bulgaria

The post of US ambassador to Bulgaria has been vacant since Kenneth Merten’s resignation in January 2025.

Holder, born in the state of Georgia in 1966, attended Middle Tennessee State University, where he got a degree in political science.

He moved to Florida in 1997.

Holder’s Linkedin entry shows him as president of Doug Holder Real Estate Services from August 2005 to present and a partner in the Legis Group, a lobbying firm, from January 2017 to present.

He was a member of the Florida House of Representatives from 2006 to 2014, when term limits meant that he could not continue in office. Holder was a candidate for the Florida Senate in 2018 but lost in the Republican primary.

He is a lifetime member of the National Rifle Association.

On June 1 2026, Holder was nominated by Donald Trump to be the US ambassador to Bulgaria.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Parliament approves 155mm artillery, IRIS-T ground-based air defence systems deals
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Parliament voted on November 19 to approve a 696 million euro deal to acquire Caesar 155mm artillery from France, and ratified an agreement with Germany on the joint acquisition of IRIS-T SLM ground-based air defence systems.

The deal on the Caesars will see Bulgaria acquire 57 of the 155mm howitzers and additional components for them.

Financing will be done through the EU’s SAFE instrument and with funds from the budget of the Ministry of Defence.

Delivery of the equipment and weapons is planned to be completed by December 31 2030.

The investment expenditure project “Development of artillery support capabilities through the acquisition of 155 mm howitzers”, submitted by the Cabinet, was adopted with 158 votes in favour, no votes against and 19 abstentions.

It was supported by 124 MPs from Progressive Bulgaria, three from GERB-UDF, 12 from the Movement for Rights and Freedoms, 10 from We Continue the Change, and nine from Vuzrazhdane. Nineteen GERB-UDF MPs abstained.

GERB-UDF MP Hristo Gadzhev said that his parliamentary group had refrained from supporting the bill because of the increase in expenses.

Gadzhev said that the loan agreement on the deal which was ratified by Parliament was for 650 million euro. “Thirty-five million euro is no small difference,” he said.

“We cannot support it and will abstain, not for any other reason, but without having all this information about what it costs and how the prices were formed, we cannot vote for 280 million euro on good terms,” he said.

Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told the House: “In reality, these are the unforeseen costs that are added to the contract”.

“This does not mean that these financial resources will be spent. Why are there no details listed on what, how and why it is acquired? Well, because this is money for an investment expense, not a specific contract,” Stoyanov said.

“What I want to tell you is that before we sign each accompanying contract, we send it to the European Commission for review and only then do we take a position on a specific accompanying contract,” he said.

Democratic Bulgaria did not participate in the vote.

“We support the modernisation of the Bulgarian army, however, there are some feelings that there are some companies that are behind deals like this,” Democratic Bulgaria MP Ivailo Mirchev said.

“Things seem to be going well, and then the higher price is explained in another way. Now we are looking at these howitzers, in recent years several European countries have acquired such, the prices are much lower,” he said.

Parliament ratified in two readings in one sitting a Program Agreement between the Ministries of Defence of Germany and Bulgaria for the joint purchase of IRIS-T SLM systems under the Memorandum of Understanding on the Joint Purchase of Ground-Based Air Defence Systems within the Framework of the European Sky Shield Initiative.

A total of 179 MPs voted in favour, with none against. Ten Vuzrazhdane MPs abstained.

The ratification of the Program Agreement is in connection with the subsequent conclusion of a supply contract for the purpose of implementing the second stage of the project “Acquisition of Anti-Aircraft Missile Systems”, namely the joint acquisition of an additional five IRIS-T SLM anti-aircraft missile systems under the SAFE instrument, the Cabinet said in an explanatory memorandum.

Through the program agreement and supplement to the supply contract with Diehl Defence, the project for the acquisition of IRIS-T SLM air defence systems will be implemented to enhance the capabilities of the Air Force in accordance with the requirements of the security environment, it said.

(Photo of the Caesar: US Army)

World.title: Bulgarian prosecutors charge 11 over participation in ‘Ku Klux Klan’ far-right racist organisation in Plovdiv
World.content:
The Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office said on November 18 that it was charging 11 individuals, including four minors, with participation in a far-right racist organiation in Plovdiv calling itself the “Ku Klux Klan”.

The statement said that a 32-year-old individual has been charged with leading the “Ku Klux Klan organisation – Plovdiv Division”, with 10 members, from January 2025 to November 16 2026.

The organisation aimed to preach and incite discrimination, violence and hatred based on race, skin colour, origin, nationality, ethnicity and sexual orientation through speech, print, electronic information systems and otherwise, a crime under the Criminal Code.

The Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office is also charging 10 identified members of the organisation – men, including four minors aged 16 and 17, with participation in the same structure.

The statement said that on November 17, a joint special operation was carried out in the city of Plovdiv by the Interior Ministry and State Agency for National Security under the leadership of the Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office.

During searches and seizures in the city of Plovdiv and the town of Rakovski, at 14 addresses – homes and adjacent buildings inhabited by members of the structure, and in two motor vehicles, various material evidence was found – books, notebooks, badges, clothes with specific symbolism, telephones, masks, swastikas and other items proving affiliation with the far-right racist organisation.

The flag of the Plovdiv structure was also found at one of the addresses.

It was established that its members gathered from January 2025 to November 26 in various public places in the city of Plovdiv, including in restaurants.

The accused alleged leader was detained for a period of up to 72 hours by order of the supervising prosecutor.

The existence and activities of the organization became known during the investigation into the murder of 37-year-old Georgi Kuzev on Mladeshki Hulm in the city of Plovdiv on August 4 2026, the statement said.

Kuzev was murdered by a group of youths who adhered to extremist views.

The Ku Klux Klan is a US white supremacist group founded in 1865. In the 19th and 20th centuries, members were linked to extreme racist violence.

World.title: New Routes and More Flights to Croatia in Winter Schedule
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – New routes and more flights are on the cards for Croatia as part of the winter flight schedule.

Croatian airports are going to be connected by regular routes to 26 markets during the winter flight schedule, which is one more than last winter. Poslovni reports that there will be 35 airlines operating in total, or three more than before. 77 percent of operations are directed abroad with 110 unique routes, representing an increase of three routes, the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) has revealed.

HTZ collected the flight data for the winter schedule from Croatia’s airports in October. They add that the data shows positive trends continuing in the development of Croatia’s air connectivity with international markets.

“Continuous improvement of air connectivity is one of the important prerequisites for developing year-round tourism and strengthening Croatia’s international competitiveness. It is encouraging that even during the winter we see the arrival of new airlines, the introduction of new international routes, and an increase in the number of flights on a series of existing connections,” commented HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić, emphasizing the importance of connecting Croatia with new markets.

The HTZ highlights international routes such as Air China’s Zagreb – Bucharest – Beijing service, which continues to operate during the winter following its launch in September, as well as Ryanair’s Zagreb – Warsaw (Modlin) route, which will operate twice a week throughout the entire winter. British Airways will launch its Dubrovnik – London flights at the beginning of March 2027.

World.title: Vukovar: After 35 Years, a Mother Finds Her Son’s Remains
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – The siege of Vukovar and the subsequent massacre took place over three decades ago now, but after 35 long years, a mother has finally found her son’s remains.

For 35 long and painful years, the Bataković family didn’t know where Zlatko was. Index reports that they waited for an answer about his fate without a grave on which to place flowers and without the chance to properly say goodbye. After three and a half decades of uncertainty, his remains have finally been found, reports HRT. “When they told me, I felt such relief. Mum will finally get to light a candle at her son’s grave instead of in front of Our Lady,” said his brother Branko.

a quiet young man who grew up on the banks of the danube

Zlatko Bataković was 26 years old when he disappeared in wartime Vukovar. His older brother Branko remembers him as Džala, a quiet and peaceful young man who loved the Danube more than anything. “He would often come back from fishing without any fish. I would ask him: ‘So Zlatko, what do you even do there for 20 hours?’ He would reply: ‘Nothing, I just look at the water, it relaxes me.’ He would go to the Danube like that, sit and it would calm him. I couldn’t understand how someone could lose a whole day just looking at the water,” Branko recalls.

joining the national guard

Soon the time came when he could no longer sit peacefully by the river. In June 1991 Zlatko, together with three other young men from Mikluševci, enlisted in the Croatian National Guard. He had already made the decision and only came to tell his brother he was leaving. “It was the 10th of June 1991 when he told me: ‘Bajo, I’m joining the Guard.’ I asked him why, and he answered: ‘Bajo, better me than you, you’ve got two children, I have to go.’ Even then I didn’t understand it, but he left,” Branko revealed.

their final meeting

His brother last saw him in August, when he came to congratulate them on their wedding anniversary and birthday. That day Vukovar was being bombed and they came to pick Zlatko up. He started towards the vehicle but returned once more to his mother. “He came out. He was wearing a chain with a pendant that said Zlatko – we had bought it for him for his eighteenth birthday. He said to me: ‘I’m going now, I’ll give you all the money. Put it in the passport.’ I told him: ‘I won’t.’ And he answered: ‘You have to, you have to take it.’ He hugged me and kissed me,” his mother Veruška Bataković remembers.

She couldn’t know that she was seeing him for the last time ever. The war was becoming ever more brutal. Croatian defenders on positions around Vukovar were trying to stop the enemy forces. “I remember him telling me: ‘Nothing will come of this. They’ll just keep it as a buffer zone so there won’t be a conflict.’ We never even dreamed that something like this would happen,” says fellow fighter Zdenko Biki.

years turned into decades…

According to witness statements, Zlatko was captured at Ristić’s farm and taken in the direction of Negoslavci. There, his brother Branko says, he was recognised by a man who knew the family, but that did not save his life. “He told him: ‘I know you, you’re Veruška’s son. Why are you here? I’ll let you go home now.’ He took him to the back yard, fired a burst into his back and killed him,” Branko says. The years passed and every new piece of information raised hope. They searched for him among the living, on lists of prisoners and in the stories of returnees. They believed even in things that seemed impossible to others. “We even had information that the Serbs had taken them to the mines in Aleksinac to work. Mum used to dream that Zlatko was alive, that he was working in a mine in Serbia, that he had lost his memory and that he had a wife and two children,” Branko says.

zlatko was finally found, three and a half long decades later

Zlatko’s remains were found two years ago at Petrovačka dola. Branko asked Minister Tomo Medved for only one thing – that the news of the discovery not be published before he personally told his mother. He spent two days gathering the strength for that conversation. “Mum is always watching the TV. The news came at around five and I arrived at four. I called all the children to come in. She was surprised and happy. And then I hugged her and told her. That scream… it cannot be described,” Branko recalls.

For 35 years Veruška had no grave she could go to. In front of the image of Our Lady in the courtyard she lit candles, prayed and waited for the son she had last hugged in August 1991. Now she finally knows where her beloved son is. On his grave reads the name she had spoken in her prayers for decades. Behind the letters remains a life cut short at the age of 26 and a mother who waited decades for an answer. Now that she has received it, she still asks the same question.

“Why him of all people? Zlatko, you shouldn’t have gone. But we couldn’t stop him. That was his fate from birth and that’s that,” concluded Veruška Bataković.

World.title: Croatian Rest Stops Ranked Among the Best in Europe
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – Croatian rest stops have ranked among the best in Europe, coming 7th out of the 23 analysed countries.

A major analysis of rest stops across Europe was recently carried out, with Poland ranking the absolute best, and Sicily the worst. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that numerous areas of road user interest were looked into, whether it’s refuelling, using the toilet or just grabbing a coffee, rest areas are among the key elements of any motorway and travel plan.

Czechvignette.cz, an independent intermediary for the sale of Czech vignettes, conducted a study on the best and worst rest areas across Europe. It ranked as many as 5,363 rest areas along motorways in 26 European countries, based on more than seven million Google ratings and over 300,000 user reviews. The analysis covered petrol stations, classic rest areas and locations that offer both fuel and food. Countries were ranked according to the rating of a typical rest area, that is, the median rating of all ranked rest areas in the country. Only 23 countries with at least 10 ranked rest areas made the list. Finland (8), Ireland (9) and Luxembourg (8) did not have a sufficient number of rest areas.

croatia is positioned among europe’s best

According to the data, Croatia ranks 7th out of 23 countries based on the rating of a typical rest area, with a score of 4.21. It sits just behind Slovenia (4.24) and ahead of Hungary (4.15). Also in the top 10 are Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Romania, Austria, Czechia and Norway.

Toilets are the biggest source of complaints (23 percent), followed by staff and service (14 percent) and prices (10 percent). The highest-rated rest area on Croatian motorways is Krka – West on the A1 motorway in the southbound direction near Skradin, with a score of 4.62. The lowest-rated is Modruš – South on the A1 in the eastbound direction near Josipdol, with 3.82 stars. A typical Croatian rest area has a rating of 4.21 stars, which is the median score of the 90 ranked locations. Of the top 10, eight offer a full range of services. The remaining two (both Krka rest areas) have catering facilities.

Half of the 10 lowest-rated rest areas are located on the A3 motorway, while five of the 10 highest-rated are on the A1. According to the analysis, Karlovac County has three rest areas among the top 10 and two among the bottom 10.

neighbouring italy ranks exceptionally poorly

Looking at Europe as a whole, MOP Rudnik Zachód on Poland’s S19 expressway (near Kraśnik) is the highest-rated, with an average score of 4.72 stars. Poland can boast six of the ten highest-rated rest areas in Europe overall; Bulgaria has two, while Spain and Romania each have one. Returning to the top country on the list, a typical Polish rest area is rated 4.3 stars — the highest average among the 23 countries — while Belgium is at the very bottom with an average of 3.78, just behind Italy (3.79).

When looking at specific locations, the analysis shows that Area di parcheggio Costa Gaia Nord, a rest area on Sicily’s A29 motorway near Alcamo, is the lowest-rated in Europe, with an average score of 2.15 stars. France has as many as six of the ten lowest-rated rest areas. Toilets are the biggest source of complaints across Europe, they account for 23 percent of all written review complaints. Staff and service follow with 14 percent, and prices with 10 percent. Safety, parking, and fuel/EV charging each make up approximately four to six percent of complaints.

World.title: British Airways Cancels Zagreb-London Route as Ryanair Dominates
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – British Airways is cancelling its long-standing Zagreb-London route as Ryanair dominates the route from the Croatian capital to Stansted.

The famous British national carrier British Airways has decided to cancel its route between London and Zagreb. This significantly changes the flight offering between the capitals of Croatia and the United Kingdom, according to the portal Croatian Aviation.

British Airways, one of Europe’s largest airlines, is discontinuing the route that connected London Heathrow Airport with Zagreb. Index reports that for many years, this service was part of British Airways’ network and provided a direct link between the two cities, as well as onward connections to international destinations via the London hub. Last winter the airline made the route seasonal and did not operate it from the end of October until the end of March. Although the same arrangement had been announced for this year, flights have now been withdrawn from sale for next summer as well.

ryanair dominates the route – and it’s much cheaper

The market for flights between Zagreb and London has become highly competitive in recent years. Ryanair currently operates on this route, connecting Zagreb with Stansted Airport, while Croatia Airlines maintains a service to Heathrow. Ryanair’s entry has significantly affected market dynamics, especially in the segment of passengers for whom ticket price is the most important factor. Heathrow Airport continues to play a key role for business travellers and those continuing their journeys to other continents via London.

With the withdrawal of British Airways, Zagreb Airport is losing yet another major European carrier. The question arises whether the remaining airlines will be able to compensate for the capacity previously provided by British Airways. This is particularly relevant for direct flights to Heathrow, given that the airport is heavily congested and has no free slots available.

The departure of British Airways is an additional loss for Zagreb Airport, from which Austrian Airlines will also permanently withdraw in the near future

World.title: “I Couldn’t Leave”: The Pregnant Nurse Who Stayed in Vukovar Hospital
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – Zvezdana Pinjuh was very heavily pregnant in November 1991, despite that, she stayed to help the wounded and vulnerable at Vukovar Hospital instead of escaping. “I couldn’t leave”, she recalls.

Nurse Zvezdana Pinjuh was in the advanced stages of her pregnancy back in November 1991, yet she remained in the besieged Vukovar and continued helping the wounded in the local hospital. Index reports that although she had the opportunity to leave the city, she decided to stay with her colleagues and patients. On the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, she recalled those days in an interview for Dnevnik. “I stayed. I just couldn’t leave. There were very few of us medical staff, and there were a great many wounded. Every day there were more and more. I simply could not allow myself to abandon all of that even though I was pregnant,” Pinjuh recalled.

no water, no electricity, and barely any medical supplies

During the nearly three-month siege of Vukovar, the hospital was one of the few places where the wounded could receive medical help. Around 4,000 wounded passed through it, and the medical staff performed approximately 2,500 operations. Despite the markings of the International Red Cross, the hospital was exposed to shelling every day. On some days as many as 700 projectiles fell on it.

Towards the end of the siege, doctors and nurses worked without electricity, water and basic medical supplies. Despite such conditions, 16 children were born in the hospital during the war, and the medical staff also provided assistance to twenty members of the enemy forces. “The conditions were inhumane, we worked 24 hours a day, there was very little rest. We were thirsty, hungry, exhausted, but we all worked equally. That was a unity that is unimaginable,” Pinjuh recalled.

the massacre after the fall of vukovar

After the defence of Vukovar was broken on the 18th of November 1991, members of the JNA and Serbian forces also entered the hospital. On the 19th of November, numerous wounded, patients, defenders, civilians and members of the medical staff were taken from the hospital. In the following days, crimes against the prisoners followed. Around 200 people taken from the Vukovar hospital were killed at nearby Ovčara. The fate of some of those taken away has still not been clarified, and their families continue to search for the remains of their loved ones to this day.

Pinjuh said that Vukovar has been rebuilt after the war, but that the consequences of the wartime suffering are still deeply present among its inhabitants, especially because of the unresolved fate of the missing persons. “I hope that these newer generations will breathe life back into Vukovar and that it will again be a beautiful city as it once was,” she said. Today marks 35 years since the fall of Vukovar, and the central commemoration will take place with the Column of Remembrance, through which people from all over Croatia will pay tribute to the fallen defenders and civilians.

World.title: Zagreb Ranks Extremely Poorly in Terms of Air Quality
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – Zagreb has ranked extremely poorly in terms of air quality, at the very bottom of the entire European ranking.

Zagreb ranks near the bottom of the European ranking of cities by air quality, according to a new study by the organisation Clean Cities, whose results were presented by the Cyclists’ Union (Sindikat biciklista). Poslovni reports that among the 40 European cities analysed, the Croatian capital took an embarrassing 38th place, with a grade of E and 19.1 points out of a possible 60. Only Bucharest and Athens ranked worse.

The study, titled Free to Breathe, covered air quality and the progress of European cities in developing sustainable mobility. The results reveal a worrying picture: only three cities — Copenhagen, Stockholm and Helsinki – already meet the new European Union limit values for two particularly harmful groups of pollutants — nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅). This means that as many as 93 percent of the analysed cities still do not meet the new European air quality standards.

zero points for zagreb

A particularly worrying figure concerns Zagreb’s readiness to meet the stricter European standards that are due to apply from 2030. In this category, the Croatian capital scored no points at all. Overall, Zagreb collected 19.1 points out of a possible 60. For current air quality it received 13.6 out of 30 points, while for changes in pollution levels over the past ten years it scored 4.5 out of a possible ten points. It performed even worse in the category of transport policies aimed at reducing pollution. For sustainable mobility measures it received only one point out of a possible ten. Cities were assessed according to four criteria: current pollution levels, compliance with the new EU limit values, changes in air quality over the past decade, and transport and other measures that promote sustainable mobility.

only bucharest and athens are worse than zagreb

The study results show large differences between European regions. While Nordic cities achieved the best results, the bottom of the ranking is mainly occupied by cities in Southern, Central and Eastern Europe. Among the cities with the worst results, in addition to Zagreb, stand out Turin, the wider Milan area, Kraków, Wrocław, Warsaw, Rome, Prague and Budapest. The last two places went to Bucharest and Athens. Athens particularly stands out for its high concentration of nitrogen dioxide. The average value was 37.6 micrograms per cubic metre, the highest among all 40 cities analysed.

london and paris show that this issue can be resolved

Nevertheless, the study also brings positive examples of cities that have managed to significantly improve air quality over the past ten years. Among them are Copenhagen, London, Paris and Stuttgart. Their progress is linked to concrete transport and urban planning measures, such as the introduction of low- and zero-emission zones, the electrification of bus transport, the establishment of school streets, and the construction and expansion of cycling infrastructure. Some cities have managed over the past decade to reduce nitrogen dioxide concentrations by more than a third, and some have come close to a reduction of as much as 50 percent. In this way they have shown that decisive transport policies can deliver significant results in the fight against pollution. How widespread the problem is is also shown by the fact that as many as 37 of the 40 analysed cities exceed at least one of the four new air pollution limit values, while 18 cities fail to meet any of them.

much stricter rules by 2030

With the revised Ambient Air Quality Directive, the European Union is introducing stricter limit values for pollutants that member states must achieve by 2030. The aim of the new rules is to reduce the health risks associated with pollution and to bring European standards closer to the recommendations of the World Health Organisation. Along with the publication of the study results, the Free to Breathe campaign was also launched. Through it, the organisation Clean Cities calls on European cities and national governments to accelerate the implementation of measures for cleaner air. The study results clearly show that Zagreb seriously lags behind a large part of Europe in this area. Given the extremely weak result in the category of transport policies, the city authorities face a major challenge: without more concrete measures to reduce car traffic, develop public transport and encourage cycling, significant progress will be hard to achieve.

World.title: Three Months After the Omiš Fire – Still No Real Answers
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – Over three months have now passed since the devastating Omiš fire, yet the public and more importantly those directly affected are still waiting for actual answers.

The catastrophic fire that engulfed the Omiš area on the night of August the 13th to the 14th remains fresh in most people’s minds, particularly for those who were near it. Index reports that six people lost their lives as a result of that specific fire, homes were destroyed, and residents fled directly into the sea to escape the flames. Survivors described the dramatic moments, escaping from blocked roads, and boat rescues for HTV. Three months after the tragedy, they are still seeking answers regarding accountability, the warning system, and reconstruction aid.

fleeing from the flames

For the residents of Omiš and surrounding towns, the night of the fire began with the flames rapidly spreading toward their houses. Goran Lović from Lokva Rogoznica recounted how his wife called him to return urgently because the fire had already caught their building. When he arrived, the fire had spread so much that they could no longer reach their other house, about three hundred meters away, where a minor child was located.

Dubravka Marunčić from Stanići was putting her children to bed when her daughter noticed that the tree in front of the house was red. When she turned around, she realized the fire had already reached them and decided to leave immediately with the children. Gabrijela Baučić from Borak also tried to escape by car with her family, but traffic had almost come to a standstill. “My younger one, David, when he saw the flames in the rearview mirror, turned around and saw it coming close to us. ‘Mum, drive faster, we’re going to burn!’ And you’re just standing still. It’s horrendous.”

Julija Hrstić tried to protect her house by hosing it down with water, but when they lost electricity and water, the family decided to leave. They grabbed their dog and put him in the car, but soon got stuck in a line of vehicles that was barely moving.

clogged roads and an escape into the sea

Marunčić described how cars drove between flames while the wind carried embers. “It was burning on both the upper and lower sides of the road. A rain of embers was falling and it was horribly hot,” she said. When she saw that cars were also burning and people were fleeing from them, she turned toward the sea. There, she got out of the vehicle with her three children and ran toward the shore, where many people were already in the shallows. “We couldn’t breathe. Thick black smoke came down, embers were falling around us,” she recalled.

She also recounted how a young man approached them in the sea and began splashing them with seawater to protect them from the heat. “Just by him being close to me, I felt safe. I calmed down because I knew I could count on him,” she recalled. Soon, boats arrived and began transporting people to safety.

“we could hear people screaming”

Among the people who set out in their boats to help with the rescue was Mario Popovac from Omiš. With a friend, he sailed toward the endangered areas despite extremely poor visibility due to smoke. “We heard screams. We simply drove the boat right in among the people. At 200 or 300 metres from the shore, we couldn’t stand the heat,” he described. They found the first people about three hundred metres from the shore. Popovac says the smoke was so thick he couldn’t even see the bow of his own boat. During one trip, his friend warned him to stop, and in the sea they spotted an elderly man keeping himself afloat by holding onto two empty fuel cans.

“We came across him by chance. It is fortunate, in my opinion, that citizens spontaneously went out to sea,” he said. The evacuation lasted until roughly 04:30 in the morning. Marunčić also mentioned Milan Balić, who came by boat to pick up people on the shore of Mala Luka and, according to her, refused to leave until he had boarded everyone who needed help.

three months since absolute tragedy…

Six people lost their lives in the fire. Among the deceased were two female workers from the same hotel, a retired fire commander, and three members of the same family. Julija Hrstić admits that she is still overwhelmed by emotion today. “A life that is lost cannot be brought back. Neither life nor health for the people who will suffer consequences. When I think about it today, I often feel like crying,” she said. Even three months after the tragedy, residents are raising questions about how the warning system functioned. Baučić claims they did not receive timely evacuation instructions. “No siren sounded, we received no instructions. It was chaos. Nobody knew where to go or what to do,” she said.

Julija Hrstić also wonders why the SRUUK early warning system was not activated. “Could there have been a reaction to alert people? Better a false alarm than for this to happen,” she stated. Residents also pointed out neglected firebreaks and the unavailability of water. Goran Lović claims there were not enough hydrants.

left with no answers

The danger did not end when the fire was extinguished, because landslides are now threatening the area. Baučić, whose apartment burned down, described how her family lost everything in a single night. “In one night, you simply lose everything you’ve built for years. Without a home, a family nest,” she said. She warns about rocks that began falling after the fire and the danger of larger landslides due to destroyed vegetation. Goran Lović warns of the same issue, believing that urgent coastal remediation and state aid are needed because the local community lacks sufficient funds. He also adds that residents estimate the total damage to be higher than the amount mentioned by the government.

Three months after the tragedy, residents are still waiting for answers about the causes of the fire and possible accountability. “There is no information whatsoever about the investigation, accountability, and handling of the situation. We want something to be set in motion so that Omiš never happens to anyone again,” said Julija Hrstić. Lović also demands that authorities explain what happened. “We just want to know what happened, why people lost their lives, why our property is gone,” he stated. He emphasizes that residents feel forgotten and expect concrete help.

World.title: Vukovar Procession to Carry the Names of the Missing
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – The Vukovar procession will have thousands of people wearing the names of those still categorised as missing on their clothing.

Today marks the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, one of the defining moments of the Homeland War and the place of the type of massacre unseen since WWII. Index reports that in this year’s Column of Remembrance, thousands of young people will participate wearing T-shirts with the names of missing persons. This is part of the “Instead of Them” (Umjesto njih) initiative, organised for the third consecutive year by the Student Catholic Centre (SKAC) from Osijek. As part of the project, an application was also designed to permanently preserve the memories and personal stories of the people in whose name the youth will walk the streets of Vukovar.

a tribute to those still missing – all 1,725 of them

In this way, young people want to pay tribute to the 1,725 people who are still being searched for. Their message is that the memory of fallen, missing, and suffering Croatian defenders and civilians must be preserved. Many of the participants will set out on foot from Osijek toward Vukovar during the night.

“It’s a big responsibility and a very honourable role to be able to wear the name of someone who gave their life for the homeland,” said Ana Pešikan, a member of Osijek’s SKAC. Vlatka Ivančičević, head of the SKAC office, shared what motivated her to participate. “When I looked from the side and saw the faces of people searching for the name of one of their own on a T-shirt, in that moment it became very real to me,” she said.

passing on the truth about the war

Although many of those planning to march wearing the names of Vukovar’s missing were not even born during the Homeland War, today they want to pass on the truth about the events of that time. “This year on our T-shirts we’re wearing the names of missing defenders, and by wearing white T-shirts with a universal message we will pay tribute to all civilians from the Homeland War,” explained Domagoj Galić, coordinator of the “Instead of Them” initiative.

So that participants can learn more about the people whose names they wear, the organizers are recording their life stories in a special web application. “We’re aware of how grateful we should be to those people who made it possible for us to live today in a free Croatia and enjoy freedom. This is the least we can do to show them respect and gratitude,” said Ivan Galić from the organising team.

World.title: Estonian PM warns Europe against falling for 'security' talks with Russia
World.content:
Entertaining Moscow's demands for talks on European security could make bargaining chips of the Baltics and Poland, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) has warned.

In an opinion piece published in The Economist this week, Michal urged Europe to prioritize supporting Ukraine, including in any negotiated end to the war and on its path to EU and NATO membership. He compared Moscow's demand for security talks as a precondition for peace to an arsonist wanting to discuss a burning building's design before putting out the fire.

The prime minister argued that Europe's security architecture is already established through agreements such as the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter and even the 2002 NATO-Russia Council (NRC).

"Western countries stuck to these deals," he said. "Russia ripped them up."

Michal noted that Russia's previous calls to limit NATO influence to the east would effectively create two tiers within the alliance, leaving eastern members in a "NATO-lite whose members' defense rests on empty promises."

While acknowledging that Russia's latest round of demands — including regarding NATO's eastern flank — are gaining a hearing, he warned that discussion isn't harmless, and that allowing Moscow a say in Europe's security would also put the security and sovereignty of the Baltic states, Poland and other countries back on the negotiating table as a bargaining chip.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"Estonia," he added, "knows very well what happens when its fate is settled by others."

Moscow trying to distract and divide

Michal stressed that while Russia will try to shift the blame, the key to ending the war already lies in Moscow, so peace in Ukraine must remain the priority.

He urged European countries to keep arming and funding Ukraine while continuing to pressure Russia using other available means, adding that giving in to Russian pressure would only invite further demands.

"A demand for talks on 'architecture' is meant to distract us from all of this, and to divide us over it," he pointed out.

The Estonian leader also warned against yielding to Russian pressure and threats, noting that "a state that yields to blackmail will be blackmailed again."

Circling back to the burning house analogy, Michal emphasized that no one sensible would negotiate blueprints with the arsonist while the house is still burning.

Putting out the fire and holding the arsonist to account must come first, he said, "and only then do you sit down to rebuild, with the people who stayed to fight the flames and not the one who lit them."

World.title: Estonia's Paul Aron escapes unhurt amid Formula E testing crash carnage
World.content:
Estonian racing driver Paul Aron escaped unhurt after crashing out at Turn 3 during a chaotic, red-flag-strewn second day of Formula E preseason testing near Madrid on Wednesday.

Stepping in at short notice to drive the new Gen4 car for Fortescue Zero Racing alongside Briton Dan Ticktum, the 22-year-old became the first casualty of a session repeatedly halted by crashes and mechanical stoppages at the famous Jarama Circuit.

The Estonian's off-track excursion came just 20 minutes into Wednesday morning's dry session. While he was uninjured, RacingNews365 reported, the impact ended his running for the morning and left him bottom of the day's time-sheets at 1:38.008. He had previously posted the 15th-fastest time in Monday's opening test.

Turn 3 proved a recurring flash-point as drivers wrestled with Formula E's new Gen4 cars — triggering five red flags on Wednesday (12 for the week) that included a heavy crash for 2023 champion Jake Dennis — while Mahindra's Edoardo Mortara and Citroën's Jean-Éric Vergne topped the day's two sessions.

Testing in Madrid concludes on Friday.

Aron currently serves as a test and reserve driver for the Enstone-based BWT Alpine F1 Team, having stepped up to the role after finishing third overall in the 2024 FIA Formula 2 Championship with Hitech Pulse-Eight.

Earlier in the 2026 Formula 1 season, the Tallinn native made official Friday first-practice appearances for Alpine at both the Hungarian Grand Prix in July — deputizing for Franco Colapinto — and the Italian Grand Prix at Monza in September, where he filled in for Pierre Gasly.

No Estonian has yet raced full-time in Formula 1, while Aron has increasingly been linked with a full-time Formula E race seat for the 2027 season, with both Fortescue Zero Racing and Cupra Kiro reportedly in the mix.

Paul Aron is the younger brother of former racing driver Ralf Aron, 28, who won the 2015 Italian Formula 4 Championship and finished as runner-up in the 2018 Macau Grand Prix before transitioning into motorsport management.

Formula E is the world's premier all-electric, single-seater motorsport championship, often dubbed the electric counterpart to Formula 1.

World.title: Guard dogs kill juvenile wolf in rare reversal at South Estonia farm
World.content:
While media reports have focused largely on a spate of dogs being killed by wolves in Estonia, the tables were turned recently at a South Estonian farm, weekly Postimees reported .

The wolf, a juvenile member of a pack that had been preying on sheep and calves in Karula National Park, met its match in the form of several large livestock guardian dogs.

A dog killing a wolf is an exceptional event, most hunters say, and the owner of the farm affected, Liilia Tali, said she hoped the encounter will change the pack's behavior and keep it from returning to prowl around the farm's pastures anytime soon.

Tali said things at Rõõmu farm in Valga County had begun getting out of hand once the wolves started approaching the barns, noting the pack was "quite large," up to 10-strong. She puts the bold behavior down to a shortage of prey in the forest at a time of growing wolf numbers.

The pack first attacked the farm, in the village of Rebasemõisa, in mid-October, killing 20 sheep after the two guard dogs on duty retreated to a barn; an electric fence also proved insufficient to keep the wolves at bay.

A week and a half later, the predators returned to the farm, which keeps around 700 sheep, including roughly 200 lambs.

However, this time the owners were ready, putting all seven of their large livestock guardian dogs — including trained Kangals and Spanish mastiffs weighing up to 70 kilograms — on duty.

This proved not only enough to ward off the attack — not one of the livestock was harmed — but when the family inspected the scene the next morning, they found the carcass of a young wolf in the pasture.

Ants Järvmägi, a board member of the local Lüllemäe hunting society, said the loss of a young, weak wolf likely mattered little to the pack, noting that wolves maintain strict pecking orders, usually led by an alpha female, and think little of killing each other if necessary.

While Rõõmu farm was safe this time and may remain so, Järvmägi added there was no way to be certain the pack had not attacked other farms — some raids go unreported, he noted.

The original Postimees piece is here.

A surge in wolf attacks has prompted calls from lobby groups to relax hunting rules. Estonia's annual wolf cull is currently underway, having started at the beginning of November and running through the end of February. A cull quota of 110 wolves remains intact after a court overruled an appeal from conservation groups — similar appeals have previously delayed or shortened culls, particularly for bears, though this season's hunt is proceeding as planned. Estonia's Eurasian wolf (Canis lupus lupus) population is estimated at around 300, with some packs in southern border regions moving between Estonian and Latvian territory.

World.title: Estonian investors unable to subscribe to Anthropic IPO shares
World.content:
Record interest in the initial public offering (IPO) of AI company Anthropic shares stems from the belief that artificial intelligence will shape the technology market over the next decade, though herd behavior may also be playing a role, says Toomas Arak, head of financial markets at Swedbank.

U.S. artificial intelligence company Anthropic raised a record $81 billion through its IPO, surpassing the previous record of $75 billion held by space company SpaceX. The IPO subscription price was set at $83 per share, giving the company a market capitalization of nearly $1.5 trillion. Shares were oversubscribed almost sevenfold.

Arak told ERR that the extraordinary interest in Anthropic's IPO reflects investors' desire to participate in the next AI success story with significant growth potential.

FOMO can be amplified

"Interest stems both from high expectations for Anthropic as one of the leaders in the field and from a broader belief that artificial intelligence will shape the technology market and our everyday lives over the coming decade," he said.

At the same time, Arak noted that intense public attention can create excitement among investors and amplify FOMO, the fear of missing out.

"This can also lead to herd behavior, where many investors move in the same direction at once. These psychological factors can influence investment decisions, so caution is warranted. The share price may fluctuate quite sharply during the first days of trading," he said.

According to LHV senior broker Marten Arumäe, Eastern European investors were unable to participate in the IPO due to the small size of the region's markets.

Anthropic's IPO is the largest share offering in history, Arumäe pointed out. In addition to the $81 billion raised through the IPO, the company also conducted a targeted offering that brought in another $26 billion.

"The company's exceptionally successful IPO is a combination of a very hot sector overall and a company viewed as one of the likely major winners in that sector in the future," Arumäe said.

According to him, investors have long-term faith in the AI sector and regard the companies currently advancing the fastest in the field as potential major winners over the coming decades.

"The entire sector is developing at an incredible pace, and competition among companies is extremely intense. At the same time, demand for products and services offered by AI-related companies is at record levels," Arumäe noted.

Revenue surges, but losses exceed $1 billion

The LHV broker added that Anthropic's Claude AI is used primarily by business customers, the segment with the greatest revenue potential. In recent years, the company's number of customers and revenue growth have been impressive. Revenue was approximately $390 million in 2024 and nearly $4.6 billion last year.

In just the first three quarters of this year, the company's revenue has already risen to $33 billion. Despite this, Anthropic recorded an operating loss of $1.26 billion during the same period.

Arak explained that in U.S. IPOs, initial allocations are often available only to selected institutional investors and clients of brokers that belong to the underwriting network.

"In Anthropic's case, Estonia was not among the countries where retail investors were allowed to subscribe to shares," Arak said. "As a result, Estonian retail investors generally have the opportunity to buy shares only after trading begins on the stock exchange."

On the first trading day, trading usually does not begin immediately when markets open at 4:30 p.m. Estonian time. Instead, it may start several hours later, as market participants need time after the opening bell to establish the final opening price based on investor demand.

Arumäe noted that because the IPO was massively oversubscribed, retail investors elsewhere in Europe likely received either no allocation at all or only very small allocations.

"Estonian investors can purchase Anthropic shares on the U.S. secondary market starting today," he added.

Swedbank pension funds participate via Swedish arm

Pertti Rahnel, portfolio manager of Swedbank's pension funds, said the bank's actively managed pension funds participated in Anthropic's IPO through Swedish asset management company Swedbank Robur, of which AS Swedbank Investeerimisfondid is a part.

"As a result of the share allocation, approximately €6.26 million worth of Anthropic shares will be added to the assets of our seven active pension funds," Rahnel said.

He added that until now, investors have generally gained exposure to the growth of artificial intelligence by investing in the "picks and shovels" of the industry, namely semiconductor and hardware manufacturers such as TSMC, or infrastructure providers essential to AI, such as Google and Microsoft.

"Anthropic is one of the first major Western developers of AI models whose shares can be directly purchased on the stock market," Rahnel said.

The portfolio manager noted that AI is one of the most significant technological trends of our generation and that investment in its development could amount to more than 3 percent of U.S. GDP annually in the coming years.

Rahnel also stressed that, despite Anthropic's rapid growth, there are risks involved.

"Key questions include the availability of computing power and the efficiency with which it is used, as well as strong competition from other technology companies and open-source models," he explained. However, he added that Anthropic's development capabilities and the quality of its models should give it a good chance of maintaining an important position in this rapidly growing market.

World.title: Rabbit breeders showcase giants and dwarfs at Tartu exhibition
World.content:
The Estonian Small Animal and Poultry Breeders Association (EVKY) will hold a rabbit exhibition at the Tartu Söödakeskus on November 20–21. The exhibition will feature 20 rabbit breeds from 17 different breeders.

"At the exhibition, a judge evaluates the rabbit's appearance, coat quality and posture," rabbit breeder Maia Näkk said.

According to Näkk, training a rabbit is a daily commitment. "Rabbits require daily care. You take them out of the cage and hold them. Preparing one for an exhibition is a longer process. The rabbit must also be weighed and measured."

"I have a wonderful husband who built a barn for the rabbits, and we have nearly 150 rabbits along with other domestic animals. Our farm actually started with a single rabbit," Näkk said.

Rabbits. Source: Olev Kenk/ERR

"Different breeds are also shown in different poses at exhibitions. I like extremes, and I like the color black," rabbit breeder Peeter Vahtramäe said. He breeds both the world's largest and the world's smallest rabbit breeds.

According to Vahtramäe, these are the two most popular pet rabbit breeds in the world. "Both very large and very small rabbits are kept purely as pets. The smaller breed is the colored dwarf rabbit," Vahtramäe said.

"I have an Angora rabbit, which is raised specifically for its wool. It has to be shorn every three months. I spin the wool myself, knit with it myself, and it's one of my biggest hobbies. I also have a full-time job. I'm a seamstress," rabbit breeder Janika Roops said.

According to Roops, no aggressive animal is suitable for exhibition. "It would be disqualified if it started behaving nervously," Roops said.

Roops also keeps satin rabbits. "It's the only rabbit breed with a glossy coat," said Roops, who has nearly 100 rabbits at home. "My goal is breeding, and I've been doing that for nearly 20 years."

World.title: Former Icelandic prime minister: Small states must redefine the AI race
World.content:
The U.S.-China AI race and the two powers' transactional approach threaten the global order, former Icelandic Prime Minister Katrín Jakobsdóttir said during a visit to Estonia, urging smaller nations to champion human rights and ethics in AI debates.

On Wednesday, you gave a lecture at the Estonian Academy of Arts on values-based governance. Could you briefly explain how we can govern based on shared values at a time when our societies — even small ones like Estonia — are increasingly divided and have relatively few values in common? What is your recipe for success?

It's difficult to have one recipe because societies are so different. I think we've seen a drastic change in the last decade. When I formed a coalition government in Iceland in 2017, we'd had several snap elections and a lot of turmoil in Icelandic politics, really ever since the economic crisis in 2008. There was quite a strong demand from voters that people be ready to make compromises and create a functional government.

What we've seen in the last few years, however, is that compromise has become a dirty word. People and parties are very locked in their own internet bubbles, where you mainly meet people who agree with you. A real connection between people with different opinions is more difficult than before.

I'm out of professional politics now, but I think we need to demand that our leaders explain their red lines when it comes to collaboration and what compromises they're ready to make and be honest and frank about it. In the end, for a democracy, it's very important that you can make compromises and create political stability.

So, in your view, is compromise-based politics the direction we should be moving in?

No, not just that. Of course, you also want to achieve some results. I'm a politician, so obviously I have my ideas about how society should work. What I'm saying is that sometimes you can't do that in one step. You sometimes have to take many steps to reach your goal.

You are an advocate of the well-being economy. Have we become too fixated on GDP and should we be paying more attention to other indicators as well?

A well-being economy has been part of my political agenda since I began in politics. I come from the environmental movement. What we criticized in Iceland was that everything was focused on economic growth and GDP, without taking into account the environmental damage that was needed to maintain that growth.

You need to measure more than just the economic factors. You need to measure societal and environmental factors. You need to go beyond GDP, as many countries are finally agreeing within the UN.

We could just talk about climate. What are we doing when it comes to climate change? We're still subsidizing fossil fuels more than renewables at the same time as we say we want to achieve our climate goals. We're using taxpayers' money to subsidize fossil fuels and we're using taxpayers' money to fund the health effects of climate change. You have to look at things more holistically than we've been doing.

Katrín Jakobsdóttir. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

In Estonia, too, there are many politicians who view environmental protection as a luxury that stands in the way of economic growth.

You can say climate is a luxury issue, but the facts are very clear. Just look at last summer here in Europe. The heat waves had severe health effects and are also very serious for our productivity as a region. Look at the droughts and the wildfires. I live in the sub-Arctic and we're watching the ice melt in the Arctic, which is detrimental to the ecosystem and to the Indigenous communities living around the Arctic.

Some would call climate a luxury problem, but the data shows otherwise. The sad fact is that even though it's gone down on the political agenda, the climate crisis hasn't gone anywhere.

You also lead New Nordics AI, a Nordic-Baltic artificial intelligence cooperation platform. How can we use and develop AI responsibly, both in terms of the climate and humanity's survival, when the power to shape these issues lies largely in the hands of major powers?

I was listening to the news this morning. The U.S. president was saying he was absolutely against global regulation of AI. The U.S. and China, which define themselves as great powers, are in this race on AI. It's a race they define. They're competing on their own terms.

I think we, the small countries, Europe, need to redefine that race. How do we actually want to use AI? When do we want to use it and when do we not want to use it? I don't want us just to be the recipients of the technology. We need to build our technological capacities, but we also need to talk about the policies. In my opinion, it's not enough just to regulate. This is such a huge cultural change that we need a more open dialogue within our societies and between them on how we really want to work on it.

Estonia, with Latvia and Lithuania, is joining a platform I chair, New Nordics AI. I truly believe the Nordics and the Baltics can decide how to use AI for the common good while maintaining values like democracy and human rights and addressing ethical concerns. I found it interesting yesterday here in Estonia, but also when I meet with young people in particular, that they have deep ethical concerns about AI.

Is Iceland prepared to make land available for the construction of data centers?

We have some data centers. We have some renewable energy. We're sparsely populated, so we don't have the data centers within the urban areas. But in Iceland, questions are arising. How many data centers should we have? How much of our energy do we want to use on that? Even though we have renewable energy, using it means we're spoiling unspoiled nature and wilderness. It's not an easy decision.

We're having that discussion. It's specifically Icelandic, but it's still partly the same as what we saw in the U.S. before the midterms.

Katrín Jakobsdóttir. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

You mentioned the AI race between China and the United States, but there is another race underway in the Arctic region and the Arctic Ocean. How do you see that playing out?

That's a very good question. I've been in politics for so long. Iceland hosted a meeting of the Arctic Council where we had all eight Arctic countries — the Nordics, the U.S., Canada and Russia. This was before the invasion. Everybody agreed it was to be a peaceful area and that we should focus on climate and the environment because of the fragile ecosystem. This was only a few years ago, I believe in 2020 or 2021. We agreed on a ten-year vision.

Then Russia invaded Ukraine. It was an illegal, brutal and senseless invasion, which has had a huge effect on Arctic collaboration. Later we saw the U.S. interest in Greenland. As the Greenlandic foreign minister put it at the Arctic Circle Assembly in Iceland this October, a friend does not show disrespect in this way. It was a very powerful statement because this has really disrupted the alignment on the Arctic.

What would be the best solution for Greenland?

The best solution for Greenland is the one the Greenlanders themselves decide on, in my opinion. They need to decide their own destiny.

How is Iceland contributing to the defense of the region?

We've been a founding member of NATO since 1949. As you probably know, we don't have a military of our own. We provide technical support. We have a center that monitors the North Atlantic Ocean. We try to provide the assistance that's needed on the civilian side. We also have a defense agreement with the U.S.

Is the U.S. a reliable partner for Iceland right now?

Iceland has maintained good collaboration with the U.S. But the multilateral system, including NATO, the UN and more, has been quite undermined in the last few years. We're seeing the emergence of the discourse of great powers, as we see today with this meeting between Russia, China and the U.S. Three guys talking about the rest of the world.

Instead of putting the emphasis on international law, territorial sovereignty and negotiations at a multilateral level, we're seeing a more transactional kind of discourse. Small countries like Estonia and Iceland should be very clear that this is not the discourse we want. It's not the system we want.

I underline that Iceland and the U.S. have enjoyed very good collaboration. We also need to be clear that the multilateral system is important for all the countries that don't define themselves as superpowers. That's the great majority.

Why should the superpowers listen to us small fish?

If you only think about the world in terms of power, you don't have to listen to anyone. You just have to gain as much power as possible. But is that the world you really want? So why should they listen to us? I think those who lead the superpowers also have an obligation to think about the rest of the world and the common good. If you only think about it in terms of power, that's another thing.

Iceland has been a pioneer in inclusive policymaking that takes minorities into account. Is every political decision you make also considered from the perspectives of gender, disability and other minority groups?

I wouldn't go so far as to say that every decision is made that way. But we've done a lot when it comes to evaluating legislation and the budget from the perspective of gender. We've tried to address multisectoral discrimination, for example, when you look at gender, age or racial background. I think we've done many good things, but we're definitely not perfect when it comes to that.

Former Icelandic Prime Minister Katrín Jakobsdóttir. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Katrín Jakobsdóttir (50)

Katrín Jakobsdóttir is an Icelandic politician who served as prime minister of Iceland from 2017 to 2024, leading a broad coalition government comprising the Left-Green Movement, the Independence Party and the Progressive Party. She was a longtime member of Iceland's parliament (Alþingi) and served as minister of education, science and culture from 2009 to 2013.

In spring 2024, Jakobsdóttir resigned as prime minister to run for president of Iceland. She now gives public talks and lectures.

She currently heads New Nordics AI, a Nordic-Baltic cooperation platform focused on artificial intelligence.

Beyond politics, Katrín Jakobsdóttir has strong ties to literature. She studied Icelandic language and literature as well as French at the University of Iceland, earning a master's degree in Icelandic literature in 2004. Before entering politics, she worked as a language editor at Iceland's national public broadcaster (RÚV) and taught literature, among other roles.

Jakobsdóttir gained international recognition as an author in 2022 with the publication of "Reykjavík," a thriller she co-wrote with bestselling Icelandic crime novelist Ragnar Jónasson. The book has also been published in Estonian. She also has a new crime novel forthcoming.

World.title: 3 manufacturers enter bids for Tallinn's bidirectional trams tender
World.content:
Three manufacturers — CAF, PESA and Škoda — have submitted applications to participate in Tallinna Linnatransport's (TLT) procurement of bidirectional trams.

TLT plans to purchase 11 new bidirectional trams through a negotiated procurement procedure, with an option to buy another 11 vehicles at a later date.

Unlike Tallinn's current trams, bidirectional trams have a driver's cab at each end and doors on both sides. This allows them to reverse direction at the end of a line without the need for a turning loop.

The manufacturer selected to supply Tallinn's new trams will be announced by February 2 next year, TLT CEO Kaido Padar said.

"The first new trams are expected to arrive in Tallinn within 33 months of the contract being signed," he added.

Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse said the procurement of new trams is an important step in developing Tallinn's tram network.

"Modern bidirectional trams will allow us to build new tram routes and extend existing lines in stages without having to construct a separate turning loop at the end of each section. This will give the city more options for expanding the tram network while saving both space and construction costs. We hope the bids submitted in the procurement process will make it possible to purchase this new type of rolling stock," Jesse said.

Tallinn's tram network operates 46 trams during peak hours. The city's tram tracks have a total length of approximately 45 kilometers and passengers take around 20 million tram rides annually.

World.title: Tartu to provide backup power units to Ukrainian sister city Lviv
World.content:
Tartu is allocating €33,000 for five portable power stations to help Lviv maintain essential services during widespread blackouts.

The city will purchase the units in cooperation with the Estonian Refugee Council, with the equipment intended to help Lviv keep essential services running during power outages. The funding will come from the City of Tartu's reserve fund.

As winter approaches, Tartu and the Refugee Council are working closely to get the equipment to Lviv as quickly as possible. Mayor Urmas Klaas (Reform) noted that the colder months make the power outages Ukrainians continue to face during the war even harder to endure.

"We want to help Lviv prepare for disruptions so that essential services remain available to residents even in difficult conditions," Klaas said.

"Urban Resilience in Wartime: Lessons from Lviv for European Municipalities," a two-day seminar held in Tartu. November 2026. Source: Maria Grünberg

The support follows an official request from Lviv's mayor.

Sister cities

Tartu and Lviv have been sister cities since 2024. Estonia's second city has provided the Ukrainian city with humanitarian aid and practical support, including vehicles, IT and medical equipment, portable power stations, art supplies, a piano for a music school, and four used buses sent this summer.

Earlier this month, Tartu also joined the Lviv-led international Unbroken Cities network.

The initiative aims to help European cities learn from Ukraine's experience during the war and share ways to keep essential services running, support residents and maintain community resilience during crises.
