World.title: Expressways linking Cavite, Laguna to open in December
World.content:
Transportation Sec. Vince Dizon —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The government is eyeing the full opening of the Cavite-Laguna Expressway (Calax) and the Cavite Expressway (Cavitex)-Calax Link (CCLink) by next month, ahead of the initial target set in the first quarter of 2027, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said on Thursday.

Dizon said Calax was already 97-percent complete and that he would recommend its opening to President Marcos as a “Christmas gift” to Filipinos, especially those living and doing business in these two provinces in Calabarzon (Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, Quezon) region and Metro Manila.

Public Works Secretary Giovanni Lopez said the Department of Public Works and Highways would recommend the opening of the expressways to the President after a road safety audit.

Article continues after this 

READ: Calax, CCLink seen boosting economic activity in Cavite, Laguna

Calax is divided into two subsections. The first connects Centennial Road in Kawit, Cavite, to the Open Canal Interchange in Imus, Cavite. It is expected to cut travel time between Centennial Road and Open Canal Road from 25 minutes to only eight minutes.

The second subsection connects the Open Canal Interchange to Governor’s Drive Interchange in General Trias City, Cavite. Travel time between Open Canal Road and Governor’s Drive is expected to be cut from 20 minutes to 11 minutes.

Both sections are also expected to ease congestion along major roads in Cavite.

READ: Metro Pacific Tollways starts two Calabarzon toll roads in June

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, the 1.2-kilometer CCLink connects Tirona Highway to Centennial Road and Calax, providing a direct link between Cavitex and Calax. This is expected to improve connectivity between Metro Manila and Cavite.

Dizon described the expressway projects as a “total game changer,” particularly for motorists traveling between Cavite, Laguna and Metro Manila, as they would have an alternative to heavily congested roads, such as Aguinaldo Highway. —Chelsy Claire Perez

World.title: Almost P15M worth of marijuana bricks seized in Ifugao buy-bust
World.content:
Police do an inventory of seized marijuana bricks placed inside sacks following a buy-bust operation in Banaue, Ifugao on Nov. 17, 2026. —Photo courtesy of PDEA

SANTIAGO CITY, ISABELA, Philippines — Police seized some P14.64 million worth of marijuana bricks placed inside sacks from a “high-value” drug suspect in a buy-bust operation in Banaue, Ifugao, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) said.

According to PDEA, the arrested 42-year-old suspect from Rizal, Kalinga yielded four sacks loaded with 122 kilos of dried marijuana with fruiting tops.

One of the sacks with 31 kilos of marijuana worth P3.7 million was the subject of the buy-bust operation.

Article continues after this 

READ: Over P500,000 suspected marijuana intercepted at Zambo Sur delivery hub

Three more sacks were discovered after the suspect’s arrest, authorities said.

READ: Marijuana bricks fished from river in Kidapawan City

The law enforcers also seized the car on which the contraband was loaded.

A violation of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Acts of 2002 or anti-drug law is being readied against the suspect.

The operation was carried out by agents from PDEA Cordillera Administrative Region–Ifugao Provincial Office, PDEA Nueva Vizcaya Provincial Office, Ifugao Provincial Police Office Drug Enforcement Unit, and Banaue town police. /cb

World.title: Woman nabbed for possession, use of fake P1,000 bills
World.content:
CABANATUAN CITY, NUEVA ECIJA, Philippines — A 35-year-old woman was nabbed with 13 pieces of alleged fake P1,000 bills after an attempt to use one in purchasing dressed chicken inside a public market in Barangay San Isidro here on Wednesday.

Police Lt. Col. Lester Zafra, city police chief, said a female vendor, a 54- resident of Barangay Magsaysay Norte in this city, sought the help of market officials upon noticing that the money handed to her by the suspect was not genuine.

“Biniro pa niya (victim) na parang peke itong pera mo. Pero sinuklian pa rin niya ng P800 plus,” Zafra said.

Article continues after this 

The vendor then allegedly noticed that the suspect turned restless.

READ: BSP: Fake peso banknotes declined in 2025

Police said the suspect was invited and interviewed at the office of the City Enterprise Economic Management Office (CEEMO).

Upon arrest, responding policemen found 12 more pieces of falsified P1,000 from a wallet that the suspect supposedly voluntarily turned over.

READ: Public warned vs fake bills this holiday season

Article continues after this 

Detained at the police female custodial facility here, the suspect said she was promised by a person whom she did not identify, a share of P200 per P1,000 bill she could dispose of.

“Dala po ng pangangailangan ay tinanggap ko na,” the suspect told police investigators.

Article continues after this 

Charges of estafa and violation of Article 168 of Revised Penal Code or illegal possession and use of false treasury and bank notes have been filed against the suspect before the city prosecutor’s office.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) unit here, upon physical examination, confirmed the bills were counterfeit.Lawyer Mark Fajardo of BSP payments and currency investigation said the confiscated bills were indeed counterfeit, noting that the seized notes were close to genuine.“Pero nakababahala kasi medyo paganda na nang paganda ang features niya; makakabiktima na talaga ito sa publiko,” he said.He urged the public to be extra careful. /cb

World.title: Batangas municipality equips workers with sign language skills
World.content:
LUCENA CITY, QUEZON, Philippines — The municipal government of San Juan, Batangas, has conducted basic Filipino Sign Language (FSL) training for its employees to promote more inclusive and accessible public services.

Municipal personnel from various departments took part in the three-day training held on Nov. 10 to 12, where they learned basic sign language skills to improve their communication with deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals.

“The program aims to equip municipal personnel with the skills needed to provide more inclusive, efficient, and equitable public services, particularly to individuals who use Filipino Sign Language as their primary means of communication,” the local government’s Public Information Office (PIO) said.

Article continues after this 

READ: SC’s adopting sign language helps ‘break down barriers’ – NCDA

The activity was conducted upon the directive of Mayor Ildebrando Salud as part of the municipal government’s commitment to protecting the rights, addressing the needs, and promoting the welfare of persons with disabilities (PWDs).

READ: Basic phrases to get started on learning Filipino Sign Language

In 2018, then-President Rodrigo Duterte signed Republic Act No. 11106, or the Filipino Sign Language Act, declaring FSL as the national sign language of the Filipino deaf community and the official sign language of the government in all transactions involving deaf individuals.

The law also mandates the use of FSL in schools, broadcast media, and workplaces to promote accessibility and equal opportunities for deaf Filipinos. /cb

World.title: ICJ Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
World.content:
The United Nations’ top court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017, in a historic decision.

In the case brought by the Gambia, the ICJ delivered the first ruling in its 80-year history finding a state responsible for committing genocide.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, delivering the court’s verdict.

Iwasawa said around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 “clearance operations,” which also involved widespread sexual violence and violence against children, as the Rohingya fled en masse to Bangladesh.

“Records also contain evidence of intentional targeting of the Rohingya population,” Iwasawa said.

The court found that Myanmar deliberately targeted the approximately 815,000 Rohingya who lived in northern Rakhine before the operation.

Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and their populations replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, the ICJ said, ruling that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

The ICJ president said Myanmar had failed to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible for acts punishable under Article III of the Genocide Convention.

The Myanmar military also disseminated and promoted hate speech in a systematic and coordinated way during the 2017 operation, the court said.

The court ordered Myanmar to cease any ongoing violations of its obligations under the Genocide Convention and to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of those who fled the violence to their homes. It also ruled that Myanmar must investigate suspected perpetrators and prosecute and punish those found responsible, and provide compensation. The amount would be determined in future proceedings, it said.

The ruling cannot be appealed. Rather than prosecuting individuals, the verdict determined that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide.

As a result of the military operation in Rakhine, over one million Rohingya now live in what is effectively the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh. For some of them, the case offered a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

“This is a historic ruling. For the first time, the World Court has found a state responsible for committing genocide—and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president,” said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

Horsey pointed out that the court lacks the power to enforce the orders contained in its ruling.

“What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyitaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it,” he said.

Myanmar should comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya, said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” she said.

Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, said international governments should not welcome putschist president and former Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya.

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said.

All other states, including members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, must also uphold these obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law, taking every measure within their power to prevent and punish genocide, Callamard said.

She urged the UN Security Council to impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.

The Myanmar military’s 2017 “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee amid widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.

World.title: 4,500 Myanmar Refugees to Get Thai Job Training Under $3m Project
World.content:
Japan has agreed to back employment training for 4,500 Myanmar refugees and their families in Thailand under a 478-million-yen (US$ 3 million) project implemented by the International Labor Organization (ILO).

Funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the two-year project announced Tuesday will also incorporate training for trainers, job-matching services, and outreach to employers including Japanese companies.

It will cover residents of border camps in Tak, Mae Hong Son, Kanchanaburi, and Ratchaburi provinces, aiming to serve high labor demand in Kanchanaburi as well as Chonburi and Rayong, where Japanese businesses are concentrated.

More than 100,000 refugees are currently sheltering in nine temporary camps along the Thai-Myanmar border, according to the Border Consortium (TBC), the main provider of food and shelter in the camps.

The refugees continue to face “significant resource pressure” due to international funding cuts, leading to reduction of food rations, medical services, and other basic assistance, with “no clear sign of reversal,”

the group’s 2026 mid-year report said.

Thailand granted Myanmar refugees the right to work outside their camps in August 2025 after funding collapsed following the USAID freeze. Since then, more than 6,000 have entered the workforce. Feedback has been mixed, with some complaining of language barriers, skill mismatches and unstable working hours.

“Some don’t have steady jobs, working for just a few days every month and surviving on meager wages,” a manager at Maela Camp in Tak Province told The Irrawaddy, citing testimony from returnees.

“We interview them and ask why they returned. They mention discrimination due to the language barrier.”

He said refugees receive a one-day orientation before joining the workforce covering their legal rights, minimum wage, work permit rules, workplace safety, and how to get help if they face abuse on the job.

However, information gaps and inconsistencies between employment brokers and employers often leave workers facing unexpected working conditions.

Announcing the project on Tuesday, the ILO said employers would support both recruitment and integration of refugees into the workforce.

The project “will help displaced persons access safe and decent jobs, while supporting employers to meet their labor needs,” ILO Thailand country director Xiaoyan Qian said at the signing ceremony.

A Karenni resident of a Mae Hong Son camp welcomed the initiative as a pathway to employment. “I hope the training will instill the basic skills needed to join the workforce,” he told The Irrawaddy, admitting it was the first he had heard of the project.

Separately, the Mae La camp official said a Japanese organization was scheduled to visit for a meeting that could be linked to the project.

Thailand relies heavily on migrants from Myanmar to fill labor shortages in key industries like construction, agriculture, and hospitality. The UNHCR and rights groups have welcomed Thailand’s decision to grant refugees labor rights as a win-win for both sides.

World.title: Regime Media Censor Min Aung Hlaing’s Swipes at China, Thailand
World.content:
Myanmar’s state-run newspapers have censored remarks by junta chief Min Aung Hlaing that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, and accuse Thailand of facilitating “illegal trade” through resistance-held territory, despite devoting six pages to coverage of his more than two-hour address to the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament.

In Wednesday’s speech, the junta boss delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive that led to the collapse of the regime’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and marked one of the most humiliating military setbacks of the post-coup period.

Without explicitly naming Myanmar’s giant neighbor, Min Aung Hlaing emotionally suggested the offensive was made possible by outside backing.

Recalling the launch of the offensive on Oct. 27, 2023, he said the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) conducted the surprise attack with superior manpower, weapons and technological assistance from “certain people.”

“I was traveling at the time. I received a phone call very early in the morning saying fighting had broken out. I immediately took out a map to assess the size of their forces. The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he stated during his speech.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he said.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

The comments echoed earlier complaints by Min Aung Hlaing during the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

The junta chief also turned his fire on Thailand, accusing Thai authorities of encouraging cross-border commerce through resistance-controlled territory.

Referring to his Nov. 12 meeting with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Min Aung Hlaing complained that despite discussions on using official border crossings, reports of what he called illegal trade were still reaching him.

“Recently, the Thai foreign minister came and discussed border crossings with me. I said Bridges No. 1 and No. 2 at Myawaddy are open and Tachileik is open, so use those official gates and not the illegal ones. But they are still supporting the illegal gates,” he said.

He accused Thai authorities of allowing goods to move through crossings linked to what he called “insurgents” because they offered easier access for both imports and exports.

The accusation came despite Thailand being one of the strongest advocates of maintaining engagement with Naypyitaw and pushing for Myanmar’s eventual reintegration into regional bloc the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Yet neither the China-related remarks nor the criticism of Thailand were reported in Thursday’s editions of Kyemon, Myanma Alin and the English-language Global New Light of Myanmar.

The state newspapers carried extensive coverage of the speech across six full pages. However, the politically sensitive comments about Beijing and Bangkok were conspicuously absent.

Instead, the papers highlighted Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks on issues ranging from egg prices and coffee plantations to livestock breeding and other routine administrative matters.

Given the prominence accorded to far less consequential sections of the speech, the absence of his remarks on China and Thailand appears difficult to explain as an editorial decision based on length alone.

While Min Aung Hlaing continues to nurse grievances over Operation 1027, his regime remains heavily dependent on Beijing for diplomatic backing, economic support and political legitimacy. At the same time, it can ill afford a rupture with Thailand, a crucial neighbor that remains one of the regime’s few channels for regional engagement, analysts said.

World.title: What’s at Stake in Myanmar’s ICJ Trial for Genocide?
World.content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has begun the session that will deliver a landmark ruling in the case brought by the Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya.

This is the first time in history that Myanmar faces a court ruling on these crimes, not as a criminal case against individuals but to determine whether it bears responsibility for genocide as a state.

What to look for in today’s ICJ judgment

In 2017, the Myanmar military’s “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.

In 2019, the Gambia—which ratified the Genocide Convention in 1978—filed a case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the convention.

In December 2019, when the ICJ held hearings on Gambia’s request for provisional measures to protect the thousands of Rohingya remaining in Myanmar, Aung San Suu Kyi decided to lead Myanmar’s legal defense as state counsellor and foreign minister.

The following month, the ICJ ordered Myanmar to prevent all genocidal acts against the Rohingya and to take steps to preserve evidence related to the case.

Since 2022, Myanmar has been represented at The Hague by the military regime that seized power in the 2021 and is led by Min Aung Hlaing, who had overseen the atrocities as military chief.

In July 2022, the ICJ rejected Myanmar’s preliminary objections and ruled that the case could move forward. It took until August 2023 for the Myanmar regime to submit its reply to the Gambia’s original legal argument, known as a “memorial.” The Gambia submitted its reply in May 2024.

In January this year, the ICJ held three weeks of so-called “merits hearings” with arguments, evidence, witnesses, and an expert from both sides. Eleven countries—Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, the Maldives, Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Belgium, and Ireland—were permitted to intervene on treaty interpretation under Article 63.

On Thursday, the ICJ delivers its final judgment concluding the proceedings. There is no possibility of appeal.

What is the Gambia asking the ICJ to do?

The Gambia has asked the ICJ to find Myanmar responsible for multiple violations of the Genocide Convention, including committing, conspiring to commit and failing to prevent genocide, and failing to prosecute those suspected of committing it.

It has also asked the court to order Myanmar to end these violations, introduce specific legislation criminalizing genocide, prosecute alleged perpetrators, and prevent direct and public incitement to genocide.

The Gambia is also seeking reparations for Rohingya victims, such as ensuring the “safe and dignified” return of refugees as well as financial compensation and other forms of reparation.

Although the Gambia is not directly affected by the alleged genocide, it claims the legal right to seek reparations on behalf of the Rohingya victims in its capacity as a signatory to the convention. Myanmar disputes this position.

The Gambia has further asked the court to find that Myanmar failed to comply with its January 2020 provisional measures order and to require guarantees that such violations will not happen again.

What if Myanmar defies the ICJ ruling?

If Myanmar fails to comply with any ICJ judgment against it, the other party can turn to the UN Security Council, which may recommend or decide on measures to enforce it, in accordance with UN Charter article 94(2). The UNSC has never acted on this discretionary power, and Myanmar has two powerful allies in permanent UNSC members China and Russia.

What is the situation in Myanmar?

Besides the Rohingya genocide case, the Min Aung Hlaing regime faces lawsuits in six countries for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity since the 2021 coup.

The regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, and has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people since the coup, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners.

Millions of young people have fled to other countries due to forced conscription, security fears, and a lack of jobs amid inflation, widespread crime, and escalating conflict across the country.

The civilian death toll continues to grow amid daily regime airstrikes and ground attacks in resistance-held territory.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Accuses Thailand of Aiding ‘Illegal’ Border Trade
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing on Wednesday accused Thai authorities of facilitating “illegal” cross-border trade through resistance-controlled areas, ignoring his request to conduct it only through border checkpoints his military regime still controls.

In a marathon speech in the rubberstamp Parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing complained that he had raised the issue in a meeting with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow on Nov. 12 but was still getting reports of illegal trade on Wednesday morning.

“Recently, the Thai foreign minister came and discussed border crossings with me. I said Bridges No. 1 and No. 2 at Myawaddy are open and Tachileik is open, so use those official gates and not the illegal ones. But they are still supporting the illegal gates,” he said.

He accused Thai authorities of allowing goods to move through crossings linked to what he called “insurgents” for both import and export because they offer easier access.

The regime itself controls only the three major trade gateways he mentioned: the two Thai–Myanmar Friendship Bridges in Myawaddy in Karen State and Tachileik in eastern Shan, plus Kawthoung in Tanintharyi Region in the deep south. The rest are now under the control of ethnic armed organizations that are fighting the putschist regime.

The regime routinely brands commerce through them as “smuggling” since it cannot collect much-needed tax, but businesses using the official channels also have to put up with growing regime chicanery and extortion.

Although the regime reopened the No. 2 Friendship Bridge in May after nearly a year of disruption caused by fighting, traders say trade remains constrained by import-license requirements, foreign-exchange controls and lengthy approval procedures. Importers must obtain licenses and show export earnings funneled through the regime-controlled official banking system before bringing goods into Myanmar, a process that often causes significant delays.

That has increased costs and slowed shipments. Currency volatility has added further pressure, making it increasingly difficult for importers to price goods and maintain working capital. The kyat has steadily weakened against Thai baht, Chinese yuan and U.S. dollar over the past month.

In August, the regime lodged a formal protest when Thai business representatives attended the opening of a border security and trade facility in Thaw Le Hta in Hpapun Township controlled by the Karen National Union (KNU). The area lies by the Salween River which forms the natural border between Myanmar and Thailand.

The protest letter urged Bangkok to prevent any economic, social or political engagement with KNU and warned that the military would target resistance supply routes.

Relations between the neighbors swiftly turned sour in recent weeks, despite efforts by the Thai government to ease the Myanmar regime’s way back into ASEAN. Bangkok is furious that recent regime airstrikes and shelling against the Karen resistance have spilled over the border.

On Oct. 31, the Myanmar military carried out airstrikes in the Thaw Le Hta area that damaged structures on the Thai side, prompting a protest from Bangkok and calls by Thai residents for a 10-km safety buffer zone along the river.

In a meeting with Royal Thai Army Commander-in-Chief Pana Claewplodtook, Myanmar Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin also attempted to shift the blame on Thailand for online scam operations in Myawaddy, calling on Bangkok to do more to cut off essential supplies to scam syndicates operating in Karen State.

The regime has repeatedly sought to blame Thailand for the flourishing fraud industry on the border. Since early 2025, regime officials have argued that the scam compounds relied on electricity, internet connections and other logistical support from the Thai side.

Min Aung Hlaing is desperate to cut off revenue streams for resistance forces that are now able to tax border trade instead of the regime along much of the country’s borders with Thailand, China, Bangladesh and India.

World.title: Top UN Court to Rule on Whether 2017 Rohingya Crackdown Was Genocide
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The top United Nations court will Thursday decide whether Myanmar committed genocide against the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority with its brutal 2017 crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee the country.

For the more than one million Rohingya now living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice offers a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

Survivors of the violence brought with them harrowing tales of gang rapes, mass executions, and barely believable cruelty towards families and children.

Far from the squalor of the refugee camps, in the gothic splendour of the Peace Palace in The Hague, a panel of 15 judges has been weighing for seven years whether Myanmar’s actions constitute genocide.

The case has been brought by Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which requires any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II.

While the ICJ has no way of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.

He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.

Myanmar has always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

“Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein,” its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January.

‘Targeted for destruction’

Gambia’s justice minister said the country filed the case “after reviewing credible reports of the most brutal and vicious violence imaginable inflicted upon a vulnerable group that had been dehumanised and persecuted for many years.”

Gambia has the “full backing and support” of the 57-member Organization of Islamic Cooperation for its efforts at the ICJ, said the minister, Dawda Jallow.

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” added Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

The ICJ has only once before found that a genocide has taken place, the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia.

Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove in international law because the Convention requires proof of a specific “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.”

Gambia argued during the hearings that genocidal intent was clear from the “organized nature and execution” of the crackdown, its “extreme brutality”, the “pervasive sexual violence”, and the targeting of children.

Legal experts are watching the case closely for clues as to how the ICJ will handle another seminal case before it—accusations by South Africa that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

“How the court applies and interprets its current jurisprudence in Gambia’s case against Myanmar will shape ongoing and future proceedings in relation to similar claims,” said Human Rights Watch.

Survivor Mohammed Osman said he was hoping the verdict would allow him to go back home and perform last rites for his parents and younger brother killed by the Myanmar military.

“They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead,” Osman, 20, told AFP.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader Says in Talks With ‘Adversary’ US
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s coup leader turned civilian president Min Aung Hlaing said Wednesday talks were ongoing with the United States, which shunned his country after the 2021 putsch but is now eyeing its rare earth resources.

“Now, we have discussions with our adversary, great power the United States, which has been constantly having issues with us,” the former general told parliament.

“There is a certain level of engagement anyway. However, it has not yet been fully finalized. Relations and discussions are ongoing.”

Media reports said a top US official, Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, joined talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw in September—the highest-level publicized contact since the coup.

The discussions ostensibly focused on trying to free a U.S. businessman held in Myanmar.

At the time, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told AFP: “You don’t solve problems by ignoring them. You solve problems by addressing them.”

A US State Department policy document in August noted the potential for investment in Myanmar, including “opportunities to access Burma’s bountiful rare earth resources”.

It also emphasized the importance of tackling online scam networks, many of them based in Myanmar, which has been mired in civil war since the coup.

Min Aung Hlaing, who led the putsch as armed forces chief before becoming civilian president in April following widely criticized elections, said other nations were also making overtures.

“Some other countries are also making ground-level approaches to establish formal diplomatic ties and ambassador-level relations with us. It is no longer like before,” he said, without naming them.

His comments came the day before the top United Nations court rules whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted genocide—an accusation authorities have always denied.

In 2022, the United States declared violence against the Rohingya amounted to genocide, saying there was clear evidence of an attempt to “destroy” the group.

Min Aung Hlaing has spent the last few months touring several Asian nations as part of a diplomatic blitz to bring his once isolated country back into the fold.

Myanmar was largely shunned by the international community after the coup ousted the democratically elected government of Nobel peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi. She remains in detention.

Min Aung Hlaing was the top military commander during the 2016 and 2017 crackdown on the Rohingya, and remains sanctioned by the United States.

Myanmar has argued its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

World.title: Why Does China Refuse to Itemize Its Climate Bill for Developing Countries?
World.content:
On Aug. 26 an avalanche of ice and rock from Langtang Lirung sent flash floods rushing down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys. By early November, 1,341 bodies had been recovered and thousands were still missing. A week after the flood, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said China, the U.S. and India had a “historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.” But the next day, meeting China’s ambassador, he was quoted as saying that Nepal had “no intention of seeking ‘climate justice compensation’ from any specific country, including China.”

Instead Nepal turned to the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which in October approved US$20 million. Nepalese authorities put the damage at about $2.56 billion. China has not pledged a yuan to that fund.

On the legal text, Beijing is right: despite being the second-biggest economy on earth, China is nominally still a developing country. Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement obliges only developed countries to provide finance, and Article 9.2 merely “encourages” others to do so voluntarily. And Wang Yi, the vice chair of China’s national expert committee on climate change, reminded last year’s COP30 in Belém that China has no mandatory funding obligation but, as a developing country, is rather entitled to receive support—though “whether it accepts the money is another matter,” he added sourly.

Li Gao, who leads China’s COP31 delegation this year, said on Oct. 21 that the Antalya meet must confront the “old problems” of insufficient developed-country mitigation and finance.

The trouble starts with China’s own headline figure. At COP29, Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang announced that since 2016 China had “provided and mobilized” more than 177 billion yuan (about $25 billion) in project funds for other developing countries. That is the accounting language developed countries use for their obligations. Yet the same 177 billion reappears, unchanged and hedged with “according to incomplete statistics,” in the 2035 climate pledge China filed in 2025 and in the Environment Ministry’s October 2025 report. The October 2026 edition, published three weeks before this year’s COP, drops the aggregate altogether: it lists 56 cooperation documents with 43 countries and 20,000 solar systems for seven African states, but no total.

Nobody outside government knows how much of these fabled 177 billion yuan is grants and how much is policy-bank lending at commercial rates. The one instrument China did specify is lagging: in 2015, President Xi Jinping promised a 20-billion-yuan South–South Climate Cooperation Fund. By June 2023, Li Gao put the cumulative amount allocated under the program at just over 1.2 billion yuan. E3G calculated in 2023 that the fund had delivered only about 1/10 of the pledge.

What outside estimates say

The World Resources Institute estimates that China provided about $4.5 billion a year between 2013 and 2022, a measly 6.1 percent of what developed countries paid out over the same period. E3G and ODI put it at about $3 billion a year from 2015 to 2021 and falling since 2018. Some 96 percent of the bilateral money came as loans. Among dedicated climate funds, the Centre for Global Development finds China pays only into the Global Environment Facility, and has joined neither the loss and damage fund nor the biodiversity fund born of its own COP15 presidency.

Set that against capacity: China’s clean-energy industries generated a record 15.4 trillion yuan in 2025, about 11.4 percent of GDP. The same 2026 ministry report records 200 billion yuan of ultra-long special bonds allocated this year for domestic equipment upgrades. In other words, one year’s domestic program exceeds everything China says it has paid out abroad since 2016.

Why more, and why now?

One does not have to accept the rich countries’ burden-shifting argument to see China’s interest here. Beijing wants to be seen as a leader of the Global South, yet in Belém its delegations, as Kate Logan of the Asia Society Policy Institute and Lily Hartzell of E3G observed, “cautiously avoided any wording that might suggest a bid for formal climate leadership, particularly when it comes to climate finance.” Brazil’s president urged Ding to “join financing initiatives for climate transition and resilience.” But a year after the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched, eight countries have pledged $7.8 billion and China is not among them.

Chinese scholars have said as much. Researchers from Tsinghua University and the Central University of Finance and Economics argued in the journal World Environment in 2022 that, facing mounting pressure, China “could consider beginning to study and formulate a contingency plan and program for contributions under the Convention mechanism” and should disclose its South–South fund data to “reduce international pressure”. Four years on, neither has happened.

Four things to watch for in Antalya

First, an itemized number in China’s next Biennial Transparency Report: grants, concessional loans, commercial loans and mobilized private money. Second, a first payment into the loss and damage fund or the Adaptation Fund. The Baku-to-Belém roadmap pencils in about $40 billion a year from South–South cooperation by 2035. Third, a dated disbursement schedule for the 20-billion-yuan fund. Fourth, a Himalayan adaptation package: China’s early-warning products already serve more than 40 countries, and joint glacial-lake monitoring with Nepal and Bhutan would cost little.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Slovakia Discuss Trade, Energy and Transport Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Slovakia discussed expanding trade, industrial cooperation and transport connectivity during a new round of inter-ministerial consultations held in Bratislava, with preparations underway for their next economic cooperation commission meeting in January 2027.

The Kazakh delegation was headed by Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov, while the Slovak side was led by State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs Marek Eštok.

The discussions focused on implementing agreements reached during Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s official visit to Kazakhstan on June 10-11, 2025, as well as prospects for taking bilateral relations to a new level.

The officials reviewed preparations for the 11th meeting of the Kazakhstan-Slovakia Intergovernmental Commission on Economic and Scientific-Technical Cooperation, scheduled for Bratislava in January 2027.

Energy, the agro-industrial sector, information technology and education were identified as promising areas for further cooperation.

Transport and logistics also featured on the agenda, with both officials discussing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route’s potential to strengthen connectivity between Central Asia and Central Europe.

In education, the parties explored opportunities to expand academic mobility and train qualified professionals through universities in both countries. They also highlighted the need to improve the legal framework governing labor migration.

The diplomats exchanged views on regional and international developments and reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation within the United Nations and other international organizations.

World.title: Astana to Open Ice Skating Route at New Winter Park
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana is preparing to open a new winter attraction featuring a 1.4-kilometer ice skating route through Linear Park near Abu Dhabi Plaza, with the first season scheduled to run through March 31, 2027.

The new Astana Winter Park/Megaice project will hold its technical opening on Nov. 21, Kazinform reported.

Unlike traditional skating rinks, the 6,000-square-meter venue will feature extended ice pathways, allowing visitors to skate along a route surrounded by the capital’s modern architecture.

The park will include heated pavilions, skate rental services, family recreation areas, food outlets and festive lighting. Organizers are also exploring interactive lighting technologies to create visual effects on the ice.

Professional refrigeration equipment, specialized ice-resurfacing machines and modern engineering systems will help maintain ice quality, including during warmer weather, according to the city’s Akimat (administration).

The project is being developed with private investment and international expertise in ice infrastructure.

Other winter recreation sites are also being prepared across the capital, including at Triathlon Park, Kazakh Eli Square and near Astana Arena. These locations will feature additional skating rinks, ice slides and outdoor activities.

World.title: Explorers Club Launches Central Asia Chapter Based in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – The Explorers Club, a New-York based international organization dedicated to scientific exploration, opened its Central Asia chapter on Nov. 12, establishing a new platform in Kazakhstan to support international research partnerships and scientific expeditions across the region.

The launch seeks to bring Central Asia closer to the international community of explorers, scientists, adventurers and conservation professionals. The chapter was officially inaugurated at the club’s headquarters in New York, bringing together explorers, scientists, diplomats and conservation experts to discuss opportunities for joint research, according to Kazakhstan’s Consulate General in New York.

Founded in 1904 in New York, the Explorers Club brings together scientists, explorers and conservation professionals and has been associated with major milestones in exploration, including expeditions to Mount Everest, the ocean’s deepest depths and the Moon.

The initiative aims to expand cooperation between Central Asian and international researchers, with a focus on exploring the region’s archaeological and natural heritage, advancing conservation efforts and creating opportunities for young scientists to participate in international expeditions.

The Explorers Club has more than 30 national and international chapters that serve as local networks for explorers, scientists and students. According to the club, many chapters organize expeditions, lectures, seminars and educational events, while also offering field-research grants to students.

For Kazakh conservationist Albert Salemgareyev, who presented the country’s experience in restoring the saiga antelope population, the most meaningful part of the event came after his presentation, when discussions turned from Kazakhstan’s conservation achievements to the challenges that lie ahead.

Salemgareyev represents the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, a project spearheading the efforts to protect and restore the saiga antelope population, one of the country’s prominent wildlife conservation achievements.

“I came away with the sense that people wanted to understand the challenges we face now. Saiga numbers are growing, and new roads and railway lines are being built across the steppe. How do we plan to keep migration routes open as that network expands? And where saigas and livestock share the same pastures, how can we make sure there is room for both?” Salemgareyev told The Astana Times.

“I see an opportunity for international scientists and explorers to join our field teams and contribute to the research that we are carrying out through the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative. I also hope the chapter can introduce this work to potential funders. Understanding how migration routes change takes years of observation, and that requires sustained support,” he explained.

Among the possibilities that he noted are joint expeditions to study steppe ecosystems, the use of artificial intelligence to identify and count saigas in aerial survey photographs, and expanded GPS tracking to better understand animal migration.

“One promising use of artificial intelligence is to help us find and count saigas in aerial survey photographs. There is also scope to study other steppe species,” he said.

Such research could also help address tensions between conservation efforts and the livelihoods of farmers, particularly where saigas and livestock compete for pasture.

“By tracking herds over several years and comparing their movements with farmers’ observations, we could better understand when and where saigas enter farmland and under what circumstances farms experience losses. That would help us work with farmers on ways to reduce those losses while keeping migration routes open,” Salemgareyev said.

“The chapter could bring together researchers and field teams for this work and help secure long-term funding,” he added.

Salemgareyev sees Kazakhstan’s steppe and the Ustyurt Plateau particularly promising opportunities for future exploration.

“In Torgai [in northern Kazakhstan], the return of kulan and Przewalski’s horses gives us an opportunity to study how they use different pastures through the seasons and how their grazing affects vegetation and steppe birds over time,” he said.

“On Ustyurt, I would focus on saiga migration and the seasonal movements of goitered gazelles. I am particularly interested in the routes these animals take as they approach the border between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, where they cross and where they encounter obstacles,” he added.

Joint fieldwork could help researchers identify important migration crossings, understand where animals encounter obstacles and determine which routes require greater protection.

“Together, we could identify which crossings matter most for each species and agree on where to focus our efforts to keep those routes open,” he added.

The launch ceremony was attended by Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to the United States Magzhan Ilyassov, presidential representative Erzhan Kazykhan and Richard Wiese, president emeritus of The Explorers Club, alongside representatives of the scientific and diplomatic communities.

Beyond wildlife conservation, the launch highlighted the region’s broader scientific and archaeological potential. During the event in New York, British explorer Nick Fielding presented the history of ancient cities along the Syr Darya River and their role in connecting civilizations across Central Asia.

World.title: Central Asian Economies Outpace Kazakhstan in Growth, but Lag in Economic Size
World.content:
ASTANA – The Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan recorded faster economic growth than Kazakhstan in January- June, but Kazakhstan remained Central Asia’s largest economy, with GDP reaching $146.4 billion.

The figures highlight a growing contrast across the region: smaller economies are expanding faster, while Kazakhstan maintains a substantial lead in overall economic output, Finprom, a financial and analytical agency, reported on Nov. 19.

The Kyrgyz Republic posted the region’s highest growth rate at 11.9% year-on-year, followed by Uzbekistan at 8.5% and Tajikistan at 8.2%. Turkmenistan reported growth of 6.3%, while Kazakhstan’s economy expanded by 4.1%.

Among South Caucasus countries, Georgia recorded 7.8% growth, Armenia 6% and Azerbaijan 0.8%.

Kazakhstan maintains economic lead

Despite its slower growth, Kazakhstan remained significantly ahead of its neighbors in economic size. Its nominal GDP reached 71.2 trillion tenge ($160.4 billion) in the first half of the year. Uzbekistan ranked second with approximately $91.8 billion, followed by Azerbaijan at $38.4 billion and Georgia at $20.3 billion.

The economies of the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan were considerably smaller, at approximately $11 billion and $8.7 billion, respectively.

The differences in growth rates partly reflect the varying size and structure of national economies. In smaller countries, comparable increases in economic output can translate into higher percentage growth. Their performance can also be more sensitive to external financial inflows, remittances and trade activity.

For Kazakhstan, with its larger and more capital-intensive economy, sustained growth increasingly depends on productivity gains, manufacturing expansion and investment efficiency. Growth in non-resource sectors also helps offset fluctuations in extractive industries.

World.title: Amur Tigers Released in Kazakhstan Adapt Well, Hunt Wildlife, Russian Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Two Amur tigers released into Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash Nature Reserve are adapting well to their new environment and have begun hunting wildlife, marking an encouraging start to the country’s efforts to restore the tiger population, said Sergey Aramilev, director general of the Amur Tiger Center.

Speaking at a TASS press conference in Khabarovsk on Nov. 18, Aramilev said both animals were healthy and remained within the reserve’s designated area.

“Both are doing well, hunting and staying within the area designated by specialists. The tigress hunts regularly. Her prey has included wild boar, Bukhara deer and a wolf,” he said.

The male tiger, named Amur, has also made a kill, although specialists will identify its prey only after the animal moves far enough away.

First steps toward restoring the tiger population

In May, Russia transferred four Amur tigers to Kazakhstan as part of a program to restore the predator in its historical range. The animals were brought to the Ile-Balkhash Nature Reserve, where the first tigress, named Umit, was released into the wild in late July. Amur followed in late October.

More than 300 deer and kulans were introduced into the reserve to provide food for the predators.

Specialists hope the two released tigers will form a breeding pair, although Aramilev cautioned that their compatibility cannot be guaranteed.

“The female was released earlier and has already established her own temporary territory. The male should be able to detect her presence,” he said, adding that both animals were released as adults because they had reached reproductive maturity.

However, he noted that animal behavior is not governed by instinct alone and the two tigers might simply not accept each other.

The project will be considered successful if the female produces offspring.

GPS tracking monitors adaptation

Both tigers wear GPS collars that transmit location data via satellite, allowing specialists to monitor their movements and adaptation.

According to Aramilev, the tigress travels between seven and 15 kilometers per day. So far, her movement patterns, activity and resting periods resemble those of Amur tigers living in Russia’s Khabarovsk and Primorye territories.

The monitoring data will help researchers assess how the animals use the landscape and determine whether additional releases are possible.

Kazakhstan plans to release two more tigers next year, which will have reached adulthood by then.

Kazakh specialists estimate that the territory could support up to 50 tigers, while their Russian counterparts are more cautious. According to Aramilev, a sustainable population could be established with 10 to 15 animals.

The Amur tiger is the closest genetic relative of the extinct Caspian, or Turan, tiger, which once inhabited Kazakhstan and other parts of Central Asia. The restoration program aims to bring the big cat back to its historical habitat.

World.title: Kazakhstan Targets First Direct Flights to US by End of 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is working to launch direct air services to the United States (U.S.) by the end of 2027, with the two countries discussing aviation safety requirements and fleet expansion to support the route.

The ministry reported on Nov. 19 that this was discussed at a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Deputy Transport Minister Talgat Lastayev and Daniel J. Edwards, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Aviation and International Affairs, on the sidelines of the seventh International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7) in Montreal.

Kazakhstan is seeking to obtain Category 1 status from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), a key requirement for launching direct flights. U.S. experts conducted an audit in September and provided preliminary results, noting positive performance indicators, according to the ministry.

“We are interested in and actively working toward launching direct air services between Kazakhstan and the U.S. The Open Skies Agreement between our countries provides a solid legal foundation for this initiative,” Lastayev said.

Air Astana expects to receive three Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft in 2026-2027, which are planned for flights to the U.S. The ministry also noted that it signed agreements with Boeing in 2025 to supply 33 aircraft valued at $15 billion.

Lastayev said direct flights would strengthen business and tourism ties, create new opportunities for companies and improve transport connectivity between Central Asia and the U.S.

World.title: ‘Economic Outcast’: US Pressure on Iran Tests Central Asia’s Trade and Transit Ambitions
World.content:
ASTANA — Washington’s new campaign to isolate Iran is putting Central Asia’s growing trade and transport links with Tehran under pressure. The dilemma was underscored in September, when the first 55-container train carrying Chinese goods was dispatched toward Iran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, highlighting the commercial potential of a route increasingly exposed to sanctions risks.

On Aug. 24, the United States (U.S.) Department of the Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast at President Donald Trump’s direction, targeting Iran’s financial networks and economic partners. As the campaign expands, Central Asian governments and businesses face a difficult question: how to preserve access to strategically important trade routes without jeopardizing their financial and commercial ties with the United States.

The campaign soon acquired a broader diplomatic dimension. On Sept. 2, Axios reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had instructed U.S. embassies to deliver diplomatic démarches to host governments, demanding that they “immediately and systematically” sever trade relations with Iran. According to U.S. officials cited by Axios, special instructions were sent to several Central Asian capitals, including demands to close branches of Iranian Bank Melli and Bank Saderat, which Washington links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The U.S. Treasury also warned that entities facilitating financial transactions or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran could lose access to the U.S. financial system. On Oct. 1, Washington expanded the campaign to Iran’s automotive and railway sectors, authorizing sanctions against individuals and entities operating in those industries. The move is particularly significant for regional connectivity, as rail transport has become an increasingly important part of Iran’s efforts to maintain economic links with neighboring countries.

Although these measures do not automatically prohibit every shipment transiting Iranian territory, they increase the potential exposure of foreign banks, insurers, logistics companies and other businesses dealing with Iranian entities.

Why Iran matters to Central Asia

For Central Asian countries, Iran is more than a neighboring trading partner. It provides landlocked economies with access to the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman through ports such as Bandar Abbas and Chabahar, opening alternative routes to international markets. Iran’s interest in Central Asia is equally strategic. Tehran views the region as a gateway to the markets of China and Russia and an opportunity to ease its long-standing economic and diplomatic isolation. Developing transport links, including the North-South corridor and the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway, has become an important part of this strategy.

Kazakhstan has been particularly active in developing this southern direction. On June 28, Kazakhstan and Iran signed a 27-year Build-Operate-Transfer agreement for a Kazakh transport and logistics terminal at Shahid Rajaee Port in Bandar Abbas. The agreement includes a two-year construction period followed by 25 years of operation, with commercial operations expected to begin in the third year. The project is part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen the International North-South Transport Corridor and diversify export routes beyond traditional connections through Russia and China.

Trade figures also illustrate the economic importance of the Iranian market. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of National Economy, freight transportation along the North-South corridor increased 12% in 2025, reaching 3.5 million tons. Trade turnover between Kazakhstan and Iran grew 26.4% to $430.2 million over the same period.

Tehran sees Central Asia as a long-term strategic partner

For Tehran, strengthening these connections is part of a longer-term strategic orientation toward Eurasia, not simply a response to Western sanctions. Mohammad Hossein Masoumzadeh, senior researcher at the Governance & Policy Think Tank (GPTT) in Tehran, described Iran’s engagement with Central Asia as a strategic priority rather than a temporary adjustment to geopolitical pressure.

“Iran’s approach toward Central Asia is not merely a tactical or temporary reaction to the intensification of Western sanctions; rather, it is part of a fundamental, strategic, and long-term pivot toward Eurasia and a neighborhood-first policy,” he said.

Masoumzadeh highlighted railway connections through the Sarakhs and Incheh Borun border crossings, which link Iran with Central Asian railway networks. Although the countries use different railway gauges, specialized bogie-exchange facilities at border terminals help facilitate cargo movement between networks.

He also pointed to the potential of maritime connections across the Caspian Sea. Iran’s northern ports, including Amirabad and Anzali, and Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk could form part of a multimodal transport network connecting Central Asian economies with Iran’s southern ports and international shipping routes. The new China-Iran railway connection is another example of this growing connectivity. Masoumzadeh described the September shipment as a significant step toward developing alternative Eurasian trade routes.

“The launch of the container train from China to Iran passing through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan is a tangible manifestation of the revival of the New Silk Road,” he said.

He added that the route “certainly has the potential to become a regular and commercially viable trade corridor.”

Its main advantages, according to Masoumzadeh, include shorter transit times compared with traditional maritime routes, as well as an alternative to international waterways facing geopolitical tensions and rising insurance and shipping costs. However, he acknowledged that the threat of U.S. secondary sanctions poses a serious challenge for private businesses and logistics companies in transit countries.

“The experience of recent years has shown that when tangible economic interests and the political will of governments are aligned, innovative solutions emerge to manage these risks,” he said.

To maintain regional participation, Masoumzadeh proposed independent financial and banking mechanisms, including settlements in national currencies, barter systems and regional clearinghouses. He also highlighted the potential of joint regional transport companies and logistics consortiums to distribute commercial risks among participating countries.

Harmonizing customs tariffs, digitalizing border processes and removing infrastructure bottlenecks would also be essential to making the corridor commercially competitive. However, alternative payment arrangements cannot automatically shield companies from U.S. sanctions. Transactions involving designated entities or targeted sectors may still carry risks regardless of the currency used.

Secondary sanctions could reshape regional calculations

Pressure on Iran could have consequences well beyond its borders, particularly for countries that have invested in transport routes through Iranian territory. Dr. Dania Arayssi, assistant director of the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, said Operation Economic Outcast was making commercial engagement with Iran considerably riskier for Central Asian countries.

The pressure comes as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have been expanding their economic and transport links with Tehran. Banks and major companies are likely to reduce their exposure to Iran to protect access to the dollar-based financial system, while governments may seek to avoid an open rupture in relations with Tehran.

Arayssi said the campaign could fundamentally reshape Central Asia’s long-standing multi-vector foreign policy, forcing regional governments to make more difficult geopolitical choices. She also identified Uzbekistan as particularly exposed because it relies on Iranian transit routes. According to her estimate, around 60% of Uzbekistan’s transit to European and Turkish markets passes through Iran.

“Washington’s pressure does undermine the region’s connectivity plans, because an alternative corridor can itself become a source of geopolitical risk,” she said.

At the same time, Arayssi noted that Central Asian countries cannot simply abandon Iranian routes because they offer access to ports on the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. She expects Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to pursue a cautious balancing strategy rather than immediately terminate their economic projects with Iran.

“They’ll keep Iran projects alive on paper and show the U.S. they are complying through tighter banking checks,” she said, adding that governments could also seek exemptions from Washington while investing more heavily in alternative routes, including the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea and the Trans-Afghan railway.

Alternative routes offer options, but not immediate replacements

The Middle Corridor, officially known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, connects China and Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Europe through the Caspian Sea. Its growing importance reflects the region’s efforts to diversify trade routes and reduce dependence on traditional transport networks. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), cargo volumes along the corridor increased 62% in 2024 to reach 4.5 million tons. However, infrastructure constraints, port capacity, vessel availability and coordination between countries continue to affect its competitiveness.

Another potential alternative is the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA) railway project, which would connect Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan with Afghanistan and Pakistan, providing access to Pakistani seaports. On Oct. 1, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates signed a memorandum of understanding to explore the project. The parties plan to conduct technical and economic studies and assess the feasibility of the required railway infrastructure. The initiative remains at the planning stage. Both routes could expand Central Asia’s access to international markets, but they cannot immediately replace the commercial and geographical advantages offered by Iranian ports.

For Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, the challenge is therefore not simply whether to maintain trade with Iran, but how to preserve access to strategically important markets and ports while limiting their companies’ and financial institutions’ exposure to measures that could affect their broader international economic relationships. How successfully regional governments navigate the expanding reach of economic sanctions will be an important factor in determining the future of these connectivity plans.

World.title: Tokayev Sets Goal of Turning Kazakhstan Into Central Asia’s Academic Hub
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan aims to attract 100,000 international students by 2029 and strengthen its position as Central Asia’s academic hub through international research partnerships, artificial intelligence development and university modernization, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the third Strategic Partners Forum on Nov. 19.

Addressing international university leaders, scientists and education experts, Tokayev said the country must move beyond hosting foreign university branches and focus on research, technological innovation and retaining world-class expertise, Akorda reported.

“Our strategic goal is to transform Kazakhstan into an academic hub of Central Asia and become part of the global market for knowledge, particularly relevant and high-quality knowledge,” he said.

From international campuses to joint research

Tokayev described international academic partnerships as the first stage of Kazakhstan’s ambitions. Universities from 11 countries have established branches in the country, enrolling more than 12,000 students and employing nearly 1,500 lecturers, including more than 600 foreign professors.

Kazakhstan currently has 132 universities with more than 800,000 students. The number of international students has increased from 31,000 last year to 41,000, with more than 8,000 receiving financial support from Kazakhstan. The country plans to raise this figure to 100,000 by 2029 through the national Study in Kazakhstan initiative.

Kazakhstan has also become the first country in the region to join the Lisbon Recognition Convention, covering Europe, and the Tokyo Convention, covering the Asia-Pacific region. The move strengthens international recognition of Kazakh university qualifications.

The next stage, Tokayev said, will focus on scientific cooperation, joint research laboratories and breakthrough technological projects.

“Now I have set the task of retaining world-class knowledge in Kazakhstan in the form of qualified personnel, scientific achievements and innovations,” he said.

The forum also featured an exchange ceremony for a signed agreement between Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education and the United Nations University on establishing a regional research hub in Almaty.

AI and research partnerships

Tokayev highlighted the role of artificial intelligence in transforming higher education and research, noting that Kazakhstan’s universities should focus on developing practical solutions and technological innovations. He cited the development of the national language models KazLLM and AlemLLM, as well as the launch of Qazaq AI Research University, as examples of progress.

“Strong universities are the foundation of the future,” he said.

Shymkent to become a regional education hub

Astana and Almaty have traditionally served as Kazakhstan’s main centers of science, culture and intellectual development, hosting the country’s leading national universities. Tokayev said Shymkent should now become a major scientific and educational hub for southern Kazakhstan.

The city has launched an educational program with Arizona State University and opened a branch of Türkiye’s Gazi University.

Tokayev also announced his decision to grant national university status to South Kazakhstan University named after Mukhtar Auezov, saying it should become a center of high-quality education, advanced research and intellectual development for the region.

Education to support economic transformation

Tokayev linked higher education development to the nationwide People’s Construction program, which will include social, transport and energy infrastructure projects across Kazakhstan.

He stressed that universities must prepare specialists capable of supporting infrastructure development, digital transformation and the expansion of AI across industries.

“Building a knowledge-based economy has become a long-term constitutional commitment that both the current government and all subsequent governments will have to fulfil,” he said.

Tokayev also emphasized that the rule of law and anti-corruption efforts are essential to creating a stable and predictable environment for international academic partnerships.

Concluding his address, he called for deeper cooperation with international universities and researchers.

“Science is an invaluable asset intended to serve the progress of all humanity, which means that knowledge has no borders and should have none,” he said.

World.title: ‘What special status does the Russian language have?’: Russian-language education debated again in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

A lawmaker from the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Hikmat Babaoglu (Mammadov), has proposed reviewing state funding for Russian-language school education. He made the proposal on 16 November during a plenary session of the Milli Majlis, Azerbaijan’s parliament, as lawmakers discussed the 2027 state budget.

According to Babaoglu, 157,000 pupils study in Russian-language classes, compared with 1.57 million in Azerbaijani-language classes. The state spends 2,000 manats (around $1,177) a year on each pupil.

The MP stressed that “national identity and national ideology are shaped through education”. He also questioned whether Azerbaijan had any state-funded schools that taught in English or Chinese:

“Why is that? It is something worth thinking about.”

He said a similar situation existed in higher education.

Over the past two years, the future of Russian-language education in Azerbaijan has repeatedly come under discussion. This time, however, a lawmaker from the ruling party raised the issue from the parliamentary podium and backed his argument with budget figures. This raises a question:

Is this a debate about education spending, or does it reflect relations between Baku and Moscow?

What do the figures tell us?

According to the figures cited by the MP, around 9% of all schoolchildren in Azerbaijan study in Russian-language classes. Based on his estimate of annual spending per pupil, the state spends approximately 314 million manats a year on Russian-language education.

Elshan Azim, head of School No. 35 in the Kalbajar district, cited the same figure. He said that the government allocates 314 million manats a year to Russian-language education, while schools for internally displaced people receive 188 million manats (around $184.7 million). Comparing the two amounts, he stressed:

“For 30 years, these schools have played an important role in preserving the folklore, music, national values and spiritual heritage of their regions.”

Azim argues that if the authorities close schools to save public money, they should assess Russian-language schools by the same criteria.

In recent years, authorities have closed hundreds of small schools in rural areas or merged them with other educational institutions because they had too few pupils. Judging by the headteacher’s remarks, the future of schools for internally displaced people is also under discussion.

The Ministry of Education has not yet commented on the MP’s remarks.

What has the ministry said previously?

In July 2025, rumours spread widely that the authorities might close Russian-language classes. Messages in parents’ WhatsApp groups claimed that schools teaching in Russian would switch to Azerbaijani within three years. The Ministry of Education denied these reports. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova also dismissed them as “fake news” and said Moscow remained in constant contact with Baku on the issue.

In June 2026, Education Minister Emin Amrullayev said that closing Russian-language classes had “never been on the agenda”. He said it was “technically impossible” to shut them down “as early as tomorrow”, adding that parents themselves chose the language of instruction. However, he did not rule out restructuring for “objective reasons”, such as a decline in pupil numbers or a shortage of teachers.

Babaoglu’s proposal, however, concerns a different issue. The MP is not calling for Russian-language classes to close. Instead, he is questioning whether the state should continue to fund them.

Against the backdrop of improving relations with Moscow

The MP’s remarks come amid a period of improving relations between Baku and Moscow. In December 2024, an AZAL passenger plane crashed, killing 38 people. In April 2026, the two sides acknowledged in a joint statement that Russian air defence systems had unintentionally shot down the aircraft.

In September, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists – Semyon Uralov, Ivan Knyazev and Alexey Chadayev – on its wanted list over public calls for a violent change of government. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador over the matter. Moscow dismissed their remarks as “personal opinions”.

Babaoglu did not mention Russia in his speech. He justified his proposal by referring to the need to preserve “national identity” and concerns over public spending. Moscow has not yet responded to his remarks.

The draft 2027 state budget contains no separate proposal to change the funding arrangements for Russian-language education. The government has also not responded to the issue raised by the MP.
