World.title: Paralympian local MP playing her third sport for Australia
World.content:
Politician, Paralympic gold medallist and Australian Para Ice Hockey player.

The unique description belongs to 57-year-old Liesl Tesch MP, who is balancing her role as the Gosford MP with the upcoming 2026 Para Ice Hockey Women's World Championships in Newcastle this month.

After seven Paralympic Games appearances across wheelchair basketball and sailing with a pair of gold medals, most would be more than content with their sporting careers, but Tesch wants more.

While sporting success has tended to follow Tesch wherever she has gone, getting used to it on the ice was not as immediate.

"The first day I felt like a turtle upside down," Tesch told ABC Sport.

"The next day, I was like, 'oh my God, how was I so bad,' [but] I have fallen in love with this sport.

"It just gives me such a rush, and it's [wild] and brutal and crazy."

Loading Instagram content

A second chance

The 2026 Para Ice Hockey Women's World Championships will be the second of its kind, with the inaugural event held in Slovakia last year. Australia competed, finishing sixth, and losing all three of their matches in Dolný Kubín without scoring.

Lynda Holt, 54, is Ice Hockey Australia’s head of para ice hockey and also a Paralympian, and says this time will be different.

"We've all grown in the last year, we've all improved so much, and we have got some new players," Holt told ABC Sport.

"The team is great. I come from a shot put and discus background, a very individual sport on my own, and I'm just loving that we are this team that comes together."

Lynda Holt was part of the team at last year's event. (Supplied: Igor Kupco)

Australia will be joined by Canada, the United States, Great Britain, Norway, and Team World, a combination of players from countries not represented.

The six teams will be split into two groups of three, with Australia in Group A alongside the United States and Great Britain.

The game is played on sleds, and like mainstream ice hockey, it is played six-a-side, with most rules carried over.

For Tesch, it is a much-needed opportunity for women to shine.

"It's a chance for women to get together and play against women because a lot of us, we are training and playing against the blokes," Tesch said.

Australia did not win a game at the last world championships, but they are ready for the challenge this time. (Supplied: Igor Kupco)

Road to the Paralympics

Like several of her teammates, Lynda Holt knows the pressure of competing at a Paralympic Games, and being a part of landmark moments.

A shot put silver medallist at Sydney 2000, she recognises a chance now to be involved in another one, with the sport hoping for Paralympic inclusion as a full women's competition as soon as 2030.

She is not alone. Decorated swimmer Priya Cooper, who won nine gold medals across four Paralympic Games appearances, will also take to the ice, along with Susan Seipel, who won a silver medal as a Para canoeist at the Tokyo Games.

Tesch and fellow Paralympic silver medallist in wheelchair basketball, Lisa Edmonds, have both medalled on the court, and want to be part of a movement for women's para ice hockey players to have the same chance.

The push is on to get a standalone event into the Winter Paralympics. (ABC Sport: Bridget Murphy)

Para Ice Hockey has officially been a mixed gender event since the 2010 Paralympic Games, but Norway's Britt Mjaasund Øyen competed in 1994 as part of the team that won silver.

She was the first of only four women to compete at the level. Fellow Norwegian Lena Schrøder competed in 2018 and will captain Norway at this World Championships.

While the opportunity is there for women to compete alongside men, Holt is part of a wider community wanting a standalone women's tournament, something the event in Newcastle could help provide.

"Our whole goal, our whole movement we have got going on is [that] we have got to get there," Holt said.

"In order to qualify for the Paralympics, we needed to have two World Championships; this will be the second.

"We also need eight teams; we currently have five, and we have got three in development, so come next year, when they decide if we can be part of the Paralympics, we should be ready.

"This is history in the making for us."

Lynda Holt was a shot put silver medallist at Sydney 2000. (Supplied: SE Photography/Shannen Keddie)

The fight for time on ice

Ice hockey's growth in popularity around Australia has meant ice time has been harder to come by, regardless of what discipline you are attempting to play.

The Hunter Ice Skating Stadium, where the team have been training, is also home to several teams belonging to the hometown Newcastle Northstars, including its stand-up men's team, who are the Australian Ice Hockey League's most successful, having won its seventh title earlier this year.

Members of the public are also able to access the space, something Leisl Tesch knows all too well.

"Getting on here with the general public, I remember the first day I did it," she said.

"Everyone's standing up looking beautiful, and I am in this full body armour, but it is really good for speed and turn training with everyone else.

"It is also an inclusion conversation that people with disabilities can get on the ice too."

Holt and Edmonds are both based in Sydney, having to make the trip to Newcastle to train.

Loading Instagram content

"There's not enough ice time for everyone, and it's such an expensive sport, six to seven hundred dollars an hour for the ice," Holt said.

"We're all fighting for it; we've all got goals, ours is the Paralympics."

The tournament starts on November 24, with Canada's clash against Team World. Australia will open its campaign the same day, against the United States.

This content was produced for the ABC’s International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 10, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Firmus talks down 'modest' data centre in bid to avoid major project status
World.content:
Firmus Technologies is fighting a local council push for one of its proposed AI data centres to be declared a major project.

Latrobe Council in Tasmania's north-west has sought to defer a decision on Firmus's proposed 52-megawatt Wesley Vale AI data centre to the state government.

It has said the council's 1993 planning scheme is dated and councillors would not be able to consider all the relevant issues, such as energy, water and environmental impacts of a large AI data centre.

A letter from Firmus's lawyers to Planning Minister Kerry Vincent, which is assessing the request for a major project declaration, has now been made public.

"We respectfully ask that the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure not be declared a major project," the letter reads.

It states that the project would have only "modest" economic benefits and ongoing job opportunities:

Although the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is expected to generate some economic activity, these benefits are relatively modest and largely confined to employment opportunities, with approximately 70 jobs anticipated during the construction phase and around 20 permanent full-time positions once operational. Beyond these direct employment outcomes, the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is not expected to materially alter the economic structure of the region, establish a significant new industry cluster, or drive broader regional economic transformation.

The submission states the development cost of its facility would be $31.25 million.

It compared this to major projects such as Chambroad's Kangaroo Bay Hotel proposal near Hobart, which it said would support 443 ongoing jobs and generate $42.7 million in additional annual visitor expenditure.

Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania. (Supplied: Firmus Technologies)

"The economic benefits of the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure are considerably more limited in scale and are largely confined to construction activity and a relatively modest number of ongoing jobs," the letter reads.

The process of declaring and assessing a major project in Tasmania can take years, while the council approval process is usually much quicker.

A sign near Firmus' proposed AI data centre site at Wesley Vale. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Firmus told inquiry of $46b economic benefit from three projects

Last week, at a Tasmanian parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres, Firmus co-CEO Tim Rosenfield was asked about the benefits to Tasmania of its three projects in the state.

Tim Rosenfield, Co-Chief Executive Officer of Firmus appeared at a Tasmanian inquiry into data centres in Hobart. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"This is a large-scale investment we're making," he told the inquiry.

"We have actually, at the request of the government some months ago, commissioned a third-party study which is close to being finalised.

"It puts total state gross product contributions of up to $46 billion to the Tasmanian state economy through 2035.

"We're operating these supercomputers, and that requires skills, it requires on-site presence, it requires learning pathways.

"The preliminary modelled outcome shows about 8,900 ongoing FTEs [full-time equivalent jobs] through 2035 created."

Firmus is building an AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards and has approval for another at Long Reach in northern Tasmania.

The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston, showing its research and development lab. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Firmus 'deeply disappointed' by council's referral

In addition to saying the economic impact of the project would not be "significant" to the region, the letter from Firmus's lawyers also said the impact on the area's environment and social fabric would be limited.

It also said the project would not deliver advanced regional development objectives or significant public infrastructure to the region.

Premier refuses to enact data centre pause The Tasmanian premier says a moratorium would grind the state to a halt and further impact the struggling health sector.

The letter said the proposal was not complex from a planning perspective, and suitable to be considered by the council under the planning scheme.

"It does not involve the jurisdictional, regulatory, or statutory complexities typically associated with projects assessed under the major projects framework, such as cross-municipal development, multiple approval pathways, or the need for planning scheme amendments," the letter reads.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff with co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis at the Firmus Technologies site in Launceston. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Tasmanians expressed doubts about AI firm Firmus, now so have investors Firmus's failure to list on the ASX comes after months of fighting to get approval for its Tasmanian projects and win over a sceptical community.

Firmus's lawyers also expressed "concern" with Latrobe Council's decision to ask for the development to be considered a major project, pointing out the development application had been submitted to council back in late May.

"Since that time, council has accepted the application, reviewed the supporting technical reports, requested further information, considered amended documentation, and progressed the application to public exhibition," the submission states.

"Our client is deeply disappointed that, after the application has advanced through these stages of assessment, council has now taken the position that the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure should instead be referred for consideration under the Major Projects framework.

"Had council genuinely considered that the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure should be assessed under the major projects framework, it would be reasonable to expect that this issue would have been identified and raised at an earlier stage of the assessment process."

World.title: One person a fortnight reports drink spiking to NT sexual assault centre
World.content:
At least one person a fortnight walks through the doors of the Sexual Assault Referral Centre (SARC) in Darwin worried their drink has been tampered with.

Experts say a strong stigma attached to spiking means the crime remains under-reported; however, earlier this month, NT Police confirmed it was investigating "several" reports of drink spiking in Darwin's CBD.

At the time, Acting Senior Sergeant Peter Cousins labelled beverage tampering as a "serious offence" and assured the community "any report will be thoroughly investigated".

NT Police say drink spiking is regarded as a serious offence. (Supplied: Unsplash/ Haley Truong)

"We want to stress the responsibility of this behaviour remains solely with the offender and encourage any victim to come forward and make a report," he said.

" Territorians should be able to enjoy a night out with friends or family without their safety being at risk by this appalling behaviour. "

According to NT Police, four incidents of drink or food spiking were recorded between November 2025 and October 2026.

No charges have been laid, with NT Police saying the cases are not yet confirmed.

Annie Whybourne says some victims don't even know they've been assaulted due to memory blackouts. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

But given memory blackouts are one of the main indicators a person's drink has been laced, SARC medical coordinator Annie Whybourne said it can be "extremely frightening" and "disarming" for people to realise they may have been out of control for a period of time.

"Sometimes there's not a clear knowledge that they've been sexually assaulted, but there's a genuine concern," she said.

"People shouldn't be afraid to speak about this phenomenon because it's a very familiar phenomenon to the police.

"They won't be dismissed; they won't be disbelieved."

Testing in 24 hours 'crucial'

While so-called "innocent drinks" can be deliberately contaminated in many ways, alcohol remains the main substance used to alter someone's drink, which is usually achieved by adding additional shots to the beverage without a person's consent.

Often victims will have no indication their drink has been tampered with, as common drugs including GHB, Rohypnol and ketamine may not change a beverage's colour or taste.

Annie Whybourne says it's crucial to get tested within 24 hours if you think your drink has been spiked. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"People usually have quite a good understanding of how they should feel for the number of drinks they've had, but they'll say, 'I just don't understand because I should not have felt that drunk, I should not have felt that bad,'" Dr Whybourne said.

Depending on the substance used, symptoms usually clear between six and eight hours after ingestion and can vary from dizziness, nausea or vomiting to loss of consciousness in extreme cases.

Since most date-rape drugs leave the body in a matter of hours, Dr Whybourne said testing within 24 hours was crucial.

Unlike in other jurisdictions, she said SARC was the only facility in the NT that could obtain forensic specimens, with hospitals and police unable to do so.

Alcohol and Drug Foundation evidence manager Eleanor Costello warned slipping something into a person's drink was a criminal offence.

The Darwin SARC office helps hundreds of victim-survivors of sexual assault each year. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Ms Costello said some may spike their friends' drinks as a "prank", but it was also common for criminals to use it as an opportunity to sedate somebody and rob them.

"What is also most common is one in three [instances], from the data that we do know, is most likely linked to sexual attack or sexual assault, and that is quite concerning," she said.

" Most drink spikings are done by a person somebody knows, which is quite alarming too. "

Preventing drink tampering

The only data on drink spiking across Australia was collected more than two decades ago, with the Institute of Criminology finding up to 4,000 incidents were recorded between 2002 and 2003.

Ms Costello said obtaining updated figures would be difficult and required a national coordinated effort to both test for drink spiking and encourage victims to come forward.

Eleanor Costello says drink spiking is often "fobbed off" as excessive alcohol consumption. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"Often, it goes under-reported; there's also a lot of stigma attached to it because people look like they essentially had too much to drink in many situations and it's often fobbed off as, 'Oh, they just drank too much'," she said.

Do you know more? Contact Courtney Barrett Peters on barrettpeters.courtney@proton.me

on If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

Ms Costello said while it is never a victim's fault, both individuals and venues could take action to identify and prevent drink tampering.

She urged anyone who suspected drink spiking to get tested immediately, preserve the drink and alert the venue so any CCTV footage can be kept to strengthen potential criminal cases.

Bar patrons are being encouraged not to leave drinks unattended. (Supplied: Unsplash/ Create a Sea)

"Avoid sharing [drinks], avoid doing rounds [and] when you go to get a drink, go to the bar and see how it's poured," she said.

Ms Costello also urged people not to leave drinks unattended and said bar staff could proactively clear drinks if people were leaving them unattended.

World.title: Adelaide motorists asked to prepare for major traffic headaches
World.content:
Adelaide motorists are bracing for road closures and traffic disruptions around Adelaide, as a business owner says customers are being driven away by constant roadworks.

Temporary closures along South Road will be in place this weekend while road disruptions for Supercars event Adelaide Grand Final begin on Friday and would continue for two weeks.

SA transport department's Matthew Bowman said Adelaide's inner west suburbs would be affected as closures start from 8pm tonight until Monday morning as part of the multi-billion-dollar Torrens to Darlington upgrade.

"There'll be a full closure in place in both directions between just south of Anzac Highway to north of the South Road tramline there at Glandore," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"There'll also be a full closure in both directions between Sir Donald Bradman Drive and James Congdon Drive at Hilton and just the northbound lane between Ashwin Parade to Gawler Ave at Torrensville."

Road closures along South Rd will begin 8pm on Friday. (ABC News)

Mr Bowman said there was no convenient time to be closing sections of South Road, but traffic volumes were lower in these areas over the weekend.

"We've deliberately coordinated to have works at all three locations done in this one weekend to minimise that overall disruption in coming weeks," he said.

Veli Uysal, who has been serving up yiros at his Brickworks shop at Torrensville for 11 years, said constant South Road disruptions have affected his business

"Before Torrens to Darlington, my business was probably trading about 15 per cent more than now," he said.

"All my regular customers tell me they don't want to come here anymore because they waiting at the intersection on Ashwin Parade coming to Brickworks, 15 to 20 minutes to get in and another 25 to get out.

"In the long run, yes it's going to help a lot of people … but the current conditions are not helping anyone short-term — which is a lot of suffering."

Veli Uysal estimates a 15 per cent downturn for his business due to South Road roadworks. (ABC News)

The final 10.5-kilometre section of the road upgrade, which would complete 78km of North-South Corridor, is due to finish in 2031.

More delays for the eastern suburbs

More pain has also begun on the other side of the city for the eastern suburbs, starting from 6am on Friday with road closures for Adelaide Grand Final.

Wakefield Road, Bartels Road, sections of East Terrace, Hutt Street and Dequetteville Terrace have shut with some closures staying in place until Thursday December 3.

RAA's Charles Mountain said workers east of the city who have the opportunity to work from home next week should consider it.

Sections around Victoria Park and east of the city will be closed for the motorsport event. (Supplied: Daniel Kalisz)

"Traffic volumes on Friday are a little bit less than some of the other days in the week," he said.

"This will be inconvenient but perhaps not so critical as come Monday morning, when we know that is usually when we see the biggest delays in commuter traffic.

"Allow extra time for your commute … it's at least double if you're travelling realistically anytime after 7:30am."

RAA released research on last year's Adelaide Grand Final impacts to commute times in the eastern suburbs.

On the first Monday of closures last year, the median morning peak travel time on The Parade, Norwood (Portrush Road to Fullarton Road) jumped to around 29 minutes — up from the usual four.

World.title: Parents afraid to take their kids to town's only childcare centre
World.content:
Families in a West Australian country town are afraid to send their children to their community's only early childcare centre after it was taken over by an operator with a documented history of child safety incidents and compliance breaches.

Parents in Bridgetown, 257 kilometres south of Perth, say their children have suffered unexplained bruises and bites and other issues at the Stepping Stones Childcare Centre.

Operator LA Anchor Pty Ltd runs eight centres in towns across WA, and has been the subject of 21 regulatory enforcement actions since 2021.

LA Anchor operates the Stepping Stones facility in Bridgetown. (ABC South West WA: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

It has been banned from accepting new enrolments since July last year, after a ruling from the Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority.

Bridgetown mother Tess Gillham said LA Anchor's operations needed heavier scrutiny, or the Department of Communites, which regulates childcare in WA, should shut them down.

She pulled her three-year-old daughter out of her local centre last month after a series of concerning incidents.

The ABC has reached out repeatedly to Girish Chhugani, who is the owner and director of LA Anchor, for comment, and understands he is in the process of selling the Bridgetown centre to a new owner.

Tess Gillham says her daughter suffered unexplained bruising while in the centre's care. (ABC South West WA: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

Unexplained bruises and bites

Ms Gillham said she started noticing issues with quality of care, which accelerated last year.

LA Anchor took ownership of the centre in October 2023.

She said Stepping Stones stopped providing updates on her daughter's activity, and could not be contacted by phone.

Seonaid Leslie says her daughter was bitten multiple times while at the centre. (Supplied: Seonaid Leslie)

She said her anxiety soared when her daughter came home with an unexplained bruise on her "nappy area" in February 2025.

She immediately sought a medical examination, which she said found no evidence of mistreatment.

"As a mother, you feel so fearful of these things," Ms Gillham said.

" And because none of the staff said anything about it when we picked her up, I worried even more. "

She said staff acknowledged in a subsequent meeting they had noticed the bruise, though failed to report it.

Ms Gillham recalled several other occasions when her daughter came home with unexplained bite marks which were also unreported.

She said centre staff only completed and provided the required incident reports after she made repeated requests.

Ms Gillham said staff were doing their best with limited resources.

Only centre in town

Ms Gillham now takes her daughter to a daycare centre in the neighbouring town of Manjimup, more than 30 kilometres away.

Other local families in Bridgetown have no other options.

Seonaid Leslie said she had no alternative to the Bridgetown centre.

She said her family commitments made driving 40 minutes to another daycare centre not feasible.

Seonaid Leslie says the limited childcare options in Bridgetown makes the situation challenging. (ABC South West WA: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

Ms Leslie said her daughter had been bitten on at least four occasions, including one incident which was not reported to her.

"No staff had noticed it; it just shows that they're not having eyes on the kids enough," she said.

She said an essential service like regional child care should not be left to private operators.

"Child care should be treated like a school service," she said.

" That pro-market argument works in metro, but in regional areas there's no competition. "

Seonaid Leslie and Tess Gillham want regulators to take decisive action. (ABC News: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

Former workers share concerns

Former Stepping Stones staff members have told the ABC they worked hard to keep children safe.

But they said the centre was poorly resourced and managed by LA Anchor.

Former staff members say Stepping Stones Bridgetown was poorly managed and resourced. (ABC South West WA: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

Former childcare worker Kirra Heritage, 17, recently left the centre after two years of employment.

"It got to to the point where we can only do the bare minimum," she said.

"We could tell the kids were getting bored and restless, and we couldn't give them much."

Ongoing enforcement actions

LA Anchor has been found to have repeatedly breached childcare standards, with regulators taking multiple enforcement actions against its WA centres.

In 2022, the company was fined a combined $26,000 after two children went missing from centres in Gingin and Karratha.

Late last year, the Education and Care Regulatory Unit ordered the closure of its Pinjarra Prep Childcare Centre, stating it was operating in a manner that posed an immediate risk to the safety, health and wellbeing of children.

Bridgetown has a population of more than 3000, but only one long daycare centre. (ABC South West WA: Sam Bold)

The regulator issued a compliance notice at the Bridgetown centre last year, finding it contravened emergency evacuation procedures, first aid qualifications, and risk assessments around sleep and rest policies.

The Department of Communities would not comment specifically on its investigations or ongoing actions against the company.

"Where serious incidents are identified, the Department of Communities' Education and Care Regulatory Unit (ECRU) investigates thoroughly and takes appropriate actions where required," a spokesperson said.

"In keeping with our obligations under National Law, the Department of Communities is unable to comment any further; however, encourages any parents with concerns to report them to ECRU via the ECRU website."

World.title: Woman drugged and raped by men in scheme organised by husband
World.content:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of rape and sexual abuse.

A British woman who was drugged and then raped by men in a scheme her husband advertised online says the abuse has shattered her trust and destroyed her life.

Joanne Young only learned that her husband of two decades, Philip Young, was advertising her for sex with strangers on websites when detectives came to their house two years ago.

Police had been investigating extreme bestiality images which he had uploaded to the internet.

When they seized his devices, they found intimate images and videos of his wife, restrained at the wrists and blindfolded, while other men engaged in sexual activity with her — all without her knowledge or consent.

Joanne Young spoke outside court after four men were found guilty of raping her. (Reuters: Jack Taylor)

Speaking outside court after four of those men were found guilty of rape and sexual assaults, 49-year-old Ms Young said her case would mean more victims of sexual abuse could come forward, knowing they would be believed and understood.

"Consent has to come from the person themselves," she said.

"No-one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no-one should be able to rely on someone else's word that you agreed

"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.

" I live with a pain that's hard to put into words and this is something that will affect our lives forever. "

Young's case mirrors French woman's

Ms Young's case strongly echoed that of Gisèle Pelicot, a French woman whose husband and 50 co-defendants were found guilty of rape or other sex offences.

The trial at Winchester Crown Court was told Ms Young's then-husband, 50, placed advertised online for strangers of any age or race to have sex with his wife at their home in Swindon, south-west England.

Philip Young pleaded guilty in January to more than 50 charges against his ex-wife Joanne Young, including 11 counts of rape. (Supplied: Wiltshire Police via Reuters)

The former councillor drugged her, filmed the encounters in their bedroom, and later uploaded the videos to the internet.

Police found five such videos recorded between 2015 and 2022, as well as hundreds of images.

"This abuse has cost me my life as I knew it," Ms Young said.

"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way. This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."

Police and prosecutors have praised Ms Young for the poise and bravery she has shown, waiving her right to lifelong anonymity to help secure the conviction of her husband, who admitted to rape and other offences in January.

Four men were found guilty on Thursday. A fifth had already pleaded guilty.

In another echo of the Pelicot case, the guilty men had argued that they thought Ms Young had consented and that it was a shared fantasy with her then-husband.

Loading...

"It is hard to put into words the depth of Young's exploitation and abuse of Jo," Police Detective Superintendent Geoff Smith said.

"No-one should have to go through what she has experienced."

He repeated Ms Young's comments about consent and said the actions of those who exploited her at her husband's behest were clearly wrong, "as in the Gisèle Pelicot case in France".

Ms Pelicot became a symbol of female courage and resilience after her ordeal and said she hoped the enormous interest in her case would help other women who had suffered sexual abuse.

Women's rights campaigners were supporting Joanne Young during the trial. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

That message was also echoed by Joanne Young, who said she was determined not to be defined by what had been done to her.

"This abuse thrives in secrecy… I will now use my experience to try to help others. I also owe it to myself to live the best life I can with my children and loved ones as we move forward."

Reuters

World.title: Aussie has first-round lead in prestigious Tour Championship
World.content:
Emerging Australian golf superstar Karis Davidson has defied the odds to seize the first-round clubhouse lead at the LPGA's rich and prestigious Tour Championship in Florida.

In a dream debut at the $US11 million ($16.5 million) showpiece, Davidson birdied the first four holes in a flawless seven-under-par 65 at Tiburon Golf Club to nab an early one-stroke lead.

"Just honestly hit some good shots into the green," the 28-year-old said, playing down her hot start after being one of the first to tee off in the elite 60-player field.

"The greens first thing in the morning, especially the bermuda [grass], is really smooth, so I just had really good visualisation and they just went in.

"So, yeah."

Yet to win on the LPGA Tour and knowing a score around 20 under par normally prevails in Naples, Davidson was trying to remain grounded as five players sat just one stroke behind, with the likes of world number one Nelly Korda still mid-round.

American Jenny Bae, Japan's Ayaka Furue, Frenchwoman Pauline Roussin-Bouchard, England's Charley Hull and South Korean Somi Lee all signed for 66s.

Davidson's more celebrated compatriot Grace Kim is also well in contention for the $US4 million winner's cheque — the biggest prize in women's golf history — after opening with a five-under 67.

Fellow major champion Hannah Green was one under through 14 holes, while Cassie Porter started with an even-par 72.

World.content:
Breaking NationalWeight loss First GLP-1 pills for weight loss go on sale in Australia Rachel Rasker November 20, 2026 — 9:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australians can access the first GLP-1 pills for weight loss through private prescription from Friday, likely boosting sales of the popular drugs already used by more than half a million people here. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, or GLP-1s, were previously only available through a weekly injection, while the new Wegovy and Foundayo pills are taken as daily oral tablets. Wegovy has landed on shelves across Australia. Louise Kennerley Millions of Australians are expected to use GLP-1s in the coming years, with the drugs boasting powerful health effects including significant weight loss, improved blood glucose control and other metabolic health benefits. However, experts have warned there is a lack of research into the wider effects of the medications, including the risk of malnutrition, which can cause serious health concerns but go unnoticed as symptoms of nutrient deficiency mimic the side effects of GLP-1s, including fatigue, nausea, diarrhoea and constipation.



The medications work by curbing appetite, slowing digestion and promoting feelings of fullness. The Wegovy pill, manufactured by Novo Nordisk, was approved by the TGA earlier this month. It’s taken every morning on an empty stomach and stays stable at room temperature, unlike the injectable Wegovy, which requires refrigeration. The new tablet’s pricing will vary by dose, ranging from about $260 per month for a 1.5mg tablet to $395 a month for 25mg. For patients on the lower doses, this works out at less than $10 a day. The pill is cheaper than the injectable, which costs between $350 and $500 per month.



Related Article Exclusive

Health and nutrition ‘Feeling really weak and shaky’: Experts warn of malnutrition risks on GLP-1s The new tablets are available on shelves from Friday, Novo Nordisk confirmed. Competing manufacturer Lilly won approval for its rival pill Foundayo on Monday, promising availability “in the coming days”. However, while doctors could prescribe the drug from the day of approval, stocks are yet to arrive in pharmacies. Foundayo is a small-molecule, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist taken as a daily pill at any time, without food or water restrictions.



It is expected to cost between $250 and $370 per month, depending on the dose and the pharmacy. Users need to be prescribed the pills by their doctor, which may also require an out-of-pocket cost. The Australian government is facing growing pressure to add GLP-1s to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for weight loss. The high price point of the medicines mean they remain out of reach for many with obesity, which disproportionately affects low and middle-income individuals. World.title: Padel, pickleball and Pilates: the new cruising add-ons
World.content:

Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. In world full of stress inducing pressures, wellness is one of the fastest-growing areas of travel. More of us seek self-care when we go on holiday and want to replace sightseeing with more personalised, feel-good experiences. Cruising fits that brief. It’s organised and stress-free; salty air, sea breezes and gazing out at the ocean seem designed to calm our mind. But if that isn’t enough, cruise lines are developing a range of wellness treatments, activities and excursions to add extra oomph. MSC Cruises has improved its spa experiences. Go cruising and you can have your wrinkles treated and skin tightened, enjoy Brazilian bamboo massages and Mediterranean seaweed wraps, relax in salt or sensory treatment rooms, and investigate local wellness traditions ashore. Shipboard wellness centres are getting bigger and better. Regent Seven Seas’ new ship Seven Seas Prestige, sailing out next month, has the company’s biggest-ever Serene Spa & Wellness space and most expansive wellness offerings, including a hydrotherapy pool and salt-therapy, acupuncture and snow rooms.



There are also dedicated areas for yoga, Pilates, cycling classes and cardio training. A separate sports deck offers a padel and pickleball court, 18-hole putting green, yoga area and ping pong. 



Even expedition ships, which have limited room for spas, are getting in on the action. Ponant, for example, has launched a partnership with French beauty and skincare brand Carita. By the end of 2027 passengers on its entire fleet will be able to rejuvenate themselves from the ravages of jet lag, travel fatigue and lagoon salt. Wellness-themed cruises are also being offered. Among the examples are four Crystal Cruises voyages in 2027 on which experts will lead programs on fitness, nutrition, mindfulness and longevity. Guests can participate in workouts, culinary workshops, breathing classes and Pilates. Related Article Ocean cruises Guide to the best spa experiences on cruise ships: Things you need to know about spa and fitness treatments while cruising Oceania Cruises meanwhile has its eye on what happens on shore, and offers more than 50 Wellness Discovery Tours across Asia, South America and Europe that showcase local healing and mindfulness traditions, such as Kandyan dance therapy in Colombo, traditional Chinese medicine in Hong Kong, tai chi in Bangkok, and soaking in hot springs near Rome and Naples. No more flop-and-drop cruising for those with an eye on improvement. You can sail well, and return feeling better.

World.title: ASX set to fall as Wall Street tumbles despite strong debut for Anthropic
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall as Wall Street tumbles despite strong debut for Anthropic Stan Choe Updated November 20, 2026 — 8:17am ,first published 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Anthropic’s strong debut on Wall Street was not enough to carry the rest of the stock market. US indexes fell after an early-morning recovery for beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence quickly evaporated. The S&P 500 dropped 2 per cent for a sixth straight loss. That’s its longest losing streak since 2024, and it’s down 8.2 per cent from its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 2.2 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 per cent. The losses were widespread, and more than 90 per cent of the stocks that make up the S&P 500 fell. Nervousness surrounding AI continues to weigh down Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for more losses, with futures pointing to a fall of 92 points, or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday, its sixth-straight day of losses. The Australian dollar was weaker at US66.74¢. Leading them downward was Williams-Sonoma, which dropped 15.2 per cent after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street’s forecast. It also stuck with its forecast for how much revenue it will make throughout 2026, and the midpoint of that range was below what analysts were expecting.



Related Article Opinion

AI Could AI become the new subprime crisis? Anthropic investors are undeterred Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Walmart sank 1 per cent even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations. Earlier in the morning, AI-related stocks seemed to be doing well enough to more than make up for such losses. They had rallied after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold its stock at a price of $US83 each in its initial public offering. That’s more than the $US70 to $US78 it earlier thought it would get, and its price quickly surged above $US115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. Anthropic later pared its gain to close 17.1 per cent higher at $US97.17, valuing the company at around $US1.75 trillion ($2.63 trillion) Even before its stock began trading, the strong demand for Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remains among investors about the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost given many AI-related stocks have careened on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology and were bound to deflate.



But AI stocks quickly returned to their jittery ways. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared because of the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8 per cent before swinging to a loss of 2.1 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, went from a 10.5 per cent leap in the morning to a drop of 6.1 per cent. Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7 per cent and flipped to a loss of 3.3 per cent. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with the worries that have been dogging the entire industry. At first it was the longstanding criticism that AI stocks had gone into a bubble after shooting so high, along with doubts that AI could produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments in data centres worth it. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI.



Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He had been one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while also using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth. Anthropic surged at the open before paring its gains, but closed more than 17 per cent higher. AP Other stocks in the AI industry, meanwhile, offered some more encouraging signals. Palo Alto Networks climbed 6.4 per cent after the AI cybersecurity company topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also agreed to buy Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, to help customers adopt AI securely. The all-stock deal is valued at $US4.5 billion. Everpure, a company that helps businesses manage and store their data, said its revenue jumped 51 per cent last quarter from a year earlier in part because of AI-related offerings. That was more than analysts expected, as was its profit for the quarter. Everpure’s stock rose 4.4 per cent.



In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady, even though a couple of reports on the US economy came in below economists’ expectations. One said slightly more US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, though the number remains relatively low compared with history. Another said manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region is slowing by more than economists expected. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 5.06 per cent from 5.07 per cent Wednesday, after flipping between modest gains and losses. Related Article Updated

Wall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Anthropic mints thousands of instant millionaires In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent. Helping to lead the way was SoftBank Group, which climbed 4.6 per cent. It was an early investor in OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and competitor to Anthropic.



South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent thanks to strength for its stocks tied to the AI boom, but indexes were weaker elsewhere in Asia and in Europe. Germany’s DAX lost 1.1 per cent. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.content:

The bassist of Brisbane indie-rock band Bugs has died aged 31 after an 18-month battle with stage-four colorectal cancer. Jordan Brunoli was one of three members of the Brisbane band – formed in 2014 – alongside lead vocalist and songwriter Connor Brooker and drummer Brock Weston. ABC reported he passed away on Wednesday night surrounded by family and friends. Bassist of Brisbane band Bugs, Jordan Brunoli (centre), died on Wednesday following a year-long battle with cancer. Bugs / Instagram Bugs announced their “best friend and bass player Jordan” had been diagnosed with incurable stage-four colorectal cancer in June last year, and held a fundraising concert to support the then-29-year-old’s treatment.



The band continued to produce music through Brunoli’s treatment, releasing its fourth album Head Noise on August 28. Related Article Entertainment ‘Beautiful to see’: Brisbane bands unite to help bassist’s cancer fight The trio performed their final two shows at the Crowbar in Brisbane in September this year. In an interview with ABC Triple J’s Hack one week before the album’s release, Brunoli revealed recent test results indicated he had months to live. “It feels like I’m talking about someone else ... it doesn’t feel real,” he said.



The bassist said he was prepared for the news following months of declining health, but said it devastated his long-term partner, George, who he married earlier this year. Brunoli also spent the final year of his life raising awareness about colorectal cancer. He said he initially struggled to get a diagnosis due to his age, and urged young people to advocate for their own health, even if it meant getting a second opinion. “When you’re at the end you really realise who’s there for you and who’s not,” he said.



Colorectal (bowel) cancer is such a recognised danger that the Australian government sends people aged 50 to 74 a screening test in the post every two years, but is less common in people under the age of 30. However, Bowel Cancer Australia has tracked a steady rise in early-onset bowel cancer, with just under 13 per cent of those diagnosed under the age of 50 – up from 11 per cent in 2025. World.title: Lucky seven: Anthropic hits $3 trillion value in record Wall Street debut
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsBillionaires Lucky seven: Anthropic hits $3 trillion value in record Wall Street debut Dylan Sloan November 20, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has pushed the combined wealth of its seven co-founders to $US171 billion as shares of the AI lab jumped following its debut. The stock, which priced at $US83 a share, soared to $US111.50 in early trade, giving the company a market capitalisation of over $US2 trillion ($3 trillion) before paring gains. Siblings Daniela and Dario Amodei are two of the five-year-old company’s seven founders. AP Photo/Seth Wenig It was trading at $US100.74 in early afternoon trade in New York, valuing each founder’s fortune at about $US24.5 billion ($36.7 billion), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The $US107.3 billion public offering and concurrent private placement broke SpaceX’s record for the biggest-ever. The group first became billionaires less than two years ago after the San Francisco-based company raised $US3.5 billion at a $US61.5 billion valuation. Another funding round that closed in May propelled all seven onto Bloomberg’s ranking of the world’s 500 richest people.



The Claude chatbot maker has an unusually even ownership structure among its founders, with each holding about the same 1.3 per cent fully diluted economic stake in the firm. That makes the seven the largest number of individuals appearing on Bloomberg’s wealth index who work at any one company. Related Article Wall Street How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot Despite their relatively small economic stakes, the founders retain outsized control over the company through Founder LLC, an entity that owns a single Class F share carrying 50.1 per cent of Anthropic’s voting power. They will retain those voting rights as long as they collectively hold at least 2 per cent of the Class A shares they owned at the time of Anthropic’s public debut. All seven have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal company equity to philanthropic causes. Anthropic’s prospectus specifies that these commitments aren’t legally binding and constitute voluntary, revocable pledges. Actor-turned-venture capitalist Ashton Kutcher, and Guy Oseary, the legendary music manager and industry broker, are also big winners through their investment firm Sound Ventures. The company was an early investor in Anthropic and has poured some $US435 million into it and owns roughly half a per cent of the AI company, according to a person familiar with the matter. That stake is now valued at approximately $US9 billion, with the windfall projected to make Kutcher a billionaire.



Paper wealth Anthropic’s offering is a key step in the AI industry’s massive wealth boom. According to a recent Bloomberg Businessweek analysis, founders and employees at San Francisco-based AI startups together hold more than $US1.2 trillion in company equity. Although much of that paper wealth remains tied up in illiquid private company shares, Anthropic’s public debut will allow founders and employees to cash out hundreds of billions of dollars in company stock. That process won’t be immediate: Lock-up restrictions outlined in Anthropic’s prospectus prevent current and former employees from selling shares for as long as six months. The co-founders face an even longer lock-up period of up to a year. The Claude chatbot maker has an unusually even ownership structure among its founders, with each holding about the same 1.3 per cent fully diluted economic stake in the firm. AP Photo/Andres Kudacki



Anthropic’s leadership is already taking some money off the table. Each of the seven co-founders sold shares worth about $US280 million in the IPO, according to the prospectus. In addition, both Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive officer, and his sister, Daniela, its chair, participated in tender offers in June 2025 and April 2026, according to the prospectus. Other co-founders include Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah. Anthropic’s strong opening also boosted the net worth of chief financial officer Krishna Rao to $US1.1 billion. Rao, who joined the company in 2024 after roles at Airbnb and Blackstone, holds about 9.3 million vested stock options. Related Article Updated

Wall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Anthropic mints thousands of instant millionaires Founded in January 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic was valued at $US461 million in its Series A funding round that year, according to PitchBook. Since then, its valuation has climbed more than 320,000 per cent, based on the fully diluted valuation implied by the offering price.



That rapid rise and the resulting explosion of insider wealth come as tech titans account for a growing share of the world’s ultra-wealthy. Through the first nine months of the year, tech billionaires on Bloomberg’s wealth index added a combined $US845 billion to their fortunes, while everyone else on the list lost a combined $US62 billion. Competing manufacturer Lilly won approval for its rival pill Foundayo on Monday, promising availability “in the coming days”. However, while doctors could prescribe the drug from the day of approval, stocks are yet to arrive in pharmacies. Foundayo is a small-molecule, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist taken as a daily pill at any time, without food or water restrictions.



It is expected to cost between $250 and $370 per month, depending on the dose and the pharmacy. Users need to be prescribed the pills by their doctor, which may also require an out-of-pocket cost. The Australian government is facing growing pressure to add GLP-1s to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for weight loss. The high price point of the medicines mean they remain out of reach for many with obesity, which disproportionately affects low and middle-income individuals. In world full of stress inducing pressures, wellness is one of the fastest-growing areas of travel. More of us seek self-care when we go on holiday and want to replace sightseeing with more personalised, feel-good experiences. Cruising fits that brief. It’s organised and stress-free; salty air, sea breezes and gazing out at the ocean seem designed to calm our mind. But if that isn’t enough, cruise lines are developing a range of wellness treatments, activities and excursions to add extra oomph. MSC Cruises has improved its spa experiences. Go cruising and you can have your wrinkles treated and skin tightened, enjoy Brazilian bamboo massages and Mediterranean seaweed wraps, relax in salt or sensory treatment rooms, and investigate local wellness traditions ashore. Shipboard wellness centres are getting bigger and better. Regent Seven Seas’ new ship Seven Seas Prestige, sailing out next month, has the company’s biggest-ever Serene Spa & Wellness space and most expansive wellness offerings, including a hydrotherapy pool and salt-therapy, acupuncture and snow rooms.



There are also dedicated areas for yoga, Pilates, cycling classes and cardio training. A separate sports deck offers a padel and pickleball court, 18-hole putting green, yoga area and ping pong. 



Even expedition ships, which have limited room for spas, are getting in on the action. Ponant, for example, has launched a partnership with French beauty and skincare brand Carita. By the end of 2027 passengers on its entire fleet will be able to rejuvenate themselves from the ravages of jet lag, travel fatigue and lagoon salt. Wellness-themed cruises are also being offered. Among the examples are four Crystal Cruises voyages in 2027 on which experts will lead programs on fitness, nutrition, mindfulness and longevity. Guests can participate in workouts, culinary workshops, breathing classes and Pilates. Related Article Ocean cruises Guide to the best spa experiences on cruise ships: Things you need to know about spa and fitness treatments while cruising Oceania Cruises meanwhile has its eye on what happens on shore, and offers more than 50 Wellness Discovery Tours across Asia, South America and Europe that showcase local healing and mindfulness traditions, such as Kandyan dance therapy in Colombo, traditional Chinese medicine in Hong Kong, tai chi in Bangkok, and soaking in hot springs near Rome and Naples. No more flop-and-drop cruising for those with an eye on improvement. You can sail well, and return feeling better.

World.title: ASX set to fall as Wall Street tumbles despite strong debut for Anthropic
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall as Wall Street tumbles despite strong debut for Anthropic Stan Choe Updated November 20, 2026 — 8:17am ,first published 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Anthropic’s strong debut on Wall Street was not enough to carry the rest of the stock market. US indexes fell after an early-morning recovery for beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence quickly evaporated. The S&P 500 dropped 2 per cent for a sixth straight loss. That’s its longest losing streak since 2024, and it’s down 8.2 per cent from its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 2.2 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 per cent. The losses were widespread, and more than 90 per cent of the stocks that make up the S&P 500 fell. Nervousness surrounding AI continues to weigh down Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for more losses, with futures pointing to a fall of 92 points, or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday, its sixth-straight day of losses. The Australian dollar was weaker at US66.74¢. Leading them downward was Williams-Sonoma, which dropped 15.2 per cent after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street’s forecast. It also stuck with its forecast for how much revenue it will make throughout 2026, and the midpoint of that range was below what analysts were expecting.



Related Article Opinion

AI Could AI become the new subprime crisis? Anthropic investors are undeterred Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Walmart sank 1 per cent even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations. Earlier in the morning, AI-related stocks seemed to be doing well enough to more than make up for such losses. They had rallied after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold its stock at a price of $US83 each in its initial public offering. That’s more than the $US70 to $US78 it earlier thought it would get, and its price quickly surged above $US115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. Anthropic later pared its gain to close 17.1 per cent higher at $US97.17, valuing the company at around $US1.75 trillion ($2.63 trillion) Even before its stock began trading, the strong demand for Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remains among investors about the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost given many AI-related stocks have careened on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology and were bound to deflate.



But AI stocks quickly returned to their jittery ways. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared because of the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8 per cent before swinging to a loss of 2.1 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, went from a 10.5 per cent leap in the morning to a drop of 6.1 per cent. Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7 per cent and flipped to a loss of 3.3 per cent. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with the worries that have been dogging the entire industry. At first it was the longstanding criticism that AI stocks had gone into a bubble after shooting so high, along with doubts that AI could produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments in data centres worth it. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI.



Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He had been one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while also using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth. Anthropic surged at the open before paring its gains, but closed more than 17 per cent higher. AP Other stocks in the AI industry, meanwhile, offered some more encouraging signals. Palo Alto Networks climbed 6.4 per cent after the AI cybersecurity company topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also agreed to buy Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, to help customers adopt AI securely. The all-stock deal is valued at $US4.5 billion. Everpure, a company that helps businesses manage and store their data, said its revenue jumped 51 per cent last quarter from a year earlier in part because of AI-related offerings. That was more than analysts expected, as was its profit for the quarter. Everpure’s stock rose 4.4 per cent.



In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady, even though a couple of reports on the US economy came in below economists’ expectations. One said slightly more US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, though the number remains relatively low compared with history. Another said manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region is slowing by more than economists expected. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 5.06 per cent from 5.07 per cent Wednesday, after flipping between modest gains and losses. Related Article Updated

Wall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Anthropic mints thousands of instant millionaires In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent. Helping to lead the way was SoftBank Group, which climbed 4.6 per cent. It was an early investor in OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and competitor to Anthropic.



South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent thanks to strength for its stocks tied to the AI boom, but indexes were weaker elsewhere in Asia and in Europe. Germany’s DAX lost 1.1 per cent. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

The bassist of Brisbane indie-rock band Bugs has died aged 31 after an 18-month battle with stage-four colorectal cancer. Jordan Brunoli was one of three members of the Brisbane band – formed in 2014 – alongside lead vocalist and songwriter Connor Brooker and drummer Brock Weston. ABC reported he passed away on Wednesday night surrounded by family and friends. Bassist of Brisbane band Bugs, Jordan Brunoli (centre), died on Wednesday following a year-long battle with cancer. Bugs / Instagram Bugs announced their “best friend and bass player Jordan” had been diagnosed with incurable stage-four colorectal cancer in June last year, and held a fundraising concert to support the then-29-year-old’s treatment.



The band continued to produce music through Brunoli’s treatment, releasing its fourth album Head Noise on August 28. Related Article Entertainment ‘Beautiful to see’: Brisbane bands unite to help bassist’s cancer fight The trio performed their final two shows at the Crowbar in Brisbane in September this year. In an interview with ABC Triple J’s Hack one week before the album’s release, Brunoli revealed recent test results indicated he had months to live. “It feels like I’m talking about someone else ... it doesn’t feel real,” he said.



The bassist said he was prepared for the news following months of declining health, but said it devastated his long-term partner, George, who he married earlier this year. Brunoli also spent the final year of his life raising awareness about colorectal cancer. He said he initially struggled to get a diagnosis due to his age, and urged young people to advocate for their own health, even if it meant getting a second opinion. “When you’re at the end you really realise who’s there for you and who’s not,” he said.



Colorectal (bowel) cancer is such a recognised danger that the Australian government sends people aged 50 to 74 a screening test in the post every two years, but is less common in people under the age of 30. However, Bowel Cancer Australia has tracked a steady rise in early-onset bowel cancer, with just under 13 per cent of those diagnosed under the age of 50 – up from 11 per cent in 2025. World.title: Lucky seven: Anthropic hits $3 trillion value in record Wall Street debut
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsBillionaires Lucky seven: Anthropic hits $3 trillion value in record Wall Street debut Dylan Sloan November 20, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has pushed the combined wealth of its seven co-founders to $US171 billion as shares of the AI lab jumped following its debut. The stock, which priced at $US83 a share, soared to $US111.50 in early trade, giving the company a market capitalisation of over $US2 trillion ($3 trillion) before paring gains. Siblings Daniela and Dario Amodei are two of the five-year-old company’s seven founders. AP Photo/Seth Wenig It was trading at $US100.74 in early afternoon trade in New York, valuing each founder’s fortune at about $US24.5 billion ($36.7 billion), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The $US107.3 billion public offering and concurrent private placement broke SpaceX’s record for the biggest-ever. The group first became billionaires less than two years ago after the San Francisco-based company raised $US3.5 billion at a $US61.5 billion valuation. Another funding round that closed in May propelled all seven onto Bloomberg’s ranking of the world’s 500 richest people.



The Claude chatbot maker has an unusually even ownership structure among its founders, with each holding about the same 1.3 per cent fully diluted economic stake in the firm. That makes the seven the largest number of individuals appearing on Bloomberg’s wealth index who work at any one company. Related Article Wall Street How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot Despite their relatively small economic stakes, the founders retain outsized control over the company through Founder LLC, an entity that owns a single Class F share carrying 50.1 per cent of Anthropic’s voting power. They will retain those voting rights as long as they collectively hold at least 2 per cent of the Class A shares they owned at the time of Anthropic’s public debut. All seven have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal company equity to philanthropic causes. Anthropic’s prospectus specifies that these commitments aren’t legally binding and constitute voluntary, revocable pledges. Actor-turned-venture capitalist Ashton Kutcher, and Guy Oseary, the legendary music manager and industry broker, are also big winners through their investment firm Sound Ventures. The company was an early investor in Anthropic and has poured some $US435 million into it and owns roughly half a per cent of the AI company, according to a person familiar with the matter. That stake is now valued at approximately $US9 billion, with the windfall projected to make Kutcher a billionaire.



Paper wealth Anthropic’s offering is a key step in the AI industry’s massive wealth boom. According to a recent Bloomberg Businessweek analysis, founders and employees at San Francisco-based AI startups together hold more than $US1.2 trillion in company equity. Although much of that paper wealth remains tied up in illiquid private company shares, Anthropic’s public debut will allow founders and employees to cash out hundreds of billions of dollars in company stock. That process won’t be immediate: Lock-up restrictions outlined in Anthropic’s prospectus prevent current and former employees from selling shares for as long as six months. The co-founders face an even longer lock-up period of up to a year. The Claude chatbot maker has an unusually even ownership structure among its founders, with each holding about the same 1.3 per cent fully diluted economic stake in the firm. AP Photo/Andres Kudacki



Anthropic’s leadership is already taking some money off the table. Each of the seven co-founders sold shares worth about $US280 million in the IPO, according to the prospectus. In addition, both Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive officer, and his sister, Daniela, its chair, participated in tender offers in June 2025 and April 2026, according to the prospectus. Other co-founders include Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah. Anthropic’s strong opening also boosted the net worth of chief financial officer Krishna Rao to $US1.1 billion. Rao, who joined the company in 2024 after roles at Airbnb and Blackstone, holds about 9.3 million vested stock options. Related Article Updated

Wall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Anthropic mints thousands of instant millionaires Founded in January 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic was valued at $US461 million in its Series A funding round that year, according to PitchBook. Since then, its valuation has climbed more than 320,000 per cent, based on the fully diluted valuation implied by the offering price.



That rapid rise and the resulting explosion of insider wealth come as tech titans account for a growing share of the world’s ultra-wealthy. Through the first nine months of the year, tech billionaires on Bloomberg’s wealth index added a combined $US845 billion to their fortunes, while everyone else on the list lost a combined $US62 billion. World.title: Kiwis paying 'horrific' amounts to fake visa websites, travel boss warns
World.content:
Audio player for " Summer holiday goers warned about AI-generated scams " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2704390%2Fkiwis-paying-horrific-amounts-to-fake-visa-websites-travel-boss-warns

Summer holiday goers warned about AI-generated scams Nine To Noon Download MP3 10m

People are paying large sums to convincing AI-generated websites that seem to be legitimate, the Travel Agents Association chief executive says.

With the lead-up to summer holidays well underway many people are planning holidays and booking accommodation and airfares

While many Kiwis do their own online bookings, travel agents are warning about increasingly convincing scams.

Julie White Hospitality NZ

The Australian government's Smartraveller website this week issued a warning ahead of the holiday season, saying scams can affect travellers at every stage of their journey, including researching destinations, booking flights and accommodation, and while travelling domestically or overseas.

Travel Agents Association chief executive Julie White agreed scamming was ramping up in the sector, thanks in part to advances in AI and hacking with information ending up on the dark web.

Visas were a fraught area - people were paying large sums to fake AI-generated websites that seemed to have accurate information.

"There's a lot of fake and very convincing websites out there. ... People are getting caught out and paying a horrific amount of money, thinking they're booking the right visa to get into whatever country they're travelling to. Not only have they lost their money but they don't have the visa," she told Nine to Noon.

"They're just so convincing so the message is: always make sure you're dealing with the official website."

Mouneb Taim / Middle East Images via AFP

If people did their own bookings online, they also risked websites such as accommodation ones being hacked and they could receive convincing scam WhatsApp messages or emails asking for credit card details.

She advised people to go back to their original email and work through that information to confirm any request was genuine.

"Always go back to the original confirmation if you're getting any information out of the blue ... that way you'll know it's legitimate."

She recommended people do some initial online research using AI but use a travel agent for their bookings.

Travel agents would be on the side of travellers and were a point of contact when things went wrong.

White said Kiwis were more enthusiastic than ever about travelling and it was necessary to book early to get the best deals on airfares on accommodation.

"On the whole, it's really buoyant. People are out there wanting to travel domestically and also internationally."

World.title: Serious injuries as bus crashes onto the pavement and into Wellington bush
World.content:
A Wellington bus has crashed onto the pavement into a bush on the side of a residential street in Wadestown.

Police reported serious injuries but it is unclear what has happened or how many people may have been hurt.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

The rear end of the bus ended up on the pavement at the bus stop on Norwich Street.

Police have shielded the incident from view with tarpaulins.

Metlink diverted buses away from Norwich Street, which police have cordoned off.

In response to RNZ's request for comment, Metlink said it was "aware of an incident involving one of our bus drivers this morning".

It said it could not comment further as police were investigating.

It said services ending at or starting from Norwich Street would now begin from Mairangi Road, and number 22 services to Johnsonville would go via Warrick Street.

Firefighters were called to a motor vehicle crash in Wadestown around 8.13 this morning.

When RNZ contacted FENZ it re-directed all enquiries to police.

Local mailman Justin said he'd been doing the route for seven years and had "never seen anything like this".

RNZ / Mark Papalii

He said he had deliveries on Norwich St that wouldn't be done, as he expected police to be at the scene for some time.

He said it was usually a very peaceful neighbourhood.

Neighbour Karen was sleeping in on her day off when the sirens began to wake her.

She said the intersection was tricky for long buses to manage.

"That corner is quite difficult to take."

Several residents said they hadn't heard the accident happen, and only went out to have a look when they heard emergency services' sirens.

An RNZ reporter saw residents milling around, confused and uncertain as to what had happened.

They said nobody would want an incident like this to happen on their street.

The reporter could see two other buses at the scene.

Traffic through Wadestown was still flowing.

World.title: More sperm whales die after mass stranding at Ninety Mile Beach
World.content:
Three more sperm whales have died at Ninety Mile Beach overnight after becoming stranded.

Te Rūnanga Nui o Te Aupōuri chief executive Tipene Kapa-Kingi, who is at the beach, said 22 whales had died in total, after being stranded for two tides.

Kapa Kingi said there were two whales still alive on Friday, but the size of the whales and the choppy sea conditions made it nearly impossible to re-float them.

There were about 60 people from iwi around the area at the beach who would be looking after the live whales, and dealing with the dead ones.

"It's a traditional customary practice handed down from our tīpuna. Which involves processing the whales that have passed on, and then also taking them to their final resting place."

Kapa Kingi said it was a "tragic situation", but morale was strong in the group.

"We're mourning the loss of these parāoa, but we're also respecting them as taonga, and treating them as so."

World.title: Man pleads not guilty to manslaughter of Braydon Hepworth
World.content:
A man has pleaded not guilty to the manslaughter of Braydon Hepworth in Christchurch.

Hepworth's body was found buried in a shed in Linwood on 8 October after he disappeared in early September.

The 60-year-old man, whose name is suppressed, also pleaded not guilty to concealing the 21-year-old father's body and making a false statement, at the High Court at Christchurch on Friday.

Justice Mander remanded the man in custody, with a possible trial date set for late next year.

Hepworth's body was found buried in a shed in Linwood on 8 October. Rachel Graham / RNZ

A 34-year-old Christchurch man has also been charged in relation to concealing Hepworth's body.

An independent review is being carried out into the care Hepworth received at the Christchurch City Mission after he was told to leave its Whakaora Kāinga transitional housing complex less than two months before he disappeared.

Mission board chair Jane Evans said the review would examine Hepworth's time with the mission and the decision-making involved in his care.

"We take our responsibilities to our clients, our staff and the wider community very seriously," she said in an October statement.

"The mission is open to improving how it supports people in its care and looks forward to the outcome."

World.title: The electorates bucking the two-tick trend
World.content:
Most general electorates handed their favoured party two ticks this election, but seven did not.

So what's happening when an electorate backs a candidate from one party, but gives its party vote to another?

Victoria University political scientist Dr Lara Greaves said it was difficult to draw a conclusion, and each seat should be treated on a case-by-case basis, but she noted incumbency bias, candidates' visibility, and strategic voting could all play a part.

Greaves said it was incredibly hard to model what percentage of people tried to vote strategically to support the right or left bloc, versus how many simply wanted the candidate they voted for to win.

It's worth noting, too, that the final vote count is not returned until 27 November, meaning some electorates could be added to or removed from this list.

Chlöe Swarbrick. RNZ / Nick Monro

Auckland Central: a strong incumbent

Party vote went to National, but Green incumbent Chlöe Swarbrick won the seat.

This one was a landslide in the seat: Swarbrick got 46.6 percent of the vote while National's Candace Kinser reached 37.2 percent.

However, it was much closer in the party vote, with National's 26.6 percent beating out Labour's 25.8 percent (followed by the Greens' 20 percent). It's worth noting that could change with special votes - those often tend to lean left.

In 2023, National had a far stronger party vote lead with 33.1 percent, compared to the Greens' 24 percent, and Labour's 22.7 percent.

Swarbrick is a party co-leader - giving her profile - plus, she's considered a staunch and responsive advocate for her electorate, Greaves said.

"There are some local MPs that we know are really hands on in the community and spend that time quite wisely making those relationships and ... get home as much as they can to really be there for the community."

Epsom has once again backed David Seymour. Baz Macdonald

Epsom: a cup of tea hangover and a strong incumbent

Party vote went to National, but ACT incumbent David Seymour won the seat.

Epsom is home to the infamous 2011 cup of tea deal, where National and ACT struck an agreement to attempt (successfully) to get ACT into Parliament by backing then ACT member John Banks to win his seat.

That had continued since but was ditched somewhat last minute this year, with National's Paul Goldsmith actively campaigning for the candidate vote.

However, it appears voters' old habits die hard. That, and Seymour is the type of representative who will answer the phone on a Friday afternoon, as he has said consistently throughout the campaign. Plus, he was the incumbent, ACT Party leader, a minister and deputy prime minister - all of which made him a well-known political figure.

Tama Potaka. Alyse Wright

Hamilton West: a ministerial incumbent

Party vote went to Labour, but National incumbent Tama Potaka won the seat.

It's historically been a bit of a bellwether, but National's held it for most of the past two decades.

This election, Labour netted 32.4 percent while National got 29.7 percent. In the seat, Potaka got 42.7 percent while Labour's Myra Williamson got 35.9 percent.
