Potaka was a minister in the last government, so he's a known figure.

"High profile can really work to your advantage ... especially in these close races," Greaves said.

"Tama Potaka does seem to have outperformed relative to what the party vote was in that electorate."

Tim Costley. Justin Wong/The Post

Kāpiti: the new seat on the block

Party vote went to Labour, but National's Tim Costley won the seat.

The seat is new, having been created last year when three electorates - Ōtaki (Costley's seat), Mana and Ōhāriu - became two: Kāpiti and Kenepuru. For that reason, it's difficult to compare the 2026 results with previous elections. Mana was a Labour stronghold, while Ōtaki had a National MP since 2008, except in 2020 when Labour flipped a huge number of seats throughout the country.

Tim Costley's success could be down to incumbency bias, or perhaps he is considered one of those people who is visible within the community and turns up to every ribbon-cutting, as Greaves puts it.

The second-placed candidate, Labour's Sophie Handford, has never been an MP but is fairly well known in the community having served as a district councillor for two terms, and previously founded School Strike 4 Climate as a teenager.

Greg Fleming. Samuel Rillstone / RNZ

Maungakiekie: a bellwether

Party vote went to Labour, but National incumbent Greg Fleming won the seat.

Fleming took the seat comfortably with 46.5 percent of the vote compared to Labour candidate Priyanca Radhakrishnan's 37.1 percent. The party vote was, again, a close one: Labour 32.4 percent, National 30.6 percent.

While Fleming is the incumbent, Radhakrishnan has been in Parliament since 2017 and has held the seat before (in the "red wave" of 2020).

Maungakiekie is a bellwether, with its election results generally reflecting those of the nation (more on that below).

Greaves said MPs in swing seats simply had to work harder.

"You need to knock on more doors, you need to build relationships with more organisations in the community and show up to more events, so there is a little bit of an effect there."

Blair Cameron. LDR/Sara Hollyman

Nelson: the same tight race with a different outcome

Party vote went to Labour, but National's Blair Cameron won the seat off the incumbent, Rachel Boyack.

Cameron lost narrowly to Boyack in 2023 and Greaves acknowledged he had been campaigning hard since.

She said visibility within the community matters - "Are they that seen face, do they show up to every single ribbon cutting?" - but it's difficult to assess that from afar.

The party vote in Nelson flipped from 2023 too. Labour netted about 29 percent in both elections, but National's 32.2 percent in 2023 dropped to 27.1 percent this election.

Tamatha Paul. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Wellington North: a new seat leaning a little less left

Party vote went to Labour, but Green incumbent Tamatha Paul won the seat.

This is a new seat: the Wellington Central (Paul's former seat) and Rongotai electorates moved north and west respectively, and were renamed Wellington North and Wellington Bays.

The move folded affluent, right-leaning suburbs like Khandallah into Wellington North. That could have been behind the shift from Wellington Central's two ticks Green result in 2023. However, National achieved 21.4 percent of the vote in 2023, and just 18 percent this election.

It was a much closer race in the seat this time around with Paul's 39.4 percent beating out senior Labour MP Ayesha Verrall's 32 percent.

"Some of these [boundary] changes do change the nature of the vote in the electorate, and that is just something that MPs kind of have to account for," Greaves said.

What about the bellwethers?

A bellwether seat tends to reflect the way the nation votes. Traditionally, they've been Hamilton East, Hamilton West and Maungakiekie. Hutt South has come into the fold since 2017.

The preliminary party vote result has Labour ahead by a whisker - 29.4 percent to National's 29.2 percent.

This election the party vote went to Labour in all but one bellwether, while the seat was won by a National candidate in all but one:

Hamilton East: National 31.9 percent, Labour 30.3 percent. National candidate (Ryan Hamilton)

Hamilton West: Labour 32.4 percent, National 29.7 percent. National candidate (Tama Potaka)

Maungakiekie: Labour 32.4 percent, National 30.6 percent. National candidate (Greg Fleming)

Hutt South: Labour 36.6 percent, National 24.9 percent. Labour candidate (Ginny Andersen)

Greaves noted some of those results would flip once the special votes were in, and said bellwethers were a hangover from the first-past-the-post electoral system.

"The idea of a bellwether hasn't made sense in an MMP system because it is relatively easy to just poll the whole party vote, and our Parliament is meant to reflect the party vote," she said.

But now a "huge overhang" is in play. The size of Parliament is set to expand by 11 seats with National and Te Pāti Māori winning more electorates than their party vote entitles them to.

That makes winning seats more important, Greaves said.

World.title: 'Need to do better': Shortcomings found in police handling of Tom Phillips documentary
World.content:
The head of a documentary crew and a cameraman were given access to the campsite where Tom Phillips' children were found before the forensic examination had been completed, a review has revealed.

The trip was made after Dame Julie Christie and the cameraman had spent up to 30 minutes at the scene where Phillips died, after his body had been removed - but before all forensic examination had been completed.

The review says the officers in charge of both scenes were aware that granting such access was "inconsistent with best practice" and formally challenged the decision to permit access "however access was approved with communication emphasising that the agreement with the documentary crew was approved at a senior level".

It was earlier revealed a film crew from Dunedin-founded NHNZ Productions had been following the hunt for Phillips and his children for more than a year, gaining exclusive access to the investigation. The documentary would be streamed on Netflix. The documentary is being produced by Dame Julie.

In April, RNZ obtained a series of documents released by police under the Official Information Act (OIA) in relation to the documentary.

Following the release, NZ Police executive director media and communications Cass Carter said police were reviewing the processes around the management of the documentary.

The review, by Detective Inspector Shaun Vickers assisted by media consultant Gavin Ellis, was released on Friday.

The review said police entered into a formal agreement with the documentary crew to create The Marokopa Project.

Filmmakers for the documentary. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Governance was managed nationally by the Director of director of media and strategic communications Juli Clausen, with district level governance and engagement led by the officer in charge Detective Senior Sergeant Andrew Saunders.

The review said the agreement did not automatically compromise investigative integrity, but it "created conditions where integrity required active protection".

"Decisions about access to crime scenes, evidence, specialist squads, and covert operations required heightened scrutiny to avoid exposing sensitive tactics or influencing investigative phases.

"Investigators raised concerns during contested access decisions, prompting escalation to senior district leadership."

It also found that the documentary arrangement "complicated perceptions of media fairness".

The shooting scene

The review details how Dame Julie and a cameraman were granted access to the shooting scene on Te Anga Rd on 9 September, the day after the shooting.

Phillips' body had been removed, but not all forensic examination had been completed.

Dame Julie and a cameraman were allowed to attend and film from an area that had been "forensically processed".

They were accompanied by the officer in charge of the scene.

"At the time of access, key elements of the scene remained in situ, including the ATV and police vehicles.

"Forensic evidence was present and visible within the scene at this time."

Tom Phillips. Supplied

Dame Julie remained at the scene under police escort for about 25-30 minutes while the cameraman captured "exclusive footage".

The access to the scene was authorised by the Acting District Commander.

Dame Julie and the cameraman then went to the 'Pines' campsite where the children had been found the day before.

The review says they were authorised to enter the campsite and film by Saunders.

"At the time of access, the forensic examination had not been completed, and key elements of the scene remained in situ."

Both officers in charge of the respective scenes formally challenged the decisions to allow the access.

The proposal

The review says Police Commissioner Richard Chambers spoke with Christie and Karen Rutherford about the proposal.

"The Commissioner said he thought the proposal could serve as an artefact of Police work, allowing the public to see the efforts undertaken by Operation Curly staff to locate and safely return the Phillips children that were largely invisible to the public."

However, beyond his "initial expression of support," prior to the agreement being signed, Chambers involvement was "very limited".

"He was not involved in decision-making or kept informed of access given to the documentary crew. Nor was he aware his early support for the documentary crew was being referenced at various stages

to help ensure the documentary progressed."

His only involvement with the crew was being filmed, but not interviewed, when he visited during the drone phase.

Governance and management of the agreement was led at a national level by Clausen, the review said.

Both Clausen and Saunders operated with oversight from their respective supervisors, the review said.

An aerial shot of Tom Phillips' campsite. Dean Purcell/New Zealand Herald via Getty Images

The comms plan

The communications plan for the investigation, dubbed Op Curly, was created in March 2025 by Clausen.

The review identified a "lack of awareness and implementation" of the plan across the investigation.

"Several individuals indicated they were either unaware of the plan's existence or the most current version of the plan."

The plan did not have a defined governance framework, or a set review cycle or update schedule. It also did not "clearly identify or expand on" documentary related risks including expectations and

parameters.

In relation to conflicts of interest the review did not find any evidence that Police decision-making or operational activity was influenced by the presence of the film crew. However, there were several

potential and perceived conflicts of interest including mainstream media no granted equivalent access.

Police respond

Following the release of the review, executive director of media and communications Cass Carter said the review had given police "an opportunity to pause, look at works well already and where we can do better".

"While the documentary did not compromise investigative integrity, we know there was a perceived conflict, and it did create conditions where integrity required protection."

The review found there was strategic planning and consistency of messaging, but there should have been robust governance and oversight, clearer access controls, and structured escalation pathways to

safeguard investigative integrity.

"I can assure people, right from the start, there were strict settings in place to protect the children and sensitive police operational information.

"While the documentary did not compromise investigative integrity, we know there was a perceived conflict, and it did create conditions where integrity required protection. Some staff had reservations which they raised at the time."

One of the campsites. Supplied/NZ Police

Carter said police's relationship with media was also "called into question".

"That relationship is vital to the work we do every day. The media supports our ability to reach communities and get important safety messages and reassurance out to them.

"We agree that some of our decisions around the documentary meant we did not serve media in the way we should have. Police has a long history of cooperating on documentaries or programmes involving ongoing investigations, and we don't want to stop that. They offer unique and interesting insights into Police work and transparency around our work, which enables communities to have trust and confidence in their Police."

Carter said police "just need to do better in how we manage these agreements".

"I believe the documentary crew also acted with the best intent in all their dealings with our staff. However, we should have had better processes in place for both our staff and the crew, so they could have better navigated those instances where there was uncertainty."

World.title: Football club wishes manager a happy birthday, then sack him hours later
World.content:
English football club Blackpool has sacked manager Ian Evatt, just hours after the club wished him a happy birthday on their social media accounts.

Blackpool plays in League One, the third tier of English football, and is languishing in 20th position, with just three wins from 13 matches this season.

Evatt was an accomplished player for Blackpool during a successful seven-year stint, where the Tangerines rose from the third tier of English football to the Premier League.

On Thursday, the club posted on social media that morning, wishing Evatt a happy 45th birthday.

Seven hours later, the club posted on social media that he had been sacked.

On the left, Blackpool FC with coach Ian Evatt a happy birthday. On the right, the club announces his sacking on the same day. (X/BBC Sport)

Evatt took over the manager role in October, 2025, helping the struggling club avoid relegation.

But the club finds itself in another relegation battle this season.

"Blackpool Football Club can announce that Ian Evatt has departed his role as Head Coach after 12 months in charge," the club said in a statement.

"During a hugely successful playing career at Bloomfield Road, Ian made over 250 appearances for the Seasiders. In his six years at Blackpool, he played a vital role in the Club's memorable rise from League One to the Premier League, which included two successful play-off campaigns.

"The Club thanks Ian for all of his efforts during his time at Bloomfield Road."

World.title: Who knew what about Sandpapergate? The players break their silence
World.content:
In one chapter of his new autobiography, Sabr, Khawaja provided a detailed account of what he says happened during Australia's 2018 South African tour.

The former batter, who retired this year, alleged sandpaper was used on the ball during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, weeks before Bancroft was caught on camera in Cape Town.

Khawaja described a discussion before the first Test in Durban, alleging a member of the coaching staff told the team they needed to find a way to make the ball move in the air.

"We were all complicit," he wrote.

Khawaja described how Bancroft picked up the ball after a break in play during the Port Elizabeth Test and used sandpaper to roughen one side.

He said the ball was then passed around the fielding team, including to him at gully, and that he noticed how dramatically it was reverse-swinging.

Khawaja recalled one bowler commenting during a huddle:

"Guys, it's going heaps now. Just don't do anything else to it, because it's silly how much it's going."

He alleged a member of the coaching staff later approached Bancroft during the Cape Town Test and encouraged him to do more of what he had been doing to the ball.

Khawaja said that after Bancroft was caught, he argued with team manager Gavin Dovey that everyone should accept responsibility.

"We need to cop this as a team," he wrote.

" We did it as a team, so we cop it as a team. "

Khawaja said most players agreed when he raised the issue at a subsequent team meeting, but then-captain Tim Paine knew not everyone supported the idea.

The chapter ends with him saying, "I can only speak for myself, and it's very clear I knew what was going on."

In a subsequent interview with the ABC's 7.30, Khawaja said he wanted to tell his story and stand by the three players who had been made out to be the only people involved.

"It wasn't just them," he told Sarah Ferguson.

"We were all involved in it as a team, as a squad."

He declined to speculate about whether individual bowlers knew sandpaper was being used.

"Twenty-two pages is what sandpaper is," he said.

"I've tried my best in that to explain my version of events."

World.title: Matildas star Foord named best international player in Asia
World.content:
Caitlin Foord has been named women's international player of the year at the Asian Football Confederation's annual awards in Bangkok, completing a unique treble for the Matildas striker.

The 32-year-old Arsenal forward became the first player to add the international prize to the AFC's women's youth player of the year and women's player of the year gongs, which she also won in 2011 and 2016.

A decade after being named the best player in Asia, thanks largely to her storming performances for the Matildas at the Rio Olympics, Foord was this year a key performer in Australia's home Asian Cup campaign, playing in five of their six matches as they reached the final only to lose out agonisingly to Japan in Sydney.

She set up the winner in Australia's first match, against the Philippines, had another assist in the draw against South Korea and scored in the semifinal against China before laying on the winner for Sam Kerr.

Earlier in the year, Foord had come off the bench to score the extra-time winner for her club side Arsenal against Brazil's Corinthians in the inaugural global club event, the FIFA Women's Champions Cup.

It was another tribute to the Shellharbour star's enduring excellence over a career that stretches back to 2010 when Foord took her professional bow with Sydney FC.

She's gone on to win 152 caps, scoring 42 times, and helped Arsenal win the Champions League in 2024/25, alongside her fellow Matildas Kyra Cooney-Cross and Steph Catley.

Foord is the second Australian winner of the international award, following Ellie Carpenter's triumph in 2024.

AAP

World.title: Cummins's agent criticises 'hysteria' as sandpaper saga continues
World.content:
As the wounds of the sandpaper scandal fester, Pat Cummins's agent has slammed critics of the Australian captain.

In a statement issued late last night, Neil Maxwell rubbished claims the Test captain knew of efforts to use sandpaper in 2018 before the plot was carried out

"There is no serious case he was an architect of ball tampering or knew sandpaper was going on the field," he said.

The pushback from Maxwell, who represents Cummins, comes in the wake of several players, including Cameron Bancroft, declaring the entire team knew of the plot.

Maxwell was critical of the tone of discussion that he described as "an hysteria unfounded in reality", he said.

"When you go through it all calmly and in detail, Pat's eight-year-long position and 68-minute Q&A stands up."

Yesterday, media camped outside Cummins's Sydney home and peppered him with questions about his leadership of the side and Bancroft's explosive claims.

There was an extensive media presence at the practice session held at the Sydney Cricket Ground as well.

Cummins himself has not thoroughly addressed Bancroft's claims, however, his agent said he had helped change the culture of Australian cricket in the fallout of Cape Town.

Maxwell said that the furore after the third Test match led to then captain Steve Smith, vice captain David Warner and Bancroft being harshly sanctioned.

"It's also true that the players who were suspended paid far too high a price," he said.

"Year-long bans for ball tampering that players in other countries did and were suspended for just a few games. They have always been right to feel aggrieved by that."

World.title: FIFA unveils Diallo and Tashima as challengers to Infantino's presidency
World.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino's re-election bid will be challenged by the French and Japanese federation presidents Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima, the global soccer body has confirmed.

The election, set to be held in March 2027, will be the first time Mr Infantino faces a challenger after being re-elected without opposition in 2023.

Mr Infantino has faced repeated calls for his resignation since his FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, a bid to sell stakes in the World Cup and other major competitions, failed.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded The FIFA president has faced international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

But the 56-year-old Swiss native, who has been the FIFA president since 2016, maintains that he has enough support from member associations around the world to get him re-elected.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Mr Diallo announced his candidacy on Monday, with the support of UEFA member associations represented on the executive committee and the FIFA Council.

Mr Tashima had declared his bid earlier this month and formally submitted his nomination on Wednesday.

"The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidates," FIFA said in a statement.

"Member associations will be notified of the names of the proposed and admitted candidates no later than 18 February 2027."

Mr Diallo, who took over as FFF president in 2023, played a leading role as France and other European associations withdrew support from Mr Infantino last year over the FFE controversy.

"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," UEFA said on Monday.

Reuters

World.title: Sydney Marathon winner banned for three years, stripped of title
World.content:
This year's Sydney Marathon winner Peres Jepchirchir has been handed a three-year doping ban after testing positive for EPO.

The 33-year-old returned the adverse finding in an out-of-competition test in Kenya before travelling to Sydney in August.

One of the all-time greats of marathon running, Jepchirchir claimed victories in four of the World Marathon Majors; New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026), the 2025 World Athletics Championships, as well as winning gold at the 2021 Olympic Games.

Her Sydney Marathon victory has now been stripped, and legacy trashed, following her doping result.

"In an interview on [September 17], the athlete denied using EPO and said she had no knowledge of how the AAF (adverse analytical finding) had occurred," the Athletics Integrity Unit said.

"Despite her explanations in the interview, the former world record-holder in the half-marathon subsequently signed an admission of anti-doping rule violations and acceptance of consequences form."

Peres Jepchirchir won in New York in 2021. (Getty images: Elsa)

Sydney Marathon race director Wayne Larden said he was disappointed the race had been won by a doper.

"We're disappointed for every athlete, partner and fan affected," Larden said in a statement.

"But this outcome shows the system works. Alongside our fellow [World Marathon Majors], the Sydney Marathon has voluntarily invested in additional out-of-competition testing, above and beyond what is required of us, and this case is exactly why that investment matters.

"There is no place for doping at the Sydney Marathon or in the sport at all, and anyone who cheats should know they will be caught."

Jepchirchir was provisionally suspended in October after an out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya ahead of the race returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO.

She was also tested on race day in Sydney and returned a negative result, highlighting the importance of out-of-competition tests.

The Sydney Marathon announced that Kenyan runner Irine Cheptai, who finished second behind Jepchirchir on the day, will be elevated to champion.

Irine Cheptai came home second in Sydney, but is now a Marathon Major winner for the first time. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Cheptai endeared herself to the Sydney crowd, handing her drink to Australian Paralympian Michael Roeger during the race, earning her a nomination as a finalist for World Athletics' 2026 International Fair Play Award.

It is the 34-year-old's first win in one of the eight World Marathon Majors: London, New York, Boston, Chicago, Berlin, Tokyo, Sydney and Cape Town.

"Today we get to celebrate Irine Cheptai, who raced clean and with real sportsmanship, and we're proud that Sydney will be where she claims her first [World Marathon Majors] title," Larden said.

Sydney Marathon organisers said that all other tests from the event had now been cleared, meaning there would be no more disqualifications.

Cheptai finished three minutes and 40 seconds behind her Kenyan teammate, running 2:22:11.

Two Ethiopians will step up onto the podium as well; Shure Demise Ware will be credited with second after running 2:22:33, with Haven Hailu Desse up to third in 02:22:57.

Jepchirchir is yet another high-profile Kenyan athlete to test positive for doping, with more than 140 sanctioned for doping offences since 2017, when the AIU was established.

Last year, Kenya's ⁠women's marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a ‌prohibited diuretic.

Chepngetich's world record of 2:09:56 remains on the books, however, because it ​was set before her positive test.

"Out-of-competition testing is one of the most powerful tools we have in protecting clean sport," Athletics Integrity Unit chief executive Brett Clothier said.

"It reaches athletes when and where they least expect it. This case is a clear example of that, and it would not have been possible without the Sydney Marathon's voluntary investment in additional testing this year.

"We're grateful to have such a committed partner in the fight for clean athletics."

World.title: Police reveal fourth Melbourne Cup stolen as two accused appear in court
World.content:
A fourth Melbourne Cup has been stolen as police reveal the brazen theft of Makybe Diva's three Melbourne Cups and a Caulfield Cup are allegedly linked.

Police have charged Sama Mirzaagha and Chrysovalandis Tassakos over the heists, which unfolded over several days during Melbourne's cup carnival.

The 1948 Caulfield Cup was allegedly swiped from Caulfield Racecourse during several break-ins at the track between November 4 and November 11.

On Monday, thieves believed to be dressed as tradies stole legendary mare Makybe Diva's three consecutive Melbourne Cups, worth $3 million, from Flemington Racecourse.

The 1948 Caulfield Cup won by Red Fury was stolen from Caulfield Racecourse. (Supplied)

Police now allege both robberies are linked, and revealed that a fourth Melbourne Cup, a replica, had been stolen.

It was initially believed three cups won by Makybe Diva in 2003, 2004 and 2005 were the only items stolen from Flemington but police also allege a cup was stolen four days earlier.

The Victoria Racing Club has remained tight-lipped about whether it was aware of the first robbery before Makybe Diva's cups were taken.

Charged over the Flemington heist, Mr Mirzaagha, who was out on bail at the time, was not present for a brief hearing in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court, where his lawyers hit out at police.

"There seems to have been a rush to charge, and investigating later," lawyer Justin Riazaty said.

Mr Riazaty called the prosecution brief "flimsy" and said there were "serious deficiencies" in the case against his client.

However, prosecutor Jonathon McCarthy said the evidence included DNA, fingerprints and a large amount of CCTV footage. He also referred to Mr Mirzaagha and Mr Tassakos as being co-accused.

Further details about the alleged offending were not read out in court, and Magistrate Simon Zebrowski refused to publicly release a remand summary filed by police.

Mr Riazaty did not apply for bail on behalf of his client but said an application would be made "in due course".

He said Mr Mirzaagha was normally prescribed medication and requested to be seen by a nurse in custody.

Mr Mirzaagha's charges include burglary, theft and dealing with property suspected of being the proceeds of crime.

During an earlier hearing, Mr Mirzaagha's co-accused, Mr Tassakos, was granted bail on charges of burglary, theft, handling stolen goods, dealing with property suspected of being proceeds of crime, obtaining financial advantage and obtaining property by deception.

Mr Tassakos is charged in relation to both alleged heists and was supported in court by his parents.

It comes after police raided a Mount Waverley home in Melbourne's east as part of their hunt for the stolen cups, which remain missing.

Both men are expected to face court again in February.

World.title: Swans complete AFL draft heist as Port take Cochrane with top pick
World.content:
Sydney swung the biggest surprise of the AFL draft's opening night, poaching Brisbane academy prospect Caylen Murray, as Dougie Cochrane AFL's newest number one draft pick.

Nineteen selections were made across an action-packed first round of the national draft at Docklands Stadium on Thursday night that featured four academy and father-son bids, along with a raft of pick trades.

The Lions were caught three points shy of the draft index total needed to match the Swans' bid for Murray at pick number nine and hence forced to pass after no last-minute trade materialised.

The 18-year-old Murray would have added more depth to the reigning triple-premiers' rebounding defender stocks after Keidean Coleman was traded to Essendon.

Barring a trade, Port Adelaide will take the first pick of the second round (pick 20) on Friday night when the draft resumes.

Port landed Dougie Cochrane with pick number one — one of five Indigenous players selected in the first round — by matching Essendon's bid on their next generation academy player.

"I grew up a big Port supporter when I was little, and I used to cry when we lost, so it just means the world," Cochrane told AFL.com.au

"I love this club so much, and it means everything to me, so I'm going to give everything to this club, that's for sure.

The Bombers then selected Ethan Drever with their first selection.

Carlton picked up father-son prospect Cody Walker, who was bid upon by Richmond before the Tigers turned to forward Arki Butler. WA midfielder Heath Mellody went to West Coast to round out the top five.

The second round will commence on Friday night, with Port Adelaide holding the opening selection at pick 20.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

Tech.title: Meta now sells 3D movies on Quest VR headsets
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta now offers more than 150 3D movies that you can buy or rent to watch in VR on its Quest 3 and 3S headsets, the company announced today. The movies are available in Meta’s TV app and include titles like Avatar, Spider-Man: Far From Home, Jurassic World Rebirth, Wicked: For Good, and a Billie Eilish concert film co-directed by Eilish and James Cameron.

The company suggests watching movies in a Theater view that’s rolling out with a new Meta Quest update. Theater view “provides a big screen and dims your surroundings to create a cozy, personal cinema experience,” Meta says.

Related 3D movies are finally worth watching

Meta promises that the library will “keep growing, with thousands of titles and international availability coming” when it launches its VR Glasses next spring. If you’re a Disney Plus subscriber, you can also watch 3D movies on Meta Quest hardware in the Disney Plus app thanks to an update rolled out earlier this month.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.

When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.

Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.

The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.

Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.

Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

Tech.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

Tech.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.

Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says.

In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added.

The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

Tech.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.

The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.

The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450.

To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.

Tech.title: You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company says it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.

The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

Tech.title: Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.

The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.

In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.

The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.

Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.

Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

Tech.title: Sonos is taking up to 30 percent off speakers and soundbars right now
Tech.content:
Sonos speakers and soundbars aren’t exactly cheap, but thankfully the company’s Black Friday sale has already begun, making everything a little easier to afford through November 30th. Most notably, you can pick up the Arc Ultra soundbar for a new low of $849 ($250 off) from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy, or the newfangled Sonos Play for $239 ($60 off) from the same retailers (Sonos, Amazon, Best Buy).

If you’re looking to give your home theater setup a big upgrade, the Arc Ultra is an excellent soundbar. It supports Dolby Atmos and delivers more immersive sound than the original Arc, while adding Bluetooth connectivity. Dialogue also sounds noticeably clearer, and the new Quick Tune feature automatically adjusts the soundbar’s audio to suit your room using built-in microphones, so you no longer need an iPhone to fine-tune the sound for your environment. For more powerful bass, you can also pair it with a compatible Sonos subwoofer, like the Sub 4, which is also available from Sonos as part of a discounted bundle for $1,499 ($499 off).

If you’re looking for a more affordable soundbar, the second-gen Sonos Beam has also hit a new low price at Amazon, Best Buy, and Sonos’ online storefront, where you can buy it for $339 ($160 off). The sound isn’t quite as immersive as that of the Arc Ultra, but the latest Beam can still fill a room with rich, clear audio. It also supports Dolby Atmos; however, unlike the newer Beam Ultra, it lacks side- and upward-firing speakers and instead relies on software to replicate surround sound effects. It also supports HDMI eARC, providing high-quality audio from a compatible TV.

If you’re shopping for a smart speaker instead of a soundbar, the Era 100 SL is available for an all-time low of $149 ($40 off) from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy (the standard Era 100 is also down to $179 at Amazon and Best Buy). The feature-packed speakers are nearly identical, but the SL model lacks a built-in mic, and thus voice controls. Both offer excellent stereo sound and rich bass, with dual tweeters and a large woofer that delivers clear, detailed audio despite its small size. They also support Bluetooth and Apple’s AirPlay 2, and you can connect a wired audio source like a turntable using an optional USB-C adapter. For a more immersive experience, you can even pair two for stereo sound or use them as rear surrounds with a compatible Sonos soundbar.

If you want a speaker you can take on the go, the newer Sonos Play is available from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy for $239 ($60 off), which is the first notable discount we’ve seen. The portable speaker delivers clear, detailed sound that can fill both larger rooms and outdoor spaces. It also offers up to 24 hours of battery life and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance, making it a great companion for long days at the beach or other outdoor adventures. Plus, its removable carrying loop makes it easy to bring along, and you can even use it to top off your phone. Like other Sonos speakers, it supports both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and you can also group it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when you’re outdoors and away from Wi-Fi.

Last but not least, you can also buy the Sonos Ace for $229 ($120 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Sonos, which marks a new low price. The newer Ace Ultra offer better sound and improved noise cancellation, but the Ace is still a solid option, especially if you already own a Sonos soundbar. The gorgeous headphones deliver powerful, detailed sound, solid noise cancellation, and an exceptionally natural-sounding transparency mode, along with up to 30 hours of continuous playback on a single charge. Unlike the newer Ultra, though, they can’t transfer music from your other Sonos speakers to your headphones. However, their TV Audio Swap feature still lets you transfer audio from a compatible Sonos soundbar to your headphones, so you can watch movies or listen to music playing on your TV without disturbing anyone else.

Tech.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
Tech.content:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an attack that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after cyber hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the Director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21 striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

It does seem like more than a coincidence. It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice Chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer told TechCrunch, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the Senator wrote on X.

AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.

In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.

When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.

Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”

Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues.

And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.

“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

Tech.title: Uber tests rides for kids as young as 10, with extra pay for drivers
Tech.content:
Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids, launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin.

The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids.

The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off.

Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber.

Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early.

Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids webpage. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete.

The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum.

Uber first opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens, although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. As the program expanded nationwide, Uber introduced a live video streaming feature.

Tech.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
Tech.content:
Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.

U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.

The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

November 17, 2026: Nvidia posts strong quarterly earnings, says it does not plan to reinstate Huang

Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory.

“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”

Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

November 17, 2026: Huang says he sees ‘outpouring’ of calls for him to return, says he ‘would be honored’ to return as CEO

Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.



I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026

November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’

More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.

Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”

Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making.

November 12, 2026: Democrats launch investigation into Nvidia; Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick summoned to testify before Senate Banking Committee

In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy.

“Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states.

That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

“The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X.

November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters

After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia.

November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress

Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang.

Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.

Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.

“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”

The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed.

November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang

After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.

Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.

November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says

The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.

According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.

November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair

Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed.

November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO but does not take action

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156 billion to charity
Tech.content:
Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees.

As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy.

First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold.

The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans.

Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF.

Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.

Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.

All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.

Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact.

Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can. And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees.

Tech.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
Tech.content:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.

The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

Tech.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
Tech.content:
In Brief

Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”

Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

Tech.title: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
Tech.content:
